Bombay Shaving Company (BSC) founder Shantanu Deshpande said the company has revised its Switch4 advertisement in accordance with the undertaking given by the Delhi High Court (HC), while maintaining that the “facts and principles” behind the campaign remain unchanged. “Consumers deserve choice. Locking consumers in with a handle and then limiting choice on blades is an anti-market, anti-consumer business strategy … We stand by Switch4. We stand by innovation. And above all, we stand by the consumer’s right to choose,” Deshpande said in a post on LinkedIn. The comment comes a day after the Delhi HC directed the startup to remove the ad campaign at the centre of its ongoing product disparagement dispute with Gillette India. The court on Thursday recorded compliance by the startup. Gillette alleged that the advertisement disparaged its products, while the startup argued that it was a comparative advertising campaign and did not explicitly name Gillette. The court’s latest proceedings also saw Gillette object to a fresh BSC commercial, with its counsel calling the advertisement obscene and seeking intervention. The court declined to pass an order on the new commercial, saying the issue could be considered if it was formally challenged. BSC maintained that the fresh advertisement did not refer to Gillette or disparage its products. Gillette had also raised concerns over copies of the original advertisement continuing to circulate through social media accounts and influencers outside BSC’s control. The court allowed Gillette to approach the platforms directly for removal. The latest dispute is the second legal clash between BSC and Gillette over advertising. In 2024, Gillette challenged a BSC commercial for its Sensi Smart 3 razor that depicted a competitor’s razor catching fire. The matter was resolved through mediation in February 2026 after BSC withdrew the challenged advertisement. Gillette and BSC’s recent legal clash also comes on the heels of another D2C startup being taken to court by an incumbent over comparative advertising. Beco, a startup selling sustainable home care products, had run an advertising campaign titled “War on What’s Hidden” targeting Hindustan Unilever’s Surf Excel and Vim cleaning products. In the campaign, it claimed that certain ingredients in HUL’s products could lead to skin irritation and allergic reactions, and asked consumers to “Switch to BECO”. HUL challenged the ads in the Delhi High Court, alleging commercial disparagement, trademark infringement, and passing off. Ultimately, the court ruled in its favour, finding that Beco had not been able to establish its claims as factual and ordering the startup to take down all its related ads.

Pakistani forces kill 5 militants and free 23 hostages in operation
Pakistani security forces have killed five militants in a shootout and freed 23 hostages in the country's southwest
ISLAMABAD -- Pakistani security forces killed five militants in an intense shootout and freed 23 hostages in the country’s restive southwest, the military said Sunday. It was unclear exactly when the abduction took place.
The militants had established an illegal checkpoint near Kalat in Balochistan province overnight into Saturday, stopping vehicles to abduct more people for ransom, extort money and seize vehicles, according to a military statement.
The statement described the killed militants as members of “Fitna al-Hindustan,” a term the Pakistani government uses for the outlawed separatist Baloch Liberation Army and other groups operating in Balochistan demanding independence and that it alleges are supported by India. New Delhi has previously denied accusations that it sponsors militancy in Pakistan.
Security forces recovered six trucks, three buses and two cars, along with weapons, ammunition and explosives. No casualties among security forces or abductees were reported. The military said troops were searching the surrounding area for any remaining militants.
The latest operation came just over a week after Balochistan Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti ruled out negotiations with insurgents and said security operations would continue until militancy was eliminated from the province.
Insurgents often kidnap people for ransom after establishing illegal checkpoints. Last month, they killed 18 police officers after abducting them. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif praised the security forces for the operation and said counterterrorism operations would continue and vowed to eliminate what he called foreign-sponsored terrorism.
Balochistan has been the scene of a long-running insurgency in southwestern Pakistan with an array of separatist groups, including the BLA, demanding independence from Pakistan’s central government in Islamabad. The groups have staged attacks mainly targeting security forces and people from Punjab who travel to Balochistan for business or employment.
Although Pakistani authorities say they have quelled the insurgency, violence in the province has persisted.

India’s luxury hospitality landscape has received global recognition, with several iconic hotels earning MICHELIN Keys for their exceptional stays. The distinction, awarded by the MICHELIN Guide, highlights hotels that stand out for their design, service, character and overall guest experience.
Among the celebrated properties is Taj Lake Palace in Udaipur, Rajasthan. Set in the middle of Lake Pichola, the iconic white-marble palace offers a distinctive blend of royal heritage, architecture and luxury. Its setting, historic character and hospitality have made it one of India’s most recognisable palace hotels. Keep on reading to know more.
MICHELIN Guide 2026 revealed
The MICHELIN Guide has revealed its 2026 MICHELIN Key selection, honouring 2,832 hotels globally for outstanding experiences. After months of secret evaluations, the worldwide selection introduces close to 470 newly recognised hotels in 79 locations, showcasing a hospitality environment influenced by more immersive, customised and experiential visits.
India has largest number of MICHELIN Keys
India boasts the highest count of MICHELIN Key hotels among the 11 locations in this regional selection, with 47 establishments acknowledged. Two landmark properties, Taj Falaknuma Palace in Hyderabad and Taj Lake Palace in Udaipur, earn Three MICHELIN Keys, adding this honour to two of India’s most unique palace hotels.
Taj to Soho: Hotels to receive recognition
In Mumbai, The Taj Mahal Palace has earned recognition for its heritage and distinctive location overlooking the Gateway of India. The landmark hotel has played host to generations of travellers and public figures while retaining its historic character alongside contemporary hospitality. Another Mumbai hotel recognised was Soho House. The hotel received one MICHELIN Key. The MICHELIN Guide recognised Soho House Mumbai for its exceptional hospitality, world-class design and unique character. Among others are The St. Regis Mumbai and Woods At Sasan.
Hyderabad’s Taj Falaknuma Palace
Hyderabad’s Taj Falaknuma Palace has also made the MICHELIN Key selection. Perched above the city, the former Nizam residence combines grand architecture with elaborate interiors and a rich royal history. The property is known for its ornate rooms, expansive courtyards and views of Hyderabad. Apart from Hyderabad, The Kumaon in Uttarakhand, The Imperial in New Delhi, The Oberoi Vindhyavillas in Madhya Pradesh, Dolkhar in Ladakh, and Leela Palace in Chennai received the honour among others.
What is Michelin Key?
The world's most famous arbiter of dining and travel has given a prestigious nod to 36 hotels from India. A Michelin Key is an accolade from the Michelin Guide that honours exceptional hotels, similar to Michelin stars for dining establishments. These keys are granted according to standards such as architecture, interior design, high-quality service standards and character, and can be attained in one, two, or three key levels to represent a "very special", "exceptional", or "extraordinary" experience, respectively.

BMW PGA Championship 2026: JJ Spaun snatches victory at Wentworth, as Rory McIlroy comes unstuck despite late surge
JJ Spaun claimed a two-shot victory at the BMW PGA Championship on Sunday, as Manuel Elvira made double bogey the 18th hole to cede victory to the American; Rory McIlroy placed tied-second; watch the Open de France live on Sky Sports Golf from Thursday
Sunday 20 September 2026 17:58, UK
JJ Spaun outlasted a packed leaderboard of players on Sunday afternoon at the BMW PGA Championship to win his second DP World Tour event and his first outside of a major championship.
An utterly thrilling final round of golf unfolded at Wentworth, with multiple players, including Rory McIlroy, Aaron Rai and Manuel Elvira, racing to the finish line, but all struggled to pull away from the pack.
There was heartbreak for Elvira, who had the chance to leapfrog Spaun at the top of the leaderboard after tying the 2025 US Open champion with an eagle on the 17th hole.
With Spaun already in the clubhouse at 17 under, the Spaniard, who is ranked 294th in the Official World Golf Rankings, needed a birdie on the 18th to win his first-ever DP World Tour title, but he stumbled, finding a fairway bunker with his tee shot before sending his bunker shot well past the green.
He attempted to chip back on but agonisingly sent his shot into the bunker before ultimately confirming Spaun's two-stroke win with a double bogey.
Elvira would tie McIlroy, Rai, and Adam Scott at 15 under par for second place, as 13 players would finish within three shots of the lead.
McIlroy mixed in moments of brilliance with a few critical errors. The Northern Irishman also struggled to make birdie putts, but surged in his back nine, making birdies on holes 12, 14 and 17, to post a final round score of 68.
Rai, who had taken the joint lead after the first round, was equally impressive throughout his week at Wentworth, and the Englishman once again put the gas on as he tried to pull away from the chasing pack of players, taking the clubhouse lead before Spaun with a final-round 66.
Open champion Ryan Fox would join Matt Fitzpatrick, Joost Luiten and Filippo Celli tied for sixth place at 14 under.
Spaun, who was omitted from Brandt Snedeker's Team USA Presidents Cup squad, felt he had 'taken care of business this week', showing his patience to bounce back from an early bogey on the first to card six birdies, and end with a score of 67.
"We [him and captain Brandt Snedeker] haven't spoken," the 36-year-old said. "But yeah, I played with a huge chip on my shoulder.
"I'm so delighted to be here and just play this event. I've always wanted to this. The extra motivation, I think that is the willpower that you kind of have, determination.
"Being left off the President's Cup team a couple weeks ago was very disappointing and I wanted to prove that I deserved to be on that team.
"I took care of my business this week, so all the best to my mates next week at Medinah, but I'll be on the couch watching."
More to follow…
What's next?
The next DP World Tour event is the FedEx Open de France, held at Le Golf National - the venue for Europe's 2018 Ryder Cup win - and beginning Thursday.
Team USA chase a record-extending 11th consecutive victory over the International Team at the Presidents Cup, held at Medinah Country Club in Illinois and also starting Thursday.

In 2024, Donald Trump’s victory was powered in large part by massive gains with Latino voters. He won 48 percent of those voters that year, up from 36 percent in 2020 and 28 percent in 2016. But now, that support is plummeting; Trump’s approval rating among Latinos who voted for him recently fell from 93 percent to 66 percent, where it was at the beginning of his second term.
Why Trump’s Latino voters are fleeing him
The Latino backlash to Trump is a major bellwether.
Why? It has a lot to do, as with everything these days, with the economy.
It was the same in 2024. During that election, voters were experiencing rising costs and stagnant wages — the same trend that has continued until today. In 2024, though, Joe Biden and his administration — which also meant Vice President Kamala Harris — took the blame from all voters, and particularly Latinos. Today, the blame is falling on Trump.
America, Actually host Astead Herndon caught up with Stephanie Valencia, who co-founded Equis Research, a political research firm that specializes in Latino voters, to unpack some of these recent shifts and explain them.
“I think one important data point to understand about the Latino voter is Latinos make up more of the wage workforce than any other part or any other racial subgroup,” she said on the podcast. “And so what that means is when wages are down and inflation is high, Latinos feel it more.”
That’s why, when the economy is bad, this group is primed to be a “swinging giant” in US politics, Valencia explains — and right now, it appears to be swinging hard against Trump.
Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
Equis has called Latinos one of the last great wild cards in American politics. Is that because of some of the double-digit swings that we’ve seen among this voting group over the past few elections?
Yes, it absolutely has to do with that. Latinos often get given the title the “sleeping giant,” which I just want to get rid of from everybody’s vocabulary.
We should be called the “swinging giant” based on how much shift we have seen election to election. A third of Latinos consider themselves kind of independent or apolitical, and that swinging middle really is deciding every single election.
Your playbook gets into messengers and particularly how we reach folks where they are. It makes a Spanish-Spanglish distinction talking about the different types of media that Latino voters consume.
I wanted to ask, in that vein, what’s the single biggest mistake campaigns make in terms of not reaching folks where they are?
Oh man, how long do we have so I can tell you how many mistakes? They’re really simple unforced errors. I’m going to give a very concrete and simple example that I think illustrates that.
Look, I’m Latina. I grew up speaking mostly English, but I listen to Spanish-language radio. I watch a lot of YouTube, and on YouTube I’m watching people like Karol G and Carin León. A lot of people — a lot of Latino swing voters — have the same media consumption habits that I do.
The first problem or challenge that a lot of candidates make is they just simply translate their English ad into Spanish. And that is, to me, one of the biggest mistakes because there are a lot of things that people want to be communicating in Spanish that don’t translate word for word. There are sayings in Spanish that don’t translate directly from English or more direct ways you can communicate.
I’m sure it immediately reads Google Translate rather than an original message for said community.
Exactly. So that’s mistake No. 1. Mistake No. 2 is when they’re deploying that ad digitally, as a proxy for talking to people, they’re going to use Spanish-language browser settings. So they say, “We don’t want people who speak English to see the Spanish-language ad.”
So the way they find that set of voters is just by going to people who have Spanish-language browser settings.
Like I said, I don’t have a Spanish-language browser setting. Everything I consume online is set in English on Chrome, but I still watch a lot of content in Spanish on YouTube.
So you’re missing a voter like me who’s going to see a Spanish language ad from a James Talarico or a Manny Rutinel and be turned on by it because I’m going to say, “Hey, that candidate’s speaking to our community. That candidate has enough respect to develop a Spanish-language ad.”
We did some testing a couple of years ago that showed that over 70 percent of Latinos who see an ad in Spanish think that party or candidate cares more about Latinos. It matters that much.
Let’s stay in 2024 for a second longer. Your research found that Project 2025 and Trump’s mass deportation plans were not top of mind for most people, and that they were thinking about the economy. I wanted to ask about that because I remember the RNC signs at the convention saying, “Mass deportations now.” One number says that 62 percent of Latinos now think that Trump wants to deport undocumented immigrants broadly.
Why did it take till post-election to realize those threats of mass deportation were real considering they were so front and center during his campaign?
I think this is really important for us as avid news consumers to understand the kind of news that the average voter, and especially that voter who’s coming in and out of elections, is consuming.
What they were seeing on mainstream media, perhaps even Fox News at the time, was a focus on people or Trump surrogates who said he was going to focus on serious criminals, securing the border, and violent criminals.
And so that’s what people bought. Fast-forward to 2026; the people who feel most regretful who voted for Trump in 2024 are most regretful because of immigration. They feel like there was a broken promise there.
They were told he was going to focus on the border, which everybody agreed was chaos, and he was going to focus on violent criminals and serious threats, and at the end of the day, he has not complied with that.
And then add that to the litany of broken promises.
I’m hearing a distinction between a focus on the border, which Republicans did try to prioritize rather than the interior deportations that may have been more attributed to Stephen Miller than Donald Trump. But we have certainly seen that be a focus of the administration once they came back into office.
You mentioned the shift that has happened since 2024, and that’s really important, of course. Trump’s approval rating with Latinos is now worse than with non-Latinos, a stunning reversal in 18 months.
You mentioned the factors that have contributed there, but is this really just the economy?
It’s the economy, it’s the war, and it’s immigration. It’s those three things.
One thing that is really interesting to note about Trump’s approval, other than that it’s at basement levels — and he’s very much pulled down the GOP with him broadly and with Latino voters — is that in Trump 1.0, his approval on the economy and the cost of living was actually better than his everyday approval on his total job.
And he has been underwater with Latinos almost this entire term so far on the cost of living and the economy. It’s almost been a complete and total reversal.
Listen, you tell people you’re going to fix egg prices and gas is going to go down, and then you do the opposite, and we’re hearing that story universally across different electorate groups.
You’re saying that’s still the main story when it comes to Latinos also?
Yes, it’s still the main story. I think one important data point to understand about the Latino voter is Latinos make up more of the wage workforce than any other part or any other racial subgroup. What that means is when wages are down and inflation is high, Latinos feel it more.
We have less savings. We have lower rates of home ownership. So the safety nets that other people might have, we just don’t have.
That really has exacerbated the kind of impact that people are feeling right now as they’re trying to make ends meet.
You mentioned the exponential growth in the terms of people who now regret or are disappointed with their vote for Donald Trump. Does that mean a preference for Democrats? How should we think about the binary choice between D and R versus what is a clear story about a backlash to Donald Trump’s actions?
I think it is a huge mistake for Democrats to rest on their laurels and think that because of what people are feeling about Trump and Republicans and the sense of disappointment and promises broken that that is automatically going to translate for them as a party and as a brand.
Right now, the Democratic brand has suffered a repeated set of blows among Latino voters. Twenty years of comprehensive immigration reform hasn’t been delivered. It’s a thing that comes up in almost every focus group.
And part of what the build-up to 2024 was, was not only 20 years of a promise undelivered; it was the chaos at the border, it was feeling like Democrats were focused on everything but Latinos and their families, or everyday Americans and their families, and that they had lost that thread.

It has been over a week since Jish (name changed to protect privacy) arrived in India after completing his mandatory military service in Israel. He savours a lemon pie and ginger tea at a popular vegan bakery-cum-café located in the narrow market lane of Dharamkot, a misty village in Himachal Pradesh’s rain-washed pine forests. A popular destination among Israeli backpackers along the Hummus Trail, Dharamkot is about two-three kilometres uphill from Mcleodganj. “This is my second visit to India,” he says, just before setting off for his painting class — one of the ways he chooses to unwind in the Himalayan landscape.
He felt compelled to visit last year in May, hearing stories through the drumbeat of social media and his friends’ first-hand accounts. He stayed in the country for nearly five months, first alone, and then for two and half months with his wife. “I travelled mostly in the Himalayas on a motorcycle. I came to Dharamkot, then went to Manali’s Parvati Valley, and then to Ladakh. On my second visit to India, we [my wife and I] have come together,” says Jish, who has served his conscription term of two years in the Israel Defense Forces (IDF)’s reserve military service.
Even as the former soldier made plans to travel, the ongoing US-Israel war with Iran left its mark on his life. “Since October 2023, we have lost many friends and many civilians. It’s like an endless war between two nations, the Jewish nation and the Arab nation. Just one month before Hamas attacked us in October 2023, I got engaged. I was on the battlefield. My fiancé prepared all the stuff, you know, the wedding dress, and so on. It’s difficult,” says 25-year-old Jish, who says he joined the IDF when he was 19.
Dharamkot is known as Mini Israel, because a number of Israelis flock here after they complete their conscription terms. Around 80,000 Israelis visit India annually, according to a paper, ‘Decoding the hummus trail of India: regaining the lost prudence’, published in 2022 in Anatolia, an international journal of tourism and hospitality research. “Last year, a little over 1 lakh foreign tourists visited Himachal. This included visitors from Europe, Canada, the U.S., and Israel among other countries,” says Bhanu Gupta, joint director at Himachal’s Tourism department.
This year, however, Dharamkot’s narrow, stone-paved roads lined by tall pine trees look relatively deserted. The influx of Israeli travellers has been skewed and uneven, according to local hospitality players. Yet, over the years, the steady footfall of foreign tourists has helped the economy of this tiny village, even as the locals worry about the adverse impact of drug-laced raves in the forest.
Trailing peace
Jish says he and his wife are “here to relax” and will soon head out on their hired bike to Delhi and onward to Rajasthan. In Dharamkot, “There are different courses, like music sessions, yoga, drawing, and painting — there are so many options to unwind. In India, unlike Israel, there is more peace and Nature, landscapes, and special people,” he says, as he grabs his belongings to move for his painting class in lower Dharamkot, run by residents largely through hired instructors. Charcoal painting and pencil sketching are popular among foreign tourists in this Himalayan village.
For Jish, the trip to India is more than just about travelling. “There is a strong and deep connection between Israel and India, like a religious connection and some shared values between these two nations. India is different from Western societies that are materialistic. The trust factor is what’s really attractive in India,” says Jish, who will soon start a course in Judaism philosophy in Israel this October. He will be in India until then.
The Hummus Trail gets its name from hummus — a Middle Eastern food traditionally made from cooked chickpeas, tahini (sesame paste), lemon juice, garlic, and olive oil. The trail has many cafés and restaurants catering to Israeli travellers. The route spans several places in the mighty mountains of the Himalayas, like Kasol, Old Manali, Rishikesh, and Ladakh. It stretches across Uttar Pradesh’s Varanasi and Pushkar in Rajasthan, extending to South Goa, Gokarna and Hampi in Karnataka, and Vattakanal in Tamil Nadu.
Hodaya, 23, also from Israel, has come to Dharamkot with her friend, drawn by the popularity of the Hummus Trail. “Most Israelis follow the Shvil Hummus (Hummus Trail) route in India and Nepal, as it has many cafés with Hebrew menus, Israeli music, and food. I have been in India for about two months now, travelling between Manali, Leh, and Dharamkot. It’s relaxing here,” says Hodaya, who is set to return to Israel in a couple of days. Asked how she feels about the ongoing conflict, she shrugs it off with a smile, saying, “I am used to it, so I am not stressed anymore.”
Monetising Israeli tourism
The stone walls across Dharamkot are dotted with posters in Hebrew, alongside English. In lower Dharamkot, more accessible by road than the upper areas, the bulletin boards outside cafés, restaurants, roadside stalls, and homestays on the market stretch, serve as a news feed for different events for the village’s international community. There are wellness workshops, music and art events, community activities, and notices for parties.
Narender Pathania, 54, who runs an eight-room guest house in Dharamkot, points out that the flow of Israeli travellers has been unsteady for the past three years. The first lull, he says, was in 2023. That year, on October 7, Hamas-led Palestinian armed groups crossed into southern Israel, killing more than 1,200 people.
Soon, the century-old Israel-Palestine conflict — one of the longest and most-violent in the world — escalated, as Israel intensified attacks on Palestine. At least 20,179 children were killed and 44,143 children injured as a direct result of attacks on Gaza between October 7, 2023, and October 7, 2025, according to a UN commission report released on June 23, 2026. “The current total is certainly higher. Thousands of children are feared to be buried under rubble. In the 300 days after the ceasefire was announced 300 more children were killed — one child every day with still hundreds more, injured,” according to UNICEF.
The tourists, Pathania says, further dropped after the US-Israel and Iran conflict broke out in February 2026. “Almost all of them had left when the war with Iran started. Now some have returned, but the flow is lower. All my rooms, which used to be packed during these days, are vacant. It eventually brings loss. Tourism is the primary livelihood for many in our village,” he says.
Pathania adds that Israelis’ Indian sojourn lasts several months, so they prefer budget-friendly homestays over expensive hotels. “Of late, tourists come with their children. Many cafés here cater specifically to the food preferences of Israelis. They visit Manali, Srinagar, Ladakh, and even trek to Chamba from here. They go to meditation centres, lean towards spirituality. Many lie in the lush green field for hours, just relaxing,” he adds.
Vivek Kumar hails from neighbouring Dharamshala, manages routine affairs at ’Dharamkot studio’ that offers pottery and ceramic courses in Dharamkot. He says, “Among the foreigners who come to us, Israelis make up the largest share. We have different courses ranging from five to 35 days. A minimum two-hour workshop is also available to experience the process of shaping wet clay into finished objects. Most of those who enrol with us are Israelis. In their country, these things are quite expensive, as I understand from speaking with them,” he says.
Sanjeev Gandhi, chief advisor to the Hotel and Restaurant Association, Smart City, Dharamshala, who himself runs Hotel Gandhi’s Paradise at Dharamkot, shares his experience on why Israelis are drawn to the town: “Most Israelis come carrying the weight of war and stress. They come to forget. What they value most about Dharamshala is the silence,” says Gandhi, recalling a number of them telling him that the biggest draw is that they don’t hear gunshots.
Not all Israelis need to serve conscription though. There are military exemptions for Israel’s ultra-Orthodox Jewish community, who constitute about 13% of the population. This has triggered protests in the past, also leading to some stress among communities.
Rage against the rave
The Hummus Trail, also notorious as the Hashish Trail, is a route taken for readily available cheap drugs, says the Anatolia paper. In June 2026, taking suo motu action, the Himachal Pradesh High Court directed the transfer of three senior officers, including the then Deputy Commissioner and Superintendent of Police of Kullu district, in connection with the alleged nexus between officials and organisers of big-scale rave parties in Kullu district.
The drug issue was addressed in the 2007 Israeli-Canadian documentary Flipping Out, directed by Yoav Shamir. It follows Israeli soldiers after their discharge as they travel to India, exploring drug use and the psychological breakdowns some experience. The film also documents Israeli officials’ response, including a meeting between the then Deputy Prime Minister Eli Yishai and former soldiers.
Om Prakash Sharma, a former Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) officer, who handled several enforcement operations in Himachal, Punjab, and Jammu-Kashmir, while he worked with the NCB’s Chandigarh zone from 2002 to 2007, asserts that cultivation of cannabis and opium in remote areas of Kullu district and Mandi district of Himachal continues unabated.
“The narcotics trade cannot survive unless there’s support from the socio-political and administrative strata. Foreigners have been found involved in the illicit drug trade,” he says, adding that regular Himachali people get involved because of “local poverty” and “easy money”. The modus operandi is simple — they throw money at people. They know that forest lands and even private lands are available for cultivation at a meagre sum, he says. “These people, usually with Nepalese and other labourers, then cultivate and harvest it, after which the networks of foreigners operate its trade. Foreigners have even been marrying local women as a part of their strategy as well.”
During his tenure, Sharma busted many drug deals, including 155 kilograms of charas (hashish) in Chandigarh, smuggled out of Kullu by Israeli, Czech Republic, and Indian (Kullu) nationals, and bound for Amsterdam in 2005. “During our operations, we had recovered the foreign strain of the cannabis seeds from some foreigners’ houses. That was a hybrid seed, which clearly points to the extent of foreign involvement in the illicit drug trade,” says Sharma, who has also served as convener-cum-advisor of the Himachal Pradesh Nasha Nivaran Board, formed to curb the drug menace.
“Rave parties in secluded forest areas are being organised in the name of tourism, which is not possible without the shelter of bigwigs and administrative machinery and local political patronage,” he adds.
Monika Pathania, former councillor of Dharamkot ward, which falls under Dharamshala Municipal Corporation, says, “People talk about rave parties happening here, but that’s simply not true. Such things don’t happen at all in the village. It could be happening in remote areas where police presence is minimal, but in Dharamkot and neighbouring Bhagsunag there are police check posts to keep a tab on unlawful activities.” She insists the village is only known for its meditation centres.
Ashwani Bamba, president of the Dharamsala Hotel and Restaurant Association, explains that Israelis tend to travel in groups and usually they prefer to spend less on accommodation, but are willing to indulge when it comes to food and, as he puts it, “Other things.” Recalling that things were different a decade or so ago, Bamba points out that then, drug consumption was open. Now, not so much.
Gandhi is worried that locals too are impacted by drugs. “We have been urging the locals and administration to create a joint team to tackle the drug menace,” he says.
For many young Israelis like Jish, Dharamkot is an escape from war, a holiday of healing and hash.

LeBron the star as Angola aims to cash in on E1 racing
- Published
It is difficult to imagine an electric powerboat racing series capturing the attention of an Angolan audience for whom football and basketball is king, but the presence of NBA royalty LeBron James certainly helped.
The 41-year-old was among the A-listers in Luanda as the E1 World Championship rolled into southern Africa for the first time at the weekend, having made its debut on the continent last year in Lagos, Nigeria.
"It's not a short trip, but he [LeBron] is here because he believes in what we're doing," E1 chief executive Jamie Copas told BBC Sport Africa in the Angolan capital.
"You can't underestimate the value of it. They [the celebrity owners] come with huge followings."
James, like fellow sport stars Rafa Nadal, Tom Brady, Didier Drogba and Virat Kohli and actor Will Smith, is an E1 team owner after buying into the series.
Similar to Formula E on land, it aims to blend sport with strong messaging around sustainability and green technology.
James said Angola had made his first trip to the country "super welcoming" after visiting the National Museum of Slavery.
"Obviously there is a lot of history here," the new signing for the Philadelphia 76ers told local media.
"A lot of history that not only is here in the country but also [crosses] over to America."
Angola's men are reigning African basketball champions, securing a record-extending 12th continental title on home soil last year, and unsurprisingly spectators of the E1 racing at the Clube Naval de Luanda clamoured for a glimpse of one of basketball's biggest icons.
Journalist Omar Prata, covering the race for the Jornal de Angola, admitted that E1 was not on his radar until Hollywood star Smith, whose Westbrook Racing team is sponsored by Visit Angola, announced in March that a deal had been agreed to race in Luanda for the next three years.
"I see the potential it could bring to project the city at a time when the government is trying to work on tourism," Prata said.
"And of course it means a lot to have LeBron James here. Angolans have seen him on television, they try to emulate him on the street courts, they have his posters."
Boosting Angola long-term
The star power of E1's owners is helping to bring eyeballs to what is a traditionally niche sport where powerboat pilots skim and bounce around tight courses at speeds close to 100kmph.
Yet, on a calendar that features traditional celebrity haunts like Miami, Monaco and Lake Como, Luanda's name seems an outlier.
Among those taking in the action from the fanzone was local resident Edson Cabeta.
"It is the first time I have seen anything like this," he said.
"Today it is foreigners doing this; tomorrow, perhaps we could have an Angolan team."
The aspiration is that hosting an E1 race will help Angola boost visitor numbers, with minister for tourism Marcio de Jesus Lopes Daniel saying enhanced foreign awareness of the country is the "first step" in a long-term plan.
"Our ambition is not simply to make Angola famous," Daniel told the BBC.
"It is to make Angola more desirable to visit, invest in and do business in."
Angola has not been afraid to speculate to accumulate in the past, bringing Lionel Messi's Argentina side to Luanda for a football friendly last November to celebrate 50 years of the nation's independence.
Daniel said it would be "premature" to assess the economic impact of this weekend's race in Luanda.
"An event of this scale generates demand across several sectors and it creates opportunities," he added.
"We want to turn the international attention generated by E1 into future trips, stays, private investment and jobs. That is the real return we are looking for."
Sustainability challenges
Beyond the spectacle and waterfront backdrops, E1 aims to transcend motorsport.
Sustainability has been one cornerstone, and marine conservation efforts around the race in Angola included mangrove restoration.
Putting sustainability front and centre inevitably invites scrutiny - particularly when races have taken place in Saudi Arabia, the United States, Nigeria and now Angola, all major oil-producing nations.
"The world's on a journey," Copas said.
"We're welcomed in places that do have a lot of fossil-fuel infrastructure.
"Each one of those markets is conscious of it and wants to be doing more from a green point of view. If we can help, why wouldn't we?"
Copas told BBC Sport Africa that E1 would only consider air freight as a last resort for transporting its teams and that they aim to showcase their technology on each stop, persuading people that electric charging is a viable alternative to diesel even on water.
But as the global series expanded to 10 teams and seven races in 2025, its own emissions rose from 1,672 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in its first season to 4,049 tonnes in its second, according to E1's own annual sustainability report.
"We need to travel to meet new people, to tell our stories, which we would hope would be of greater benefit than the carbon footprint that we have," Copas explained.
"We work really hard to offset our carbon and to make sure every stage of our logistics journey is done in the most sustainable way.
"It would be crazy for us to say we're not going to travel and we're not going to race, because then we can't do the job that we're here to do."
There is an acknowledgement within E1 that the work is unfinished and that more active reductions are needed.
'Continuing the story'
E1 was due to return to Lagos in October, but Nigeria's race was cancelled earlier this month, perhaps showing how the series is still working to establish itself.
It means its longer-term impact in Africa will take time to judge, but the effect of its celebrity owners was obvious around the paddock in Luanda.
After visiting his pilots, Will Smith stopped for selfies and handshakes with fans, telling the crowd it was "great to be here".
On the water, however, there was no fairytale result as Westbrook Racing's hopes of victory were ended by a mechanical fault, with Team Brady taking the inaugural Luanda title.
Smith could have used the help of Kianda, the mermaid-like Angolan water spirit traditionally regarded as a protector of fishermen.
It will take one of her miraculous interventions if electric powerboat racing is to usurp football or basketball in Angolan affections, but Copas hopes E1 can leave a different legacy.
"I think it's for us to help tell Angola stories, and for Angola to help tell ours.
"We will be back next year, we will be back the year after. It's not just about what we're doing in the few days we're here.
"We'd love to see the journey they're on develop even more, and us playing a part in that."

Millions without power as Cuba hit by latest major blackout
- Published
Millions in Cuba were left without power on Friday as the country was plunged into yet another major blackout.
The country's entire electricity grid suffered "total disconnection" that triggered a nationwide outage, Cuba's energy ministry said.
Power was restored to some priority areas by late evening, including those near hospitals and water pumping stations in the capital Havana, grid operator UNE said.
It is at least the sixth partial or total blackout to hit Cuba this year, where ageing electricity infrastructure and chronic fuel shortages have been placed under further strain by a US blockade on oil shipments to the communist-run nation.
UNE said the outage started just before 14:00 local time on Friday (18:00 GMT) due to a transmission fault coupled with poor weather conditions in central Cuba.
Protocols to begin the "gradual restoration" of power were activated, the operator's national load dispatch director Felix Estrada said, with the process ongoing on Saturday.
Cuba relies heavily on fuel imports, meaning tight US sanctions and an oil blockade since the start of the year have exacerbated existing shortages.
Food and medicine have also become more scarce, with hospitals struggling to function normally and schools and government offices having to close.
"Lately, it's becoming a habit," Havana resident Frank Lorenzo told news agency Reuters on Friday.
"Before it happened less frequently - once a month… just yesterday we were 24 hours without electricity, they turned it on for just an hour and it went down again."
"It's one thing after another: no water, no gas for cooking, no electricity," 36-year-old schoolteacher Lidia Fernandez told news agency AFP. "Honestly, I don't know how we haven't gone crazy."
Francisco Rodriguez, 78, said his home had already gone without power for 28 hours on Friday and feared he would not have light "for several days".
The repeated blackouts have prompted rare protests in Cuba, where unauthorised demonstrations are illegal and those who defy the ban risk being jailed.
Havana has blamed its fuel crisis on the Trump administration and denounced all of its sanctions - including a new round announced in August - which are part of a wider pressure campaign against the Caribbean island's leadership.
Cuba's regional ally Venezuela was believed to have sent it around 35,000 barrels of oil a day - about half of its oil needs - until Venezuela's own supplies were cut off following the US seizure of its President Nicolás Maduro in January.
US President Donald Trump has threatened tariffs on countries shipping oil to Havana, and a number of such shipments have been seized by the US.
Washington meanwhile attributes Cuba's energy crisis to poor internal management and has accused it of posing a "national security threat". Trump has openly discussed toppling its leadership, including threatening a "friendly takeover" in March this year.

Cambridge curriculum aligns with NEP 2020 vision of greater choice for students: Official
Mumbai, Cambridge offers schools flexibility in choosing subjects and combinations based on students' needs, aligning with the National Education Policy 2020 vision of greater choice and learner-centred education, a top Cambridge University Press official has said.
Cambridge has a significant presence in India, with around 850 schools offering its curriculum and examinations, a number growing by about 15 per cent annually, Cambridge University Press and Assessment Group Managing Director, International Education, Rod Smith, told PTI.
Across South Asia, Cambridge has a presence in approximately 1,200 schools.
"Cambridge offers schools the flexibility to choose subjects and combinations based on their students' needs. This closely aligns with the NEP 2020 vision of moving away from rigid streams and a one-size-fits-all approach toward greater choice, flexibility and learner-centred education," Smith said.
It also allows learners to make choices progressively, based on their developing interests, strengths and aspirations, rather than being defined too early by a fixed academic pathway, he stated.
"India's NEP 2020 has already articulated a progressive vision in response to many of these shifts, with its emphasis on multidisciplinary learning, flexibility, subject choice and holistic development. The global experience can complement this vision by offering perspectives on how these principles can continue to evolve," Smith said.
However, learners should be given opportunities to explore different subjects before choosing their specialisations, and this process should begin at the school level, he opined.
"Early assessment can help schools understand learners' strengths and areas for development, while exposure to different subjects and careers can help learners understand what interests them. This can support more informed pathway choices, rather than choosing a career first and discovering later that it does not align with their interests or strengths," Smith said.
"It can also contribute to learner wellbeing by helping them pursue directions that better align with who they are," he added.
For Cambridge in India, the global experience is not about adopting another model but learning from how education systems worldwide are responding to a changing world, while strengthening the vision outlined in NEP 2020 and helping learners understand themselves, explore possibilities and make informed choices about their future, he said.
Smith said that teachers and school leaders are critical to making this happen.
Cambridge, therefore, invests significantly in professional development, helping educators strengthen learner-centred approaches, active learning, assessment for learning, metacognition and differentiated teaching, he added.
The objective is to help learners explore their strengths and make informed academic and career choices, while helping parents understand wider pathways and make more informed choices for their children, according to the official.
"We have also enabled our schools to have open conversations with parents about academic rigour in an AI-enabled world, the growing importance of judgement and multidisciplinary approaches, and the varied academic and career destinations available. This year, our leadership is taking this conversation directly to parents in over 500 schools, helping them better understand these possibilities," he added.

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.
Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.
The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.
Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.
“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”
Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.
Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.
Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.
The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.
Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.
The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.
The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.
Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.
“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”
Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”
The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.
They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.
Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”
The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.
Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.

PHOTOS: The precarious life of fisherfolk
He works from 2 a.m. to 7 a.m. every day. In pitch darkness, he carries baskets of fish on his head from boats in Kasimedu harbor to the auction house, navigating slimy and damp pathways littered with fish scales and wet with seawater. It's a third of a mile each way. He makes the trip 40 or 50 times during his shift for the daily auction, which begins at 4 a.m.
Pavadairayan, who is 60 years old and goes by one name, is one of hundreds of workers known as basket men. It's a tough job. Each basket weighs about 35 pounds. Their bosses don't trust them: "If supervisors think that fish are missing, they can dock your pay and fine you several thousands of rupees. Basket men have few rights," he says.
They earn about $5 a day.
Despite the hardships, Pavadairayan says he loves the job because the rest of the day is his own. He spends his mornings sleeping and lounging.
"Many other basket men go out and do other odd jobs," he says. "But I always refuse. This money is enough for me. Sleeping with a full belly under open skies, a salt sea breeze fanning your face: that's what I call heaven."
A smuggler's story
Pavadairayan is one of around 30,000 people who are part of the bustling scene at the Kasimedu harbor in the southern Indian city of Chennai. In addition to basket men, there are fishermen, auctioneers, fish hawkers and wholesalers, transport workers, ice suppliers. The harbor itself is overcrowded, built for fewer than 600 boats and now estimated to be serving over 1,000.
They have stories to tell about their labors and their lives. Their experiences testify to the struggles they face — and to their undying love for the sea.
Nandu Kumar, who is 65, says he used to be a smuggler.
Dressed in a grey shirt and a checkered lungi (a traditional garment men wear, made of light cotton and wrapped around the waist), Kumar is seated on an overturned boat on the harbor's sandy shores. In the pale light of early dawn, he looks vulnerable, almost fragile, with a wispy white beard and contemplative eyes.
He's always worked as a fisherman. But in the early '80s, desperate to make a living, he says he'd help smuggle in imported alcohol and cigarettes on his boat. This was the time when India imposed steep customs duties and limits on consumer-goods imports. Smuggling was profitable until 1991, when economic reforms began taking effect.
So Kumar gave up on his illegal cargo and went back to battling the sea for fish.
Years later, in December 2010, tragedy struck., Kumar says. His daughter's husband, who drank heavily, toppled off his boat and drowned. "This fishing life — it's harshest on the body," Kumar says. "Your shoulders ache all the time. Sometimes, alcohol is the only way you can cope and forget the pain."
His daughter struggled to come to terms with her loss. Months later, she took her life, ingesting the pesticide she had bought to weed the garden.
After his daughter's death, Kumar took in her infant daughter and son — and soon realized that spending weeks at sea was no longer practical. Fishing was a gamble. A group of ten fishermen would go out to sea for three weeks or months in a boat, and sometimes, come back empty-handed. Kumar needed a steady income to care for his grandchildren. "With the support of my two sons, I decided to start selling fish," he says.
Today, he runs a shop at the harbor and does brisk business.
A risky business
Members of fishing communities in Kasimedu are well aware of the risky nature of the business, says Bhagat Singh, a researcher, social worker and member of the Coastal People Rights Movement, a grassroots campaign led by fishing and indigenous communities to protect their traditional marine livelihoods against corporate displacement and unregulated development.
Singh's own father was a fisherman, and he knows the community well. ""It's feast or famine. That is the rhythm of life at the harbor. For workers and fishermen here, earning a living is hard enough. One bad season, one poor catch, or one spell of illness can be enough to push a family into dire poverty. There are no safety nets. Worse, they have little access to government support and their labor remains largely invisible, " he says.
On an average, the fisherman at Kasimedu earn around $200 a month, he says — if they have good catches. The precariousness of the job is a reason why the younger generation seeks out more reliable employment. But that need for independence that is so inherent to their personalities eventually surfaces, he says. "Many of my friends are not happy in corporate jobs or in related industries. Eventually, they do find their way back fishing again, and many make this career change mid-life."
Nizamuddin, 25, belongs to the younger generation of fishermen. He's also the only man in the entire harbor wearing a wet suit. When he's not out fishing, he helps repair nets, dock boats and haul fish from the hold to pass onto the basket men.
The power of the sea
He is aware that young people his age are conspicuously absent from Kasimedu, but he's always embraced his job. "It's a hard life but I wasn't very good at studying," he says. "This is the only work I know and it has helped my family survive." He's put two older brothers through school and college. They now have good jobs, he says, but he's never regretted his own career choice.
The fisherman-turned-fish vendor Kumar knows all too well that the seas hold power over those who've worked there. "It's like your mother's lap. You may travel far and wide, and don't need it anymore, but you will return for the warmth and comfort it gives you," he says.
Every now and then, in the early hours of the morning, Kumar sits in the stillness to watch the fishermen return with their catch and feels a pang of longing. "Life on a boat is hard, but it is also exhilarating," he says. "There are moments when you never know what will happen next. I quite miss that."

Senior journalist Payal Mehta passes away; PM Modi, Rahul Gandhi, CMs offer condolences
Mehta was on a visit to Mumbai when she developed uneasiness early in the morning. She was rushed to a hospital, where she later passed away.
Senior journalist Payal Mehta passed away on Sunday. Mehta, 46, was on a visit to Mumbai when she was rushed to the hospital after sudden uneasiness.
"On a visit to Mumbai, she developed uneasiness. Around 2 am she was taken to the hospital. Before any treatment could be administered, her pulse went silent," said senior journalist Sheela Bhatt in a post on X.
"Payal was one of the standout political reporters of her generation — deeply respected, remarkably well connected and a formidable presence in Parliament. Her access was matched by her understanding of national politics, and her relentless commitment to being on the ground made her reporting stand apart," said a post by CNN-News 18, while paying tribute to the late journalist.
PM Modi, Rahul Gandhi and more offer condolences
Prime Minister Narendra Modi also condoled Mehta's death. He emphasised that beyond her work, Mehta would be remembered for the kindness and warmth with which she touched many lives.
"Payal Mehta Ji was a hardworking journalist who remained firmly connected to the ground, bringing a deep understanding of national issues to her reporting," Modi said in a post on X.
"Her sudden and untimely passing is extremely saddening. My condolences to her family, friends and colleagues. May they find strength in this difficult hour. Om Shanti," he said.
Hailing Mehta as a thorough professional committed to delivering detailed information about various issues, home minister Amit Shah remarked that the passing of such a talented journalist is an irreplaceable loss to the field of journalism.
"I extend my deepest condolences to her grieving family and friends and pray to God to give them the strength to bear this profound pain. Om Shanti," he said.
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh also expressed his deep shock and sadness at the news of Mehta's passing.
"She has left us far too soon. Payal was an extremely hardworking and dedicated journalist who covered the Parliament beat with great commitment and professionalism," he said.
Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge also condoled her death, adding that Mehta was a hardworking and diligent journalist who had a keen understanding of public affairs.
"Her untimely passing is deeply distressing. My heartfelt condolences to her family, friends and colleagues. May they find strength in this difficult hour," he said.
Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi also expressed sadness over Mehta's demise, saying, "My sincere condolences to her family, friends and colleagues," he said.
Meanwhile, Lok Sabha speaker Om Birla said that Mehta's passing is a profound loss to journalism. "May God grant peace to the departed soul and strength to the bereaved family," he said.
Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis said he was deeply pained to know about the sudden demise of the "very hardworking" journalist. "She used to meet me whenever I was in New Delhi and always on the field. She will be remembered for her dedication towards journalism. My deepest condolences to her family and friends," he said.
Assam Chief Minister Sarma expressed his sadness upon hearing of Mehta's passing. "I have known her for a long time. She was full of life and brought an infectious energy to everything she did. Yet for all her dedication to her work, what stood out most was how deeply she valued her relationships," he said.
Conveying his deepest condolences to Mehta's family, Sarma said, "I pray they find the strength to navigate this difficult phase. Prayers for her sadgati. Om Shanti".

Neither Keith Ellison or Letitia James’ offices responded Sunday to Deadline’s request for comment on any settlement or gearing down. Three dead and eight injured in Philippines school shooting
- Published
A 16-year-old gunman has shot two students dead and injured eight others at a Philippine high school, before killing himself.
The two deceased victims were 14-year-old pupils at a school in Banga in the southern province of Mindanao, the local mayor told the BBC.
Albert Palencia said four of the injured were in critical condition.
The education department said in a statement it was "deeply concerned" by the reported incident which took place on Friday afternoon at Banga National High School.
This is the third deadly school shooting in the Philippines since June this year.
"Our immediate priority is the safety and well-being of our learners, teachers and school personnel," the education department said, adding it was coordinating with authorities to verify the incident and provide necessary support.
"We urge everyone to remain calm and refrain from sharing unverified information as authorities continue their investigation."
Palencia told Reuters news agency that during a lunchtime conversation on Friday, the gunman had urged friends to go home "because after lunch, [he would] be executing [his] plan".
"His friends laughed because the shooter was a known joker," Palencia told the news agency.
"After lunch, he started shooting students. He hit 10 students before killing himself."
Classes have been suspended "in all levels in the entire municipality of Banga" due to the shooting, disaster management authorities said in a statement.
The Philippines Red Cross said it was alerted to the incident at 14:00 local time (06:00 GMT) and had dispatched an ambulance with four paramedics to provide life-saving assistance.
Police are at the site investigating the shooting, local media reported.
Gun crime is not uncommon in the Philippines, which has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the region. Broadly speaking, school shootings are rare, but today's incident marks the third deadly campus shooting in the last four months.
In June, three students were killed and more were injured after their peers opened fire at a high school in central Philippines. Investigators believed the deadly shooting had been motivated by a "grudge" over bullying.
In August, a student at a Catholic junior high school in the southern Philippines shot dead a fellow student and later took his own life. In this case, the suspect had fired at the teacher, but missed, then moved to another classroom and shot a student, who later died.
Following the shooting on Friday, Reynaldo Tamayo, the South Cotabato governor, urged adult gun owners to "be responsible in storing firearms" and ensuring that minors do not get access to them.
"We cannot expect a handful of security personnel to monitor thousands of students. We need to work together because otherwise this will be very difficult for us to address," he told Reuters.

Trump’s efforts to turn DC into a gilded bunker reflect his increased political isolation
Donald Trump announced Sunday that his planned 'triumphal arch' would be the latest D.C. structure weaponized to satisfy his war-happy image. In reality, it reflects his administration's descent into irrelevance, writes John Bowden
Will Donald Trump put a drone port on every roof in Washington D.C.?
No. But that would be the impression one could get from reading the president’s latest post on his planned “triumphal arch” Sunday morning — that every inch of the nation’s capital is slowly (or not so slowly) becoming a fortress.
In reality, it’s an open question as to whether either the arch or his other beautification-plus-fortification project, the White House ballroom, will ever see the light of day. Beset by lawsuits and lacking formal congressional approval, it’s quite possible both projects could be cancelled by the incoming president in 2029.
Just as likely, if not more, is some combination of Congress and the Pentagon deciding that Arlington National Cemetery is possibly not the most necessary space to install a sniper’s nest.
But Donald Trump is pushing forward full-steam with his latest D.C. renovation project. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Trump’s dressalike loyalist deputy, announced earlier in September that ground would break on the first construction project related to the arch in the coming weeks. There’s a reason for this: It’s just about the only thing the president can do at this point.
With the war in Iran having gone very sour, the Trump 2.0 White House is at its most isolated.
Trump’s approval ratings have hovered near rock bottom levels in the mid to low 30s for weeks, with polling showing Americans widely against the war and Trump’s own ability to extract the U.S. from another costly conflict. A new poll from Fox News this past week found that a wide majority of Americans do not believe the president’s stated claim that the war was an unavoidable investment required to stop Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
Worse, affordability concerns remain top of mind for American voters heading into the midterm elections, less than two months away.
It isn’t just among Republican voters where Trump is isolated. On Capitol Hill, the president is in less good favor with Republicans than ever: Senate leadership still fumes over the utter destruction the president has wreaked across their midterm map as the president has spurred the retirement of one incumbent, forced out another, and made a political environment possibly untenable for several others.
In the House, the president remains extremely close to Mike Johnson, the GOP speaker.
But moderates in purple and purple-red districts like Reps. Mike Lawler, Maria Salazar and Sen. Susan Collins have all found it necessary to run on their own independence from the president in recent weeks, while Trump’s endorsements have once again gone to right-wing firebrands and loyalists who will put MAGA above all else, often at the cost of experienced and scandal-free leadership.
Trump’s frustrations with these dynamics are clearly at an all-time high, and last week he lashed out in his latest attempt to banish his critics from the spotlight, hoping to stem the bleeding of support. CNN, MS Now and Politico found themselves banned from the White House, apparently for the remainder of Trump’s presidency — though the outlets have indicated that legal action to restore their status is likely. The move couldn’t even find support from senior Republican leadership on Capitol Hill, who’ve dealt with Trump’s antics and refusal to accept reality for months.
“I don’t know why he did it,” claimed Rep. Steve Scalise, the House Majority Whip. He went on to falsely claim that the Biden administration “banned” hundreds of journalists, who failed to renew their press passes, from the White House.
Sen. John Barrasso, Scalise’s counterpart in the upper chamber, repeatedly declined to outright endorse Trump’s decision on NBC’s Meet the Press.
But while the president’s approval ratings are now hovering around what seems to be his floor, the president is choosing to focus on D.C. renovation projects and the handful of other issues firmly within his purview.
He has renewed efforts to close down and refurbish the Kennedy Center amid a fight over adding his name to the building, and other random acts of executive power, too narrow in scope to address the widely-felt economic pain of Americans who once again are watching Washington fiddle while Rome burns around them.
Gas prices are on the rise, past $4 a gallon at the national average and driving prices higher across economic sectors. Other concerns and voter priorities — AI regulation, immigration reform, healthcare policy — it’s all taken a back seat, or worse, been bogged down into the muck of the Senate stalemate swamp by the president’s insistence that every issue take a lower slot on the pecking order than his voter ID push, which just last week sank Washington’s first real attempt at AI legislation — the CLARITY Act.
Trump, when he took office in 2025, was faced with a political reality: two razor-thin majorities in Congress, with a highly-skeptical but also bruised and timid Democratic minority presenting his only path to pass more substantial pieces of legislation.
Instead of embracing that reality, Trump spent the next year and a half cocooning himself inside a bubble of altered expectations, where aides do not bother him with that mathematical fact and his refusal to accept it has pushed him apart from Hill leaders, particularly John Thune in the Senate.
Now, that cocoon of disinformation is affecting another reality: The Iran war.
With almost all dissenters exiled from his administration, Trump has wedged himself firmly into a conflict and its resulting international economic crisis, with no ability to extract himself or bring it to a decisive conclusion.
And with Republicans facing an electoral house fire in the coming weeks, the president is choosing to isolate himself one last time — this time, from the presumption that his party’s imminent drubbing could have anything to do with him.

A former police officer allegedly developed an “infatuation and obsession” with one of his victims, and disguised himself as an Uber Eats rider before shooting two men, a court has heard.
Beau Lamarre-Condon, 31, pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter as his trial began in Sydney’s supreme court on Monday.
He has been accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird, 26, and Baird’s partner, Luke Davies, 29, with his police service weapon at Baird’s Paddington home in February 2024.
Appearing in the dock at the King Street courthouse in a light grey suit, dark tie and white shirt, the 31-year-old repeated his pleas.
He offered to plead guilty to an alternative charge of manslaughter, but it was rejected by the prosecution.
As the jury selection process began on Monday morning, crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield said Baird and Lamarre-Condon had become romantically involved from late 2022 and into 2023.
“[Lamarre-Condon] developed an infatuation and obsession with Jesse Baird which manifested itself in a range of compulsive behaviour,” Hatfield told the jury panel.
This behaviour escalated after Baird ended all contact with Lamarre-Condon in November 2023, the court heard.
The crown alleged Lamarre-Condon began planning the murder of Jesse Baird in early 2024.
He started investigating ways to conceal the sound of gunfire, hired a vehicle under his mother’s name, and bought a surfboard bag to dispose of the body, Hatfield told the jury members.
Lamarre-Condon retained his police service weapon when he had “no need to be using it” and disguised himself, the court heard.
On 19 February 2024, he wore a motorcycle helmet and dressed as an Uber Eats rider to enter Baird’s house with a key he had previously obtained, the court heard.
“He then proceeded to the kitchen, where he shot Jesse twice, he then proceeded back to the bedroom where he shot Luke Davies,” Hatfield said.
Their bodies were found almost 200km away in Bungonia, eight days after they were killed.
The prosecution said Lamarre-Condon had earlier unsuccessfully tried to sink the bodies in a nearby dam.
Lamarre-Condon’s case has attracted significant attention, with members of the public and media filling out the entire courtroom on Monday morning.
Baird and Davies’ loved ones, including their mothers and siblings, also watched proceedings at the courthouse.
The jury has been chosen and the trial is expected to continue for another two to three months.

'It's like a dog set loose on us' - fear over Kenya's crackdown on foreign traders
- Published
For Ndaikech Ali, who has been traversing the streets of the Kenyan capital eking out a living as a tuk-tuk driver for the past nine years, Nairobi's traffic - not xenophobia - has been his biggest concern.
During his time in the East African nation, the Burundian says he has always found Kenyans to be friendly and welcoming - that is until last week, when the president ordered a crackdown on foreigners working as traders or operating small-scale businesses.
"Now they have turned against us," he told the BBC at the Burundian embassy in Nairobi where many have been queuing this week for documents to allow them to travel back home.
"The threats are many… even from children," he said, adding: "It's a like a dog has been set loose upon us. We have been bitten."
President William Ruto made his remarks last week when addressing Kenyan traders gathered at state house - in reference to legislation before parliament that seeks to exclude foreign nationals from petty trade and to mandate the local sourcing of certain materials.
During his speech, he said that all foreign nationals operating small businesses had until 7 September to pack up shop, saying such low-level jobs should be reserved for Kenyans.
Ali, like others, panicked, saying it seemed the president's announcement had been interpreted by some Kenyans as a signal that foreign nationals were no longer welcome in the country.
"We face harassment and can't work," he says. "If our work is stopped, we lose the income that enables us to pay rent and buy food. When those jobs are taken away, the only option left is to return home."
Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees"
Other Burundians and some other foreign nationals have rushed to border crossing points to leave the country, with reports suggesting that a number have ended up stranded there.
Some couples fear they will be forced to separate - and some families have already been divided.
"I have been here from 2019," said a Burundian man, who identified himself only as Prosper and who has a child with a Kenyan woman.
"When I heard the announcement, it was very painful because when I go, I'm forced to leave my family... and I love my family," he told the BBC.
In Nairobi's low-income neighbourhood of Majengo, Kenyan Grace Wamaitha said her Burundian husband had already gone - leaving the day after the president's 3 September directive.
She is distraught as she has been left trying to feed their five children - and has taken on extra work washing clothes.
"Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees? I don't know what to do. Let them come back," she told the BBC.
In Nairobi and other major towns, migrants from the region can be found working in barber shops and salons, construction, operating motorbike taxis and street vending, as well as selling clothes, food and household goods.
Some have fled conflicts or economic hardship at home, while others have moved to Kenya in search of better opportunities. Within the East African Community (EAC), a regional bloc made up of eight countries, including Burundi and Kenya, the relative free movement of people is allowed - but employment and long-term residence do require permits.
Kenyan law also recognises the right of refugees to work and operate businesses, although they are also required to obtain the appropriate documentation.
Filmon Eyob, a co-ordinator within Nairobi's Eritrean community, agrees with concerns that the crackdown order will be used as pretext to harass foreigners.
He told the BBC that while many Kenyans had been supportive and welcoming, some Eritreans and Ethiopians had closed their businesses and stayed at home over the last week as a precaution.
The president's remarks also sparked a diplomatic row, with the Burundian foreign affairs minister warning that "hate speech against Burundi" could have repercussions for Kenyans abroad.
The authorities in Kenya have struggled to contain the fallout - and as the matter came to a head, Kenyan foreign affairs official Korir Sing'Oei visited and apologised to Burundians at the embassy this week, assuring them of protection from violence.
Critics argue that Ruto's remarks were a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia, although the government has denied this.
Since then, a series of official statements have sought to clarify the directive.
The government has now given a 90-day window for undocumented foreign nationals running small business to register and comply with local laws. During the process, those undergoing registration will be presumed to be living legally in Kenya.
Yet observers and those affected argue that it did not have to be this way.
Academic Hesbon Owilla told the BBC the president's comments were bound to be misinterpreted, especially by people who did not have the right documentation.
He says that while the proposed policy is good for Kenya and in line with global migration protocols, the communication about it ought to have been more diplomatic.
For those not in the audience, Owilla says people interpreted the president words as saying: "We are kicking these guys out."
The president did not stop at small-scale traders. A day later, he ordered India's Tata Chemicals to leave the country, saying the company had not provided sufficient benefits to the local Maasai community in Kajiado county.
Tata has been mining soda ash for years in Lake Magadi, a vast area often covered by a whitish salt crust. The lake's extreme briny environment sustains algae blooms that attract flamboyances of pink flamingos that thrive in the area.
Mining operations began at the lake in 1911 under a British colonial arrangement that is said to have remained largely intact, despite long-running land and resource disputes pitting the company and its predecessors against community and the government.
Economist Odhiambo Ramogi argues that the move to restrict foreign nationals from businesses is too broad - and could do with finessing.
He points out that Kenya hosts hundreds of thousands of refugees as well as other migrants, mostly from the EAC region, as well as other international investors.
Ramogi says that Ruto's intention seemed to go beyond "just protecting jobs for Kenyans".
The president's remarks have prompted a wave of support for foreign nationals, including by civil society groups and ordinary Kenyans who have criticised his approach.
In the wake of the criticism, Ruto, who is up for re-election next year, has sought to counter the backlash.
"Kenya will remain an open, secure and welcoming country, protecting opportunities for its citizens, safeguarding the rights of all persons lawfully within its borders," a statement by his spokesman said.
"Kenya's commitment to the East African Community of the African continent remains firm."
Ramogi says that in the end, it is Kenya that stands to lose when citizens of neighbouring countries are targeted.
He points out that Kenya earned $56m (£41m) in exports to Burundi last year, adding that the country would still benefit by allowing competition, as "locking out aliens simply means you don't want a competitive economy that gets to grow a lot faster".
"Now, if you got $56m out of a country, why are you worried about a hawker who's just trying to make, say, $200 in a month?
"It absolutely makes no sense what the president has done."
For Nairobi resident Lima Kabura, whose husband is Tanzanian, the president's remarks were just too hasty. She says he should have first established those who were in the country illegally.
"When they are forced out, I'm left with no work, no business and no husband," she said.
