The Indian spacetech ecosystem is entering its most critical phase yet. After years of experimentation and ambition, spacetech startups must now prove they are on a path to commercial viability. Investors are already betting on this transition. According to Inc42's data, homegrown spacetech startups have already raised $252.9 Mn so far this year, nearly double what the sector raised in 2025. Leading the momentum is Skyroot Aerospace. The startup became India’s first spacetech unicorn in May after it raised a $60 Mn round. Subsequently, it was successful in becoming the first Indian private company to place a rocket into orbit with its Vikram-1 mission. It is now lining up a bigger $200 Mn round. Earlier this month, Temasek-backed hyperspectral imaging startup Pixxel’s $100 Mn Series C round made headlines as the single-largest funding round raised by a spacetech startup in India. So, why are spacetech startups suddenly the flavour of the season? A key reason is the deepening policy push. The Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) earlier this year began deploying capital from its ₹1,600 Cr Antariksh Venture Capital Fund. Similarly, the state-backed ₹1 Lakh Cr Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) fund also recently allocated nearly ₹834 Cr to spacetech startups in its inaugural cohort. The buzz around the sector hasn’t just been about money coming in, but real achievements too. GalaxEye recently became the first Indian startup to secure a US patent for its OptoSAR satellite imaging technology. Agnikul Cosmos also completed a test firing of its Agnite engine, which boasts India’s first semi-cryogenic engine and the largest 3D-printed single-piece rocket engine in the world. Despite this, finding commercial viability is a looming concern for many spacetech startups. In addition, there are concerns around the frothy spacetech valuations. Under the current scheme of things, can Indian spacetech startups convert milestones into scalable and sustainable business models? What Are VCs Betting On? Earlier this year, Union minister of state (MoS) Jitendra Singh pegged the size of India’s space economy at around $9 Bn and projected that it would grow to nearly $45 Bn over the next decade. Behind this projected market size is an entire value chain: First comes the infrastructure layer that enables launches, including ground stations, launch vehicles, and the components that act as inputs for the rockets Then come payloads – the satellites and sensors that hitch a ride on the rocket and generate data from orbit From there comes the ‘downstream’ data intelligence and applications layer, comprising analytics and services that process the raw data from the previous step. It is this ‘downstream’ layer that Viju George, a partner at Mela Ventures, believes has the most promise. “Revenue models in satellites tend to be very lumpy and capex-driven, whereas data streams tend to be high-margin recurring revenue,” he observed. The upstream input layer is relatively more commoditised, as per George. But that doesn’t mean it’s not investable. “If you’re able to take the shovels approach, where you provide the components to satellites like avionics, communication infrastructure, and others, that is a kind of a multipurpose play. With that positioning, you're not really dependent on a single satellite brand winning or losing,” he added. Ashish Taneja of GrowX Ventures, an early investor in Pixxel, also believes that the nascent earth observation segment is a huge market opportunity. He added that the infrastructure layer is a “big thing too” as it continues to be a supply-constrained market. But have the potential and the promise of spacetech taken investors too far? The Gap Between Hype & Market Demand The rapid influx of capital into the spacetech sector is creating concerns around valuations, market size and whether the demand required to justify these bets has materialised yet. “I worry about the valuations because now somehow we are in the FOMO zone,” George said, adding that he is unsure whether the market is large enough to support current valuations. The risk, he said, is “whether you are paying a little bit more for market demand that is not yet evident.” The valuation question is especially pronounced for capex-heavy businesses, where large cheques are being signed based on potential future launch cadence and scale, even as India’s launch capacity is still developing. Space hardware also carries risks around technology, manufacturing, launch and satellite longevity. Satellites are expected to operate for around five to six years, but India does not yet have enough historical data to establish how reliably newer constellations will perform over that period. Because of limited launch experience and deployments, investors are finding it tough to benchmark execution capability or predictable revenues. The growing number of startups is also raising the investment bar, with multiple ventures now attacking similar problems. To achieve scale, spacetech startups will need to expand their base beyond government buying, which has, thus far, acted as an anchor customer. These emerging players will also need to tap into foreign sovereign buyers and commercial enterprises as well. But demonstrating competitive cost, reliability, performance and consistency will be key to competing in international markets. As such, GrowX’s Taneja remarks that “not many people will make the cut” in attracting sustained capital, predicting consolidation as startups expand beyond their initial products and become vertically integrated space infrastructure companies. Simply put, he believes that stronger players could eventually acquire or absorb smaller companies. What Will It Take To Win Capital? The first phase of Indian spacetech hinged on visions and ideas. But growing market maturity and an influx of new ventures have turned investor focus to identifying which businesses can turn technical breakthroughs into large, durable markets. A startup may solve an extremely difficult engineering or deeptech problem, but that alone does not guarantee a scalable business. “Early stage investors like to see milestones because we think they are the precursor to valuations and revenues. But once growth investors come in, they like to see tangible metrics,” said Mela Ventures’ George. In 2018-19, investors were largely evaluating founder quality, technical capabilities, and whether building satellites and propulsion systems out of India was even possible. This is no longer the case. “I want a precise use case. I want clarity on the use case. I want a differentiated solution which is defensible in the long run,” said Taneja. Investors also want clarity on who will buy the product, how it will be used and what makes the offering difficult to replicate. Hence, established spacetech startups have more of an advantage now in attracting growth funding as they have a track record to show. Signs of market maturity are also evident with global investors now participating in larger rounds, while domestic growth-stage funds are also beginning to enter Series B and beyond. But the funding pool remains smaller, particularly for capital-intensive spacetech businesses that require significant funding before reaching scale. This could make the public markets increasingly relevant to the sector's long-term funding cycle. Once companies have spent years building technology, establishing revenues and reaching sufficient scale, public listings could provide another route to capital and liquidity. For early investors, meanwhile, the long development cycle itself can create multiple opportunities for valuation repricing as spacetech startups move from technical milestones to commercial deployment. Taneja cited a 17X outcome over around five years, following the sale of a small portion of GrowX’s stake during Pixxel’s recent $100 Mn fundraise. Regardless, the investment thesis has evolved substantially from when the first spacetech startups created the market a decade ago. The real challenge now is not reaching the stars, but turning that journey into a stellar business.

The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has issued an alert on the use of unauthorised cosmetic products manufactured in Pakistan, which are on sale in India.
A public notice dated September 8, 2026, stated that cosmetic products named ‘Goree Beauty Cream’ and ‘Chandni Whitening Cream’ are unauthorised for sale and no trade registration certificate was issued to the manufacturers.
“To manufacture cosmetics for sale and distribution, a licence must be obtained from the State Licensing Authority... For the import of cosmetics, the products must be registered with the Central Licensing Authority in accordance with prescribed rules,” the notice said.
The products are unauthorised and contain excessive levels of heavy metals beyond the specified limits, which may pose health risks to consumers, including toxic effects, said CDSCO.
The drug regulator warned people not to purchase or use the products. It also asked consumers not to use similarly named cosmetic products if they had already purchased them.
It also informed that all concerned establishments/individuals were warned not to sell, distribute or advertise these products.

Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa
- Published
"What we are going to do, I have no idea," sobs Nokwanda Matshikiza, reflecting on the murder of her niece Dineo Motapane. "But something must give."
"For us, for all the other women. How many other bodies will be found before something happens?"
Nokwanda is speaking to the BBC from the family home near South Africa's main city, Johannesburg, just two days after relatives identified Dineo's body.
The 38-year-old mother-of-two was last seen alive last Sunday. Her battered body, partly burned, found later in the residential region of Ekurhuleni.
Nokwanda weeps as she describes how the family will have to face, at some point, the grim task of telling Dineo's daughter of her death.
"How do you explain that your parent was brutally murdered, dumped in a field, and just left there, discarded like a piece of rubbish.
"There's no coming to peace with it," she adds. "It's something that you can never reconcile yourself with, that you can never get over."
Dineo's death this week has come amid a series of comparable incidents in Ekurhuleni – her body one of three discovered there this week. In total, nine bodies of murdered women have been found in similar circumstances in the region since July.
The problem has always been there but this spate of grim discoveries has once again sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country – which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world.
Themba Kekana is also living in shock at the death of a loved one.
His sister, Itumeleng, was one of the first to disappear in Ekurhuleni.
The 32-year-old shopkeeper's body was found in July, 17 days after she was last seen alive. Her body was badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge.
"We are devastated with grief," says Themba, wet eyes shining.
"I look at my sister's young daughter and my eyes fill with tears, I know there is no way that I can ever take this pain away from her.
"No family should have to deal with what we are faced with."
Only one arrest has been made in connection with the murders – and that was two days after the first body was discovered on 15 July.
Nobody has been detained following the murders of Itumeleng or Dineo or the other six Ekurhuleni women.
Most of the victims were young, in their 20s or 30s, and almost all had suffered extreme violence before their deaths.
Police have said they are not sure if they are hunting a serial killer. It is possible the cases are not linked.
Either way, what has happened in this residential district east of South Africa's biggest city has traumatised the nation, shining a spotlight on a situation that many believe is a crisis.
South Africa's police issue detailed crime statistics every quarter, which show that during the last quarter – between April and June this year - 5,427 people were murdered.
The official data does not distinguish between the genders of the victims, but this week the country's Human Rights Commission released figures showing that 569 women had been killed in that period (six a day on average), with another 1,052 who faced attempted murder.
Many women - already feeling unsafe - have been left reeling by recent events.
And it has put pressure on the government, less than a year after ministers acknowledged the scale of the issue and declared gender-based violence a national disaster.
Announcing the move last November, Minister of Social Development Nokuzola Sisisi Tolashe said treating the issue as a national disaster would help the government tackle the crisis.
It followed weeks of protests, culminating in a "Women's Shut Down" march as South Africa hosted the G20 summit.
This week has seen a chorus of calls for things to go further.
Rights group Amnesty International said an important first step towards protecting South Africa's women was to recognise femicide as a separate crime.
"Every day that femicide remains unrecognised as a crime is a failure to confront the targeted killing of women," said Amnesty's country director Shenilla Mohamed in a statement. "It is time to call it what it is: Femicide.
"Femicide is a gender-motivated crime. It is the killing of a woman because she is a woman."
Amnesty says femicide is criminalised as a specific crime in 33 countries, including Gabon and Morocco in Africa.
It argues that making that change in South Africa could help focus on the scale of the issue.
"It would compel the state to confront their failure to protect women and girls from violence," says Mohamed. "You cannot fix what you are not tracking."
Almost everyone in South Africa agrees more needs to be done.
President Cyril Ramaphosa this week pledged to leave "no stone unturned" in investigating the crimes in Ekurhuleni, adding: "As a nation, we must stand up for the rights, safety and dignity of women and girls."
Lebogang Ramofoko, an advocate for gender and social justice, said the levels of violence against women in the country were symptomatic of a much bigger problem – a lack of regard for humanity.
"The bodies of black women have been treated as disposable in this country for time in memorial, passed down from colonisation through to apartheid," she tells the BBC, referring to the legalised system of racism that was in place until 1994.
"What we see happening to women is testimony to legacies of violence from those systems whose traumas were never addressed.
"This is not to say black men are inherently violent, but in systems where violence was meted out against them for decades, historically black women were the people that that violence would be taken out on - that cycle has not been broken."
In Kempton Park, a district of Ekurhuleni where five of the nine recent bodies were found, Lumka Maqhubela is part of the Girl2Woman Foundation group which has held protests to raise awareness of the crimes.
"We are grieved, we are scared," she says. "If the police cannot protect us any more the government should step in and do something.
"It's clear that we are not safe, we cannot be told by the police to be more vigilant. They should be doing more to make our communities safe – what else are we expected to do? We are not safe anywhere, not in our homes, not in the streets, it needs to stop."
"I feel uncomfortable," says Thulisile Sibande, 32. "When I go to a shop, I have to look around. I'm shocked and scared. So scared, it's a trauma."
Thembi Mabena, 60, tells the BBC she lived in the same neighbourhood as Dineo Motapane.
"She was laughing every day, with everybody," she remembers. "Now I'm worried.
"I know many children, girls, who tell me they are afraid to go to the shop alone. There is no safety, even for me too. I am old, but there is no safety."
"In South Africa," says Lerato Mzizi, 20, simply, "women are not safe any more."

You may be familiar with the various memes detailing the fact that once you reach middle age, you're automatically sorted, Harry Potter hat-style, into one of a handful of hobbies, such as sourdough bread making, gardening, or bird-watching. I can't contradict this, since I'm a middle-aged person who got sorted into bird-watching. But I do know that enjoying birds and their various activities is fun for all ages. Birds are beautiful, interesting, and unpredictable, and it's fascinating to keep a running life list of all the birds you've seen and hope to see in your lifetime.
Whether someone you know is in their bird-watching phase, preparing for this phase, or has been in it for decades, all of these unique gifts—for traveling bird-watchers and backyard bird enthusiasts alike—are things either I or another bird-loving Reviews team member tested, was gifted, or bought IRL and enjoyed.
For more specific equipment recommendations, check out our guides to the Best Smart Bird Feeders and the Best Binoculars. For other gift ideas, check out all our gift guide coverage, including the Best White Elephant Gifts, Best Gifts for Men, and Best Viral TikTok Gifts.

Featured Gifts
Our Favorite Smart Bird Feeder
If you love birds, nothing beats seeing them up close and personal, conducting all their birdy activities. I have learned more about birds in the past two years of testing smart bird feeders than I have over my entire lifetime, such as the fact that cowbirds will lay their eggs in other birds' nests (such as juncos) and the “host” birds will raise the cowbird chicks as their own, even if they look nothing alike. Or that jays and other corvids are scatter-hoarders and will spend an entire day picking nuts out of a feeder's seed mix to hide caches around the yard. There are many smart seed feeders on the market, but Birdfy's high-quality basic model (available with a blue or yellow roof) stands out for its balance of price, features, reliability, and usability without a subscription, making it a great gift option that I have personally given.
A Family Pick
My mom gifted this to my family about 10 years ago, and to this day, it is the single most-played and most-enjoyed game we have ever owned, in any genre. Shuffle the small cards and call them out; players place a blue cardstock square on their bingo card if they have that bird. My son loved it, his friends loved it, neighbors loved it, extended family loved it—it can be played by up to six people at a time, and is suitable for all ages. No reading or parsing of rules required. Best of all, neither my husband nor I minded playing it multiple times a day for years on end (a bonus feature important for any parent of young kids).
For Beginning Birders
Experienced birders probably already have a decent set of binoculars, but for the birding-curious, kids, or someone just starting out, quality binoculars and a life list journal ($22) would make a great gift. WIRED contributing reviewer Caramel Quin declared these the Best Budget Binoculars. I bought a set for each member of my family for a cruise to Alaska last summer, and I'm glad I did. They're lightweight (7.2 ounces) yet sturdy, with an aluminum casing instead of plastic, and small enough to slip into a pocket if you'll be hiking and don't want to deal with them around your neck.
A Customized Bird Seed Subscription
The one thing a bird-watcher could always use more of is seed, and this service offers a fun spin on what would otherwise be a boring gift. You can choose either a subscription or a one-time purchase of three boxes: The Starter consists of one 10-pound bag of seed custom-blended to appeal to birds in your recipient’s zip code. The Simply Seeds (pictured above) adds a 5-pound bag of a specialty blend (I received a fruit and nut mix), and the Splendid tacks on suet and mealworms. The blend for my yard—black-oil sunflower seeds, peanut splits, safflower, and millet—was spot-on; birds loved it so much there was little to no mess. (Though you can also specifically opt for No Waste, Hot Pepper, and No Starling versions of your blend.) Each box comes with a personalized letter from founder Susan Vandergriff about which birds to look out for in your area. This latter part needs a bit of fine-tuning, as my letter featured blue jays and summer tanagers, neither of which exist in my region, but I found the whole package charming nonetheless.
A Bird Nerd Classic
This 8- by 11-inch hardcover by famed ornithologist David Sibley (known for his Sibley field guides) may be too big and too heavy to fit in a backpack for field reading, but it remains the definitive source for interesting bird facts. Did you know mallard nestlings have only a 15 percent chance of fledging, and that once they hatch, fewer than half of ducklings survive? And that jays in the Northeastern US often eat paint chips in search of calcium, which doesn't occur naturally in that region's soil? Or that chickadees specifically seek out spiders to feed their young for the first week after they hatch, as spiders are high in taurine? Whether you want to or not, you will learn all these things and more if you give someone close to you this book.
A Different Kind of Bird Food
My husband and I received this feeder basket and some suet cakes as a gift about 10 years ago. The basket has fallen on the ground countless times; been chewed on and used as gymnastics equipment by squirrels; and survived windstorms, snow, and pretty much everything Pacific Northwest winters have to offer. Sure, looks-wise, it's seen better days, but it still does the job.
Suet—beef fat, if we're being explicit; the solid-form cousin to rendered tallow—attracts a different variety of birds than seeds, primarily insect-eaters like woodpeckers and bushtits. It tends to melt and go rancid in the heat, so I like the melt-free hot pepper variety, which can be used year-round and has been deemed unpalatable by our neighborhood squirrels.
Camera Lenses for Your Phone
Phone cameras keep getting better, but photos taken with that tiny lens aren't going to win you any awards. If you want more detailed and dramatic photos from your birdwatching expeditions but don't want to schlep a full camera setup around, try a professional-grade phone lens. WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu has tested several of these from Moment and recommends the 1.33X Anamorphic Lens for cinematic video, the 10X Macro Mobile Lens for close-ups, and the 14-mm Fisheye Mobile Lens for fun.

Note that Julian doesn't recommend buying these lenses if you have a Google Pixel or Samsung phone, as Moment seems to have stopped making cases for Android.
The Ultimate Bird Poster
If you've ever wondered how many birds live in North America, this poster displays all 740 of them in one chart, both native and non-native, arranged by size and order. It's educational and a surefire conversation starter. In fact, I’ve had this chart framed in my home's entryway for almost eight years, and I don’t think a single person has visited my house for the first time and not commented on it, regardless of their ornithological interest level. It's really fascinating in person, and even if your giftee is already well-versed in birds, they'll probably still learn something new.
For Birders Who Love Adventure
Until reading this book, I had never heard of Blakiston's fish owl. And apparently neither had the author, bird-watcher and biologist Jonathan Slaght, until he caught sight of one—the world's largest living owl. What followed was a five-year passion project to catalog the owl in a remote region of eastern Russia. Part travel adventure, part scientific study, part memoir, this much-lauded nonfiction book reads like a novel and will be a page-turner for anyone who enjoys birds, exploration, or the outdoors.
Make Your Existing Bird Feeder Smart
If your recipient has an existing bird feeder they like, or a seasonal nesting site somewhere around their home or property, they might love a stand-alone bird camera. This one is the best I've tested, compatible with both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz Wi-Fi networks. The cute green owl face streams 4K HD video and pushes 1080p pics to the Hibird app. There's access to AI identification (which I found to be just OK), livestreaming, and Hibird's “Dr. Bird” ChatGPT-like help feature, which allows you to ask bird-related questions. (I didn't find it to be particularly helpful, but YMMV.)
The auxiliary solar panel can be mounted separately, or you can just take the camera inside to charge when the battery runs out, as I did—the battery lasts at least several weeks. The camera comes with a bracket and bendable arm for precise positioning, or you can jury-rig a custom solution. No subscription is needed, though a Hibird rep says that may change in the future.
For Bird-Loving Gamers
WIRED reviewer Simon Hill, our staff board game aficionado, says this award-winning card-driven game will appeal to anyone interested in birds, as it pairs strategy with plenty of educational information about different bird species. It can feel complex at first, so it's probably best for families with kids older than 10, but once you get the hang of it, it can be addictive. (Up to five people can play, but you can also play solo.) Playing time is 40 to 70 minutes.
A Smart Birdhouse
Contrary to popular belief, birds don't always sleep in birdhouses. Some cavity-nesting birds may use them for shelter during inclement weather, but where I live on the West Coast, birdhouses are primarily used for nesting, which happens during the spring. This is not my first go-round with a smart birdhouse; I tested the interestingly shaped Birdfy Polygon last year, which did not attract any birds then, and this year it kept going offline. As an alternative, I tried Birdfy's newer Nest Duo, which has two 2-MP cameras, one facing the entrance and one tucked discreetly inside. This one worked perfectly, both connection-wise and in terms of bird interest—mine raised a family of black-capped chickadees, and seeing their activity on the Birdfy app each day has been the most fun bird-watching experience I have ever had.
Become a More Observant Naturalist
In his guide to Gifts for Hikers, Backpackers, and Outdoorsy People, WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson said he loved this book by John Muir Laws (no relation to the famed naturalist John Muir) so much that it changed the way both he and his kids looked at the world, allowing them to see a level of detail they'd never noticed before. You don't even have to be an artist to appreciate this one, as it's more about the art of observation. He recommends including these pens with the book, which I have also owned in the past and love.
A Perfect Puzzle
If you're a puzzle enthusiast and haven't yet tried wooden jigsaw puzzles, you must. Though it's only 511 pieces, they are all individually shaped, many with a bird theme, which makes this puzzle both beautiful and extremely challenging.

Delhi records slight dip in dragonfly, damselfly numbers; two new sightings: Survey
Delhi’s seven biodiversity parks recorded 11,154 dragonflies and damselflies, down from 13,253 last year. Erratic rains and dry conditions may explain the dip.
Delhi’s seven biodiversity parks recorded 11,154 dragonflies and damselflies in a survey, down from 13,253 in 2025, with erratic rains and dry conditions contributing to a marginal dip in their diversity and numbers, officials said.
The three-day survey, conducted from September 17 to 19, recorded two new sightings: the Yellow-tailed Ashy Skimmer at Aravalli Biodiversity Park and the Blue Grass Dart at Yamuna Biodiversity Park.
Faiyaz Khudsar, scientist-in-charge of the Delhi Development Authority (DDA)’s biodiversity programme, said, “Dragonflies are amazing insects, but they’re not easy to raise or use for mosquito control. Dragonflies have complex life cycles and highly specific habitat needs that make them difficult to raise and release on any meaningful scale. Most of their lives are spent as aquatic nymphs, living in ponds or wetlands for months or even years. These nymphs are territorial, predatory, and require clean, stable aquatic environments.”

“Therefore, clean and functional wetland ecosystems alone can sustain their population, which in turn helps in mosquito control in surrounding areas, and restored DDA Biodiversity Parks provide such pristine ecosystems,” he added.
Experts and college students affiliated with the University of Delhi participated in the survey, which was carried out across the DDA’s seven biodiversity parks: Yamuna, Aravalli, Neela Hauz, Tilpath Valley, Kamla Nehru Ridge, Tughlaqabad and Kalindi.
Speaking about the survey outcomes, entomologist Mohd. Faisal said that there had been a minor dip in the diversity as well as density of dragonflies, adding, “Delhi has seen erratic rains and adverse weather conditions with an increase in dry areas and a lack of formation of water pools in biodiversity parks.”
“This year, a new species seen in DDA Aravalli Biodiversity Park was the Yellow-tailed Ashy Skimmer (Potamarcha congener). Last year, it was observed for the first time in Yamuna Biodiversity Park, so its range has increased. We also had an interesting sighting in the form of the Blue Grass Dart for the first time in Yamuna Biodiversity Park,” he added.
Yellow-tailed Ashy Skimmers perch on dry twigs near ephemeral ponds and marshes, while the Blue Grass Dart is seen perching on water plants in lakes and in marshes with well-developed vegetation along the banks. The presence of these dragonflies indicates a healthy ecosystem. These insects form a part of the “odonata” family. Odonatans are characterised by large round heads, compound eyes, two pairs of long, transparent wings and elongated abdomens.
Some of the most commonly seen species across the seven biodiversity parks include the Scarlet Skimmer, Ditch Jewel, Wandering Glider, Coromandel Marsh Dart and Ruddy Marsh Skimmer.

Quick Answer
The iPhone Duo hides several firsts and oddities: horizontal rear cameras, vertical UI elements, top-mounted volume buttons, Apple Pencil support, titanium construction, Smart Take, a circular status bar, unusual USB-C placement, and no Action button or Pro camera controls.
Apple launched many devices at its recent Surprise and Shine event, but there was no doubting the star of the show. It was the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, and the device that many are expecting to do for foldables what the iPhone did for smartphones almost two decades ago. Small wonder then that the past few days have seen everyone and their grandmother discussing the iPhone Duo.
Debates have been raging over its animations, its crease, its cameras, its apps, and of course, its price. Some are hailing it as the coolest thing since sliced bread, while others insist it is a spawn of Satan in smartphone shape. But in all this debate and discussion, some important aspects and features of the Duo have either escaped attention or have not been adequately covered.
Here are ten things you might have missed about Apple’s first foldable.
Table of Contents
The first iPhone with horizontally arranged cameras on the back…selfie cameras on the corners
iPhones have been coming with multiple cameras (two or three) on their backs for a while now. However, they have always been arranged vertically, one below the other, or in the case of some Pro devices, with two cameras one below the other and the third one placed between them but slightly to the side, forming a triangle of sorts. The iPhone Duo thus becomes the first iPhone to have cameras placed next to each other horizontally, in what some would term a very Pixel-like style. The selfie cameras also get new locations – moving to the right corner of the external display and close to the right corner of the internal display (when opened), where it actually lies under the display. Regular iPhone users are sure to notice a change in perspective.
The dock, navigation, and even the Dynamic Island just got radically right, and utterly vertical
The cameras on the iPhone Duo might have gone horizontal, but some elements of the UI have gone vertical! While everyone has been focusing on the crease in the middle of the iPhone Duo and its visibility (it’s not easy to spot, by all accounts). Apple moved many iOS elements to the right side and gave them a vertical orientation. Lock screen controls, navigation buttons, the home screen dock, and even the Dynamic Island are on the right side of the iPhone Duo, and what’s more, are arranged vertically.
The Dynamic Island even slides open vertically to show information and updates. Evidently, this was done because of the width of the iPhone Duo (it is also the widest iPhone ever), which would have made it difficult to reach these elements. They have therefore been placed on the same side as the display unlock/power button, which is also a fingerprint scanner. This is pretty right-wing in UI terms, literally.
Volume buttons on the top
The iPhone Duo comes with a rather different volume button placement from other foldables. While it is conventional for most foldables and indeed, most ‘normal’ phones, to have volume buttons on the right or left side, the iPhone Duo actually has volume buttons on the top, aligned slightly towards the right. This is a volume button placement we have seen on the newer iPad minis but not on any other iPhones or iPads. It is a rather odd location in our opinion, and if opened and rotated clockwise, it would place the buttons on the lower part of the right side, and on the top of the left side if rotated anti-clockwise.
Camera Control? Present! Action button? Er…
While the iPhone Duo comes with a Camera Control button like other recent iPhones, it, rather surprisingly, does not have an Action button, which is generally seen on the left side of most iPhones and can be customized to carry out a number of tasks. It used to toggle Silent mode on and off, before being changed to an action button. Clearly, it was either not good enough to make the cut for the Duo or perhaps there simply was not enough space for it.
Apple Pencil support exists, but only for the Type-C one
The iPhone Duo is the first iPhone to come with Apple Pencil support. What’s more, it supports the Apple Pencil on both its internal as well as external display. But there is a catch – it only supports the basic Apple Pencil (USB-C). This means that while one can scribble and sketch easily, there’s no pressure sensitivity and no support for double taps. One will also need a Type-C cable to charge it, as it cannot charge magnetically. Given the price and potential of the device, it would have been good to have Apple Pencil Pro support on it.
Only new iPhone with Titanium
Remember how Titanium was the coolest thing in premium phones a few years ago. Well, while it still remains a very premium material, it has largely disappeared from the smartphone scene, with even Apple seemingly moving on to other materials, with only the iPhone Air using Titanium last year. This time around, it is the iPhone Duo that carries the Titanium legacy forward. While the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max use “forged aluminum” and ceramic glass, the iPhone Duo comes with a main chassis made with grade 5 Titanium, and 3D-printed titanium is also used for the hinge cover.
The only iPhone camera with Smart Take
Although its cameras might not seem as formidable as those on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, the iPhone Duo has a slice of camera magic up its sleeve that no other iPhone has. This is Smart Take, which, with some AI magic, automatically works out when you are perfectly placed for a photograph and takes it without you needing to hit a capture button or prompt the device in any manner. It is supposed to work very well with individual and group selfies, and uses the rear cameras while showing you a preview on the cover display. While the feature is designed mainly for the fold form factor, it would be great to see it on “normal” iPhones too, although one might not be able to see previews!
A Type-C port placed under the cover display
In another case of rather unusual placement, the Type-C port of the iPhone Duo is actually placed on the base of the cover display or the upper panel. In many foldables, the charging port is placed on the lower panel, so that the phone can be opened without moving the charging cable. That is clearly not going to be possible on the iPhone Duo.
The status bar is closed…and is now a circle
The move to a foldable form factor has led to a redesign of some UI elements on the iPhone Duo. Perhaps the most surprising of these is the status bar. Until now seen in the top right corner, and displaying signal strength, Wi-Fi, and battery, it has now been changed to a circle, with the battery life and signal strength being on the circumference and Wi-Fi being at the center. It is not really as intuitive as its predecessor, but we guess users will get the hang of it.
No Pro controls in the camera
The iPhone Duo comes with two 48-megapixel cameras on the back – a new Fusion Main camera, and the same ultrawide that is on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. But while these pack in a lot of features such as three photographic styles, smart focus tracking, next-generation portraits, macro photography and more, the iPhone Duo’s camera app does not come with the Pro Controls seen on the 18 Pro and Pro Max, which let users play around with shutter speed, white balance, and aperture. This l is a bit of a pity, especially given the vast viewfinder the open Duo can serve up. But well, to be fair, this was never meant to be a camera phone.

Researchers Say They’ve Found the Truth About Thomas Jefferson
A secret 15-year effort has produced genetic evidence that one of the nation’s Founders fathered children with a woman he enslaved.
Three hours after Thomas Jefferson died at his Monticello home on July 4, 1826, his personal secretary, Nicholas Trist, snipped a lock of the Founder’s gray hair, still faintly reddish blond. Trist then tied the hair with orange thread and placed it in a paper packet, along with a short note describing what he’d done.
In an era before photography or modern embalming, hair was an easily preserved reminder of a beloved friend or relative who’d died. Trist did not know that he was also securing physical evidence that, two centuries later, would help resolve one of the nation’s oldest and most contentious historical debates: whether the author of the Declaration of Independence, the nation’s third president, had children with Sally Hemings, a woman he enslaved for half a century and never freed.
After a covert and exhaustive 15-year effort led by the Smithsonian Institution, a team of geneticists, genealogists, historians, and anthropologists believe it has found proof that Jefferson fathered at least two of Hemings’s six children. On Tuesday, Richard Kurin, a Smithsonian cultural anthropologist, who led the multidisciplinary research effort, will publish a book detailing the team’s findings. A scientific paper is currently under review for publication in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS). The researchers, who agreed to speak with me about their results before publication, relied on the latest genetic techniques to reassemble Jefferson’s genome from the Founder’s hair. They then matched that sequence with DNA from descendants of two of Hemings’s sons, Madison and Eston. (Of her other four children, two died in infancy, and the other two didn’t have any known offspring.) Not only did the researchers find that Madison’s and Eston’s descendants share Jefferson’s DNA; many of them had more of it than do his known descendants by way of his wife, Martha Wayles.
For many Americans, the matter was already laid to rest years ago. In 1998, the scientific journal Nature published a two-page peer-reviewed paper titled “Jefferson Fathered Slave’s Last Child.” Newspaper stories declared the case solved, and Oprah Winfrey staged a tearful family reunion of Jefferson’s descendants. Most historians came to accept the finding when it was combined with other evidence from the era.
But a vocal minority has continued to doubt that the two had a sexual relationship. Some have pointed out, correctly, that the limited biological data used in the Nature study did not definitively prove that Jefferson was the father of Hemings’s children—only that he was one of several candidates in the Jefferson male line. These doubters also disparage as unreliable or wishful thinking the oral histories passed down by Hemings’s descendants who have placed Jefferson in their family tree.
Some detractors saw a more nefarious agenda. One researcher called the 1998 study “a deliberate attempt to select and mold the evidence to fit a pre-selected theory.” Other critics, many of them white Virginians, joined in the defense of the Founder. “Jefferson’s personal reputation has been all but assassinated,” wrote William G. Hyland Jr., a lawyer and author. “The face on Mount Rushmore has been vilified as a slave-owning hypocrite, misogynist, and racist.”
Though the new results might convince some holdouts, the backlash has already arrived, and more will likely follow. The Heritage Foundation has previously criticized Monticello’s depiction of Jefferson in part for failing to tell visitors “that historians disagree about Jefferson’s relationship with Sally Hemings.” The Thomas Jefferson Heritage Society, a nonprofit formed in response to the Nature report, still accuses “historical revisionists” of inaccurately portraying Jefferson as a “liar, fraud, hypocrite, and child molesting slave rapist.” The Trump administration has made clear that it wants to present a version of American history that doesn’t disparage the Founders. In a report released on the Fourth of July, the White House condemned what it asserted is “extreme political activism” guiding the 180-year-old Smithsonian, which President Trump has said is too focused on “how bad Slavery was.”
For Clara Nutt, though, the results are simply confirmation of a long-known fact. Her African American father told his freckled daughter at an early age that she was a direct descendant of Jefferson through Madison Hemings. Nutt provided the researchers with saliva samples that found 5.1 percent of Jefferson’s genetic makeup in her DNA—nearly twice the amount expected by genetic averaging. She was delighted but not surprised to have scientific proof. “I have always known who I am,” Nutt told me.
That the very person who made famous the phrase “All men are created equal” repeatedly impregnated a woman he held in lifetime bondage first surfaced in a Richmond newspaper in 1802. The writer, a Scottish-born journalist named James Callender, had once been a Jefferson champion, and had received financial support from him. But when Jefferson won the 1800 election, he denied a government job to the volatile Callender, who had been jailed during John Adams’s administration for sedition. Ally turned enemy. “By this wench Sally, our president has had several children,” Callender wrote in The Recorder. “The AFRICAN VENUS is said to officiate, as housekeeper at Monticello.”
The Hemings-Jefferson matter became one of the nation’s first major political scandals—and one of its most enduring. “This engaged six of the seven first presidents,” Richard Kurin told me. “You could call it the longest-running American soap opera”—one, he notes, that involves the issues of race, inequality, and liberty.
Jefferson, after all, declared in 1814 that “amalgamation with the other color produces a degradation to which no lover of his country, no lover of excellence in the human character can innocently consent.” By that date, his youngest child with Hemings, Eston, was 6 years old. Jefferson’s granddaughter Ellen Randolph Coolidge, in an 1858 letter to her husband, referred to the possibility of a relationship with Hemings as that which “will not bear telling. There are such things, after all, as moral impossibilities.” The Founder went to his grave without publicly acknowledging the relationship or any children he’d had with Hemings.
A 1974 book by the historian Fawn Brodie reignited the debate with fresh historical evidence of Jefferson’s long-term liaison with Hemings, but Brodie’s assertions gained little traction among scholars and intellectuals. If the Hemings story was true, one skeptical historian wrote in 1977, then Jefferson “deserves to be regarded as one of the most profligate liars and consummate hypocrites ever to occupy the presidency.” Gore Vidal summarized the prevailing sentiment in an interview: “No gentleman would have gone to bed with a slave. Since Thomas Jefferson was the greatest gentleman of his period, he could not have done so either. That takes care of that.”
Two decades later, the Harvard law professor Annette Gordon-Reed sharply criticized the academic community for spending “generations either ignoring or explaining away” the nearly four-decade relationship and accepting white narratives denying the tie while dismissing those left by Black families that asserted otherwise.
The 1998 Nature report brought the new tools of genetics to bear on the dispute. The authors based their biological data on the Y chromosome, passed down by Jefferson’s male descendants. But some researchers accused the authors of misleading the public, and the authors were forced to acknowledge that Jefferson could “neither be definitively excluded nor solely implicated” by their data. Other candidates included his younger brother, Randolph, a frequent visitor to Monticello. One enslaved informant had called Randolph “a mighty simple man” who “used to come out among black people, play the fiddle & dance half the night.”
A month after the Nature study’s publication, the Thomas Jefferson Foundation, which owns and operates Monticello, convened a group of scholars to examine the genetic and historical data. A 2000 statistical analysis by a Monticello archaeologist strengthened the case made in Nature by examining the timing of when Jefferson was present at Monticello and when Hemings’s children were conceived. A majority of the foundation’s panel found “a high probability” that at least one of Hemings’s children had been fathered by Jefferson, and likely all six. A minority, however, rejected the conclusions, calling the research a cynical campaign by academics and the media “to denigrate and destroy the legacy of one of the greatest of our founding fathers and one of the greatest of all our citizens.”
Critics united to form the Thomas Jefferson Heritage Society, which undertook a second independent review of the findings in the Nature study, and declared the Thomas Jefferson Foundation’s report “the product of shallow and shoddy scholarship” that had ignored exculpatory evidence “in order to achieve an apparently desired conclusion.” John Works, a Jefferson descendant and founding member of the society, wrote that defending the author of the Declaration “has come to mean defending what America means, and we feel compelled to rise to that defense.” The report that the society’s panel of scholars released in 2001 found the Nature results “almost certainly false,” and insisted that “Sally Hemings appears to have been a very minor figure in Thomas Jefferson’s life.”
The controversy spawned books with subtitles such as An American Travesty, and Fallacies, Omissions, and Contradictions in the Hemings Genealogical Search, which expanded on critiques of the genetic study and the historical data. “Jefferson is completely innocent of this sordid charge,” William Hyland maintained in his book In Defense of Thomas Jefferson, citing “an obsessive agenda on the color of Sally’s skin, and slave status.” Another doubter, David N. Mayer, a law and history professor in Ohio, fingered “‘political correctness,’ radical multiculturalism, and postmodernism.”
Hemings was born in 1773 as the youngest child of the enslaved Elizabeth Hemings, described by one enslaved man at Monticello as “a bright mulatto woman.” Sally, he recalled, was “mighty near white” and “very handsome; long straight hair down her back.” One of Jefferson’s grandsons described her as “light colored and decidedly good looking.” Both enslaved and free contemporaries reported that her father was John Wayles, the father of Jefferson’s wife, Martha. If true, then Hemings was Martha’s half sister.
On her deathbed in 1782, Martha is said to have made her husband promise not to remarry. Five years later, he was in Paris serving as the minister plenipotentiary when his daughter Maria arrived, accompanied by the 14-year-old Hemings. Madison Hemings later claimed that Jefferson and his mother began a sexual relationship while in France, where she was legally free, and that she agreed to return to the United States on the condition that any future children would be freed at age 21.
In an interview with a journalist, Madison stated that his mother was pregnant by Jefferson on their return to the United States in 1789, though it is unclear whether any child from that time survived. Hemings went on to serve in the main house of Monticello while her owner joined George Washington’s Cabinet as the nation’s first secretary of state, and then became president from 1801 to 1809. As he did with all of his human property, Jefferson recorded the birth of Hemings’s six children, including a son, Beverly, in 1798; a daughter, Harriet, in 1801; a son, Madison, in 1805; and another son, Eston, in 1808. Two other daughters, one born in 1797 and another in 1799, died in infancy. The three sons trained as carpenters, and Harriet spun and wove cloth.
Both Beverly and Harriet fled Monticello in 1822. Jefferson, who often posted rewards or hired slave catchers to return those who escaped, did not attempt to recover either. By Madison Hemings’s account, Beverly went to Washington, D.C., passed as white, and married a white woman. Monticello’s former chief overseer later claimed that Jefferson had arranged for Harriet’s departure, giving her spending money and stage-coach fare to Philadelphia. She “married a white man in good standing” in the capital, Madison recalled in his later years.
In Jefferson’s will, made out months before his 1826 death, he granted Madison and Eston Hemings their freedom once they reached 21, and gave both men “my last, solemn, and dutiful thanks.” He also asked the Virginia government—which required those emancipated to leave the state—to allow the Hemings brothers to remain “where their families and connections are.” Sally Hemings was never officially freed, although Jefferson’s daughter Martha later let Sally live with the freed Madison and Eston in Charlottesville until her death, in 1835. Her burial location, like that of so many enslaved African Americans, is unknown.
Both Madison and Eston later moved to Ohio. Eston died in 1856 in Wisconsin. His two sons fought for the Union in the Civil War, and the family obscured its African American heritage. “We identified as white,” Arthur Westerinen, Eston’s fifth-generation descendant, told me. Westerinen’s mother, Julia, learned of the connection when she stumbled on it while doing a college ancestry project.
Madison’s branch, however, retained its African American identity and passed down the story of Jefferson’s paternity. When a teenage Clara Nutt visited Monticello on a school trip in the early 1970s, she was eager to see the home of her famous ancestors. “I got off the bus with my head held high,” she recalled. Shown Jefferson’s bedroom, she asked a docent where Sally Hemings had slept. “That woman never stepped foot in this house,” the docent snapped. Nutt was devastated. “With every breath,” she said, “I silently sobbed.”
In his new book, the Smithsonian’s Kurin tells the story of how he and his fellow researchers tracked down Jefferson’s DNA. In October 2011, Kurin was reviewing a film to accompany a Smithsonian exhibit displaying what is known as The Jefferson Bible. After retiring to Monticello, Jefferson compiled the volume by painstakingly cutting and pasting sections of the New Testament that were focused on morality and stripped of what he called the “artificial vestments” of miracles and superstitions. The film included a segment featuring a reenactor working with a sharp penknife under candlelight. Kurin, then the Smithsonian’s secretary for history, art, and culture, mused to himself that if he had taken on such a delicate task, he would have repeatedly cut himself. That idle thought prompted him to contact a curator who had worked on the bible’s conservation to see if he had encountered any blood splotches that might contain Jefferson’s DNA.
The curator told Kurin that he had found no blood but had encountered a couple of hairs. One was pasted down on page 73 and was light red, like Jefferson’s hair. At the time, extracting DNA from old hair was cutting-edge science; light and humidity can quickly degrade genetic material. Only in the previous year had a Danish team succeeded in sequencing an ancient genome using a clump of 4,000-year-old human hair that had been well preserved in the ice of Greenland.
With approval from Smithsonian leaders, Kurin launched an investigation to reconstruct Jefferson’s genome using the hair found in the bible, while also gathering saliva samples from dozens of living individuals who were known or suspected descendants. By comparing the first with the second, he hoped to produce unequivocal evidence of the paternity of Hemings’s children.
From the start, the ambitious effort was kept secret from the public. “We didn’t want people to assume results until we were really, really sure,” Kurin told me. A colleague of his reached out to a couple in the genetics field, the molecular biologist Beth Shapiro and her husband, Richard Green, a computational expert who had made a name sequencing the Neanderthal genome. They were starting a paleogenomics lab at UC Santa Cruz. “We knew the technology was getting better,” Shapiro told me. “And this looked cool, interesting, and fun.”
Years into the project, Shapiro and Green’s lab determined that the bible hairs had not, in fact, belonged to Jefferson. A reliquary at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, purporting to contain hair from the first 14 presidents, also proved a dead end. “I thought that was it,” Shapiro said. Kurin, however, had already begun to scour other collections. Monticello’s storage areas yielded several samples of Jefferson’s hair encased in gold lockets, glass ampules, and the packet assembled by Nicholas Trist. Kurin also found additional corroboration of the latter’s validity: In 1899, Trist’s daughter had mailed the packet to her cousin, writing that the hair was “in the same paper in which they were placed on that day nearly 74 years ago,” and which “I know to be authentic.”
With the permission of the Thomas Jefferson Foundation, the geneticists examined the hair strands and found viable DNA. “We’ll exhaust it and sequence the crap out of it,” Shapiro assured Kurin in 2017. Lab workers gradually assembled a library of Jefferson’s genome. “We went from a long-shot fishing expedition to a slam dunk,” Green said. “From then on, it was pretty straightforward. We spend a lot of time getting DNA out of difficult things like hair.” (Many of the lab’s recent projects have centered on identifying victims and suspects in cold cases, including the Gilgo Beach murders.)
Kurin, meanwhile, traveled the country to meet with known and possible Hemings-Jefferson descendants, including Julia Westerinen and Nutt. He explained his mission, gained consent, collected saliva samples, and secured promises that they would keep the matter private. This second library of material allowed the geneticists to compare the DNA from descendants of Madison and Eston Hemings with DNA from Jefferson.
The match proved indisputable. On average, a fifth-generation descendant retains 3.125 percent of their ancestor’s genetic material, though the precise amount can vary considerably. Two fifth-generation descendants of Jefferson and Martha Wayles showed 2.6 percent and 2.7 percent of Jefferson’s genetic material. Nutt’s percentage was nearly twice that. Other Madison relations shared significant amounts of the third president’s DNA, as did descendants of Eston. The scientists had found their proof, thanks to Jefferson’s hair. “Once you have a common ancestor,” Green said, “the accuracy is absolutely stunning.”
The research effort has begun to face criticism even before it is publicly released. One descendant of Madison Hemings, Mary Brady-Atkins, provided DNA samples for the study, but criticized Kurin this week in an interview in The Chronicle of Higher Education. Brady-Atkins said she was concerned that Kurin’s book would be published before the scientific paper.
Last month, the 98-year-old Brady-Atkins asked that her saliva samples be destroyed. “It was her right to withdraw from the study,” Kurin told me today. “And yes, we destroyed her DNA, and withdrew data from the study, but the findings are still the same.” He acknowledged that the book would come out before PNAS has accepted the paper, and noted that Brady-Atkins’s request to be removed from the project came after the book was already printed. But Kurin and Green insisted that the study was undergoing appropriate peer review. Green added that a draft of the paper with detailed data will be released on Tuesday, at the same time as the book.
According to the Chronicle, Brady-Atkins supports a competing research effort led by Works, the Jefferson descendant who helped found the Heritage Society; he has long argued that Randolph Jefferson, rather than his brother Thomas, was the father of Hemings’s children. Last year, Works petitioned a county court in Tennessee to exhume the body of Randolph’s son from a Nashville cemetery, with the goal of extracting DNA that Works believes might clear Thomas Jefferson’s name. The city opposes the petition.
Some descendants worry that the new research from Kurin and his colleagues will only infuriate die-hard Jefferson apologists further. “It will be ugly,” Nutt predicted. Unlike during her first Monticello visit, however, she now feels supported. After the Nature paper came out, she attended a reunion of her late father’s family and was drawn into the community of Hemings’s descendants. In 2001, she participated in a White House event hosted by President George W. Bush that brought together Jefferson’s progeny on both sides of the color line. “Whatever comes, I can lean into my family—and my new family,” she said, including the researchers who gathered the hard data confirming her family’s ties.
One likely flash point will be the policies of the Monticello Association, a private organization that oversees the Jefferson-family cemetery at Monticello. The group has long refused to allow Hemings’s descendants to join the association, much less be buried alongside their white relations. “They are invested in this idea of Thomas Jefferson on a pedestal,” Arthur Westerinen said. He told me that he has been in contact with several association members who have pressed for the acceptance of the Hemings branch of the family, though without success. (Lucy Taylor, the association’s president, did not respond to requests for comment.)
Another “giant question,” Green said, is what becomes of Jefferson’s genome. According to Green, two major National Institutes of Health–funded genetic-data banks recently rejected the team’s request to submit its detailed sequence. This is in part because Jefferson is a known figure; if Jefferson’s genome is made public, then his descendants’ privacy will be at risk. “The descendant community will need to weigh in,” Green said. “My lab worked hard on this, but I don’t want to be the one who decides who gets access.”
At the same time, the data, were they publicly released, could allow individuals to determine their own relation to the third president—and, perhaps, pinpoint descendants of Beverly and Harriet Hemings to see if they, too, were born of the Hemings-Jefferson relationship. By recovering the genome of Jefferson’s wife, Martha, researchers also could confirm whether she is Sally Hemings’s half sister.
More broadly, the UC Santa Cruz team’s success might spark a rush to recover the genomes of other famous people—Beethoven’s, for example, was recently sequenced from locks of his hair. Such an effort would have intriguing but unsettling implications. “You could search to see if Abraham Lincoln’s melancholy was genetic,” Kurin suggested. Green fears that rapid technological advances might lead to a genetic Wild West. “Genes are not necessarily fate; most simply create a predisposition,” he said. He worries that members of the media will fail to convey this complexity, much as the 1998 Nature headline was misleading. He also fears a backlash that might result in unreasonable barriers to research.
When it comes to Jefferson and Hemings, Kurin is confident that the team’s careful work over a decade and a half will convince doubters of the accuracy of their finding. “For me, it had nothing to do with an ideological or political agenda,” he writes in his new book. “I was using evidence, logic, and the available tools and methods to follow a trail.” He also takes Jefferson at his word. “There is not a truth existing which I fear,” the Founder wrote two months before his death, “or would wish unknown to the whole world.”

As many as 71% of consumers surveyed in Mumbai said chemists never or rarely refused to sell medicines without a doctor’s prescription, compared with 64% nationally, according to a LocalCircles survey published on September 18, 2026. The findings come as the Centre has proposed mandatory CCTV surveillance at medical stores selling prescription drugs, and the Maharashtra FDA has intensified enforcement against retailers.
The Mumbai survey by LocalCircles, which received more than 20,000 responses across its questions, also found that only 28% of respondents said they were assisted by a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always, while 21% said they were assisted by someone who was not a qualified pharmacist.
On prescription checks, 36% of 3,697 Mumbai respondents said chemists never refused to give them medicines without a prescription and another 35% said they did so very rarely. Only 9% said chemists refused such sales most of the time and 5% said they always did so.
The gap was also visible in home deliveries. Of 3,122 respondents, 18% said their chemist never demanded a doctor’s prescription during ordering or delivery and 40% said this happened very rarely. Only 23% said a prescription was sought most of the time or always.
The survey showed that neighbourhood chemists remain the main source of medicines in Mumbai. Of 3,012 respondents, 57% said they visited or sent someone to a local chemist, while 26% ordered from their chemist through phone calls or WhatsApp for home delivery. Only 17% primarily used e-pharmacy apps.
The national survey, published a day earlier on September 17, 2026, showed similar, though somewhat lower, levels of reported non-compliance. Across India, 64% of consumers surveyed said their chemist never or rarely insisted on a doctor’s prescription, while only 15% said chemists did so most of the time or always. Only 31% said they were assisted by a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always, while 13% said the person assisting them was not qualified.
The nationwide survey received more than 106,000 responses from consumers across 327 districts. It also found that 41% said chemists never or rarely sought prescriptions during home delivery, compared with 58% in Mumbai.
The findings come as the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has floated draft amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, proposing mandatory CCTV surveillance at medical stores supplying medicines sold on a registered medical practitioner’s prescription.
The draft, issued through Gazette notification G.S.R. 791(E) dated September 8, proposes inserting a new sub-rule after Rule 65(2). It states that retail supply of prescription medicines should take place under CCTV surveillance installed and maintained at the premises. The proposal is aimed at strengthening oversight of the sale of Schedule H, H1 and X drugs and curbing sales without valid prescriptions. The government has invited objections and suggestions before finalising the amendment.
The proposed rule comes amid a sharper enforcement drive by the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration. Between June and August 2026, the FDA inspected 2,902 drug establishments, including 2,295 sales establishments and 607 manufacturing units, and initiated action against 880 licensees.
Of these, 677 licences were suspended, and 203 were cancelled, with 740 of the 880 actions involving retailers and wholesalers. During the same three-month period, the FDA conducted 104 search-and-seizure operations, seized illegal drugs and cosmetics worth Rs 11.41 crore, registered 20 FIRs and made 21 arrests.
FDA inspectors flagged several of the same issues reflected in the consumer survey, including the sale of medicines without registered pharmacist supervision, dispensing prescription medicines without valid prescriptions, incomplete Schedule H1 records and sales without proper invoices. Other violations included expired medicines being kept in sale stock and inadequate temperature controls for products such as insulin and vaccines.
The Mumbai survey also found billing gaps. While 76% said they generally received a printed GST invoice and 3% received a manually prepared GST bill, 20% effectively did not receive a proper GST bill.
LocalCircles said the Mumbai findings would be shared with the Maharashtra FDA, Union Health Ministry and CDSCO, and called for stricter verification of registered pharmacists, prescription checks for phone and WhatsApp deliveries and better documentation of medicine sales.

The signing of the ‘Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026’ marks a significant escalation in the use of US President Donald Trump's “coercive geopolitics” and geoeconomics, according to Raj Yadav, Assistant Professor at the Centre for Russian and Central Asian Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU).
Yadav said that “energy security is crucial for India,” as New Delhi warned that the sanctions could impact bilateral ties.
He also questioned the timing of the legislation, saying that it came days after the India-chaired “BRICS Summit succeeded in building consensus despite concerns “over differences among member countries.”
Trump signed the legislation into law on 18 September. The move significantly increases US economic pressure on Russia over the war in Ukraine and opens the door to 100% tariffs on countries, including India and China, for maintaining energy ties with Moscow.
India has maintained that its decision to purchase oil from Russia will be guided by “national interest”, including adequate availability and prevailing global oil prices.
Yadav said the legislation needs to be viewed against the backdrop of a changing global economic and geopolitical order, particularly as countries such as India continue to maintain energy ties with Russia despite Western sanctions.
“The timing and context are important. Just a few days ago, on 12-13 September, India chaired the BRICS Summit and was successful in building consensus amid speculation over differences among member countries such as Iran and the UAE, as well as issues concerning supply chains and energy security,” Yadav said.
The US legislation comes at a time when India is seeking to strengthen its role within BRICS while simultaneously maintaining a significant economic and strategic relationship with Washington.
India is a strategic partner of Russia, and the two countries have maintained extensive bilateral ties across areas, including hydrocarbons and defence.
Russian oil exports to India increased substantially after the Russia-Ukraine war, particularly as Western sanctions disrupted Russia’s traditional energy markets. India subsequently emerged as one of the major buyers of Russian crude.
Yadav pointed to the broader sanctions environment surrounding Russia and the importance of energy supplies for India.
“Russia, being rich in hydrocarbon resources, has seen impressive exports of the same towards India since the Russia-Ukraine war, while Russia has been slapped with almost 13,000 sanctions. India had to move away from Iran for crude oil towards Russia since Iran was sanctioned,” he said.
“Energy security is crucial for India. India has to meet its requirement either from Russia or Iran. India is one of the largest importers of hydrocarbons, hence getting a regular supply of energy is crucial for India’s economic growth,” Yadav added.
India has maintained that its purchase of Russian oil is linked to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people.
Yadav emphasized that the proposed tariff mechanism also needs to be understood in the context of India’s broader trade relationship with the US.
“The imposition of a 100% tariff on India by the US signifies that the US is giving a signal to India that either India should not buy Russian oil or be prepared to sell India’s products in the US at higher prices. In other words, buy crude oil from the US and be a non-tariffed trade partner,” he said.
Yadav also highlighted another often-overlooked factor in discussions of crude oil imports — the compatibility of different crude grades with refinery infrastructure.
“It is also important to factor in the refining capacity and technology related to refining, since there lies the difference in types of crude oil and the refining technology required,” Yadav said.
The issue is therefore not limited to the availability of crude oil in the global market. The type of crude and the refining technology required to process it are also important considerations for an importing country such as India.
The dispute also highlights the balance India seeks to maintain between strategic partnerships and national economic interests.
India has repeatedly maintained that its energy purchases are guided by "national interest", adequate availability and prevailing global oil prices.
Yadav invoked former British Prime Minister Lord Palmerston’s famous observation to describe the principle he believes is relevant to India’s approach:
“We have no eternal allies, and we have no perpetual enemies. Our interests are eternal and perpetual, and those interests it is our duty to follow.”

The Mumbai Police has transferred the case to the Crime Branch after the student’s father filed a complaint
NEW DELHI: Congress spokesperson Shama Mohamed on Monday expressed solidarity with an IIT Bombay professor accused by the father of a second-year BTech student of harassing his son, saying that students in her generation were “mentally strong”.The student, from IIT Bombay’s Department of Energy Science and Engineering, allegedly died by suicide on Friday evening after he was found using a mobile phone during a mid-semester examination.The Mumbai Police has transferred the case to the Crime Branch after the student’s father filed a complaint alleging that IIT Bombay professor and exam invigilator Suryanarayana Doolla had hurled casteist slurs at his son over the past three months. An FIR has been registered against Doolla.Reacting to the controversy, Mohamed wrote: “In this suicide, I stand with Professor Doolla. If a student is caught cheating, it is normal to admonish him & ask him to leave the room. If the student was harassed due to his caste, he should have complained to the SC/ST department.”She added: “When we were kids - we were admonished by teachers, parents for our wrongdoings but our generation was mentally strong.”
Mohamed also called for greater mental health support for students, writing: “I would request colleges to have mental health therapists for the wellbeing of the students.”According to IIT Bombay, the student was found with a mobile phone in the examination hall and had uploaded the question paper on ChatGPT to seek answers. The institute said no disciplinary action had been initiated against him.
The IIT Bombay Faculty Forum has also expressed solidarity with Doolla, saying he was following institute-approved procedures after detecting the alleged academic malpractice. It said the professor reported the incident to the authorities for further action.The institute said Doolla and the Head of Department had counselled the student and assured him that the incident would not adversely affect his academic career. The student subsequently returned to his hostel room, where he was later found dead.The incident has since triggered student protests on campus, with students demanding accountability and transparency from the administration.
