'Agent Layla': Sex assault victim turned secret agent brings her abuser to justice
Vienna Luke became an undercover RCMP operative to get a confession in a historic sexual assault
WARNING: This article may affect those who have experienced sexual violence or know someone affected by it.
On a Friday morning in 2021, just a couple of days before Halloween, Vienna Luke zipped up an oversized puffer jacket with a big hood, and put on sunglasses to hide her face.
In a SUV outside her home, plainclothes RCMP officers waited to whisk her away on a secret mission — a face-to-face meeting with the man responsible for the worst night of her life.
Luke, a fitness instructor and mother of two children, was the key undercover agent in an RCMP operation that — if successful — could lead to the rarest of outcomes: a criminal conviction in a sexual assault that that had occurred 14 years earlier.
If Luke failed, her case and the truth about what had happened that night would almost surely be lost to time.
The police referred to Luke using a code name: Agent Layla.
CBC has obtained the surreptitious recording of that mission. It shows an extremely rare instance of RCMP turning the victim into an agent in her own case.
The RCMP sergeant who led the investigation say it’s an approach that is almost never tried — especially in sexual assault cases.
"For the victim to have the strength, and the investigative team [to have the] determination[...] is almost unheard of," said Sgt. Joëlle LaChance.
Facing the man who assaulted her, her estranged brother-in-law, "Agent Layla" presses him for answers over the course of 70 minutes. Luke ultimately elicits a confession that surpassed even the highest hopes of the RCMP team gathered in a nearby hotel room listening in over a wire. The breakthrough was so moving that it brought tears to a hardened undercover officer accustomed to working with drug dealers and murderers.
"She literally took her life back in her hands," said one of the officers from the undercover unit, working with LaChance.
"There wasn’t a dry eye in that room," said LaChance.
That recording — along with interviews from Luke, her middle sister Shawnessy Luke, and the police officers involved in the sting — is part of a new four-part CBC podcast called Personally: Agent Layla.
The podcast details how Luke managed to get the truth, put the man who assaulted her behind bars, and begin to heal from an incident that left her traumatized, detached from her own body, and at odds with members of her family who at times failed to take her side.
A night with only one memory
At 20 years old, Luke was living at home with her family in the Vancouver suburbs after attending a Bible school overseas. Her life had been sheltered; she says she had never been kissed, or even held hands with a man.
While she contemplated her future, she decided to move in with her eldest sister, brother-in-law and their sons in the small B.C. town of Fort St. John — a 14-hour drive north from where she was raised.
Her brother-in-law, Justin Sewell, was a respected veterinarian who was active in a local Christian church. Sewell was 11 years older than her and he had been a trusted member of the family since Luke was a child.
During a week when Luke's sister and nephews were out of town, Sewell proposed a plan. He suggested she get drunk for the first time at home with him, in what he described as a "safe place."
Luke says she had heard of another Christian girl who had done something similar to experiment for the first time with drinking, so she went along with his idea.
WARNING: This story contains graphic details about sexual abuse.
According to testimony presented in court and extensive interviews conducted by the CBC, Luke only sipped the cocktails he made — one of them a Kahlua-based "Brown Cow."
As she and Sewell danced to country music in the living room, Luke remembers her legs buckling. As the world went black, she felt nauseous and thought to herself that drinking alcohol didn’t seem so fun after all.
Aloud, she spoke a phrase that only drives home how naive she was to what was about to happen.
"I just love Jesus," she said. "I just love Jesus. And then I was out."
For Luke, everything about the rest of that night is blank, except for one memory that would both torment her and propel her to seek accountability in the almost two decades to come: a brief moment when she says she awoke mostly naked in her bed.
"I was looking at myself, from above, to my brother-in-law taking off my underwear," she said.
'We gotta tell mom and dad'
In the aftermath of that horrible evening, Luke says she tried to "shelve" what happened. For months, she fought what she described as a war between her body that remembered, and her brain trying to forget.
She moved back home to her parents’ home near Vancouver and didn’t come face-to-face with Sewell again until half-a-year later at Christmas when the entire family went to Florida for a cruise. But when they said their goodbyes at the airport, her middle sister, Shawnessy Luke, noticed something was off.
"I remember it like it was yesterday," Shawnessy Luke said. "The way he hugged her. And I think that’s strange. That’s prolonged. And I knew something was going on."
Shawnessy Luke describes herself as a person with great intuition and "like a dog with a bone." She waited until she and Vienna Luke got back to their parent’s home to ask questions. She was doing her laundry in the family’s narrow utility room when she insisted that her sister explain.
"She definitely pulled it out of me," said Vienna Luke. "I did not volunteer."
Vienna Luke told her sister what happened in the days leading up to the drinking game, facts that were accepted in court: How Sewell had held her hand, how he called her up from her basement bedroom to watch a lightning storm and then massaged her back, and how he told her he loved her.
Then she shared how Sewell proposed she get drunk, and how she couldn’t remember much more than that.
"In my moral compass brain, the minute I heard those things, I was like, I don’t need to know anymore, I believe you," said Shawnessy Luke. "We’ve got to tell someone about this because [...] whatever happened to you [...] was wrong."
Shawnessy Luke says she insisted they tell their mom and dad.
The night in question had happened in June 2007, about 10 years before the #MeToo social movement. As Vienna Luke told her parents about Sewell holding her hand and massaging her back, she stopped short of sharing the most damning memory of all — that she woke up to Sewell removing her underwear. She felt like her parents didn’t know how to handle what she was saying, and didn't have the vocabulary at the time to talk about sexual assault.
"I knew that I couldn’t share more," she said.
Her father called Sewell right away. She didn’t overhear their conversation, but she recalls her father handed her the phone and she found herself suddenly on the line with Sewell.
Vienna Luke pleaded with Sewell to tell his wife what had happened, hoping her oldest sister would take her side. She still doesn’t know if that happened, only that her oldest sister has continued to stand by her husband and is still married to him today.
Her parents declined to be interviewed for this story. In a victim impact statement filed in court, they wrote: "Our effort to uncover the full story was unsuccessful. Lacking information and clarity, we had no path forward. We felt uneasy about what we knew, but did not pursue this matter further."
Years of numbing
In the years that followed, the Luke family struggled with the divide created by that night: Vienna’s oldest sister and Sewell on one side, Shawnessy and Vienna Luke on the other, and their parents trying to walk a line between all three of their daughters.
"It was easier to take Justin for his word," Vienna Luke said. "He was the one that knew what happened. He got to write the story."
With no clarity about what had actually happened and that one horrific memory of him removing her underwear replaying in her head, Luke says she spent years feeling like a robot trying to numb her pain.
She also moved out of her parent’s house and moved to Vancouver, got a job, and met a man who she credits for showing her how to love herself again.
When they started a family, Luke says something inside her started to shift. She knew she’d have to tell her children the truth someday, and something about birth reconnected her to her body.
"My body wasn’t just laboring," she wrote in her journal. "[It was] waking up."
Twelve years after the assault, and weeks after she delivered her second child, Luke called up her sister Shawnessy.
"Hey, I’m ready to deal with this," she said.
So the two sisters made a list.
The sister detectives
Together, they wrote down all the names of people they suspected had soured on Sewell after he had disclosed to his wife and friends two extramarital affairs five years earlier.
Shawnessy Luke's first call was to one of those ex-lovers, a female veterinarian who had worked at Sewell's clinic.
In a recording of that phone call shared with CBC and in court testimony, the woman said she and Sewell were discussing previous sexual experiences when he said something shocking.
"So what he told me was that he put ketamine in [Vienna’s] drinks," the ex-lover revealed during a phone call Shawnessy Luke recorded. "But he didn’t know how much was enough to like, make her forget."
The sisters say this new information validated a hunch they had come to believe: that Vienna Luke had been drugged.
It also gave her a little piece of evidence to march into the Vancouver Police Department and report.
'I do my job for the victims'
Vienna Luke's file was transferred up to the small RCMP detachment in Fort St. John. Against all odds, it landed on the desk of Sgt. Joëlle LaChance, a female officer with a special commitment to cases that many officers would simply dismiss as too hard and too old.
"My whole life I have been a champion for the underdog," she said. "Being able to stand up for the victim … it's why I do my job."
LaChance said she knew Sewell — with his stellar reputation in the community, had a lot to lose. So instead of going directly to the veterinarian to question him, she called on other RCMP units for help, including the undercover unit.
Together, they hatched a plan.
Court records show Sewell had emailed Vienna Luke several times in the years since the night of the drinking game, asking her to accept that he had changed and hoping that the extended family could be together again.
Luke showed the police those emails. Together, they crafted back emails that suggested there could be a possibility for family reconciliation, but first Luke would need the whole truth and they’d have to meet face-to-face.
They pitched Sewell on a plan to fly to Vancouver to meet Luke.
Unbeknownst to Sewell, Luke would be prepared.
For weeks, she trained, preparing to grill him for the facts. She spent a couple of days in a hotel room, sitting across from an undercover RCMP officer who role played with her. The officer worked to get her comfortable asking tough, direct questions, using words like "vagina" and "ejaculate" — specific terms that would be necessary for charges to be laid.
"This isn’t a trained hitman," the undercover officer said. "She’s very polite, very soft-spoken. And I knew that was exactly the opposite of what we were going to need to do."
On the day of the sting at Vancouver airport, everyone involved held their breath. RCMP had laid the groundwork, but as soon as the tape started recording and Sewell walked in, it would be entirely up to Luke to get the truth.
For the plan to work, Luke would need to be both victim and hero. The RCMP believed it was the best chance at bringing charges. Luke knew it was her only chance to get answers.
"You think I'm exactly the same," Luke remembered thinking. "You think I'm gonna play your same little game, but we've got a new game and I'm writing it."
An extraordinary encounter – and as much truth as she’ll ever get
In the recording, Sewell sits down across from Luke and quickly tries to take control. He claims pornography and a culture that objectifies women is part of why he assaulted her that night.
"Okay, but you’re not actually telling me what happened," Luke replies. "Let’s get back to the night and what actually … happened."
The undercover officer who had spent time coaching Luke for this moment felt proud.
"Take control of that conversation," he said in an interview while listening back to the recording. "Don’t just accept a two-minute fluffy bullshit answer."
Luke persists, peppering Sewell with questions seeking specific details, seemingly undeterred by the fact she’s learning this information about the worst night of her life for the first time.
On tape, Sewell confesses to drugging her, removing her clothing, masturbating and ejaculating twice on her body, and taking 30 photos, including ones where he is spooning her naked body and one where his penis is near her face.
As Luke prepares to wrap up, she lobs an open ended question.
"Is there anything that I’m not asking?" Luke said.
"No reason for me to disclose this. But I took pictures of you at other times," Sewell replied.
His response allowed the RCMP to recommend another charge, this one for voyeurism.
A rare conviction in a historic sexual assault
In the morning of April 26, 2022, Fort St. John RCMP arrested Sewell as he left his home for work.
Sewell pleaded guilty to one count of sexual assault and two counts of voyeurism — one for the photos he took of her the night he assaulted her and one for times he had watched her through her bedroom window. Crown agreed to stay a charge of administering a drug with intent to commit a sexual assault.
In the courtroom, Luke’s mother, father, and Sewell’s supporters listened to the recording from the airport.
A provincial court judge sentenced Sewell to house arrest. Crown appealed and the Court of Appeal judges determined the lower court judge had overstated the mitigating fact of Sewell’s confession.
They issued a sentence of 33 months less a day in prison for his crimes.
Luke asked the court to remove the publication ban on her name — something that is standard in cases of sexual assault to protect the victim’s identity.
As she began to tell friends and acquaintances her whole story, that she was the unnamed victim, she says she realized how important it was to her that she could also say she was the secret agent.
"It took this … experiment of the police saying, 'Hey, how about you go undercover as yourself' for me to realize, whoa, look at the advocate I can be for myself," she said.
"I was Agent Layla. That's me."
The CBC podcast Personally: Agent Layla is available wherever you get your podcasts.

Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing over a thousand people in Nepal and Tibet last month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found.
Researchers identified unusually warm conditions before the glacier’s collapse, which sent an avalanche of 110m cubic metres (3.885bn cu ft) of snow and ice into the valley below. This triggered flash floods on an almost unprecedented scale, hitting communities downstream without warning.
“Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,” said Dr Friederike Otto, a climate science professor at Imperial College London, which carried out the study.
“When warming destabilises the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction. Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come.”
More than 1,300 people were killed and more than 5,000 people remain missing after a massive section of overhanging glacier and rock measuring roughly 200,000 sq metres (2,153,000 sq ft) fell from Langtang Lirung mountain on 26 August.
It dropped about 1,400 metres (4,660ft), slamming into the valley floor with such intensity that it registered as an earthquake, liquidising ice and sparking a freezing flood that careened downriver at speeds exceeding 110 mph.
The devastating flood of water, ice, rock and sediment swept away families, homes, settlements, roads, bridges and other infrastructure, leaving survivors stranded and cut off.
“Rock avalanches of this size are rare, with annual frequency estimates of approximately one event this size every 1,000–10,000 years,” the study said. “This event shows that limits to adaptation are already being reached.”
The research was unlike previous studies by Otto and her team at World Weather Attribution (WWA) – a collaborative project between Imperial and other climate specialists worldwide – in that the role of climate breakdown could not be ascribed to one particular weather event.
Instead, the researchers found the disaster was the result of a compound crisis, with a number of factors made worse by decades of atmospheric heating as a result of greenhouse gas pollution.
Dr Ben Clarke, who researches extreme weather and climate change at Imperial, said the “fingerprints of climate change” were clear in the long-term changes that happened around the glacier before its catastrophic collapse.
Among the study’s key findings were:
- 
  In the region where the collapse happened, climate breakdown has caused about 2C of warming since pre-industrial times, and about 1.5C of warming in July and August specifically;
- 
  July and August 2026 were the warmest on record locally, reaching 5C above the 30-year average in the days before the collapse;
- 
  The freezing threshold in the Himalayas has risen by about 100 metres per decade since the 1980s, with higher and longer thaw temperatures weakening mountain slopes shaped by permafrost;
- 
  The warming temperature had already driven substantial glacier recession, removing stabilising ice from around the site where the collapse occurred and contributing meltwater;
- 
  A 7.8 magnitude earthquake in 2015 further contributed to slope failure, though its specific contribution to the disaster in August could not be confirmed.
Otto, Clarke and the WWA team said their study did not directly ascribe climate breakdown as the fundamental cause of the catastrophe. Instead, it was best understood as a destabilising factor on the existing geology.
Clarke said: “We found that climate change is transforming the high mountain environment, influencing many of the possible drivers of this collapse.”
Nepal has filed a formal request with the UN loss and damage fund for financial support to address the destruction caused by the flood, a process that requires proof of a link to the climate crisis. The country’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, has also demanded that top emitting nations such as China and India “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for the disaster.
Madhab Uprety, senior technical advisor for the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, which is part of WWA, said only aggressive cuts to global emissions could begin to address the “losses and damages faced by vulnerable frontline communities”.
He added: “In addition to the human tragedy on an unimaginable scale, the cost of recovery for this disaster is substantial. For a nation that’s done virtually nothing to contribute to this problem, it underlines the need to find fairness in helping climate vulnerable nations cope with the problems they have not unleashed.”

Thousands march in France against ‘licence to kill’ draft law
In July, deputies in the National Assembly approved the bill which says any police official who uses force is assumed to have acted legally
Thousands of people marched in Paris and other French cities on Sunday against a proposed law on the legitimate use of force that critics say would be a “licence to kill” for police and gendarmes.
In July, deputies in the National Assembly approved the bill which says that any police official who uses force is assumed to have acted legally when using their weapon. It now faces a vote in the Senate.
Politicians, rights groups and other activists joined the Paris demonstration, among them Mathilde Panot of the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party.
“The police kill already,” Panot told the crowd, calling for the bill to be voted down in the Senate.

SIR appeals pile up in WB, EC says hike number of tribunals
NEW DELHI: The innumerable voters in West Bengal who were removed from the electoral rolls after special intensive revision (SIR) may not be able to vote for more than a decade as appellate tribunals set up by Supreme Court could take more than 12 years to decide on their appeals for inclusion, going by the present pace of adjudication.An affidavit filed by Election Commission before Supreme Court says 1,26,194 applications have been decided by tribunals in the last five months since they started functioning in mid-April. So, on average, 25,238 cases are being decided by the tribunals in a month when even Saturdays and Sundays are included as working days. The total number of pending cases as of Sept 16, when the affidavit was filed, was 37,05,235. At current speed, if the tribunals work seven days a week, it would take 146 months to decide all cases.
Excessive backlog
Admitting that the present infrastructure and number of tribunals are insufficient to handle the Herculean task of adjudicating 37 lakh cases, the poll panel pleaded with the court to increase the number of tribunals in the state from 24 to 42, almost double the present strength, and allow judicial officers to work from home.
"With a view to further streamlining and expediting the disposal of the pending appeals, it is proposed that the number of appellate tribunals in the state of West Bengal may be considered for increase to correspond with the number of parliamentary constituencies in the state, so as to facilitate expeditious disposal of the pending appeals," said the affidavit, filed in response to a petition from TMC MP Derek O' Brien. Allowing judicial workers to conduct hearings and undertake other proceedings from home "would assist in expediting the disposal of pending appeals by minimising the time lost in conveyance", it said.In another affidavit filed in response to a petition on the functioning of the tribunals, the commission said they were constituted pursuant to the directives of the apex court and the standard operating procedure (SOP) governing their functioning has been formulated by the committee constituted for this purpose, comprising, inter alia, former judges of the high court at Calcutta.
"It is humbly submitted that the reliefs sought by the petitioner pertain primarily to the functioning, procedure and accessibility of the appellate mechanism and, therefore, fall within the domain of the SOP governing the functioning of the appellate tribunals and the authorities entrusted with the administration thereof. The feasibility, modalities and implementation... are matters best left to the consideration of the concerned appellate tribunal..." the affidavit said.

(Bloomberg) -- Dutch police broke up a far-right protest of several hundred demonstrators in The Hague after it turned violent on Saturday.
Protesters gathered in the center of the Dutch administrative capital under the banner “We Are the People,” with some displaying extremist symbols and slogans. Clashes broke out as demonstrators threw fireworks and other objects at police. The riot unit in turn pushed crowds back to prevent them from blocking major roads, Dutch news agency ANP reported. 
Deputy Mayor Richard de Mos halted the planned march through the city due to ongoing disorder, violence against officers, and the presence of masked individuals. The municipality also issued an emergency decree covering parts of the city, a spokesperson for de Mos said, making it easier for police to arrest anyone contributing to unrest.
Justice Minister David van Weel condemned the violence on social media, citing what he described as “disgusting images” including Nazi salutes, antisemitic slogans, and attacks on police. He called for a firm response. 
The rise of the far right, fueled by structural problems such as inequality and distrust in institutions, has become a headache for European policymakers in recent years. Like other European countries, the Netherlands has experienced a fragmentation of the political center, with fringe groups increasingly sowing chaos and fueling discord.
The riots follow a turbulent week in the country. On Tuesday, the official opening of parliament was disrupted by the sabotage of rail lines and roadside fires, plunging parts of the country into chaos. Some of these actions have been linked to farmers angry over proposed legislation to curb nitrogen emissions.

In March, the Federal Communications Commission banned new consumer internet routers manufactured outside the US, citing national security concerns. The ban doesn’t affect any routers already in American homes or currently on sale in the US, but all new routers aimed at the consumer market will need to be approved. That has inevitably included some of the best new routers to come out in the past six months.
While the headline is that foreign-made consumer routers are banned, manufacturers can apply for exemptions, and some have been approved. There's no need to throw out your router, and you'll still find plenty of mesh systems on the store shelves. But what does this mean for you?
Updated September 2026: I added the news that Conditional Approval has been granted to several more companies, the biggest being Asus.
Why Are Foreign-Made Routers Banned?
“Malicious actors have exploited security gaps in foreign-made routers to attack American households, disrupt networks, enable espionage, and facilitate intellectual property theft,” the FCC wrote. “Foreign-made routers were also involved in the Volt, Flax, and Salt Typhoon cyberattacks targeting vital US infrastructure.”
Foreign-made consumer routers were added to the Covered List, which details equipment and services “deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States.”
Bogdan Botezatu, director of Threat Research at cybersecurity firm Bitdefender, says this ban is a step to harden the cybersecurity readiness of US households, given ongoing geopolitical tensions.
“Consumer routers sit at the edge of every home network, which makes them an attractive target and a strategic risk if compromised at scale,” he says. Asked whether he thinks the risk is real, Botezatu says yes, though there’s no easy way to prove intent. “[Internet of Things] devices, including routers, are a weak point across the internet.”
Which Routers Are Banned?
The ban only affects the sale of new Wi-Fi routers and mobile Wi-Fi or hotspot devices aimed at consumer households. The ban does not apply to existing FCC-approved routers on sale in the US or to phones with hotspot features. Previously purchased routers already in use in homes across the country are also fine and aren't part of the ban, according to the FCC’s FAQ. These routers can continue to be sold, used, and updated with new firmware, at least until January 1, 2029.
Any new router manufactured outside the US now requires FCC approval before it can be imported, marketed, or sold in the US. This includes routers from US companies manufactured overseas, which is the vast majority of the market right now.
What Does Foreign-Made Mean?
This is decidedly murky. The ban is concerned with “consumer-grade” routers and could include any designed or manufactured outside the US or manufactured by companies that are not completely US-owned and operated. All the major players in the market, including Netgear, TP-Link, Asus, Amazon’s Eero, Google’s Nest, Synology, Linksys, and Ubiquiti, fall under the definition. As do most, if not all, of the routers supplied by internet service providers in the US.
Just like the recent federal drone ban, or the even more recent robot vacuum ban, the router ban only applies to new devices, but manufacturers can apply for Conditional Approval from the Department of Defense and the Department of Homeland Security.
What Is Conditional Approval?
There are three main elements to securing a Conditional Approval in the official guidelines:
- Corporate Structure: This must disclose the ownership, board membership, and “any foreign government ownership, control, influence, financing, or material support.”
- Manufacturing and Supply Chain Disclosure: Router manufacturers must submit detailed reports that break down where every major stage of production happens, covering manufacturing, assembly, design, and development. That means listing every component in every router or hotspot they manufacture and explaining where it comes from.
- US Manufacturing and Onshoring Plan: This must include “A detailed, time-bound plan to establish or expand manufacturing in the United States for the router for which the applicant is seeking Conditional Approval" to qualify for FCC authorization, along with details about any existing US manufacturing and quarterly status updates on progress.
Companies that receive Conditional Approval can continue to sell and update existing devices and release new routers, mesh systems, and mobile hot spots for 18 months. This includes firmware and other software updates for existing and new devices. All new devices are subject to the regular FCC approval process.
Companies With Conditional Approval
So far, several companies have been granted Conditional Approval. Here’s the FCC list.
- Netgear, a popular US manufacturer of Orbi mesh systems and Nighthawk routers, has been granted a Conditional Approval until October 1, 2027.
- Eero, Amazon’s mesh router brand, was granted a Conditional Approval until October 31, 2027.
- Asus, popular maker of many routers and mesh systems, was granted a Conditional Approval until March 6, 2028.
- Arcadyan, which makes routers for AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, was granted a Conditional Approval until December 12, 2027.
Other companies that have been granted Conditional Approvals so far include Zyxel, Gryphon, SpaceX, Adtran, Calix, Nokia, and Sagemcom.
Outside the guidelines, the Department of Defense, Department of Homeland Security, and FCC have not released any further information on why certain companies have been granted Conditional Approvals. None of these companies has released any detailed information on how they secured a Conditional Approval or about plans for US-based manufacturing.
The Consumer Technology Association (CTA) has appealed via this FCC filing for greater clarity and clearer guidelines. It also raised concerns about software patching and component updates.
What About Software Updates?
While the FCC initially published a waiver covering software and firmware updates until March 1, 2027, it has now extended that waiver “at least until January 1, 2029.”
What happens after that date is not clear. The fear was that companies that failed to secure Conditional Approval before the original deadline would not only be unable to sell new routers but also unable to update existing routers.
“The biggest practical security risk with routers is not only who made them, but whether they remain patched. Routers sit at the edge of homes, businesses, and critical networks. When they stop receiving updates, known vulnerabilities remain exposed, attackers gain durable footholds, and consumers are left with equipment they cannot realistically secure on their own," says Matt Wyckhouse, Founder and CEO of Finite State. “The original restriction risked creating exactly that problem: millions of deployed routers frozen in time, unable to receive security fixes. I appreciate the FCC recognizing that preventing updates could unintentionally make Americans less safe."
The majority of routers compromised and used in cyberattacks are older (end-of-life) devices that no longer receive security updates.
What About Foreign-Made Components?
Due to the vagaries of international supply chains, it is very common for router manufacturers to substitute certain components in existing devices. How this fits with the router ban is unclear, but companies are clearly worried enough about it that the CTA has asked the administration to consider “additional waivers of Class I permissive change rules for changes that do not materially change the security posture of the device, for example, routine parts substitutions that do not materially affect the device’s RF characteristics.”
Well, the FCC provides some clarification in its FAQ (“covered” here means banned):
“Non-'covered' devices do not become ‘covered’ simply because they contain a 'covered' component part, unless the 'covered' component part is a modular transmitter under the FCC’s rules,” it says. “Therefore, a router produced in the United States is not considered ‘covered’ equipment solely because it contains one or more foreign-made components.”
Manufacturers importing components from China but assembling them in the US will presumably be OK, though it’s far from clear. “Applicants will need to be able to have sufficient evidence that the routers were not produced in a foreign country to make this certification, but there is no specific documentation or evidence required,” according to the FCC.
Netgear Has Approval
Netgear published a letter from its CEO to announce its Conditional Approval. While it is a US-founded and headquartered company, Netgear’s routers are manufactured abroad, mostly in Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia, and Taiwan. The company has moved away from China in recent years. Netgear has been lobbying the government on “cybersecurity and strategic competition with China.”
“We commend the administration and the FCC for their action toward a safer digital future for Americans,” a Netgear spokesperson tells WIRED. “Home routers and mesh systems are critical to national security and consumer protection, and today’s decision is a step forward.”
Netgear is a publicly traded company on Nasdaq, mostly owned by institutional investors, including BlackRock and Vanguard. The company’s stock rose on news of the ban.
Will TP-Link Be Banned?
Since all of its routers are made overseas, TP-Link must apply for Conditional Approval or spin up manufacturing in the US to sell any new routers. Estimates vary, but TP-Link’s US consumer router market share is somewhere around 35 percent, with Netgear and Asus accounting for another 25 percent or so.
The US Commerce, Defense, and Justice departments have reportedly been investigating and considering a ban on TP-Link routers for more than a year over concerns about the company’s links to China. No ban has been enacted until now, but Texas attorney general Ken Paxton sued TP-Link in February, claiming the company allows the Chinese Communist Party to access American consumers’ devices. Detractors have also criticized perceived predatory pricing, claiming TP-Link flooded the US market with a wide range of affordable routers to establish dominance.
TP-Link has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and claims it has divested from its Chinese roots and is now headquartered in the US with the bulk of manufacturing in Vietnam. TP-Link’s cofounder and CEO, Jeffrey Chao, recently applied for permanent US residency through President Trump’s Gold Card program, according to the Times of India.
“Virtually all routers are made outside the United States, including those produced by US-based companies like TP-Link, which manufactures its products in Vietnam,” a spokesperson from TP-Link tells WIRED. “It appears that the entire router industry will be impacted by the FCC’s announcement concerning new devices not previously authorized by the FCC.”
TP-Link is a privately owned company and not publicly listed on any stock exchange. Chao and his wife, Hillary, are listed as the company's sole owners.
Asus Has Approval
Asus primarily makes its routers in Taiwan, though it has production facilities in China and works with several third-party manufacturers. Recent tariff pressures led the company to branch out to Thailand, Vietnam, Indonesia, Mexico, and the Czech Republic, but the bulk of its routers still come from Taiwan or China.
Asus posted after securing Conditional Approval in September, 2026, stating, “We are honored to announce to users worldwide that ASUS has successfully passed the U.S. FCC’s rigorous cybersecurity review for consumer networking equipment, receiving official conditional approval and being listed as a Trusted Consumer Router Vendor.”
Asus is listed on the Taiwanese Stock Exchange and is mostly owned by public shareholders. The ban doesn’t appear to have impacted its stock price.
Are Any Routers Manufactured in the US?
The only routers I know of that are manufactured in the US are some Starlink Wi-Fi routers, which are primarily made in Texas. Starlink is part of Elon Musk's SpaceX company, but many of the components in these routers come from East Asia.
Botezatu says what matters more than geography is the security model behind the product. Companies that invest in “long-term firmware support, vulnerability management, and built-in protection layers” offer stronger security.
How Will the Router Ban Impact Ordinary Folks?
It’s not entirely clear, but it probably won’t have a huge immediate impact. There is already a wide range of Wi-Fi 7 routers and mesh systems on the market that will continue to be sold—they enable speeds well in excess of what most people need at home. Whether companies spin up manufacturing in the US or find other ways to satisfy government agencies that their wares are not a security risk, the result is likely to be higher prices for consumers.
"This ruling has the potential to significantly disrupt the US consumer router market," Brandon Butler, a research manager of Network Infrastructure and Services at IDC, tells WIRED. “In the near term, much will depend on how quickly conditional waivers are processed. Most vendors are likely to pursue them, but any delays could constrain supply and create upward pressure on pricing.”
If you haven't upgraded to the latest Wi-Fi 7 standard, now might be a good time to do it. But it's worth keeping in mind what you're buying. Botezatu says consumers should “stick with reputable manufacturers that have a track record of issuing updates and maintaining their devices. Check that your router is still supported and running the latest firmware.”
When current stocks run low, the ban could have a serious impact on the router market in the US. Not only will spinning up US manufacturing take years and increase costs, but the ban is also likely to limit choice in the market, as smaller companies may struggle with the compliance burden, and chipset vendors and OEMs, turned off by a slowdown and unpredictability in the market, may deprioritize the US, according to a Global Electronics Association report.
Unanswered Questions
The ban does leave several unanswered questions. Why is it being applied only to consumer routers? Why are some manufacturers being granted Conditional Approvals and not others? Why are the foreign-made routers currently on sale and in our homes deemed safe? What happens when the software update waiver runs out? The FCC did not address these questions.

At the start of September, about two weeks before she was due to compete at the Asian Games, Vidarsa Vinod Kochalumkal finally bought her first 10m air rifle.
It was a steel-grey Feinwerkbau 900 ALU. The decision was something of a gamble, not least because the rifle cost about Rs 5 lakh.
For the past five years, the 27-year-old had been shooting with a Walther that once belonged to her husband, Manu. It was old and had been modified and adjusted countless times. More importantly, though, it produced results.
It was on that same rifle that Vidarsa had come through a fiercely competitive national selection process to earn her place on the Asian Games team.
“It was a risky move to change something she had worked with for so long. But she took that risk,” says Manu.
ALSO READ | Indian shooters are taking year-old bullets to Aichi-Nagoya; here’s why
The gamble has already paid off.
On Sunday, Vidarsa — on her Asian Games debut— partnered Sonam Maskar and Elavenil Valarivan to win silver in the women’s 10m air rifle team event. Her score of 630.4 contributed to India’s aggregate of 1898 points, with only China finishing ahead.
As she held the silver medal between her fingers, Vidarsa admitted she could hardly believe what she had accomplished.
“When I started shooting, I never thought that one day I would be competing at the Asian Games and I’d have my own medal,” she says.
For much of her career, Vidarsa had never even intended to become an air-rifle shooter.
Growing up in Kozhikode, Kerala, she first became fascinated by shooting as an NCC cadet. And it wasn’t the air rifle that caught her attention.
“I wanted to try shooting only because I wanted to touch an actual gun,” she remembers.
On her first day, with virtually no training, she was the best shooter in the group. The result encouraged her to continue. But it was only the following year, after she joined the Kerala Rifle Association and won 12 medals at her first state competition, that she began to believe shooting could become a profession.
The early years, however, were not easy.
At the NCC, Vidarsa used an old rifle and ammunition that she felt was of poor quality. Her shooting jacket belonged to someone else and did not even fit her properly. Eventually, she and her father took a loan to buy her own 50m rifle.
She moved to Delhi in 2021 to train with national coach Manoj Kumar. Even at that stage, the 10m air rifle event held little attraction for her.
ALSO READ | Japanese triathlete Takumi Hojo wins first gold medal of Asian Games 2026
“I was forced into shooting it,” she says. “Manoj sir told me that if I shot the air rifle, it would help me develop my standing shooting in the 50m rifle three-position event.”
Vidarsa still wasn’t convinced.
“I didn’t have the resources to buy a new gun. I’d used everything I had in buying my 50m rifle. I really didn’t want to buy another rifle for something that wasn’t even my primary event,” she says.
Eventually, her friend Manu — himself a shooter who had supported her before they eventually married — provided the solution, sharing the Walter rifle that belonged to him.
That rifle would become an unlikely but important part of Vidarsa’s journey.
Her 50m performance improved and she made her international debut in 2025. But, unexpectedly, it was the event she had initially regarded as little more than a training exercise that began to produce results.
“I first started to believe I had potential in the 10m event after I reached the final of the National Games in Dehradun in 2025. After that, I felt maybe I shouldn’t just see this as a training exercise,” she says.
She began making her presence felt at the national selection trials. Her first international appearance in the 10m air rifle came at the Munich World Cup in June 2026, where she shot 630.6 in qualification. She followed that with an appearance at the Hangzhou World Cup the following month.
There were no medals at either event, but Vidarsa was steadily building a case for herself.
By the time the Asian Games selection process was complete, she had qualified for both the 10m air rifle and 50m rifle competitions.
It was only then that the decision was made that the Walther had finally reached the end of its utility.
“The rifle she had originally bought was meant for her husband. Vidarsa is a much smaller shooter — she is only 152cm tall. So we adjusted it as much as possible, but eventually it was not possible. So it was time to get her a new rifle,” says Manoj.
For years, Vidarsa had hesitated to spend money on another rifle. Now, with an Asian Games place secured and her old equipment no longer capable of being adjusted sufficiently to suit her, there was little reason to hesitate.
The timing could hardly have been more dramatic. She had only about two weeks to become comfortable with the new Feinwerkbau ahead of her Asian Games debut.
There was, naturally, some apprehension.
ALSO READ | Elavenil Valarivan’s silver worth its weight in gold
“A lot of people doubted the choice but I completely trusted Manoj sir,” Vidarsa says.
For his part coach Manoj Kumar says he’s satisfied with the outcome.
“Vidarsa shot about as well as she always has. I was hoping she would have improved on her average score but I couldn’t have asked for more,” he told Sportstar.
For her part, Vidarsa feels she certainly can. Her current Feinwerkbau has served its purpose but she’s not done yet.
“I’ve got so much confidence. I still have my 50m rifle event to go. I will do my best in that as well. But from now on, I think the 10m air rifle is not my secondary event anymore,” she says.

Xi rolls into Trump summit with China's trade engine roaring
While thorny issues like Taiwan may surface, the main focus of the upcoming meeting is whether Xi and Trump will signal an extension to a trade truce struck last year that averted a major shock to the global economy.
BEIJING: In the four months since the leaders of the two global superpowers last met, Xi Jinping has overseen a surge in China's trade with the world while Donald Trump has struggled with falling approval ratings at home.
That shift in fortunes has tempered expectations for their summit in Washington this week, analysts say, with Xi in no rush to make concessions and Trump constrained by a costly war with Iran that has hurt both his popularity and Americans' wallets.
While thorny issues like Taiwan may surface, the main focus of the Sep 24 meeting is whether the leaders will signal an extension to a trade truce struck last year that averted a major shock to the global economy.
"Xi is not really looking for anything tangible. He wants to extend the gentleman's agreement with Trump so that China has time to fortify itself," said Jon Czin, a foreign policy expert at the Brookings Institution who formerly served as China director at the US National Security Council.
"LIVING IN XI'S WORLD"
White House officials have sought to downplay the potential for major breakthroughs. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng helmed preparatory talks in New York on Sunday (Sep 20) aimed at teeing up some potential agreements on AI guardrails and trade in non-sensitive products.
That is a far cry from Trump's vow when he returned to office in 2025 to use tariffs to address a trade imbalance with China that was "killing" the United States.
But since agreeing to the truce with Xi in October of that year, his attention has been divided among myriad other foreign policy battles, from the wars in Iran and Ukraine to disputes with Europe over free speech.
China has faced its own challenges, such as slowing domestic demand and a protracted property crisis, but the export juggernaut that Trump sought to tame has kept roaring in what economists are increasingly referring to as China Shock 2.0.
China's global trade surplus is on pace to top US$1 trillion for a second straight year.
While US efforts to curb the cheap parcels that online retailers such as Shein and Temu rely on have worked, more than half of the roughly 6,500 product categories China sold to the US so far this year have grown compared to 2025.
A delegation of Chinese business leaders, potentially including some firms facing US regulatory scrutiny as they seek greater market access, is set to accompany Xi to Washington.
The Trump administration "thought they could use massive unilateral pressure to force China to make concessions, and that did not occur," said Scott Kennedy, an expert on the US-China economic relationship at Washington-based think tank CSIS.
"Now this is Xi Jinping's world, and we're all living in it."
TAIWAN AND TRADE WINS
If Xi is in the driver's seat as analysts suggest, that will further unnerve US allies in Asia who expect the Chinese leader to push Trump to soften Washington's support for Taiwan, the island claimed by Beijing.
Xi repeatedly asked him about Taiwan when they met in Beijing in May, including about arms sales and Washington's resolve to defend the island, Trump told reporters.
The US president described a pending US$14 billion arms package for Taiwan as a "negotiating chip" with Beijing.
Some officials in Taipei and Tokyo worry he may be tempted to cash in that chip for political wins ahead of November's midterm elections, which could prove challenging for his Republican Party.
That could include Chinese purchases of Boeing jets or farm goods, or commitments to curb the flow of fentanyl precursor chemicals that have fuelled the US opioid crisis.
"China-US ties have become more transactional," said Wu Xinbo, a professor at Shanghai's Fudan University who advises China's foreign ministry.
While Washington may want to prioritise trade talks, for Beijing, the US approach to Taiwan could be key, he said.
"If you accommodate our concern on the Taiwan issue, then we would be willing to accommodate your concerns on other issues, be it law enforcement or on purchases of US agricultural products," Wu said.
PUTTING PRESSURE ON IRAN
Washington also sees Xi as uniquely able to exert pressure on Iran to bring an end to the war that has dragged Trump's approval rating to the lowest of his political career.
However, Xi has shown little inclination to do so. Reuters earlier this month reported that Beijing is selling billions of dollars' worth of goods to Iran through a sanctions-evasion scheme. China's foreign ministry says it is not aware of such a scheme.
US threats last month of secondary sanctions on countries doing business with Iran - which Bessent called an "Economic D-Day" - appear not to have yet been wielded against Tehran's largest trading partner.
That is more evidence, analysts say, that Trump is eager to keep relations with Xi steady as he focuses his energies elsewhere - an arrangement that also suits the Chinese leader.
"Both Xi and Trump feel it's quite helpful to have stability in the relationship so that they can focus on more pressing things," said Ruby Osman, senior geopolitical researcher at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change.
"For Trump, that is Iran. For Xi, that is building out China's domestic resilience for whatever comes after Trump."

WHO and Switzerland have announced the renewal of their cooperation strategy for the period 2024-2028. In 2013, Switzerland became the first high-income country in the WHO European Region to pilot a cooperation strategy with WHO (hereafter referred to as the WHO-Switzerland Cooperation Strategy). In 2022, WHO and Switzerland jointly decided to update and renew this cooperation strategy, which was done on 4 March 2025 at the Regional Office of the WHO in Copenhagen, Denmark.

Iran has issued warning that any renewed military action by the United States and its allies would trigger “continuous, effective and painful” attacks on US bases and interests across West Asia, while countries supporting Washington would be treated as parties to the conflict.
The warning was issued on Sunday by Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, the country's central military command, which said Washington was preparing to resume military action against Tehran with the backing of some regional countries.
“Should the United States make any mistake against the Islamic Republic of Iran, all its bases and interests in the region will be targeted in continuous, effective and painful attacks without any limitation or consideration,” the command said in a statement carried by state-run IRNA, as quoted by ANI.
The Iranian command also warned regional countries against supporting any US military action, saying those that aligned themselves with Washington would be considered participants in the conflict and could no longer expect restraint from Iranian forces.
The warning came as the US maintained a naval blockade on Iranian ports. US Central Command said its forces had redirected 109 commercial vessels as of September 20 as part of efforts to enforce the blockade.
The standoff has raised further concerns over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key global energy corridor. Iran has continued to restrict most shipping through the waterway and has said it will not reopen it until the terms of a June ceasefire agreement, as Tehran interprets them, are met.
US President Donald Trump has meanwhile warned Tehran of severe consequences if it does not agree to a deal, saying Iran could face economic collapse or attacks on its leadership. Trump said he was in a “deciding mode” on Iran and warned that “very big things” could happen.

Meanwhile, Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei said Tehran had conveyed conditions for ending the conflict through Qatari mediation, including an end to hostilities, the release of frozen Iranian funds and the lifting of the naval blockade.
The latest escalation followed renewed attacks by Iran-backed Houthi forces targeting Saudi Arabia, including claims of strikes on Riyadh and an oil facility in the Red Sea port of Yanbu. Saudi Arabia did not immediately comment on those claims, while a Saudi-led coalition said it had foiled other attacks.
Amid the looming threat, the US State Department had on Saturday warned Americans in the region of the potential for “unforeseen escalation”, urging them to exercise greater vigilance and prepare for possible flight cancellations and airspace closures.

18వ బ్రిక్స్ (BRICS) సదస్సు 2026 12,13 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 తేదీల్లో న్యూఢిల్లీలోని భారత్ మండపంలో జరిగింది. ఈ సదస్సులో బ్రిక్స్ సభ్య దేశాలతో పాటు భాగస్వామ్య దేశాలకు చెందిన నాయకులు పాల్గొన్నారు. ఈ నేపథ్యంలో రష్యా అధ్యక్షుడు వ్లాదిమిర్ పుతిన్, బ్రెజిల్ అధ్యక్షుడు లూయిజ్ ఇనాసియో లులా డా సిల్వా, యూఏఈ అధ్యక్షుడు మహమ్మద్ బిన్ జాయెద్ అల్ నహ్యాన్, భారత ప్రధాని నరేంద్ర మోదీ, చైనా అధ్యక్షుడు షీ జిన్పింగ్, టర్కీ అధ్యక్షుడు రెసెప్ తయ్యిప్ ఎర్డోగాన్, దక్షిణాఫ్రికా అధ్యక్షుడు సిరిల్ రమాఫోసా, ఇరాన్ మాజీ అధ్యక్షుడు ఇబ్రహీం రైసీలతో కూడిన సెల్ఫీ చిత్రం సోషల్ మీడియాలో విస్తృతంగా షేర్ చెయ్యబడుతోంది (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ). ఈ చిత్రం నిజమైనదేనా అనే విషయాన్ని ఇప్పుడు పరిశీలిద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: 2026 బ్రిక్స్ సదస్సులో ప్రపంచ దేశాల నాయకులతో కూడిన నిజమైన సెల్ఫీ చిత్రం.
ఫాక్ట్ (నిజం): ఈ చిత్రం AI ద్వారా రూపొందించబడింది. ఇందులో సదస్సుకు హాజరుకాని వ్యక్తులతో పాటు మరణించిన వ్యక్తులు కూడా ఉన్నారు. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టు ఫేక్.
ఈ పోస్టును పరిశీలించినప్పుడు మేము వైరల్ చిత్రంలో కొన్ని తప్పులు గుర్తించాము. బ్రెజిల్, యూఏఈ, టర్కీ అధ్యక్షులు 2026 బ్రిక్స్ సదస్సుకు హాజరు కాలేదు. బ్రెజిల్ తరఫున విదేశాంగ మంత్రి మౌరో వియెరా, యూఏఈ తరఫున క్రౌన్ ప్రిన్స్ ఖలేద్ బిన్ మహమ్మద్ బిన్ జాయెద్ అల్ నహ్యాన్ ప్రాతినిధ్యం వహించారు. అంతేకాకుండా, చిత్రంలో ఇరాన్ మాజీ అధ్యక్షుడు ఇబ్రహీం రైసీ కూడా కనిపిస్తున్నారు. అయితే, రైసీ 2024 మేలో హెలికాప్టర్ ప్రమాదంలో మరణించారు.
అంతేకాకుండా, ఈ చిత్రాన్ని AI detection టూల్స్తో పరీక్షించాం. Hive Moderation ఈ చిత్రం 99.9% AI ద్వారా రూపొందించబడిందని తెలిపింది. Sightengine కూడా ఇది 99% AI-generated చిత్రం అని తెలిపింది.
సదస్సులో పాల్గొన్న నాయకుల చిత్రాలను ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ చూడవచ్చు.
చివరిగా, ఈ AI రూపొందించిన చిత్రాన్ని, 2026 బ్రిక్స్ సదస్సులో ప్రపంచ దేశాల నాయకుల నిజమైన ఫొటోగా షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

On September 10, two days after researcher Jacob Coxon, who had recently quit his job at Anthropic, sounded the alarm about the industry potentially bringing about the end of humanity, the New York City Democratic Socialists of America posted a carousel of images on Instagram. The first slide was a drawing of an ouroboros—a dragon eating its own tail—set against a hot pink background. “AI alarmism and AI hype are the same story: both keep your attention on a science-fiction future to distract you from the real harms experienced in the present,” the image reads.
The post was authored by the NYC DSA’s Tech Action Working Group, which focuses on tech regulation issues for the chapter, the largest in the country. It garnered more than 25,000 likes on Instagram. But not everyone agreed with the post: “Horrible and dangerous take,” one comment reads. “Sometimes sounding the alarm is justified.”
As politicians scramble to understand AI safety, an ideological split is opening on the American left. Among the questions it’s centered on is whether to believe tech companies’ claims that their products are so powerful that they could end the world.
Some on the left question the value in elevating theoretical concerns about AI over actual harms. They believe repeating claims promoted by the frontier labs about the dangers of AI empowers the AI companies, turning attention away from regulating the current harms of the technology and toward an impossible future.
“AI has become the latest tool of capitalist exploitation. The damage that unregulated and misused AI is already causing is clear across the country,” Alan Dang, a member of Tech Action, tells WIRED. “As socialists, we don’t trust these corporations to craft their own regulations.”
But others are following the direction of Senator Bernie Sanders, the unofficial leader of the American left, who has enthusiastically taken up the AI safety issue, asserting that AI has the potential to eliminate humanity. They say that it’s possible to address all harms from AI—both those happening now and those that could happen in the future—at once.
“The same people concerned about frontier governance and the development of superintelligence are also addressing those current harms,” says Alexander McCoy, a Democratic strategist working on AI issues. “We should address all these other important factors. Those frontier AI abilities are true and increasing in power. They are not fake or hype.”
Over the past year, Sanders dove head-first into the world of AI safety, bringing conversations that were previously happening in Bay Area circles to Washington and his large populist base. The 85-year-old was early to both opposing data centers—a massive organizing pole for the left this year—and speaking out about AI’s potential harms, from job loss to existential dangers. His data center moratorium bill, released in March, explicitly linked pausing construction with the need to pass federal regulation to protect “the future of humanity.”
Sanders’s positioning on this issue has put him in some unusual alliances, most notably with Steve Bannon, President Donald Trump’s former adviser and a right-wing populist podcast host. It has also seemingly inspired a raft of messaging from left-wing candidates running for office across the country, many of whom have been tying broader concerns around AI to the furor over data centers. On September 9, a day before the New York DSA post, six candidates affiliated with the Working Families Party, including four backed by Sanders, released statements on the need for Washington to regulate AI to prevent existential threats to humanity.
This has come with both public and private criticism. AI researcher and tech industry critic Timnit Gebru has accused Sanders and others on the left of “taking their cues from literal doomsday eugenicist cults,” referring to the effective altruist and rationalist philosophies, which underpin AI safety conversations in Silicon Valley. And Sanders’s moves have inspired some private agita within certain left-wing circles.
“Some of us are looking at Bernie and saying, what happened?” one NYC DSA member with a tech background tells WIRED.
Rumman Chowdhury, CEO and founder of the nonprofit Humane Intelligence, understands the concerns expressed by the DSA working group. Chowdhury, who formerly led the machine learning ethics, transparency, and accountability team at Twitter, thinks that all the attention that the AI safety discourse is generating will ultimately be beneficial to frontier labs.
“[The companies] grab all the attention, time, energy, and money by spouting really extreme perspectives. But then they actually backtrack to where we sit, all while they discount all of our expertise,” she says. “I think it's hard for normal people to think of how the mind of a venture capitalist works and these investors work. The scarier and more fantastic these CEOs make these companies seem, the more investors want in on it.”
For AI companies—particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, which aim to go public in the coming years—the attention and scrutiny on their products now could also be a boon in the long run. “Part of IPOing is sharing a lot of diligence documentation on risks and how risks have been addressed,” says Chowdhury. “This way, they can say, there is a full regulatory regime that they are part of establishing in this industry to guard against the worst risks, and that we have all established exactly what the ‘worst risks’ are.”
Pragathi Barusubramanian is a member of the NYC DSA’s Tech Action working group and a leader in the group’s anti-data center organizing, which netted a major win earlier this year by helping New York pass a one-year moratorium. Barusubramanian feels there may be a disconnect in the conversation around what exactly constitutes the most pressing AI-related harms to regulate. “When it comes down to what's happening on the ground,” they say, the conversation about existential risk “doesn’t come up at all.” Instead, they say, “there's an understanding that AI and data center companies don't have our interests at heart.”
McCoy, who is advising several Congressional candidates on AI, asserts that there is no real divide between actual leaders on the left on the issue. McCoy noted that several members of the DSA, including New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, have come out with recent statements about Coxon’s warnings and the Hugging Face hack.
McCoy says Gebru and similarly-minded critics are “marginal, unrepresentative, and also, frankly, picking an unnecessary distinction. It’s yes and. We should address harms like surveillance and Flock cameras, and other important factors. These do not come in any way at the expense of governing frontier AI capabilities.”
Phil Aroneanu, executive director of Irreplaceable, a left-leaning pro-AI safety organization, says that his time working as a climate activist has informed his approach to the AI regulation question. He believes that addressing both AI’s immediate and existing harms as well as future threats is both needed and possible. (McCoy helped found Irreplaceable with an initial seed fund from the Center for AI Safety.)
“This very similar intersection between the direct impact of fossil fuel extraction, people's homes getting flooded out because of climate-change-fueled storms, and then the broader movement focusing on the longer-term issue of risks and emissions,” he says.
Sanders and New York representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez don’t appear to be on the exact same page, either. While she cosponsored Sanders’ data center moratorium legislation, including the language around AI threatening humanity in her own House version of the bill, she has not participated in the high-profile AI safety discussions that he has been present for. While Sanders has called AI “the most transformational technology in the history of the world,” much of Ocasio-Cortez’s language around AI thus far has focused on data centers and the harms to jobs the technology could create, and worries that the industry is creating a bubble.
When asked by a reporter about AI safety last week, Ocasio-Cortez threaded a careful line, saying that “two things can be true at once,” noting AI “can be very dangerous when pursued without any guardrails,” and warning that “we could be seeing an economic bubble collide with a technological frontier.”
As the safety conversation quickly coalesces in Washington and in statehouses around the country, the ultimate question for the left is not whether to support AI regulation, but what regulations the movement should put its time and resources behind. Dang told WIRED that the DSA Tech Working Group supports “comprehensive AI and tech regulation at the federal, state, and city level, addressing frontier model regulation while also fighting back against the ways that corporate AI is already being used.”
A convention resolution currently before the DSA, meanwhile, proposes organizational support for Sanders and representative Greg Casar’s bill to ban superintelligence altogether—hardly something the frontier labs would agree on. And any ideological concerns within the DSA itself may not matter too much when voters get a say. A Politico poll released Wednesday shows that two in three Americans think that there is at least some risk that AI could “destroy humanity.”
Barusubramanian says that, if nothing else, they’re “happy that everyone is talking about AI now.”

An Australian man accused of murdering a Thai teenager and putting her body in a suitcase pleaded not guilty on Friday in a hearing in the seaside resort city of Pattaya, a court official said.
Simon Peter Carman, 45, was arrested in June after 17-year-old Tunchanok Donhomla was reported missing in Pattaya City, about 150km south-east of Bangkok. A suitcase containing her body was found shortly after.
Police said she died of suffocation.
Carman appeared on Friday at Pattaya provincial court, where he pleaded not guilty to all charges, a court spokesperson said.
He had been charged with murder, concealing a body and taking a minor for indecent purposes. The next court date was set for 12 October.
Police previously said CCTV footage showed him entering a condominium in Pattaya with the girl in the early hours of 25 June, and leaving that evening carrying a large black suitcase.
In a police interrogation video shared online by Thai media, Carman has said he was acting in self-defence because the girl was threatening him with a knife.
The case put the spotlight on Pattaya, which is popular with foreign tourists for its beaches and nightlife, but also has a reputation for sex tourism.

Senegal job an 'absolute dream' for new boss Vieira
- Published
Patrick Vieira says it is "an honour" to become Senegal head coach, with the decision to take the job "one from the heart".
The 50-year-old was born in the West African nation but subsequently represented France as a player, winning the 1998 World Cup and the 2000 European Championship with Les Bleus.
The former Arsenal midfielder spoke of his "immense pride" to begin his first international job, following stints with New York City, Nice, Crystal Palace, Strasbourg and Genoa, at his unveiling by the Teranga Lions on Friday.
"Being head coach of the Senegal national team is an absolute dream," he told a news conference in Dakar.
"I was born here, my parents were born here, and it really is a homecoming.
"From the very first meetings I had with the [Senegal football federation] president, I accepted this challenge straight away, because there was also an exceptional generation of players.
"I realise the expectations of the people - all 20 million Senegalese. And I know that with the experience I have, with the determination I have, I'll be able to see this project through."
- Vieira named new Senegal head coach 
  - Published18 August
Taking over after the dismissal of Pape Thiaw, Vieira inherits a Senegal side which exited the 2026 World Cup in dramatic fashion in the last 32, throwing away a 2-0 lead after 85 minutes against Belgium before losing 3-2 following extra time.
Before that the Teranga Lions claimed the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) title with a 1-0 extra-time win over Morocco in January.
However, the ultimate destination of the trophy will be decided by the Court of Arbitration for Sport after a walk-off by some Senegal players and staff protesting against a penalty decision in the final resulted in the trophy being handed to the North African hosts instead in March.
"Today, Senegal is among the major nations in world football," Vieira said.
"Senegal's objectives aren't what they were 10 or 15 years ago. On the back of its recent results, Senegal has moved forward, has reached new levels.
"The demand for results has also stepped up. We need to lay solid foundations."
Vieira plans to build a side with "a very precise structure" which can play with "intensity and aggression".
"What matters to me isn't starting again from scratch," he added.
"It's about respecting what the federation has put in place over the last few years and building the next stage, opening a new chapter.
"A new chapter meaning my job isn't to tear everything down, it isn't to throw everything out of the window.
"It's about keeping this team's strength: its identity, its unity, its ability to suffer together.
"To make this project work, I'll need the whole nation united. I'll work heart and soul to restore the team's pride."
Starting with two away trips
Vieira has been thrust straight into competitive action in qualifiers for the 2027 Afcon with two fixtures in this international window, two more in November and the final two rounds in March 2027.
His stint in charge was due to begin with a home match against Mozambique on Friday, 25 September but the fixture has been reversed as Dakar is in the midst of preparations for the 2026 Youth Olympic Games.
"Of course, I'd have preferred to play the first match here in Dakar but unfortunately, with the federation, we all felt the best decision was to postpone the match and go and play in Mozambique," Vieira explained.
"Those are difficulties we're going to accept and deal with."
Senegal will be without several notable names for the trip to Maputo and the subsequent away game against Ethiopia on 29 September.
Long-time number one Edouard Mendy, 34, has retired from Teranga Lions duty and Vieira said talismanic forward Sadio Mane will be absent with "a bit of a physical issue".
Despite previous speculation that Mane, also 34, could follow Mendy into retirement, Vieira said the former Liverpool and Bayern Munich man will "surely" be part of his next selection, fitness permitting.
Right-back Krepin Diatta has been left out because he is currently without a club, while forward Ismaila Sarr, who is yet to feature for Crystal Palace this season because of transfer speculation and a groin injury, is also absent.
'No doubt' about his managerial ability
Vieira's career as a player was trophy-laden but he has found the same kind of success hard to come by as a manager.
He departed Palace in March 2023 with a record of 22 wins from 74 games in all competitions and, after a season at Strasbourg, has been out of work since being sacked by Genoa in November last year with the Italian club bottom of the table.
He had guided them to safety in Serie A in the 2024-25 campaign but was then dismissed after six defeats in nine league games at the start of last season.
"When you talk about my coaching career, or a certain amount of experience, I've always been someone who stays positive," Vieira said.
"That means you learn, and there are always positive things to take from it. I'm a better coach today than I was in my last spell at Genoa, because that experience helped me grow and made me realise certain things.
"Given the experience I have as a manager, I've got no doubt about my ability to meet the expectations of fans."
Vieira was warmly received when he arrived in Dakar on Thursday evening, with video clips posted on social media showing him holding a Senegal flag aloft while shaking hands with a throng of fans gathered at the capital's airport.
"I couldn't have been given a warmer welcome. I saw the supporters' enthusiasm and I thank them for it.
"Taking charge of this national team isn't just a new stage in my career - it's coming back home."

Markets regulator SEBI has greenlit the proposed listing of audio OTT startup Kuku Technologies months after it filed its draft IPO documents confidentially. As per its latest update, it had issued its observation letter for Kuku’s offer documents last Friday (September 11). In SEBI parlance, the observation letter signals the regulator has given its go-ahead to a company to proceed with its public issue. Kuku filed its confidential DRHP with the SEBI in June. Kuku plans to deploy the capital to upgrade its tech, AI infrastructure, content production and fuel geographic expansion. Founded in 2018 by Lal Chand Bisu, Vikas Goyal and Vinod Meena, Kuku offers audiobooks, podcasts, and original audio shows via its Kuku FM brand, while also operating microdrama platform Kuku TV and microlearning platform Guru. The startup’s content library spans more than 20,000 titles across seven languages and multiple genres including drama, finance, and well-being. It claims to have more than 1 Cr listeners and creators on its platform and 400 Mn app downloads across its portfolio. Kuku has raised over $156 Mn to date from the likes of Fundamentum Partnership, Krafton, Vertex Ventures, IFC, 3one4 Capital, among others. Kuku competes with the likes of Pocket FM, Flick TV, ReelSaga and Miniplix, as well as OTT majors like Amazon, JioHotstar and Zee5, in this segment.

An Etihad Airways flight from Delhi to Abu Dhabi was cancelled late on Saturday evening due to a technical issue with a Boeing 787 aircraft, leaving around 200 passengers stranded. A number of passengers who had booked tickets for the flight EY217 from Delhi to Abu Dhabi told PTI that the flight was scheduled to depart at 9:15 pm. All passengers were asked to deboard the aircraft, with the crew telling them that there was a technical issue with the aircraft. After a few hours, the airline made an announcement that the flight had been cancelled. The fact that the passengers had already boarded does not by itself remove the cancellation protections guaranteed to them. As per the DGCA, a 'cancellation' of a flight means non-operation of a flight that was previously planned and had at least one passenger reserved on it. Thus, despite passengers having boarded the aircraft, it still qualifies as a cancellation since Eithad did not operate the flight. Thus the airline is technically required to provide passengers with an acceptable alternate flight or compensation along with a full refund. For an international flight that has a block time of 2+ hours, the compensation guideline is ₹10,000 OR the booked one-way basic fare + airline fuel charge, whichever is lower. Airlines are also required to provide passengers who had reported for the original flight with meals/refreshments and, where necessary, hotel accommodation including transfers. DGCA says that for a foreign carrier (Etihad in this case), the compensation has to be as per its country of origin or the corresponding prescribed amounts by the DGCA. However, airlines are exempted from providing compensations if the reason for cancellation is beyond their control. This can happen in the case of natural disasters, ATC issues, strikes, government orders, security risks etc. However, Etihad has just said technical error. As per a PTI report, specific details about what the technical issue was could not be ascertained. If the issue arises from manufacturing defects or sabotage, this can potentially be treated as an issue beyond Etihad's control. However, Etihad's current Conditions of Carriage do state that it does not override applicable law in a country and its India-specific page also shows DGCA-prescribed compensation amounts depending on flight duration. While the refund amount is sent to the original source using which the ticket was bought in the first place, the compensation amount, which is a separate component, is paid by cash, bank transfer, or a travel voucher if the passenger agrees. Passengers should note that an airline cannot force them to accept a travel voucher. It always creates apprehension because the sight is somewhat gory, but a nosebleed, in general, isn’t a cause for major concern. Occurring mostly in the under 10s and the over 45s, nosebleeds are very common: about 60% of the population is estimated to experience one in their lifetime. They can occur in one or both nostrils, but usually affect one. The medical term for a nosebleed is epistaxis.
How do they occur?
Our noses are lined with a moist, delicate tissue, the nasal mucosa. This lining cleans the air that we breathe in, and also warms and moistens the air. The mucosa is made of many tiny blood vessels, lying to close to the surface. These blood vessels can easily be irritated, injured and broken. When they break, they cause a nosebleed.
There are two types of nosebleeds: anterior and posterior. An anterior nosebleed, which is the most common type, starts at the front of the nose. These types of nosebleeds can mostly be treated at home. A posterior nosebleed takes place place deep at the back the nose, may cause heavier bleeding and could result in blood going down the back of the throat. This type of nosebleed requires medical attention.
Why do they occur?
Common causes include the inside of the nose becoming dry, usually due to a change in temperature, picking the nose, or blowing the nose too hard.
When the air is very dry, it causes the nasal mucosa, which is meant to be moist, to dry out, making it prone to crusting and bleeding. Dry air can occur in hot places with low humidity, areas of high altitude and in air-conditioned or heated spaces. People with upper respiratory infections, sinus infections, allergies or other ailments such as rhinitis may also sneeze, cough or blow their nose frequently, making them more prone to bleeds. The frequent use of medications such as antihistamines, nasal sprays or blood thinners, could also make people vulnerable to nosebleeds, as could breathing in strong fumes.
Nosebleeds can also occur due to injuries to the nose, the insertion of objects into the nose, a deviated septum, recreational drug use as well as less common causes such as having blood disorders, alcohol use, nasal polyps or tumours.
Being pregnant may also increase the chances of nosebleeds.
When to see a doctor
In general, nosebleeds aren’t serious and can be treated at home. In some circumstances, however, it is best to consult a medical professional. You should see a doctor if: the nosebleed has followed an injury or accident; if there is heavy bleeding or the bleeding lasts longer than 30 minutes; blood has been swallowed; if there is a feeling of weakness, dizziness, lightheadedness or if you have breathing difficulties, chest pain or a rapid heart rate. A doctor should also be consulted if the person with the nosebleed has other health issues such as a bleeding disorder, or high blood pressure, or if the person is a child under two years old.
How to stop a nosebleed
To stop a nosebleed, there are some first-aid measures that can be taken:
- Sit upright so the head is above the level of the heart, lean forward slightly
- Breathe through the mouth and gently blow the nose to clear it
- Use the thumb and index finger to pinch the both nostrils shut. Do this for 10 minutes.
- Use an icepack on the bridge of the nose at the same time as the pinching
- Check in 10 minutes, and if the bleeding has not stopped, repeat the pinching for another 10 minutes
- Once the bleeding has stopped, lean forward and clean the nose with lukewarm water
- See a doctor immediately if the bleeding does not stop in 30 minutes
Preventing nosebleeds
Using a humidifier in the house especially in dry air conditions, trimming children’s fingernails, managing allergies, using a nasal saline spray or petroleum jelly to keep the inner lining of the nose moist and avoiding smoke exposure can all help prevent nosebleeds.
