In March this year, the American College of Cardiology (ACC) and the American Heart Association (AHA), both globally recognised premier organisations in cardiovascular medicine, handed down their newest dyslipidemia guideline, and gave universal Lipoprotein(a) screening in every adult a ‘Class I’ recommendation -- the strongest tier there is. The High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein (hsCRP) test got a lighter endorsement: checked selectively, alongside coronary calcium scoring, to sharpen risk estimates when they’re uncertain. These two long-debated biomarkers, were both freshly blessed by the field’s governing societies.
Then arrived the irony. On July 31, pharma major Novo Nordisk’s ziltivekimab — a drug built to block the inflammatory pathway behind elevated C-Reactive Protein (CRP) — fully hit its target in a Phase 3 clinical trial and still didn’t move the needle on heart attacks or strokes. Five weeks later, pelacarsenm, a drug that lowers high levels of Lp(a) failed the same way. Within six months of the guideline telling every clinician to start checking these numbers, the two flagship drugs built to act on them came up empty.
It’s a familiar shape for cardiology. Heart disease mortality fell almost every year through the back half of the last century — statins, blood pressure control, smoking cessation, better acute care — and that decline has visibly slowed this past decade, even as the drug arsenal has never been more sophisticated. LDL (’bad cholesterol’) is already driven remarkably low in anyone on a serious statin; medicine needed a new lever, and reached for the two candidates the guidelines had just endorsed. Neither has delivered yet.
What actually happened
On September 4, Novartis announced pelacarsen missed the primary endpoint of Lp(a)HORIZON, the first cardiovascular outcomes trial ever run for a drug built to lower lipoprotein(a). Pelacarsen is an antisense drug — a short, lab-made strand of genetic material injected monthly, designed to intercept the liver’s instructions for building Lp(a) before it’s ever made, rather than mopping up what’s already circulating. In 8,323 patients with established heart disease, it cut Lp(a) by roughly 80%. And yet, there was no reduction in heart attacks or stroke.
What we were taught
Lp(a) was drilled into me in medical school as one of the ‘unfair’ risk factors — a number you’re essentially born with, indifferent to diet or willpower, and loaded disproportionately onto South Asian patients, who as a population carry some of the highest mean Lp(a) levels of any group studied. It helped explain a pattern every cardiology rotation eventually shows you: South Asian patients with premature, multi-vessel disease and normal LDL numbers. That teaching isn’t wrong, and this trial doesn’t overturn it — Lp(a) is a real, heritable, biologically active risk factor. What it disputes is narrower: whether lowering it, this late and this fast, changes what happens next.
What Lp(a) actually is
Here’s the plain version of how a heart attack builds. LDL particles, commonly known as ‘bad cholesterol’ work their way into the artery wall and get stuck there. Once trapped, immune cells chemically alter them and swallow them up, ballooning into fat-filled ‘foam cells.’ Over years, those dying cells pile up into a fatty core, and the artery seals it off with a cap of scar-like tissue. When that cap eventually cracks or wears thin, a blood clot forms on top of it — that’s the heart attack.
Statins, ezetimibe, and the newer PCSK9-inhibitor injections all lower LDL through different mechanisms, but the trial data lines up the same way every time: about a 22% drop in heart attacks and strokes for every 39-point drop in LDL, no matter how you get there.
Lp(a) is an LDL particle with one extra piece stuck to it — a protein called apolipoprotein(a), built from the same molecular parts as the protein your body uses to break up blood clots. But it’s a decoy, not a copy: it fits into the same docking spots on a forming clot, without carrying the working part that actually gets activated into a clot-dissolving enzyme. So instead of helping to break clots down, it crowds out the real thing and makes clots a little harder to clear. That’s what makes Lp(a) different from LDL: it builds plaque the same way LDL does, but it also nudges the body toward clotting rather than away from it. And unlike LDL, your Lp(a) level is almost entirely set by your genes at birth — diet, exercise, and statins barely move it.
Why did the trial fail?
A floor effect: Mean background LDL in the trial was 66 mg/dL as most patients were already on aggressive therapy. Whatever risk Lp(a) adds on top of that may be smaller than older, less-treated cohorts suggested, offering little room for an 80% reduction to matter.
Too late in the game: Every patient entered with 50-plus years of Lp(a) exposure already built into their arteries. Lowering the level for three or four years in someone’s sixties, after a cardiac event, may be too late to undo a lifetime of exposure the genetic data actually measured.
This isn’t cardiology’s first time at this wall. The CANTOS trial suggested a decade ago that quieting the immune system could work, independent of cholesterol reduction. Hitting the biomarkers still doesn’t seem to be enough: Lp(a) may just be writing the newest chapter of the same story.
Back to basics
The interventions with the deepest trial evidence are still the boring ones: eat well, move, don’t smoke, stay lean. LDL, blood pressure, glucose, and tobacco remain the pillars with decades of reproducible data behind them.
Lp(a) will likely still matter — as a flag for who needs those basics enforced hardest, and maybe eventually as a target that is treated decades earlier than this trial tried. But for now, the fanciest number on the panel failed its biggest test, and the oldest advice in medicine didn’t.
No antisense drug, no anti-inflammatory antibody, has found a way around the same wall. In Greek mythology, Icarus didn’t fall because he was foolish — he flew exactly as high as anyone reasonably could, and the sun turned out to be closer than he’d been told. Despite everything medicine can now measure, alter and silence, the quest for a healthy long life perhaps rests on the same principles it has rested on for centuries: eat well, move well, sleep well.
(Dr. Dinesh Arab is director, interventional and structural cardiology, AdventHealth Daytona Beach and clinical assistant professor of medicine, Florida State University. dinarab@yahoo.com)

Football Sundays are officially back, and my recipe for easy slow-cooker Buffalo chicken dip is guaranteed to be the MVP at any party.
Practically every time I entertain friends — be it for game day, the Super Bowl, or any party — I'm always asked if I'll be making my famous Buffalo chicken dip.
Over the years, I've tweaked recipes I've seen online to come up with the easiest, most crowd-pleasing dip. It requires only six main ingredients, plus seasonings you'll probably already have in your pantry.
Here's how to make my easy slow-cooker Buffalo chicken dip.
My recipe for slow-cooker Buffalo chicken dip requires only six main ingredients.
To make the dip, which feeds about 10 people, you'll need:
- A 6-quart slow cooker or Crock-Pot
- A rotisserie chicken (or 1 lb of cooked chicken)
- 12 fluid ounces Frank's RedHot Buffalo sauce
- ½ cup ranch dressing
- 16-ounce cream cheese
- 1 cup shredded cheddar cheese
- 1 cup shredded mozzarella cheese
- Salt, pepper, garlic powder
I always start by separating the breasts from the rotisserie chicken and removing the skin.
I like to use rotisserie chicken for this recipe because it's often easier and cheaper than buying chicken breasts and boiling them myself. I find that the rotisserie chicken also packs much more flavor, and saves me from having to do any actual cooking.
When it comes to game-day recipes, easiest is usually best.
Then I shred the rotisserie chicken.
I usually do this step by hand, but you can also use two forks to shred your chicken. By the end, you should have about 3 cups of shredded rotisserie chicken.
I put the cream cheese in the slow cooker and cut it into cubes with a knife.
This helps ensure the cream cheese melts evenly and is well-distributed throughout the dip.
You can use full-fat or low-fat cream cheese for this dip, depending on your preference — I've had success using both.
I then add the rotisserie chicken to the slow cooker and season it.
I usually eyeball how much seasoning I use, but typically go for about a tablespoon of garlic powder, a tablespoon of salt, and a few dashes of pepper.
I add the two types of cheese.
I use 1 cup of shredded, low-moisture mozzarella cheese and 1 cup of shredded sharp-cheddar cheese.
Next, my wet ingredients go on top.
I use a whole 12-ounce bottle of Frank's RedHot Buffalo sauce, but you can use whichever brand of Buffalo sauce you prefer. I then add ½ cup of ranch dressing on top.
I mix the ingredients with a wooden spoon until everything is evenly distributed.
You don't need to overmix it — as the dip cooks, the ingredients will melt and combine.
Scoop along the sides to make sure nothing is sticking to the walls, put the lid on the slow cooker, and walk away. It's that easy.
I heat the dip on high for 1 to 2 hours, or on low for 3 hours.
I stir the dip with a wooden spoon a couple of times while it's cooking to prevent any spots from burning on the side and to help it cook evenly.
The dip should be smooth and slightly bubbling when it's done, with all the cream cheese and cheeses fully melted and combined.
I serve the finished Buffalo chicken dip with tortilla chips.
Whether you're making it for the Super Bowl, a last-minute party, or an easy weeknight snack, this six-ingredient slow-cooker Buffalo chicken dip shows that crowd-pleasing food doesn't have to be complicated.
Simply toss everything in, let it cook, and you'll end up with a creamy, spicy dip that disappears almost as fast as it comes together.

Herpetologists first discovered in 1933 that rattlesnakes are immune to their own venom. Native to the Americas, rattlesnakes are pit vipers, a family of vipers with a heat-sensing pit organ between each nostril and eye.
Venom resistance in snakes comes in two forms: either the targets in their bodies have evolved such that the venom doesn’t attack them, like in cobras, or they possess specific molecules in their bloodstream that serve as “toxin sponges”, like in vipers, Sean B. Carroll, chair of biology at the University of Maryland, U.S., said.
In 1972, Japanese researchers discovered the first example of a so-called toxin sponge — a serum protein dubbed Fetuin-A — from Okinawa habu (Protobothrops flavoviridis), a pit viper endemic to the Ryukyu Islands. Fetuin-A could inhibit metalloproteinases, a class of venom toxins that could cause haemorrhage, damage tissue, and disrupt the coagulation system.
Metalloproteinases are the most abundant toxin family in rattlesnake venoms, and researchers have studied metalloproteinase inhibitors such as Fetuin-A in great detail. However, only recently did they discover that Fetuin-A belongs to a larger family of FETUA proteins.
In a 2022 paper, Dr. Carroll and his team identified four FETUA proteins from the western diamondback rattlesnake (Crotalus atrox).
Curiously, understanding the principles of venom resistance from C. atrox led the researchers to leverage these antitoxins, which had evolved over millions of years, for human benefit.
In a new study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team at Maryland has shown that specific combinations of C. atrox FETUA proteins can fully neutralise rattlesnake venom lethality in mice, with roughly 10-times the potency of commercial antivenom.
‘String of surprises’
On discovering metalloproteinase-inhibiting FETUA-2, 3, 4, and 5 proteins from C. atrox, the research team studied their antivenom potency. By injecting various protein combinations preincubated with C. atrox venom into experimental mice, they found that some combinations successfully blocked haemorrhaging, while some even staved off death.
“Rattlesnake venoms have 10-15 different kinds of toxins,” Dr. Carroll said. “So it was entirely unexpected that just blocking metalloproteinases would block the lethality of the venom.”
The test results that followed were a “string of surprises”. Encouraged by the success of FETUA proteins against C. atrox venom, the team tried them against the eastern diamondback rattlesnake (Crotalus adamanteus), which proved successful. Then they tested them against two Asian snakes: the Malayan pit viper (Calloselasma rhodostoma) and the Chinese moccasin (Deinagkistrodon acutus). The proteins could protect against those as well.
The team then moved to candidates outside of pit vipers. Of the two true vipers they tested against, the proteins protected significantly against the Sochurek’s saw-scaled viper (Echis carinatus sochureki) — but none against the puff adder (Bitis arietans).
“Our surprises ran out, you could say,” Dr. Carroll said.
According to him, an antivenom needs potency and broad reactivity. And not only could these proteins recognise and neutralise the venom of a spectrum of distant species, when tested against CroFab, a commercial antivenom obtained from animals immunised with four pit viper venoms, including C. atrox, the proteins proved tenfold more potent.
The findings are a “real advance” for antivenom development, according to Kartik Sunagar, an associate professor at the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru; he was not involved in the study. “The paper shows convincingly that a combination of naturally evolved FETUA proteins can fully neutralise rattlesnake venom lethality by inhibiting metalloproteinases alone.”
However, Dr. Sunagar also pointed out that the study did not exactly measure clinical capacity.
“Every efficacy experiment premixed venom and inhibitor before injection,” he said. “So the study measures neutralising capacity, not treatment of an animal already envenomed, which is the clinically relevant scenario.”
Next-generation antivenom
According to Dr. Carroll, unlike lab-made compounds, FETUA proteins have been tested in nature.
“Rattlesnakes have evolved these proteins for 50 million years, with remarkable specificity and potency to inhibit their own venom, which gives me the sense that it is worth exploring,” he said.
Manufacturability and purity are added advantages, he added: “We can make recombinant FETUA proteins in the lab in unlimited quantities — whereas traditional antivenom requires animals to be immunised, and then the obtained antibodies have to be purified.”
Dr. Sunagar also shared the view that the recombinant and defined nature of FETUA proteins will help sidestep the low purity of animal-derived products.
While the study showed that these proteins can protect experimental mice from venom lethality, toxins other than metalloproteinases will have physiological effects on humans, Dr Carroll said: “What we don’t know is what else we will have to use in conjunction with these proteins to make an antivenom” for humans.
“FETUAs do nothing for the neurotoxins that dominate many medically important venoms,” Dr. Sunagar said. “The honest reading is that these proteins form the metalloproteinase-neutralising component of a next-generation antivenom, but it is not yet a standalone therapy.”
Dr. Carroll also said his team has found a new component that could aid human antivenom development, but did not elaborate on ongoing research.
Implications for India
In countries like India, which host both vipers and elapids such as cobras, FETUA proteins alone cannot provide a complete antivenom solution, Dr. Carroll said.
Although the study revealed partial protection against saw-scaled vipers (Echis carinatus sp.), one of India’s ‘Big Four’ and a major cause of death and disability, partial cross-reactivity need not translate into clinical protection, Dr. Sunagar added.
But India’s bigger takeaway is the strategy: “The logical path for India is to identify and test FETUAs from our own vipers rather than relying on rattlesnake versions, and to pair them with agents covering the neurotoxic elapids the FETUAs cannot touch,” according to Dr. Sunagar.
Nikhil Sreekandan is an independent journalist.

The closures in Assam and Kerala are linked to Janmotsav of Srimanta Sankardeva and Sree Narayana Guru Samadhi Day, respectively.
Banks will remain closed in Assam and Kerala on Monday, September 21, according to the state-wise bank holiday calendar. Customers planning to visit a branch tomorrow (September 21) should check whether their local bank is observing the regional holiday.
The closures in Assam and Kerala are linked to Janmotsav of Srimanta Sankardeva and Sree Narayana Guru Samadhi Day, respectively.

Bank branches in other states will remain open on September 21, according to the available state-wise holiday lists.
Why are banks closed on September 21?
In Assam, banks will be closed for Janmotsav of Srimanta Sankardeva. In Kerala, the holiday is observed for Sree Narayana Guru Samadhi Day. Both are listed as regional holidays for September 21.
Srimanta Sankardeva Janmotsav in Assam
Srimanta Sankardeva Janmotsav is primarily observed in Assam to mark the birth anniversary of saint, poet, social reformer and Vaishnavite sage Srimanta Sankardeva.

Alexis Ohanian says he and Serena Williams have one rule for letting their daughters chart their own paths.
"The one rule in the house is we don't care what you want to do when you grow up, as long as you do your best at it and you're doing something useful," Ohanian told E! News on Saturday at Athlos LDN26, the inaugural London edition of the women's professional track-and-field series he founded.
Ohanian said he was on "dad duty" supervising their eldest daughter, Olympia, who was "working the event."
"We've got her interviewing a few of the ladies who are on their way in," the Reddit cofounder and venture capitalist said.
On the other hand, he said Williams "drew the short straw" and was watching over their youngest daughter, Adira.
Ohanian said the couple also tries to keep their daughters grounded as they grow up around elite athletes and attend high-profile events.
"We both go out of our way to normalize a lot of this stuff," Ohanian said.
That same idea shapes how Ohanian thinks about women's sports and the example he wants to set for his daughters. While he sees women athletes as inspirational role models, he said that shouldn't be the reason they are celebrated.
"In a way, sort of ironically, if the only thing that I focus on and talk about is the sort of normalcy of celebrating greatness, and they just happen to be women, I feel like it actually helps us get a little closer to the end goal that we all want," he said.
Ohanian has previously spoken about giving his daughters room to explore their interests.
In a July 2023 interview with People, he said he and Williams enjoyed watching Olympia try different hobbies.
"Like any parent, we just want her to have fun, and we're fortunate enough to be able to expose her to anything she could be interested in. It's already been an interesting journey, seeing the stuff she's into. We don't want to limit that," he said.
Williams has also spoken about how she has no interest in grooming her daughter to be a tennis star.
"I would hate her to have to deal with comparisons or expectations. It's so much work, and I've given up so much. I don't regret it, but it's like 'Sliding Doors': Go through a different door and lead a different life. I'd like her to have a normal life. I didn't have that," Williams told Vogue in February 2018.
Other celebrities have also shared the values and expectations they hope to instill in their children.
Guy Fieri has said his children must earn two college degrees before they receive an inheritance. Matthew McConaughey's mother, Kay, has said her sons had to follow her rules while they lived under her roof, which helped them become "loving and productive" men.

'I don't even know if my parents are alive' - the war heroes jailed 25 years ago
- Published
Hanna Petros Solomon breaks down in tears as she recalls how she and her siblings effectively became orphans 25 years ago when their father was arrested in Eritrea and jailed without trial. Their mother was subsequently detained - and no-one has heard from either of them - or of them - since.
"He had a towel on his shoulders like a sportsman," she tells the BBC about the last time she saw her father when she was 10 years old, and he had gone out for a jog.
"He used to work out every morning."
Her parents met when they both fought in the long liberation war that saw Eritrea gain independence from Ethiopia in 1993.
Her father Petros Solomon had been one of the senior leaders during the war and is regarded by many as a national hero for his critical role.
After independence, he had served as defence minister, then foreign minister and had been heading the fisheries ministry when his troubles began.
That was in May 2001 when he and 14 other high-profile politicians signed an open letter to President Isaias Afewerki calling for the implementation of a constitution that was ratified after independence and demanding national elections. They became known as the G-15.
Isaias, the leader of the Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF) which had fought against Ethiopia, did not take the criticism well.
Unbeknown to Hanna, her father had been dismissed as a minister, though he still went out early to get some exercise each day.
It was not until a few days after 9/11 - when the world was distracted by the al-Qaeda attacks on the US - that the country was to discover the full extent of Isais's displeasure in what became a watershed moment in Eritrea's history.
In the early hours of 18 September, the security forces positioned themselves outside the homes of 11 senior government officials in the capital, Asmara, on the president's orders.
Petros was picked up by security agents as he left in his tracksuit.
The family had no idea what had happened to him. Hanna and her three siblings went to stay with their paternal grandmother as their mother, Aster Yohannes, was away studying in the US.
It was only some days after Petros had disappeared that things became clearer, says Hanna about the painful memories.
"My classmates told me that my father sold out his country.
"That is when I understood how serious the situation was, and how people framed my dad and his colleagues who fought for the independence of their country. I was hurt."
In the US, Aster was shell-shocked by what had happened - and was in a very bad way. She asked government officials if they could issue the children with passports - but they refused, telling her to come home.
After agonising about the situation for two years and reportedly receiving assurances from government officials, she packed her bags to return.
Hanna and her siblings desperately wanted her back - but they were also worried.
"I told her on the phone: 'What if they arrest you?'" Hanna remembers.
"She insisted nothing would happen to her, saying: 'I haven't done anything wrong, and am only coming to raise my children.'"
Hanna says she learned later that President Isaias himself had promised Aster that she would be safe. But while the family waited at Asmara International Airport on 11 December 2003, she failed to emerge through arrivals with the other passengers.
Their hopes began to wilt along with the flowers they had brought: "It was a long, long wait. Eventually we gave up and went back home.
"First we called to the US, friends and relatives told us they saw her off at the airport."
Then ominously an official called from the airport asking Aster to collect her luggage. That is when they realised she had arrived in the country but would not be coming home.
All pleas and requests for information fell on deaf ears in the months that followed. Instead Hanna's grandmother was warned by authorities to stop inquiring.
The family later heard that Aster was being held in the infamous jail known as Karshelli in the heart of Asmara.
Hanna's father is believed to be detained, with the others arrested on 18 and 19 September 2001, in the remote, hostile and highly secretive prison known as Ela-Ero, located in eastern lowlands north-east of Asmara. Accused of treason, none of them has ever been brought to trial or allowed to see their relatives.
At around the same time, the government also shut down all the fledgling independent newspapers and detained their editors and journalists - also believed to be imprisoned in Ela-Ero.
The Eritrean government - including its embassy in the UK - has not responded to the BBC's request for comment regarding the whereabouts of the prisoners or whether or not they are alive.
Hanna, like many thousands of young Eritreans fleeing conscription and in search of better opportunities, left the country - travelling secretively over the border without a passport.
Now 35 years old, she is married and lives in the US, working as a trauma specialist - but still feels traumatised herself by how she lost her parents.
As she stares at old pictures of her parents, she worries her memories will fade of the happy times before their arrest - the laughter, the family gatherings, the birthday parties: "My dad always wanted to gather people in the house, they were good days."
She also hankers after her mother's "unmatched" egg and potato sandwiches.
On trips down to the coast when her father was the minister of fisheries, Hanna remembers him organising singing competitions in the car: "He would ask us to sing one by one and whoever won would get a present."
One of his favourite songs included the lyrics: "I had a sweater, a blue sweater, that my sister took" - which reminded him of his sister who was also a freedom fighter and had been killed during the war.
She also has memories of her mother loving music - playing and singing hits by Abba, Dolly Parton and Whitney Houston.
Until her father's arrest, Hanna remembers September as being full of hope with its three big Orthodox Christian festivals, including the Geez New Year. Now the month brings her no joy.
Ibrahim Sherifo knows exactly how she feels. Both his parents, who were senior members of the ruling People's Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ), were among the G-15 people arrested 25 years ago.
He was 13 years old at the time
"For me 18 September 2001 is a dark day, but not only for me, it is a dark day for Eritrea and its people, because it is the day when law and democracy was detained," he tells the BBC.
He is now 38 and living in exile in the Netherlands, where he was granted asylum, and is pursuing an MA in political science - following in his father's footsteps.
His dad Mahmoud Ahmed Sherifo was the local government minister and de facto deputy president before his detention.
Ibrahim was with his mother, Aster Fissehatsion, staying with her sister when he remembers security agents knocking on the door early in the morning and taking her away in her pyjamas.
Worried about his father, Ibrahim immediately ran to his nearby house but was told he had already been picked up when he had gone out for exercise.
Both Hanna and Ibrahim say they are forever grateful to the friends and family who offered them care and supported them as they grew up without their parents, despite the risks.
They are also proud of what their parents stood for and daring to call for reforms.
"They had conscience and couldn't observe idly while what they fought for what had been hijacked by Isaias and his coterie," says Ibrahim.
"As a family, we should be informed whether they are alive or not," he adds, accusing the government of wanting to erase all memory of the political prisoners.
Hanna also wants the plight of the many others whose relatives have disappeared over the years to be heard too.
Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down"
Human rights groups, including the UN, consider the G-15 prisoners of conscience and have been calling for their release.
President Isaias, now 80, has still not implemented the country's first constitution - approved in 1997 - and remains in power without ever holding an election.
Hanna recalls that on the eve of her father's disappearance, she had a "bad feeling" - and had crept into his bed and tied his legs to her own with string while he slept.
"In the morning he woke up to find he was tied up and to release himself he pulled my legs and I woke up. I begged him not to leave but he assured me that he would return [after his run]."
Describing the years of sorrow since, she says it is like living in the deep sea.
"Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down.
"Sometimes you lose hope and you are out of breath."
Asked what she would say if she could get a message to her parents, she replies: "Don't worry about us.
"Like you survived the struggle through sheer steadfastness, we hope you can pull through this too and return to us."

Russia's first wartime parliamentary election shows Kremlin dominance all but assured
The election was virtually devoid of opposition to President Putin's policies.
Russia's first wartime parliamentary election was due to end Sunday, virtually devoid of opposition to President Vladimir Putin's policies and all but certain to cement the Kremlin’s dominance. The last day of the election came as Ukrainian forces fired more than 1,000 drones at Russia overnight, including hundreds that were launched toward Moscow.
The vote began Friday, and authorities encouraged online balloting to boost turnout among its 111 million eligible voters.
For the first time, the election included residents of four Ukrainian regions that Moscow illegally annexed after the war began but still doesn’t fully control. Voting is also taking place in Crimea, the Black Sea peninsula that was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014.
Authorities in Kyiv denounced the voting in the Russian-held areas as illegal and urged foreign governments not to recognize the result. The European Union on Friday called the action a “blatant violation of international law.”
The Kremlin wants the parliamentary election — the first since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — to showcase popular support for the war and legitimize its action. It has sought to avoid political risks by stamping out any dissent.
A massive state media campaign and tight control over the election in the absence of genuine opposition all but assure the Kremlin will keep tight control of Russian politics amid mounting economic costs and increasing Ukrainian drone attacks deep inside the country.
Voters cast two separate ballots, filling half of the Duma’s 450 seats by selecting political parties listed on the ballot. The rest are contested in single-seat constituencies, with voters choosing individual candidates.
Preliminary results are expected within hours of voting ending in the country’s west.
The main Kremlin party, United Russia, is widely expected to retain its overwhelming control of the lower house, the State Duma. Several smaller parties of the “systemic opposition” that vote in sync with Putin's views on all key issues also are expected to maintain their presence.
The liberal Yabloko party, the only registered political entity that dared to publicly criticize the war, was removed from the ballot last month by Russia’s Supreme Court, and only has a few dozen candidates in the single-constituency races. Additionally, some anti-war politicians were imprisoned or forced to flee abroad ahead of the campaign.
Yabloko and the Communist Party, which has criticized some aspects of government policy but carefully avoided any criticism of Putin, said many of their observers were turned away from polling stations.
Russia didn’t invite observers from the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe, with the Russian Foreign Ministry accusing the body of “double standards” for its criticism of Russia. OSCE Parliamentary Assembly President Pere Joan Pons said that the decision was a breach of Russia’s commitments as a member state of the organization.
Yabloko reported that one of its observers lost consciousness while being arrested by police at a St. Petersburg polling station on Saturday, after officials accused him of trying to “disrupt the elections” and called police.
The parties reported violations including sealed ballot boxes being opened, doors to polling stations not being secured overnight, and a refusal to issue paper ballots. The claims could not be independently verified.
At one polling station in the Russian-held part of the Donetsk region, voters dropped their ballots in a box as an armed Russian soldier stood nearby and watched.
Ella Pamfilova, head of Russia’s Central Election Commission, said Sunday that the electronic voting system in Moscow was targeted by cyberattacks. She blamed one of the “systemic parties” — meaning one of those taking part in the vote, without specifying which one.
SotaVision, an independent Russian news outlet, said Sunday that voters were reporting glitches in the electronic registry systems at polling stations across Moscow. People were not issued paper ballots and instead were asked to vote via an electronic terminal, the outlet said on Telegram.
Leonid Volkov, a close associate of the late Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny, suggested the supposed breakdown of the system used to issue paper ballots in Moscow may have been deliberate, aimed at pushing voters toward electronic voting.
“Demand a paper ballot!” he wrote on X on Sunday.
Lines formed outside polling stations as many voters refused to vote electronically.
Having urged supporters to spoil party-list ballots, Yabloko party leader Nikolai Rybakov cast a ballot in St. Petersburg on Sunday, covered in bright green writing declaring “For freedom," “For peace,” and “Yabloko.”
Russia’s exiled opposition, including the widow of Alexei Navalny, Yulia Navalnaya, called on anti-war Russians to cast their votes at noon on Sunday.
Thousands of Russians living in Armenia took part in the vote, lining up outside the Russian Embassy in the capital, Yerevan. Some of them joined the “Noon for a Peaceful Russia” anti-war demonstration, holding anti-war and anti-Putin posters.
Mark Podberezin, a journalist, said members of the election commission in Yerevan made remarks that felt like “outright intimidation.” He said he had heard comments "along the lines of, ‘You’ll have to return to Russia sooner or later, keep that in mind.’”
Lidiya Klimenko said she did not think her vote would have any real impact. The most useful thing to do, she said, was “to see other people who are also against the war, to be together in a shared cause.”
In Germany, voters cast their ballots at the Russian Embassy in Berlin. Andrei Pivovarov, a dissident and former head of the Open Russia group, addressed a protest gathered outside the building.
The election's last day came against a backdrop of a major wave of Ukrainian attacks. Russia’s Defense Ministry said Sunday that its forces shot down a total of 1,110 Ukrainian drones across Russia, as well as over the annexed Crimea and the Black Sea.
Two people were killed and 20 wounded across the wider Moscow region, local Gov. Andrei Vorobyov said.
The election follows a summer of Ukraine’s long-range drone strikes on oil refineries that triggered a widespread fuel crisis. Warehouses belonging to online retailers Wildberries and Ozon also were attacked. Those attacks have exacerbated economic problems and brought the war home for millions.

The city’s Vinayaka Chavithi festivities culminated over the weekend in a mix of colour and chaos, as hundreds of devotees carried idols to the coast for immersion while clean-up crews grappled with the aftermath by Sunday morning.
Processions through the night featured tableaux of mythological figures, folk dance troupes and drummers, drawing large crowds on the streets leading to RK Beach and other immersion places. Families, many with children in tow, gathered at the shore to bid farewell to their idols amid chants and applause, underlining the festival’s continuing pull on the city’s public life.
Immersion points
The Greater Visakhapatnam Municipal Corporation (GVMC) had designated immersion points across the city, including Sagar Nagar, Jodugulapalem, Lumbini Park, Bheemili Beach, the Gosthani river near the Tagarapuvalasa flyover, Mangamaripeta Beach, Annavaram Beach, the IT SEZ beach cutting point, the area opposite the Naval Coastal Battery, Yarada Fishing Jetty and Appikonda Beach. Officials had directed that barricades, lighting, lifeguards, boats, cranes, drinking water and medical teams be stationed at each point, with dedicated routes kept clear for ambulances and fire engines.
Devotees were also asked to avoid using fresh water for immersion, given the city’s water stress, and to confine idol immersion to the designated beach points.
That advisory, however, appeared to have been only partly heeded. By Sunday morning, several stretches of the coast, including Pedda Jalaripeta beach, not all of them official immersion sites, were strewn with idol frames, flowers, plastic bags and other puja waste, forcing sanitation workers to begin large-scale clearance operations soon after sunrise. Discarded straw-and-bamboo frames and remnants of larger community idols lay abandoned on the sand alongside piles of flowers, banana leaves and plastic waste.
Harming marine life
Environmentalists said the scale of the waste pointed to a larger, recurring problem. C.V. Naidu, Head of the Department of Meteorology and Oceanography at Andhra University, said the dumping of plastic and Plaster-of-Paris idols into the sea harmed marine life, with fish ingesting plastic that could eventually enter the human food chain as microplastics. “Plastic carry bags, water bottles and PoP idols should either be banned or their use restricted. Both the government and the public have an equal responsibility to protect the environment. Only clay Ganesha idols should be used,” he said.
With sanitation staff working through the morning to restore the beaches, the contrast between the previous night’s festivity and the visible cost it left behind was, once again, difficult to miss.

Residents of Bengaluru who have witnessed hot and humid weather for the last couple of weeks woke up to a rainy Sunday morning.
According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD) data the city received widespread overnight rainfall with the Kempegowda International Airport (KIA) weather station and HAL Airport station recording 94.2 mm and 66 mm rainfall respectively for a 24-hour period ending 8.30 a.m. on Sunday (September 20, 2026). Bengaluru city recorded 15.9 mm rainfall.
The rainfall also brought down the temperature by a few degrees Celsius. It had been hovering above 30°C for the last couple of weeks.
The maximum temperature in Bengaluru city station dropped to 28.3°C on Sunday compared to 31.2°C the previous day.
The heavy downpour at KIA resulted in one international flight being diverted to Chennai and one domestic flight was delayed by 30 minutes.
“The rest of the operations continued as usual,” airport officials said.
IMD said that there is a low-pressure area over the North Andaman Sea and adjoining areas which has moved west-northwestwards and is located over the North Andaman Sea and adjoining East-Central Bay of Bengal.
It said that the associated cyclonic circulation extends up to 5.8 km above mean sea level.
“The system is likely to move west-northwestwards and gradually intensify, becoming a depression over the East-Central Bay of Bengal on September 21 and a deep depression over the West-Central Bay of Bengal on September 22.
It is likely to continue moving west-northwestwards and reach the West-Central and adjoining Northwest Bay of Bengal, close to the South Odisha–North Andhra Pradesh coast, by the morning of September 23,” IMD said.
IMD officials said under the influence of this weather systemt there would be widespread rainfall across all districts of Karnataka till September 24.
Yellow Alert
“All districts in south interior, north interior and coastal Karnataka will receive widespread rainfall till September 24. Bidar, Kalburgi, Yadgir, Vijayapur, Belagavi, Dharwad, Haveri, Gadag, Shivamogga, Chikkamangaluru, Hassan, Kodagu, Bengaluru, Kolar, Chikkaballpur and Bengaluru South districts will receive heavy rainfall and yellow alert has been declared,” said IMD Scientist C.S. Patil.
The forecast for Bengaluru for the next 24 hours states that there would generally be cloudy skies, light to moderate rain/thundershowers accompanied with gusty wind at speeds of 30-40 Kmph. The maximum and minimum temperature are very likely to be around 32°C and 20°C respectively.

When Gloria Steinem’s plane touched down in Bombay in 1957, she could not have known that her stay in India would become what she later called a “pivotal, life-dividing event [that] made me who I am”.
She was 22, with a degree in government from Smith college and was travelling on a Chester Bowles fellowship.
India was “not only a place I’d always wanted to go, but (also) an escape from a very kind and tempting man to whom I was engaged and knew I shouldn’t marry,” Steinem later wrote. The prospect of marrying Blair Chotzinoff, a pilot from a well-connected New York family, depressed her “enormously because marriage meant the end of life to me”.
Funds were short, so she wangled a free airline ticket in exchange for an article “that I still feel guilty to this day because I never wrote”.
While in London waiting for her Indian visa, she discovered she was pregnant and obtained an illegal abortion – an experience that underpinned her conviction that, without control over reproduction, women could not control their own lives.
Steinem, who died this week at the age of 92, arrived in Delhi with romantic expectations of “ageless beauty and jewelled elephants”. They were quickly displaced. Driving from the airport, she had what she called her “first glimpse of Asian poverty”, seeing people sleeping on pavements and doorsteps.
She lived at Miranda House, one of Delhi University’s leading women’s colleges, immersing herself in student life.
“At night in our rooms we have long sessions and are asked everything: the Christians’ conception of God, the intricacies of western lingerie, the dating system, how much milk the American cow gives,” Steinem wrote.
Steinem’s Indian years have been extensively documented by Rashida Shafiq of Southern Methodist University, who drew on her fellowship reports and other archival material for a recently published PhD thesis.
She adopted the sari as everyday dress, writing: “Saris make one stand straighter and walk more slowly and worry less about time and efficiency.”
India was not entirely unfamiliar territory. Her mother and paternal grandmother had been Theosophists, part of a spiritual movement that drew heavily on Hindu and Buddhist ideas such as karma and reincarnation, and at college Steinem had written a paper on the Communist party of India.
When her fellowship money ran out, she supported herself by writing for Indian newspapers, doing advertising work and taking occasional modelling jobs – including posing in saris.
Wider travel in the country brought some of her most important encounters.
She met Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the former princess and follower of Mahatma Gandhi who became independent India’s first health minister, and spent two hours with Indira Gandhi, whom she described as “shy to uncertainty, gentle and a little whimsical”.
At a Radical Humanist study camp in Mussoorie, followers of the former communist MN Roy debated democracy, individual freedom and political organisation. Steinem later said she learned there that “radical” need not mean violent or extremist, but could mean “going to the root,” and that “the means we choose dictate the ends we achieve”.
But some of her most lasting political education happened on the road.
On a journey from Calcutta to Kerala, Steinem travelled third class in a railway carriage reserved for women, which she later described as “a dormitory on wheels”.
Women settled in with children and food, nursing babies, sharing tiffins and talking. They wanted to know everything about her and conversations ranged across marriage, childbirth, contraception and family life. “Had I been isolated in a car, this talking circle could never have happened,” Steinem wrote later.
Years before American feminist “consciousness-raising” groups brought women together to discover that supposedly private problems were widely shared, Steinem had watched women in India exchange intimate experiences among themselves.
But the experience she regarded as most important came after caste violence erupted in what was then Madras state in 1957.
Steinem joined workers associated with the movement of Vinoba Bhave, a leading disciple of Gandhi, who were walking from village to village trying to counter rumours, discourage revenge and bring people together to talk.
She travelled with little more than “a cup, a comb and the sari I wore”.
In settlements scarred by violence, meetings were held beneath trees and in village courtyards.
“I listened as villagers narrated burnings, murders, thefts and rapes, with fear and trauma needing no translation,” she wrote.
The lesson was to listen before offering solutions. “Ask the people what they want, don’t tell them what they need,” was how Steinem later described it.
She remembered “the ancient and modern magic of groups in which anyone may speak in turn, everyone must listen and consensus is more important than time”.
“If you want to know how people live, you have to go where they live; if you want people to listen to you, you have to listen to them,” she later said. “I believe I learned that in India.”
Steinem returned to the United States in 1958, more than a decade before she became one of the leading figures in the women’s movement.
“I couldn’t integrate into the rest of my life these two very, very crucial years,” she recalled. “It was only after the women’s movement started that links began to be forged.”
She repeatedly connected her later organising methods with India. “The first organising I did was in India, though I didn’t realise it then,” she said.
Her years travelling across America as a feminist activist, she later wrote, were “just a western version of walking in villages”.
And when Ms. magazine, which Steinem co-founded, produced its spring 1972 preview issue, its cover featured an American housewife depicted as the many-armed Hindu goddess Kali, pregnant with her hands clutching a frying pan, duster, telephone, iron and other symbols of the domestic demands placed on women.
Steinem said the image “had come out of my Indian past”.

Trump Is Betting on the Wrong Europe
The far-right parties the White House favors have a foreign-policy agenda that won’t serve American interests.
Donald Trump says he wants a Europe that is more capable of defending itself. But the nationalist-populist movements he is championing there will not advance this agenda and may put Europe at odds with the United States over China.
Earlier this month, the nationalist-populist Alternative for Germany party came just a few seats short of an outright majority in a regional parliament, its best-ever result. This Sunday, Germans will vote in two more regional elections. The ruling Christian Democrats are behind in both races, and the AfD is expected to do well in one. On Wednesday, Chancellor Friedrich Merz canceled his visit to the United Nations General Assembly next week, sparking speculation that he could soon be forced to resign.
U.S. officials are ebullient. Trump greeted the AfD’s recent electoral victory with a triumphant message on Truth Social that finished with “MGGA” (Make Germany Great Again). Richard Grenell, Trump’s former ambassador to Germany and now a presidential envoy, called the result “a huge win and a new day in Germany.”
The Trump administration has consistently embraced Europe’s nationalist-populist parties as ideological partners, and even launched a State Department fund to support MAGA-aligned European groups. It surely sees the AfD’s ascendance as a sign that politics are moving in its direction. But that is true only if Trump’s real goal is a fragmented Europe that accommodates Russian and Chinese power and is unable to punch its weight. Such an outcome would be catastrophic for U.S. interests.
Some people in the administration insist that the idea is not to weaken Europe but to shift the burden for its conventional defense to the Europeans themselves. Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, for example, reject claims that the administration is soft on Russia and say that they are calling instead for greater European self-sufficiency. Colby advocates for what he calls NATO 3.0, in which Europeans would take on the primary responsibility for their conventional defense.
But the nationalist populists do not share this view. The AfD has called for an end to all arms deliveries to Ukraine and a lifting of all sanctions on Russia. Its co-leaders, Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, boycotted Volodymyr Zelensky’s speech to the Bundestag in 2024, dismissing the Ukrainian president as a “war and beggar president.”
In France, Marine Le Pen, the parliamentary leader of the nationalist-populist party National Rally and the front-runner for next spring’s presidential election, has promised to take France out of NATO’s integrated military command (France would remain a member of the alliance). Such a withdrawal would hardly help the Trump administration shift the burden of NATO’s defense to Europe.
The Trump administration’s affinity for Europe’s nationalist-populist right seems to be almost entirely cultural and civilizational, and based on the notion that Europe’s populists are fighting the same culture wars—including against immigration—as their counterparts in the United States. J. D. Vance explicitly praised then–Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán as an ally in defense of Western civilization at an election rally in Budapest on the eve of the Hungarian elections. And the Trump team seems to see the European populist right’s enemies—the European Union and national political establishments—as versions of its own domestic foes. This commonality appears to take precedence over foreign-policy concerns.
Trump officials have blasted centrist European governments for being too soft on Beijing but have said nothing about the populist right’s position on China. Some of these parties—particularly the AfD and Fidesz, in Hungary—favor much closer ties to the American adversary. The AfD’s Weidel lived in China for six years, speaks Mandarin, and wrote her doctoral dissertation about China’s pension system. Chrupalla, her co-leader, accused the German government of waging “economic war” against China for proposing a tougher trade policy toward Beijing. They have both called for warmer relations with China. Orbán, who was defeated in the Hungarian elections earlier this year, blocked the EU from criticizing Beijing, initiated an “all-weather comprehensive strategic partnership” with China, and welcomed Chinese investment in Hungarian infrastructure.
These largely transactional attitudes toward China and Russia may reflect a broader worldview among the nationalist populists, who praise Trump but are deeply skeptical of American power. In an analysis for the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Jeremy Cliffe argued that the AfD supports a multipolar world order and believes that great powers, such as China and Russia, should possess spheres of influence—a perspective that Trump seems sympathetic toward. The AfD, Cliffe wrote, “may regard Trump as a civilizational ally, but its senior figures have long described the United States as a raumfremd in Europe, a hard to translate German word that means something like ‘territorially alien.’”
If parties with these views take power, they could reduce American influence in Europe while making common European action on Russia and China much more difficult. They will also make Eastern Europeans nervous about German rearmament. In 2011, Radek Sikorski, Poland’s foreign minister, said, “I fear German power less than German inaction.” He recently revisited that remark, telling the German newspaper Handelsblatt, “We want Germany, under democratic leadership and as the largest economy in Europe, to play a strong role in securing our common security. But we remember all too well where a rearmed Germany can lead in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party—and that is exactly what the AfD represents.”
Senior Trump-administration officials say they are building a Europe that will carry its own weight. Maybe they are so beguiled by the nationalist populists’ domestic agenda that they have not yet realized it will come at the expense of NATO 3.0. Or maybe Trump doesn’t care about Europe’s defense, doesn’t see it as a U.S. interest, and doesn’t believe that Europe has any contribution to make to America’s security.
Trump and Vance seem to be laying the foundation for a more divided Europe that is incapable of deterring Russia, ever more dependent on China, and at odds with itself. If the administration continues on this path, it may get the European culture war it wants, but the United States will lose its ally.

Neville calls Man Utd 'pathetic' - but Carrick maintains belief
- Published
Gary Neville took a deep breath after Lisandro Martinez's own goal put Fulham ahead just over an hour into what had been a laboured Manchester United performance, and delivered his verdict.
The former United skipper is never short of a scathing word, but even by his standards, this was brutal.
"I've watched Manchester United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen," he said. "Absolutely pathetic.
"I've never seen such a lack of effort. What must [Michael] Carrick be thinking?"
For context, Neville was part of the United side beaten 3-1 by Sunday's opponents Fulham at Old Trafford in October 2003. In recent memory they have also lost 7-0 at Liverpool and 6-1 at home twice, to Tottenham and Manchester City.
Neville's words came after a poor quarter of an hour from the start of the second half to Martinez's moment of ill fortune, before United went on to snatch a 1-1 draw thanks to Matheus Cunha's deflected strike in the 89th minute.
It seemed an extreme reaction. But in a week when United lost the Manchester derby to a City side reduced to 10 men midway through the first half, then against Brighton for the first time in more than 50 years were beaten at home after giving away a two-goal lead, frustration among the fanbase is high.
Questions over fitness were first raised during pre-season when midfielder Youri Tielemans revealed United were not prioritising running.
While Cunha did not exactly agree with Neville in his post-match interview with Sky Sports, his comments will have fuelled more debate around the issue.
"At the beginning of the second half they put in more energy than us," said the Brazilian. "We cannot accept this."
Unsurprisingly, Carrick had a different take. He used the way his side tried to pressure the home team in the latter stages, leading to Cunha's equaliser, as evidence his squad is fit enough.
"The way we finished the game, actually, it didn't look like that. We finished the game really strong actually, and kept pushing. I don't think that's an issue, no," he said.
United must shut out 'noise'
Cunha also mentioned the "noise" around United when he spoke to BBC Match of the Day.
Neville is a significant part of that noise, either directly or through his growing media empire.
Carrick has previously said he can shut it out.
It cannot be quite so easy though when United fans - who usually back their team through disappointment - followed up chants on Wednesday in disgust at the Brighton debacle by here booing Carrick's decision to take off popular England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo 11 minutes from time.
"There's always going to be certain reactions when you're making changes," said Carrick. "I've spoken to Kobbie after the game and he's absolutely fine.
"I understand at times when we are chasing the game, everyone's a little bit emotional. The supporters are, as well they should be, desperate for us to do the right thing.
"But I don't take any negatives or offence to it. I think we've just got to try and keep doing the right things to get back into the game.
"The supporters were unbelievable today, I have to say, all the way through, and stuck with the boys and supported them. At least we've given them something small at the end to take from it, and I'm sure there's more to come."
And that is the key point.
A draw at Fulham is "something small" considering the home side started the game at the foot of the Premier League - and have now swapped places with Tottenham.
Five points from five games leaves United 12th, an incredible 10 points behind pacesetters Manchester City already.
Their £70m summer signing Carlos Baleba is still to make his debut, and long-term injury victim Matthijs de Ligt was not involved at all, even though both were part of the squad that travelled south on Saturday.
Striker Benjamin Sesko also missed the game after suffering a recurrence of the shin problem against Brighton that he was troubled by for an extended period last season before submitting to a recovery programme that ruled him out for more than three months.
Carrick says "at this point" the extent of the damage is unknown.
This would all be pretty underwhelming were it not for the ticketing issues instigated by the club's touting crackdown that has annoyed so many in the fanbase.
On Wednesday, United will release their full-year financial results to 30 June, around which the full extent of their current debt will be revealed.
Then there is the general debate about the wisdom of new stadium, which is set to cost in excess of £2bn, with planning permission potentially submitted with the main Old Trafford masterplan, which is earmarked for late 2027 or early 2028.
Little wonder, after leading United back to the Champions League so unexpectedly last season, Carrick is presiding over a club whose supporters feel deflated, even if he does not recognise that.
"It's still a big season ahead," he said. "It's a long season and you're going to have spells through a season. That's part of the journey.
"It's not a sprint, it's a long effort.
"I'm not playing it down, you know. We wanted more points, so I'm not saying everything's great. I understand the frustration. We wanted to be better and we wanted to do other things.
"But deflation is certainly not what we have within the club and within the group. The players didn't have that on the pitch today and that's what will carry us through the season without a doubt."

I've never been good at sports, and I've never been fond of exercise, so you might be wondering why I chose the Chicago Athletic Association when booking hotels for my first-ever trip to the city.
I wanted to step back in time. The Gilded Age hotel was a private club where professional athletes and high-profile individuals trained and socialized from 1893 to 2007.
Following its closure and a lengthy transformation project, the Chicago Athletic Association reopened as a hotel in 2015. I spent one night there in February for $250. It felt extremely luxurious for the price point, and some surprising details made me certain I'd book it again.
Parts of my stay felt like a time warp, but the hotel's history also came out in ways I didn't see coming.
Welcome to the Chicago Athletic Association, the 19th-century private club that's now a hotel.
The Venetian-Gothic-style building was designed by architect and club member Henry Ives Cobb, who took inspiration from the Doge's Palace in Venice, according to the hotel's website.
The hotel stood out to me among modern buildings on Michigan Avenue in Downtown Chicago. It's just across from Millennium Park and the Bean (formally known as Cloud Gate) and within walking distance of many tourist hot spots like the Art Institute of Chicago, the Chicago Theater, and the Chicago Riverwalk.
Inside, the past lives on.
The Chicago Athletic Association began as a Gilded Age gentlemen's club joined by influential sports icons. Membership opened to women in 1972.
It was a stomping ground for industry moguls like William Wrigley and Marshall Field. It was a training base for five-time Olympic gold-medal swimmer Johnny Weissmuller and the first professional football player, William "Pudge" Heffelfinger.
The building's history is celebrated inside the hotel, with 19th-century relics and refurbished materials, from wood paneling to marble flooring, Elizabeth Story, the hotel's sales and marketing director, told Business Insider.
As I stepped into the lobby, I felt like I'd traveled back in time.
The lobby, also known as the drawing room, looked as if it had been designed 100 years ago, with restored 19th-century trim, moldings, and replicated historic details.
"Teams of craftsmen restored the 1893 grandeur of the Lobby Lounge by removing, refinishing, and reinstalling every piece of millwork, and recreating original light fixtures from old photographs," Story said.
I noticed other contemporary details that pay tribute to the city and club's history. The check-in desk, designed with long strips of wood in different colors, was inspired by vintage athletic equipment.
"A mural above the desk depicts the elevated train tracks that encircle Chicago's Loop," Story added.
Restored Gilded Age interiors made communal spaces look as lavish as they were historic.
I was mesmerized by the preserved luxury finishings as I walked through the hotel. Restored Italian columns, stained-glass windows, and golden doors made me feel as if I were inside a palace.
The ballrooms had an old-world, luxury feel.
The hotel had many event spaces, including the White City Ballroom. During the restoration process, Story said that the Italian Carrara marble floor was buried under an inch and a half of carpet, glue, and concrete.
I was surprised by another event space that used to be a swimming pool.
Known as "The Tank," this space still has the swimming lane flooring tiles from its pool days.
"Artists hand-made 167 individual stalactites as part of the atmospheric design," Story said.
Although the highlight of this room is the historic pool tiles, I thought repurposing the space for events was surprising and innovative.
The game room had a mix of historic and fresh details.
The game room was the billiards room back in the club days, Story said.
It didn't feel frozen in time like some of the other spaces. The walls blended antique woodwork with whimsical murals, such as chalkboard sketches of athletes and an aerial view of a basketball court. I thought it was a playful, creative way to showcase the building's history.
Some aspects of the hotel were completely new, like the rooftop bar and restaurant.
"The past was honored at every turn, but the transformation also called for thoughtful new additions," Story explained.
For example, Cindy's, the rooftop restaurant and bar, was built ahead of the hotel's 2015 opening.
I thought the space had a midcentury modern vibe with vintage influence. Cindy's brought the outdoors in with a steel-framed, windowed pavilion inspired by 19th-century train sheds.
The fitness center was sleek and modern.
Here, I found cardio machines with tablet attachments and fun cartoons of men stretching on the walls. The fitness center is open 24 hours a day.
My room had a vintage aesthetic without feeling dated.
I booked a standard room with a comfy king-sized bed and a downtown view for about $250 a night. I immediately noticed the custom metal bedframe with brass accents — a vintage design inspired by the 19th-century club.
The furniture creatively combined elements of old-fashioned gym equipment in a functional way.
The desk was unlike any I'd seen before. Wooden bars, inspired by stretching racks, climbed the wall to a netted shelf that appeared large enough to hold a typical checked suitcase.
The bars were cleverly used as vertical storage, with leather pouches of varying sizes hanging from them. I used these pockets to store my wallet, keys, and chargers during my stay.
The bathroom blended old-school locker room vibes with opulence.
"The bathrooms were conceived as a quiet luxury counterpoint," Story said. A black-and-white palette and a simple striped backsplash were paired with a Carrara marble vanity and a rainfall shower.
There was also a boxing-style robe in the bathroom, which almost made me feel like an athlete myself.
At the Chicago Athletic Association, I got my trip back in time, with some surprises.
While parts of the hotel felt 100 years old, fresh designs inspired by its private-club past gave other spaces a modern twist.
"The goal was never a museum-quality freeze in time, but something more alive," Story said. "A touch of disorder in the new space was introduced to draw in a younger generation, balanced bravely with references to the building's past."
From the palace-like common spaces to the creative nods to the past, the Chicago Athletic Association was more luxurious and distinctive than I expected for $250 a night. I would definitely stay there again, and maybe next time, I'll bring a jock with me.

Ukraine fires over 1,000 drones at Russia, including hundreds launched at Moscow
Ukrainian forces fired more than 1,000 drones at Russia overnight, including hundreds that were launched toward Moscow, officials said Sunday as the Kremlin was wrapping up the third and last day of its parliamentary elections.
Moscow's mayor described the wave of drones as the "largest ever" attack on the Russian capital and said there had been damage to a Moscow oil refinery and a residential building.
Across the wider Moscow region, the attack killed two people and wounded 20, local Gov. Andrei Vorobyov said. The dead were a 74-year-old man and a 44-year-old woman, he said.
Writing on social media, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Kyiv had used a range of missiles and drones in the attack — including Ukraine's domestically made Flamingo and Pelican missiles — to hit oil and logistics facilities.
"These are billions of dollars that sustain the war machine," Zelenskyy said, referring to the financial pressure that Kyiv hopes to put on Russia's economy.
The voting underway in Russia is the country's first wartime parliamentary election — balloting that has been virtually devoid of opposition to President Vladimir Putin's policies and is all but certain to cement the Kremlin's dominance.
Russia was also holding the vote in the four Ukrainian regions that Moscow illegally annexed after the war began but still doesn't fully control, and in Crimea, the Black Sea peninsula that was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014. Kyiv has denounced the action as illegal.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said that its forces shot down 1,100 Ukrainian drones across the country, as well as over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the waters of the Black Sea.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that 450 drones had been destroyed en route to the Russian capital, and that the attack had damaged the Moscow Oil Refinery and a residential building.
He said the "unprecedented attack" on Moscow was an attempt to disrupt the elections. "The enemy failed in this regard," he said.
Since Russia's invasion more than four years ago, Ukraine has become a global leader in military drone technology, deploying domestically produced long-range drones alongside missiles for strikes deep inside Russia. Its drone technology has impressed governments and defense manufacturers around the world.
Kyiv is aiming to make the Russian public feel the war's consequences and pressure Russian President Vladimir Putin into negotiating a peace settlement. Putin has so far shown no signs he intends to stop the invasion.
Instead, Moscow and Kyiv have been drawn into an escalating duel of long-range aerial strikes as fighting along the roughly 1,250-kilometer (780-mile) front line in eastern and southern Ukraine has slowed, restricted by large numbers of drones and ground robots threatening troop movements.

The Delhi Chief Electoral Officer clarified on Sunday that receiving a notice during the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls does not automatically mean that an elector’s name will be removed from the voter list. This comes after former deputy prime minister L K Advani and former Delhi deputy chief minister Manish Sisodia, Foreign Minister S Jaishankar were among the prominent Delhi voters included in the list of 33 lakh electors being sent notices over "discrepancies" in the information submitted during the SIR exercise. The CEO’s office stressed that no voter can be deleted from the electoral roll without first being given an opportunity to present their case. It added that any such deletion must follow a proper, speaking and appealable order. The clarification followed reports circulating about notices being sent to prominent personalities and other electors as part of the SIR exercise in Delhi. According to the CEO’s office, the draft electoral roll was compiled using details submitted by voters through Enumeration Forms during the exercise and handed over to Booth Level Officers (BLOs). The draft was published on August 31. The electoral roll is available for public access through the CEO Delhi website, offices of Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) and Assistant Electoral Registration Officers (AEROs), as well as designated polling station locations, according to ANI. The Election Commission of India launched the SIR in Delhi on May 14, stating that the exercise was aimed at ensuring that "No eligible citizen is left out while no ineligible person is included in the Electoral Roll." According to the latest press note issued by the Delhi Chief Electoral Officer, electors included in the draft roll have been divided into two broad categories — those whose names, or whose progeny entries, could be linked to the electoral rolls from the previous intensive revision, and those for whom such a link could not be established. Notices are being sent to voters whose records could not be linked to the electoral roll from the last intensive revision, as well as those whose linked details contain "logical discrepancies". The CEO's office said the list of electors who have received notices has been uploaded on the websites of the CEO Delhi, District Election Officers and Voter Centres. Clarifying the purpose of the notices, the office said, "All stakeholders are hereby informed that issue of Notice does not mean that their names will be deleted from the electoral rolls of NCT of Delhi." It added that the system-generated notices are intended to facilitate correction of data in ECINET. The CEO's office reiterated that "No name can be deleted without giving an opportunity of being heard and a proper speaking and appealable order". It also rejected reports suggesting that the notices had created a "no existential crisis", saying there was "no existential crisis" arising from the notices. Electors who receive notices can file their responses along with the required documents before the concerned ERO or Booth Level Officer (BLO). The Delhi CEO’s office clarified that the list of documents prescribed by the Election Commission of India is "only Indicative not exhaustive". It said EROs, being statutory authorities, will assess each case individually and make a final determination after considering the documents submitted and the report prepared by the BLO. The process of deciding the notices is expected to conclude by October 29. The names of eligible electors covered by the exercise will subsequently be included in the final electoral roll, which is scheduled to be published on November 4. The Delhi Chief Electoral Officer’s daily SIR bulletin said 84,263 Form-6 applications were submitted across the national capital between August 31 and September 19. This was in addition to 2,12,400 such applications received up to August 30. Form-6 is used by citizens to seek inclusion of their names in the electoral roll. During the August 31-September 19 period, the authorities also received 174 Form-6A applications, 1,396 Form-7 applications and 29,705 Form-8 applications. The CEO’s office urged residents to verify their names in the draft electoral roll and, if missing, submit Form-6 along with the required declaration and supporting documents. Those who will turn 18 on or before October 1, 2026, are also eligible to apply through Form-6. Form-8 can be submitted for changing an address or making corrections to existing electoral roll entries. Claims and objections submitted by September 30 will be processed by October 29, while the final electoral roll is scheduled to be published on November 4, according to the latest bulletin. The CEO’s office has also scheduled special camps at all polling station locations on September 20 and September 27, where citizens can access various electoral services. With US President Donald Trump having signed the Lindsey Graham Sanctions bill that allows him to impose steep tariffs, as high as 100% on India and China, the biggest buyers of Russian oil, Vladimir Putin might have to look towards Africa to continue sustaining its wider networks.
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 was signed by Trump on 18 September once it cleared the US Congress.
As per the provisions of the law, the US President can impose sanctions of up to 100% on countries buying oil from Russia.
India's Confederation of Indian Textile Industry (CITI) has urged the central government to engage with Washington in order to protect Indian exporters, ANI reported.
“Any additional tariffs under this Act will be very difficult to absorb for the MSME-dominated Indian textile and apparel sector already under stress due to several factors, including the continuing turmoil in West Asia. It will severely impact our ability to sell in the United States, our most significant market by a distance,” CITI Chairman Ashwin Chandran said, as per ANI.
Can Russia depend on African network?
With western countries cutting their imports of Russian oil after the war with Ukraine began in 2022, Moscow had
turned towards its partners in Asia. With the latest sanctions threat looming over both Beijing and New Delhi, Moscow will try to explore its options in Africa to sustain its wider network.
Russia has political, military, as well as logistical ties across Africa although no African country is a major buyer of Russian crude.
The sanctioned tanker Progress was spotted in January when it ran into some difficulties while carrying around 730,000 barrels of Urals crude from Russia while it was moving towards the Suez Canal.
Another LNG carrier from Russia, Arctic Metagaz, entered the search-and-rescue zone of Libya after it suffered damages in the Mediterranean.
Egypt is the African country with the most direct involvement in the energy trade of Russia, Business Insider Africa revealed. The country, in August, became the fifth-largest buyer of Russian fossil fuels, when it purchased goods worth €513 million, as per the CREA.
Moscow has also been deepening its military logistics network, which now links Mali, Burkina Faso, as well as Niger.
As per an investigation carried out by the US-based Center for Advanced Defense Studies (C4DS), 75 flights were identified which resupplied Russia-aligned military operations in countries like Niger, Burkina Faso, and Mali during the period of January 2025-July 2026.

In a bid to boost tourism, the Kozhikode district administration has decided to resume boating services at the Peruvannamuzhi reservoir and introduce a new boating service at Thonikadavu.
The decision was taken at a meeting of the Tourism Management Committee held recently in the presence of District Collector M.S. Madhavikutty and Perambra MLA Fathima Thahiliya. Thonikadavu, a 15-acre land known as ‘Heart Island’, is located within the reservoir. The meeting decided to invite expressions of interest from boat operators to run the service at Thonikadavu. Solar-powered boats will be used to minimise pollution.
The meeting also decided to make temporary appointments required for the operation of the tourism facilities. A special meeting will be held soon to discuss the comprehensive development of the destination.
Boating through the reservoir, which has 13 islets, is envisaged as a key attraction in efforts to develop Peruvannamuzhi as a major tourism destination.
“Boating will offer visitors an opportunity to experience the reservoir, its islets and the surrounding forested landscape. The idea is to develop Peruvannamuzhi as a major tourism destination by leveraging its natural beauty, water resources and potential for adventure tourism, particularly among young people,” said Ms. Thahiliya.
A ₹3.13-crore tourism development project was implemented at Peruvannamuzhi in 2021, with facilities, including a children’s park.
Two solar-powered boats were launched at the Peruvannamuzhi ecotourism spot in 2022, helping to increase tourist footfall and generate revenue.
The service was initially suspended during the heavy rains in the 2024 monsoon and has remained stalled since then. Sources said it had been stopped following an engine failure. Despite several notices issued by the Irrigation department to resume the service, the operator failed to restart it.
The prolonged suspension has deprived visitors of one of the destination’s major attractions, leaving them with little option but to visit the dam and return. It has also resulted in a loss of potential revenue.
