What’s this @TwitterIndia ? @alok_bhatt has tweeted about Hindu girls being kidnapped, r@ped and forcefully converted to !slam in Pakistan and his account has been suspended, What kind of nonsense is this? Explain!#BringBackAlokBhatt pic.twitter.com/w4T3epRn6t
— संवैधानिक डकैत (@Shivam_h9) May 29, 2020
The Pamphlet-Savitr Analytics-Alok Bhatt Connection
In 2022, Bhatt took on a directorial role at Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation, a company that was incorporated in April 26 that year, with Bhatt and Ashish Nautiyal initially named as directors. According to documents filed with the Union ministry of corporate affairs (MCA), Bhatt holds 9,500 shares, or 95 per cent of the company, while Nautiyal holds the remaining 500 shares, or 5 per cent.
Interestingly, Nautiyal is also the founding editor of the Right-wing media outlet, The Pamphlet.
Savitr Analytics has no website or online presence. We went through its financial records filed with the MCA for the financial years 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25, and found that it was registered as a Section 8 company, i.e., a non-profit. In the 2024-25 financial year, its total revenue from operations was Rs 2.7 crore.
The organisation’s revenue across all three years comes from ‘sale of services’, and the rows for ‘Grants or donations received (relevant for Sec 8 companies)’, present in the 2022-23 and 2023-24 filings, are left blank in 2022-23 and 2023-24. In 2024-25, the row does not exist.
Under ‘Corporate Information’, they state ‘Research and awareness about Indian culture and heritage…’, ‘Promotion of commerce, art, science, sports, education, research, social welfare, religion, charity, and environmental protection…’ and ‘Advancement of education, learning, and skills development…’ as their activities.
There was a category called ‘professional expenses’ in the 2022-23 filing that was later relabeled as ‘content production expenses’. Rs. 41,48,600 was spent in the first year, Rs. 95,36,600 (filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the second year, and Rs. 1,38,53,200 (also filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the third year.
Next, we found that an individual named Ridhika Aggarwal stated on LinkedIn that she worked as a content writer for Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation until August 2023. We went through her X timeline (linked to her LinkedIn profile) and found that she wrote at least three articles for The Pamphlet during her tenure at Savitr. None of the articles are currently available on the website.
Ridhika is also listed as a non-official member of a steering committee formed by the Union ministry of environment, forest and climate change in 2023.
The Pamphlet, previously known as The Indian Affairs, posted for the first time on Facebook in April 2022, which is the same time when Savitr Analytics was incorporated.
ठीक 2 साल पहले देहरादून में आज ही के दिन @Pamphlet_in ऑफिस निर्माण की शुरुआत हो गई थी, उत्तराखण्ड चुनाव निपटने के बाद मैं २० दिन के अपने नैनीताल और लैंसडाउन प्रवास के बाद दून घाटी में उतरा था।
आज ही के दिन साल 2019 में लोकसभा चुनाव का रिजल्ट भी आया था और प्रधानमंत्री… pic.twitter.com/6lAVSW3twN
— V Ashish Nautiyal (@ashu_nauty) May 15, 2024
The Pamphlet claims to “cut through the noise of the modern information ecosystem by offering readers and viewers clarity, depth and perspective on issues that shape India and the world.” Its reports have seem to be echoing pro-BJP narratives. An August 11 video report, for instance, was captioned: “Questions raised in the public domain regarding the credentials of two CJP leaders, Abhijeet Dipke and Saurav Das, have brought up several serious concerns”. It questioned Dipke’s Boston University degree, academic timeline and funding, as well as Das’ property, tenancy, rent, police verification, and electoral records.
During the CJP protests, another report took a swipe at Mohammed Junaid, who had been feeding protesters, with the reporter noting that “such bhaijaans were also seen” at the protest sites in Shaheen Bagh and Farmers’ stir. Thumbnails of these reports carried AI-generated visuals of individuals critical of the Union government, their faces distorted through AI to portray them in a negative light. This is a tactic common across Right-wing outlets and social media troll handles.
More recently, the outlet, alongside Abhijit Iyer-Mitra, Law Beat, The Jaipur Dialogues and The Sunday Guardian, was summoned by the Delhi high court over a Rs 2 crore privacy suit by Cockroach Janta Party spokesperson Saurav Das, who alleged that they had disclosed his home address and other personal details online. The case will be heard on September 14.
The video below depicts a time when the outlet was still called The Indian Affairs, and Nautiyal (in striped shirt) can be seen with his colleagues alongside educator Pawan Gupta.
The Indian Affairs @ForIndiaMatters Coming Soon

— The Pamphlet (@Pamphlet_in) July 22, 2022
Nautiyal’s last video with The Pamphlet was uploaded in December 2024. In June 2025, Nautiyal was pictured with the OpIndia team. His first video for OpIndia, an interview with Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Dhami, came a month later, in July 2025.
Nautiyal is now the multimedia & digital head and editor at OpIndia, and is no longer listed as a director of Savitr on the MCA website.
It is worth noting that The Pamphlet’s website does not disclose any parent company, ownership, editorial team, funding details or board of directors. Its ‘About Us’ page offers only a description of what it does, while calling itself ‘an independent digital media platform’. The only publicly mentioned funding source we could find was YouTube memberships of The Pamphlet costing Rs. 119 to Rs. 3199 per month.
Nautiyal is not the only link between Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet. An individual named Shiv Kumar Mishra was appointed the director of Savitr Analytics in April 2023. In March 2023, Mishra was announced as the CEO of The Pamphlet.
Please welcome @shivkmishr, Founder & CEO, The Pamphlet https://t.co/U53aK62Fzo
— The Pamphlet (@Pamphlet_in) March 14, 2023
In other words, two of the three directors of Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation have held senior positions at The Pamphlet. And in both cases, the appointments to Savitr and The Pamphlet came in close succession. This raises the question of whether the two entities are formally linked.
We also found that The Pamphlet had an office space from its inception in Dehradun, and it is evident from a photo posted by Nautiyal that it began with a team of at least 20 people. Bhatt, the reader would remember, also claims to be from Dehradun.
While all of this points to a connection between Bhatt and The Pamphlet, there appears to be a concerted effort to keep that relationship under wraps. Hence, we tried to dig more.
Is Bhatt Linked to The Pamphlet? We Asked The Pamphlet
We sent an email to The Pamphlet on September 3 asking them about the relationship between Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet, and whether Alok Bhatt was connected to The Pamphlet, given that he holds a 95% stake in Savitr Analytics, a company whose other directors have held senior positions at The Pamphlet. We also asked them about their funding sources, since nothing is mentioned on the website.
In reply, they asked us to send our queries to another email ID of The Pamphlet and also to Alok Bhatt, Nirwa Mehta, Ashish Nautiyal and Shiv Mishra. Interestingly, they provided us with the email IDs and phone numbers of each of these individuals. This, in itself, might be considered an indicator of some sort of link between The Pamphlet and Bhatt. It is unlikely for an organisation to provide the direct contact details of someone with whom it has no professional association.
We then sent our queries to all of them.
Nautiyal responded to us saying that his reporting manager, OpIndia editor Nupur J Sharma, “suggested” him “not to give (you) any quotes or information as a matter of policy of not engaging with entities that don’t act in good faith”. A day later, he took to X to let the world know that a woman from Alt News “with a Hindu-sounding name” had approached him with some questions.
Pamphlet editor Nirwa Mehta sent us a 1,071-word response, but did not answer any of our questions. Instead, she sent a detailed set of reciprocal questions concerning Alt News’ funding transparency, the outside associations of its founders and editor, and grants received by individuals associated with Alt News, both currently and in the past. She offered to answer Alt News’ questions in writing once Alt News answered hers first.
It is worth noting that The Pamphlet published a video on Alt News on August 16, 2026, without seeking a response from the organisation.
This correspondent responded to Mehta, stating that questions concerning Alt News’ funding should be directed to its editor, while questions concerning any of the founders’ personal assignments should be directed to the person concerned. We also reminded her that a so-called expose on Alt News’ founders had been published by The Pamphlet without either of the concerned persons being approached for a response — a violation of basic journalistic ethics.
In her final response, Mehta did not address the question of ethics. Instead, in a demand that many may find bizarre, she asked this correspondent, “as a responsible employee”, to take her questions to the Alt News directors.
At this point, we felt there was no point continuing the conversation.
We will update our article if The Pamphlet answers Alt News’ questions on whether Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet are connected in any way, and whether Alok Bhatt, BJP’s new IT cell member who continues to remain away from X, holds a position at The Pamphlet.
Social Media Posts Answer the Question
The connection between The Pamphlet and Alok Bhatt is one of internet’s worst kept secrets, it seems. We found several instances on social media where well-known faces from the Right-wing ecosystem tagged Alok Bhatt alongside members of The Pamphlet team — whether to thank them for invitations to Delhi Shabdotsav 2026, where The Pamphlet Panchayat featured on the itinerary, or in connection with other events involving the organisation.
On January 5, 2026, Right-wing influencer Abhijit Iyer-Mitra, who was recently criticised for comparing Newslaundry journalists to prostitutes, thanked The Pamphlet team — including its editor Nirwa Mehta, anchor Shreya Arora, and Bhatt — for inviting him to speak at The Pamphlet Panchayat.
Responding to Iyer-Mitra, Nirwa Mehta and another The Pamphlet employee, Pratibha, thanked him for being a part of the session. The exchange is significant because it can be seen as an acknowledgement by the Pamphlet editor and another employee of Bhatt being a part of the organisation.
Delhi Shabdotsav 2026 was a three-day cultural and literary festival held from January 2 to January 4, 2026, organised by Suruchi Prakashan with the support of the department of art, culture and languages of the Delhi government. The Pamphlet was the digital partner at the event and hosted ‘The Pamphlet Panchayat’ at the fest. The Pamphlet team held and moderated several discussions over the three days, including those with Sanjeev Newar, Vijay Patel, and Subhi Vishwakarma. The subjects of the discussions ranged from ‘Love Jihad: factsheet’ to ‘Bharat’s Hostile Neighbourhood & Need to Regain Shatrubodh’.
We went through the images posted on Shabdotsav’s website and found that Bhatt was present at the event.
The link between Alok Bhatt and The Pamphlet becomes more apparent in another conversation on X in which Iyer-Mitra directly addressed Mehta as Pamphlet and Alok Bhatt’s ‘staff’. Iyer jokingly rebuked Mehta for liking a certain kind of car. Tagging Bhatt, he wrote, “Do @Pamphlet_in and @alok_bhatt @shreya_arora22 approve of these disgusting and extremely hateful statements by their staff?” Mehta responded to Iyer-Mitra’s post, but did not object to the ‘staff’ reference.
On June 1, 2023, a little more than a year after The Pamphlet’s inception, one @saket71 posted a picture with Ashish Nautiyal, who was working at The Pamphlet then, and called him a ‘Media Mughal’. He later tagged Alok Bhatt and Shiv Mishra, praising them for “putting a great team together.”
Such a pleasure to meet the young stars of @Pamphlet_in , @RitikaChandola @himanshi__bisht and the whole team. Such a great young team, full of hope and dreams, and a visible sense of great camaraderie. Kudos to @alok_bhatt and @shivkmishr for putting a great team together. https://t.co/NnmHkA9rQO
— saket साकेत ಸಾಕೇತ್ 🇮🇳 (@saket71) June 1, 2023
Several people have congratulated Alok Bhatt at various points of time upon The Pamphlet reaching certain milestones.
To sum up, what raises serious questions about the BJP’s decision to name Bhatt as its social media co-convenor is not just his past social media conduct, but also the opacity surrounding his professional associations. One organisation he appears to be associated with, The Pamphlet, does not publicly disclose its ownership, editorial team, board or funding sources. Without any apparent source of funding, it starts off as a 20-member organization. Who pays their salary? How are establishment costs met? There are no answers. Again, another corporate entity closely linked to him, Savitr Analytics, has no website or public online presence despite reporting Rs 2.7 crore in operational revenue in 2025.
Things get murkier when one takes into account the desperate efforts by Bhatt’s associates to conceal his association with The Pamphlet, evident in the organisation’s refusal to answer direct questions regarding this.
In other words, a man linked to organisations with questionable records, and whose involvement with a pro-government outlet is abundantly visible in public, but markedly absent from the outlet’s own disclosures, has now been given a formal position in the BJP’s social media cell.

As Jeremy Strong delivers his portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg, Aaron Sorkin has shed some light on the method actor’s process for this role.
The Social Reckoning writer/director was “not shocked” that Strong didn’t tell him about writing an email to Zuckerberg, confirming that the Oscar-nominated actor stayed in character as the Meta founder and CEO between takes.
“Jeremy does a lot of his own work. He does a tremendous amount of work before he shows up on your set,” he explained to NYT’s The Interview. “He did not speak in his own voice on the set or walk the way Jeremy walks.”
Sorkin continued, “I told all the other actors in his scenes: ‘Guys, he’s not going to be hanging out with you at craft service. He’s not going to be yucking it up with you between takes. He’s probably not going to speak to you at all. He is going to treat you the way he imagines Mark treats the people around him.’ And that’s what happened. You cannot argue with the results.”
Watch on Deadline
Strong previously revealed that he emailed Zuckerberg before making the film to tell him he takes “this responsibility very seriously, and the veracity of it seriously, and I’m approaching it with respect.”
After The Social Network (2010) recounted Zuckerberg’s creation of Facebook and the controversy that ensued, screenwriter Sorkin returned to write and direct the upcoming sequel, which premieres Oct. 9, focusing on a 2021 document leak that exposed harm Facebook caused on society.
In The Social Reckoning, Facebook engineer Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) goes to Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White) with the social media platform’s most guarded secrets. Bill Burr, Wunmi Mosaku, Billy Magnussen and Betty Gilpin also star.

Israel’s president has pardoned a combat medic who shot dead a badly wounded Palestinian attacker who had stabbed a soldier in the occupied West Bank, in a case that divided the country a decade ago.
Elor Azaria’s conviction in 2017 for manslaughter and his release after serving two-thirds of his 18-month sentence drew enormous attention in Israel, where military service is compulsory for most Jewish men.
In his first interview after his release, Azaria said he would “act exactly the same, because that’s how I needed to act”.
Azaria had approached Abdel Fattah al-Sharif as he lay on the ground, unarmed and badly hurt, after stabbing a soldier in the city of Hebron. A mobile phone video captured Azaria shooting al-Sharif in the head.
The office of president Isaac Herzog said in a statement on Saturday that he acted on the recommendation of defence minister Israel Katz. The statement cited the time that had passed, and the spirit of the approaching Yom Kippur, or Day of Atonement, holiday as among the factors in the decision.
Herzog’s office also said that Azaria, who was 20 when he was sentenced, had “expressed his sorrow” in his request. The statement noted that in an earlier request, he called his gunshot an “operational error”.
In a separate statement, Katz called it a “right, humane and fitting decision” and said Azaria had been in a “complex operational mission”.
But the military’s chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, had said in a letter to the defence minister that the pardon should not be granted, Israeli media reported.
The conviction was a rare case of a military court ruling against a soldier for deadly action taken in the field. Top generals had pressed for his prosecution, while many in the Israeli public supported Azaria at a time when there had been a series of stabbings and car-ramming attacks by Palestinians or Israeli Arabs. Some supporters protested outside his trial.
On Saturday, Israel’s hard-line national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said in a statement that “cancelling the criminal record of someone who killed a terrorist makes me emotional and very happy”.
Some Palestinians and human rights groups had described Azaria’s sentence as far too lenient. Prosecutors had sought a sentence of three to five years.
The statement by Herzog’s office on Saturday said that his decision “does not constitute a reassessment of the case”.
The divisions over Azaria’s case led to public polling and political pressure that led the defence minister at the time, Moshe Ya’alon, to resign.
After the verdict, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for Azaria to be pardoned.
After the sentencing, the Palestinian government minister in charge of prisoner affairs, Issa Karaka, called it a “joke”.

Listed NBFC Kissht has secured board approval to raise up ₹832.2 Cr via a preferential issue of equity shares to 34 investors and entities. In a filing with the exchanges, the company said that its board has approved the issuance of 2.6 Cr fully paid-up equity shares to the investors at an issue price of ₹314.11 apiece. The NBFC did not disclose how it plans to utilise the fresh proceeds from the issue. The allotment is still subject to regulatory and shareholder approval. The company has also convened an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders to seek approval for the preferential issue. “Funds raising by way of a preferential issue on a private placement basis of up to 2,64,93,882 fully paid-up equity shares of the company… for cash, at an issue price of ₹314.11 per share… for an amount aggregating to ₹832.19 Cr to identified investors (non-promoters), in accordance with the provisions of… applicable laws….,” read the filing. Among the investing companies, Axis Flexi Cap Fund, Axis Multi Cap Fund and Axis Small Cap Fund together will receive 63.7 Lakh shares worth nearly ₹200 Cr. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, via two entities, will also receive 27.1 Lakh shares totalling ₹85 Cr. Envision Capital will also get 12.7 Lakh shares valued at nearly ₹40 Cr, while PE firm First Bridge will lap up 12.1 Lakh shares for a sum of ₹20 Cr. Kissht will also allot 23.9 Lakh shares to three entities linked to Ashoka WhiteOak Capital for a consideration of nearly ₹75 Cr. Other investors that will receive allotment under the preferential issue include 360 One, Alchemy Capital, Groww, Bandhan Small Cap Fund, Unity Small Finance Bank, among others. In terms of the other individual investors, Ameeta Rajendra Naik will receive 63,671 shares worth ₹2 Cr and Anil Shah will get 1.6 Lakh shares valued at nearly ₹5 Cr. The latest fundraise comes barely four months after the NBFC made a strong debut on the exchanges, listing at a premium of 11.7% on the BSE compared to its issue price of ₹171. Its public issue comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹850 Cr and an OFS component totalling ₹76 Cr. Founded in 2015 by Ranvir Singh and Krishnan Vishwanathan, Kissht is a lending tech platform that offers digital personal and business loans of up to ₹5 Lakh. It also offers health-related insurance products and secured loans through loans against property. In July, it also received regulatory approval to begin distribution of mutual funds through its wholly-owned subsidiary Invincible Minds. The NBFC claimed to have 45+ active lending and co-lending partners under its belt at the end of June 2026. It also operated 101 offline branches across eight states and union territories, and managed to more than double YoY its active customer base to 3.49 Mn in Q1 FY27. On the financial front, Kissht’s consolidated net profit zoomed 59% to ₹95.1 Cr in Q1 FY27 as against ₹59.7 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Meanwhile, operating revenue zoomed nearly 45% to ₹669.5 Cr during the quarter under review as against ₹463.1 Cr in Q1 FY26. Shares of the NBFC closed Thursday’s trading session 5.08% higher at ₹359.7 on the BSE.

As a teenager, I'd sit on my bed flipping through glossy magazines, fascinated and completely absorbed by the empowering stories about women. The news felt dominated by men, but magazines seemed to offer a different world — one where women's lives, bodies, careers, and opinions were worthy of entire pages. I knew from an early age I wanted to help bring more of those stories to life.
In 2012, after studying journalism at Northeastern University, I moved to New York City as quickly as I could, interning at Ladies' Home Journal and Self, then gravitating toward parenting publications including What To Expect, American Baby, and Fit Pregnancy.
Motherhood fascinated me long before I became a mother. It was the same intrigue and interest that drew me to magazines — the power of women, what their bodies could do, and the enormity of the identity shift involved in raising a child. Writing about pregnancy and parenting somehow felt very natural to me, even when I understood both mostly in theory.
I loved editing, but I wanted to write
Working at magazines wasn't quite how I'd imagined it from my childhood bedroom. I loved editing: finding the heart of a story, moving pieces around, and helping a writer say what they were trying to say. My boss, Mindy, was one of the first people to make me believe that my creativity and instincts were worth trusting. She taught me nearly everything I knew about shaping a narrative.
But I also began to feel restless. I was putting so much of myself into stories that ultimately ran under somebody else's name. I longed for that authorship and craved the terrifying privilege of starting with a blank page, figuring out what I had to say, and hoping it might matter to even one reader.
Mindy warned me that freelancing would be hard. I believed her and quit anyway. I had just gotten engaged, was planning a wedding, and was already thinking about having children. I also knew that if I kept waiting to feel established enough to become a writer, I might spend my entire career editing other people's work.
I was scared to give up a steady paycheck, especially while planning a wedding and thinking about starting a family. Dan, my now-husband, understood the risk but supported me taking the chance. Neither of us knew whether I could make a sustainable living on my own; I only knew I would regret it if I didn't try.
The transition happened faster than I expected. Within the first few months, I had more assignments than I knew what to do with, partly because leaving my 9-to-5 meant I could attend daytime events, meet editors, and build relationships that led to more work. My income still varied from month to month, but it was far steadier than I had feared. By my second year of freelancing, I was writing at an almost ridiculous pace for around 20 magazines and websites and earning nearly four times the roughly $30,000 salary I'd once made as an editorial assistant.
My career became so much bigger after I left my staff job, but it looked so different from what I could have imagined.
Moving home changed the picture completely
Life started looking even more different in 2018, about a year after I began freelancing, when my husband lost his job. Because I didn't have employer-sponsored health insurance of my own, I had been covered through his job, so we lost coverage along with his paycheck. Our lease was also ending, and we wanted to start a family. Leaving New York suddenly felt less like giving something up and more like the only decision that made sense.
We moved to my hometown north of Boston, where my parents and oldest friends still lived. I became a mom the following spring, April 2019. Less than a year later, COVID turned the world upside down, and there wasn't a single person whose life looked the way they had imagined it.
My working life went from events, meetings, and crowded New York sidewalks to writing alone in the corner of a small, old house, albeit with an ocean view. There were no coworkers nearby, no glossy proofs circulating, and no one across the desk to bounce an idea off. There was just me, my laptop, my cat, and, during several stretches, a pregnant belly.
My hardest experiences became part of my work
Motherhood was so different from what I'd imagined, and so was my path through it. While trying to grow my family, I suffered two miscarriages, which drastically changed the way I understood pregnancy, loss, and the motherhood journey in its entirety. I was so fortunate to have two healthy pregnancies afterward, but I couldn't shake everything the process had shown me.
I was inspired more than ever to create — to bring to life the kinds of platforms and communities I'd needed myself. I co-founded Miscarriage Movement, to make pregnancy loss feel less isolating, as well as The Mother Chapter to talk honestly about motherhood, identity, mental health, and ambition. Neither platform was part of a careful business plan. Both grew from experiences and questions I couldn't leave alone.
My career today looks nothing like the one I imagined as a teenager. I miss parts of New York and the collective energy of a magazine office. Freelancing can still be unpredictable, and running my own platforms means the work is never exactly finished. But I get to write, edit, create, and build something that belongs to me. I'm also close to my parents and present for the small, ordinary parts of my children's lives.
The magazines on my childhood bed made me want to tell women's stories. All these years later, that's still very much what I'm doing. I just couldn't have imagined where I'd be doing it — or how much of my own life would eventually find its way onto the page.

During the seventh edition of Semicon India today, Odisha’s chief minister (CM) Mohan Charan Majhi shared that the state is planning to set up an ‘Odisha Silicon Valley’ across an 870 acre stretch between Cuttack and Bhubaneswar. The state aims to transform from a mineral-rich region into a high-tech chip-making powerhouse. The CM said that the administration is in conversations with international semiconductor companies based out of countries like Sweden, Japan, and others to discuss potential projects pertaining to semiconductors, AI, and data centres in the state. As of now, construction across the state has begun on two central government-approved projects: Sicsem Pvt Ltd’s first-in-India silicon carbide fab and integrated packaging facility, and 3D Glass Solutions’ glass-substrate packaging facility, the CM announced. Efforts have also begun to launch a Phase 2 project with Sicsem to establish a silicon carbide epitaxy and packaging facility, per CM Majhi. As of now, the Odisha government has approved five additional semiconductor projects worth approximately ₹11,000 Cr, which are estimated to create around 4,500 direct jobs and over 16,000 indirect jobs. While RiR Power Electronics, Sancorn Technology, and ASP Semiconductor have signed MOUs for semiconductor projects, Intel and 3D Glass Solutions have also signed an MOU for a partnership aiming to bring $3.3 Bn (₹30,550 Cr) in investment and over 1,800 direct jobs to the state. To support research and commercialisation, Odisha is also investing ₹125 Cr towards a ₹452 Cr National Industry Co-Development Hub on Integrated Power Electronics alongside IIT Bhubaneswar and the National Research Foundation. The state government has also amended its semiconductor policy and committed up to 25% capex for projects approved under the India Semiconductor Mission, the CM revealed. “With this credit, along with full infrastructure support and incentives, Odisha's offering is very attractive and competitive, ensuring our success,” he said. CM Majhi also highlighted specialised training programmes at the World Skill Center in Bhubaneswar developed in partnership with the Singapore government through which the government is aiming to meet the demand for highly skilled labour from the technology ecosystem. “We are focusing heavily on emerging technologies like semiconductors, AI, and data centres. Beyond the World Skill Center, we have developed key ITIs into Institutes of National Excellence equipped with labs and modern training infrastructure,” he added. He further said the government aims to prioritise skill-based employability over local hiring quotas in order to ensure the youth of Odisha can be integrated into the tech ecosystem.

One dead and multiple injured after driver, 93, crashes into brunch diners on Jersey Shore
The driver reportedly hit the gas instead of the brake
One person was killed and seven others were injured when a 93-year-old crashed her SUV into a patio teeming with brunch diners on the Jersey Shore over the weekend.
The crash unfolded just after 11 a.m. on Saturday at Meg’s Grill in Lavallette, as a driver of a 2014 Buick Encore was reportedly trying to park — but hit the gas instead of the brake, sending her vehicle speeding into a group of diners, News 12 New Jersey reported.
The Buick plowed through the restaurant’s outdoor patio area and into the building, the Lavallette Police Department said.
Seven restaurant patrons were injured and taken to the hospital with varying degrees of injury.
A 56-year-old woman from Toms River, New Jersey, was killed in the crash, authorities said.
The 93-year-old driver, who was from Lavallette, suffered minor injuries from the crash.
The Lavallette Police Department has not publicly identified the driver, or shared the names of any of the victims.
None of the staff working at Meg’s Grill were injured in the crash, and the building was undamaged, the restaurant wrote on Facebook. Meg’s Grill is located just across the street from the local police department.
“Our building is fine and was undamaged. But I can’t say the same for our hearts. All of our thoughts and prayers are with the people who were hurt. We are closing tomorrow and Monday out of an observance of compassion for my staff and those affected,” the restaurant wrote.
“We plan to reopen Tuesday. If anything changes we will update. Please give an enormous hug to your loved ones tonight.”
Photos published by NJ.com from the scene showed significant damage to the exterior wall of the liquor store next door to the restaurant.

Carney touts Arctic alliance with Norway during PM's visit to Ottawa, amid Russia threat
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre warns of 'real threats' from the Kremlin
Prime Minister Mark Carney says his focus on building international relationships, including with Norway, is part of the answer to renewed threats from Russia.
During a news conference with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre in Ottawa on Sunday, both leaders were asked about warnings from the Polish prime minister that Russia may be planning attacks on European countries that support Ukraine.
Støre said those warnings should be taken seriously and that Norway's intelligence has concluded there are "real threats coming from hybrid activity, ranging all the way to potential sabotage."
Carney didn't comment on the credibility of the threats but said he agreed with Støre's statements.
"One of the advantages of this relationship and deepening across a broad range of relationships is, yes, greater intelligence sharing, greater perspective, greater capacities that are built together," he said.
Carney said that includes having the "right partners" among Arctic nations working together. "The phrase that always sticks with me ... is 'High North, low tension,'" he said.
The way to accomplish that, he said, includes submarine and space capacity.
In July, Carney chose to buy a dozen submarines from a European shipbuilder instead of a Korean firm, after a months-long, hotly contested bidding process. The chosen partnership involves a German company but partners with Norway, with the three nations collaborating to produce and maintain the submarines.
Carney said the "time spent, whether it's in the high north in Norway, a meeting with the French president who's directly implicated in a number of these decisions, our meeting today and beyond, it's all connected."
Before his meeting with Støre in Ottawa, Carney travelled to Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon to meet with French President Emmanuel Macron earlier in the day.
Støre's visit comes as Carney looks for closer ties with Europe, including potential "associate membership" in the European Union.
Norway is not a member of the EU, but for three decades the country has had a deal with the political and economic bloc that gives both sides free access to each other's markets for goods and services — and gives Norway access to most EU programs.
Carney is courting deeper defence ties with Norway, as well as investment from its massive petroleum-based sovereign wealth fund.
Carney was in Norway in March — the first sitting Canadian prime minister since 1980 to visit the Nordic country.
During that visit, the two leaders pledged to advance collaboration in fields ranging from Arctic security and space to critical minerals and energy. Carney and Støre also touted their reputations as low-risk global oil producers, amid supply shocks emanating from conflicts like U.S. President Donald Trump's war on Iran.
Norwegian officials have often described Canada as a similar country, given that both seek to balance a large oil sector with a push for green energy and respect for Indigenous people.
They both put an emphasis on using multilateral institutions to resolve disputes while identifying as strong proponents of NATO and deeply tied with the EU, without being members. Both countries have put support for Ukraine at the forefront of foreign policy, amid Russia's full-scale invasion that began in February 2022.
Since late 2024, Canada has had an Arctic foreign policy that calls for more intense ties with Nordic countries in defence, strategic sectors and environmental issues.

Should municipalities ban smart glasses in pools and change rooms?
Privacy advocates say yes, but cities say existing rules are sufficient
Some city councils are banning smart glasses in public changerooms to prevent people from being covertly recorded, but 10 Canadian municipalities contacted by CBC News say existing rules are sufficient.
In Australia, local councils in Sydney, Brisbane and in the Melbourne area banned them from public pools and change rooms, with one mayor going so far as to call them “pervert glasses” in introducing the motion.
The glasses were also recently banned by a Toronto dance venue.
Caitlin Stockwell, a lawyer running for municipal council in Vancouver, is calling for a similar ban there.
Stockwell noted it’s primarily women, children and gender diverse people who are being covertly recorded and harmed when the videos are posted online.
In the U.K., there are also reports of people asking for money to take the videos down.
“We think if there are extra rules in place that can reduce the likelihood of these glasses being used in that way, that's something that our city hall and park board should be looking into,” Stockwell said.
So far, the idea does not seem to be taking root across the country.
CBC News reached out to 12 Canadian cities to find out if any were considering a ban.
Ten responded by deadline. Representatives all said existing rules that prohibit the use of recording devices within these facilities also apply to smart glasses.
“The regulations already in effect across all of Montreal's aquatic facilities prohibit taking photos and recording videos inside the pool areas and locker rooms. These rules apply regardless of the type of device used,” a City of Montreal spokesperson said in an emailed statement that was typical of the responses CBC News received.
The City of Ottawa’s policy is under review, according to Tracey McGarry, the city’s director of complexes, aquatics and special services.
“Any updates would further clarify restrictions related to photography, video recording, audio recording, and livestreaming in recreation facilities. We have had no issues with smart glasses in city recreation facilities.”
But Stockwell says more proactive rules are needed because of the covert nature of the glasses.
“The issue that we're seeing that's unique with wearable recording tech is that it's actually really difficult to tell whether they're recording someone or not. So, a more proactive rule in place to restrict the type of harm that they can be used for is to prohibit wearing those glasses in those spaces altogether.”
Smart glasses have a light that indicates when they’re recording, but it isn’t always obvious and some people have tampered with it, an issue engineers at Meta, one of the companies developing these glasses, are grappling with.
The idea would be to have signage indicating smart glasses are not allowed in the facilities, Stockwell said.
“Letting people know these glasses are banned, it … increases the likelihood that more people will catch it, as opposed to just the person that's targeted by the filming themselves and might see the video after the fact.”
Lloyd Richardson, director of technology at the Canadian Centre for Child Protection in Winnipeg, says their organization is already seeing children targeted by covert recording.
This was the case before smart glasses, and it's not always clear what type of device was used to make the recordings, but the glasses make it easier to be inconspicuous, he says.
"We've seen what are obviously surreptitious recordings of children in bathrooms. We've seen it in daycares, we've seen it in pools. "
Richardson says he agrees with a ban in municipal facilities, but believes it needs to go further.
"I think we really need to like stand up to sort of sovereign law here and say ... you can't design a device like this. This is privacy invasive. It's harmful. And ... you can't ship them into Canada."
Stockwell says there are change rooms in Vancouver where cellphones aren’t allowed, and she was once reminded by another patron to put her phone away.
The Sydney-area ban excludes people with impairments who use the glasses for accessibility reasons, and Stockwell says she envisions a Vancouver ban having the same exemptions.
Policies
CBC News asked 12 municipalities whether they’re considering a ban on smart glasses in public facilities.
These responses have been edited for length and clarity.
Toronto: For any filming and photography in city parks, recreation facilities and recreation programming, an individual must not engage in filming and photography in washrooms and change rooms and obtain permission from staff prior to taking photographs or filming in active recreation spaces. We continue to review and evaluate our education and enforcement practices. Further refinements to our practices surrounding all filming tools, including smart glasses, will take place as we learn more.
Montreal: The regulations already in effect across all of Montreal's aquatic facilities prohibit taking photos and recording videos inside the pool areas and locker rooms. These rules apply regardless of the type of device used. Additionally, in several of its new facilities, the city has set up universal (or gender-neutral) locker rooms where nudity is not allowed.
Vancouver: The Vancouver Board of Parks and Recreation's pool guidelines state that the use of photographic devices, including cameras and cellphones, in fitness centres, swimming pools, and connected change spaces is not permitted without prior staff approval. While the park board does not currently have a specific policy regarding smart glasses, all patrons are expected to respect the privacy, safety and comfort of others when using our facilities. We continually review emerging technologies and consider their potential impacts on the privacy, safety and experience of patrons using our spaces.
Ottawa: The City of Ottawa’s current policy prohibits the use of electronic equipment with photographic capabilities in change rooms, washrooms, exercise rooms and swimming pool areas. It applies broadly to devices that can capture images or video and is not limited to specific technologies. Smart glasses with photo or video recording capabilities would be subject to the same restrictions as other photographic devices within these areas. The policy is currently under review, and any updates would further clarify restrictions related to photography, video recording, audio recording and livestreaming in recreation facilities. We have had no issues with smart glasses in city recreation facilities.
Edmonton: City of Edmonton recreation facilities prohibit the use of recording devices in change areas. This includes all devices that can record (photograph/picture, video and/or audio) and including, but are not limited to, cellphones, cameras, video recorders, laptops and tablets. Given that smart glasses have recording capabilities, they would also be prohibited in change areas. Recording devices can be brought into the space, but must be turned off and stored out of view (pocket, purse, locker). Patrons must leave the prohibited space before using the recording device, including speaking on the phone or texting.
Winnipeg: Recording devices are not permitted in washrooms, change rooms and locker rooms at City of Winnipeg facilities. We encourage patrons to report any unusual behaviour or the use of recording devices to on-site staff.
Quebec City: Quebec City prohibits the use of all electronic devices that can record, film and photograph in its swimming pools and change rooms. Smart glasses are included in this ban.
Hamilton: While the City of Hamilton does not have a specific bylaw governing the use of smart glasses in municipal recreation facilities, as with any device that may capture photos or video, we expect all facility users to respect the privacy and dignity of others, particularly in washrooms, change rooms and saunas, where photo taking is not permitted.
Kitchener: While the City of Kitchener does not have a bylaw or policy that specifically references smart glasses, we do have an existing policy that prohibits the use of cellphones, cameras, personal digital assistants and other electronic devices with photographic capabilities in change rooms and public washrooms at all city facilities. This policy is posted in all of our municipally operated recreation facilities. Devices with photographic or recording capabilities would generally fall within the intent of the policy. Our focus is on maintaining privacy and ensuring residents feel comfortable and safe when using city facilities, regardless of the type of technology involved.
Halifax: The Halifax Regional Municipality has a policy governing image recording and broadcasting at its recreation facilities, including pools. Recording is strictly prohibited in change rooms, washrooms and similar areas at all municipal recreation facilities. Recording in active recreation spaces, including pools and pool decks, is restricted and requires permission from facility staff. Staff may require consent or waivers from participants and/or parents or guardians. The policy applies to image recording and broadcasting using photographic and modern digital recording technology of any form, means or type.
Calgary and London: No response by deadline.

WASHINGTON — Health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Thursday named eight new members to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, an influential panel of experts who assess the evidence behind a wide array of preventive medical services.
They include a number of specialists, including in clinical nutrition, gastroenterology, and oncology, as well as a finance professor who has expertise in health insurance. It’s a major departure from the past, when the panel was made up of generalists, as opposed to specialists, to avoid prioritizing one area of medicine over another.
The independent body has more than advisory power because its assessments help determine whether health insurance companies are required to cover preventive services, such as mammograms and drugs to help prevent HIV. The newly appointed chair, Seth Corey, works in pediatric hematology-oncology at the Cleveland Clinic. He replaces Michael Silverstein, who departed from his role last year.
Kennedy has been critical of the 16-person group, which has been left with at least eight vacancies this year after five members rolled off at the end of their terms and the previous chair, Silverstein, departed on his own. Two members — vice chairs John Wong and Esa Davis — were fired in letters sent to them by Kennedy on May 11. The letters, viewed by STAT, said they were terminated due to a review of the current appointments.
The panel hasn’t met in more than a year, after its meetings were canceled by Kennedy. The most recent news on the USPSTF website dates back to August 2025. The group had previously signaled it was working on recommendations related to breast cancer genetic screening, pediatric autism disorder screening, and cervical cancer screening, among others.
Last year Kennedy said he planned to remove panel members, viewing them as too “woke,” but no new members had been named until now. His ability to remove members may be traced to a Supreme Court ruling issued in 2025, in the case Kennedy v. Braidwood Management, which established that the expert task force is under the authority of the health secretary.

College Sports Are Great
The accomplishments of athletes are every bit as impressive and legitimate as those of dancers, debaters, and oboists.
For a decade, I’ve been a member of a faculty committee that works closely with the athletics department at Northwestern University. A fellow professor once complained to me about the special admissions considerations that athletes receive, arguing that we could admit more oboists if athletes didn’t get so many spots. At the time, the university was being sued as part of athletics-department scandals involving sexual harassment and hazing. One case was dropped, and others were settled without the university admitting wrongdoing. During the same period, the university announced the construction of a brand-new football stadium that would be the most expensive ever built for a college team. It was a lot to digest all at once. In answer to my colleague, I nodded in agreement, thinking, Yeah, more oboists.
But as I considered the mission of our university—helping students decide what they want to do after college, cultivating the knowledge and skills they need to achieve their goals, supporting faculty research, and raising capital to ensure that we can continue to do that work—I became less certain that oboists are more desirable, and more qualified for admission, than athletes. Why do we think that, over the course of their life, oboists will make a greater contribution to society than linebackers? (I mean you no offense, kind oboists! The duck is my favorite character in Peter and the Wolf.)
On campus, many people remain doubtful that Northwestern’s athletics and academic missions are aligned, especially as football becomes more and more of a business sheltered by a university. Critics are right to lament the increased professionalization of college sports, but they also believe that most student athletes care more about their sport than their classes. Many academics see sports as frivolous and corrupting, as a distraction from the higher purpose of moral and intellectual formation—and as the most visible sign of the commercialization and corporatization of the modern university. We worry that out-of-control spending on sports could lead us to abandon our commitment to academic achievement.
Many, maybe even most, of these negative views of athletics held by my colleague and others are based on misconceptions. Take the complaint that student athletes are paid. Other students have the opportunity to get paid for work they do for the university and on their own behalf. We have a start-up incubator that has raised more than $1.6 billion in capital. Why shouldn’t athletes profit from the work they do too?
Our college athletes are hardly dumb jocks. As part of my work on the Committee on Athletics and Recreation (now called the Intercollegiate Athletics Committee), I’ve reviewed athletes’ selection of majors, academic performance, and travel schedules. I served on committees that hired our two most recent athletics directors. In my interactions with the athletics department and with student athletes in particular, I’ve been impressed, above all, by the emphasis they place on academic success, and how much effort they put into being students. I wish more of them wanted to major in my discipline, history, but that’s a different story.
Despite the seemingly constant negative attention paid to youth sports, I’m not convinced that parents of athletes put any more pressure on their kids than the parents of kids involved in other pursuits do. Northwestern’s Division I athletes worked as hard to get here as the oboists—or dancers, debaters, and comedians—did. Their accomplishments are every bit as impressive, and their chosen path every bit as legitimate.
Yet student athletes have told me that they sometimes feel like they don’t deserve to be here; that nonathletes don’t want to do group projects with them, either because they think that their practice and travel schedules will make them unreliable partners or that they are intellectual lightweights.
In fact, athletes do as well as nonathletes in their classes, and they typically get better grades during their active season of play compared with the offseason. As the director of our American Studies program, I met frequently with majors, one of whom was a runner on our varsity cross-country team. In addition to talking about her thesis or the classes she needed to graduate, we talked about the discipline necessary for her to maintain her 3.9 GPA. Her answers combined behaviors she learned from sports and from academics: physical activity, nutrition, sleep, good study habits. I learned a lot from her about a life well lived.
Student athletes do get support from tutors and advisers whom they’re required to meet with regularly. But nonathletes also have access to advisers, tutors, and other academic-support services. They aren’t required to use them, although it would benefit them if they did.
Athletes do miss a lot of classes, which grates on professors. On average, they miss maybe five days of class per quarter. In a nine- or 10-week quarter, that could amount to 15 or 25 percent of all class meetings. When athletes arrive on campus, their advisers tell them they can major in anything they want. That’s not entirely true, because some majors have requirements, such as lab time in the natural sciences, that conflict with practice or competition schedules. I wish they really could major in anything, but all students and not just athletes decide which classes to take and which subjects to major in based on their other curricular and extracurricular commitments, including work and family obligations. They’re also the only students who have to announce at the beginning of each quarter how many classes they’ll skip.
Football and, to a lesser degree, men’s basketball are fundamentally different from our 19 other varsity teams. These two sports spend and earn the majority of athletics-department revenue, are responsible for the most controversial changes to how college sports work, and receive almost all of the negative press. They make the system run and are inextricable from it. They, too, can add academic value.
To be transparent, I’m a fan. I’ve traveled to football bowl games in Nashville and Las Vegas, and March Madness basketball games in Sacramento, where I met recent and older alumni. To demonstrate how big-time college sports can help an entire university to prosper, a trustee pointed me to the example of Vanderbilt University, whose chancellor, Daniel Diermeier—previously on the faculty at Northwestern and the University of Chicago—has invested heavily in sports (especially football and basketball), written about the benefits to the university, and seen applications skyrocket and admissions rates dip. (There are also counterexamples; Northeastern University dropped its football program in 2009 and has still shot up the rankings.)
Over the past decade or so, applications from high-school students in the Northeast to schools in the Southeastern Conference—the Big Ten’s primary rival in athletics, in terms of prestige and television dollars—have increased by more than 90 percent. Perhaps it’s a coincidence, but most SEC schools have climbed in the academic rankings over the same period. Maybe they’ve ridden the wave of social-media posts of outdoor parties in February, or Bama Rush. But maybe a good football team, along with fancy dorms and good food, is considered by many incoming students to be an essential part of university life. Meal plans and residence halls aren’t core to our academic mission, either.
This fall, we’re debuting our new $875 million stadium. Our roster of college-football players will earn $21 million to $25 million to play this year, and our quarterback will make $1 million to $2 million. We’ve lured Chip Kelly to Evanston; as the former head coach of the NFL’s Philadelphia Eagles, he will be as much of a campus celebrity as an offensive coordinator can be. We’ve also landed a $35 million gift from the Uihlein family specifically for football. Mac Uihlein was a captain of the team last year. That donation has upset some of my peers not only because of the family’s politics—they’ve donated to pro–Donald Trump super PACs and national efforts to limit abortion rights—but also because it’s further evidence of our investment in sports at a moment of austerity for much of the university. It’s a big bet that spending so much on football will lead the team to victory and that competitive success will boost the whole university.
The dramatic transformation of college sports makes it harder for me to justify my fandom—to myself and others. Conference expansion has shattered pretenses to regional coherence. Athletes now sometimes attend three, four, or five schools during their college career. Federal courts have held that student athletes can be paid directly by universities and simultaneously earn additional income from sponsorships and advertisers. Amateurism as the model on which college sports are based has always been a half truth, but today it’s basically dead. These facts are enough to make one wonder what the college half of college sports even means.
As a faculty member, I’m fine with most of this, but with many reservations. When I taught a large lecture course on the history of college sports, I learned about a tackle named James Hogan, who played for Yale University from 1901 to 1904. He was in his mid-to-late 20s and didn’t pay tuition, and the university paid for his spring breaks in Havana. His story is a reminder that money has infected college sports for a long time.
Even so, I’m concerned that the money our athletes receive will affect my interactions with them as students in my classes. Instead of learning history, will they be focused on how to invest or spend the dollars the athletics department is paying them? Their labor for the university is more valuable than mine, so will they wonder why they should have to listen to me at all?
Yet I continue to believe that a university’s athletic and academic successes are complementary, if not connected. I still disagree with my colleague’s claim that sports drag down the more elevated intellectual and creative purpose of our institution. Football games and other sports connect generations of students, faculty, and alumni. Investments in athletics can boost a university’s academic reputation, along with our roster of poet laureates, Nobel Prize winners, and Marshall Scholars, and can also be a source of financial stability or even prosperity.
Even now, I think college sports, on balance, do more good than harm. It has been a rough period at Northwestern and other institutions of higher learning. I see sports as part of what holds us together as a community at the same time that they’re one more source of tension for others, such as my oboist-loving colleague. Yes, there’s too much money in the system, and that money can invite corruption that goes against our values. But there’s also too little attention paid to what college athletes gain from a university education, and what the rest of the university gains from having first-rate athletes here, in the classroom as well as on the field. The value of big-time college sports is real—for players, for fans, for professors—although you do have to work harder than ever to see it.

On dinner timing, weight management, emerging research, pain, disease prevention, healthcare gaps and more
(In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Athira Elssa Johnson writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)
What we eat, when we eat and how we manage our weight remain important questions in health, even as advice often runs ahead of the evidence. This week,I examine one deceptively simple question: is there a right time to have dinner?
Does eating late really affect our health? Is the time at which we eat more important than what we eat? And how should dinner timing be considered alongside sleep, work schedules, physical activity and the overall quality of the diet? Doctors explain what we know about meal timing, and what it can and cannot tell us about maintaining good health.
Close on the nutrition and weight-management front is a study from the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition, which looks at what works better for lasting weight loss. The study finds that combining diet and exercise is more effective for sustained weight loss than either approach alone. The findings are a useful reminder that weight management cannot be reduced to one food, one nutrient or one short-term intervention.
Meanwhile, the focus on protein continues to grow, particularly on social media. But increasing protein intake is not, by itself, a definition of a healthy diet. Ramya Kannan looks at what constitutes a wholesome meal and the importance of considering the overall dietary pattern rather than focusing on individual nutrients or products.
Emerging research
From everyday nutrition, we move to some interesting areas of emerging research.
Researchers are exploring whether material derived from menstrual blood could have applications in the treatment of osteoarthritis. A recent study as reported by Manjeera Gowravaram examined extracellular vesicles derived from menstrual blood stromal cells and their effects on processes involved in cartilage formation. The findings are from laboratory research and do not establish a treatment for osteoarthritis, but they add to growing interest in regenerative approaches to cartilage damage.
Another study reported by Anirban Mukhopadhyay takes a closer look at the genetic basis of cerebral palsy. Researchers found that far fewer genes may have a clear and reproducible association with the condition than some earlier studies had suggested. Understanding which genetic findings hold up is important not only for research but also for how clinicians interpret genetic information in people with cerebral palsy.
Diagnosis and care
There are also important questions about what happens within the healthcare system after patients seek care.
Dr. Suvira Jain writes about why one in three donated corneas is wasted. Eye donation does not automatically translate into transplantation. The cornea has to be retrieved, assessed, preserved and transplanted within the appropriate window. Gaps at different stages can mean that donated tissue is ultimately not used, even as many people continue to wait for corneal transplants.
Pain, too, can persist long after the original injury or illness has apparently healed. Persistent pain may require specialised assessment rather than being dismissed as something a patient simply has to live with. Afshan Yasmeen looks at why persistent pain can be complex and why appropriate pain management needs to go beyond treating the original condition.
Prevention and public health
On the disease prevention front, rabies remains an important public-health concern. Maya C. reports a study from Keralam that looks at the potential impact of dog vaccination in preventing rabies, underlining the importance of controlling the disease in its animal reservoirs alongside ensuring timely post-exposure care for people. Rabies prevention cannot depend on treating people after exposure alone; sustained vaccination and surveillance of dogs are central to controlling transmission.
The issue of counterfeit medicines also highlights why the quality and safety of healthcare products matter. A large stock of suspected counterfeit medicines was seized from a private facility in Bengaluru. Such cases raise concerns that go beyond regulation: a medicine that does not contain what it claims to contain, or does not meet required quality standards, can result in treatment failure and expose patients to further harm.
Air pollution remains another persistent health concern. A study examining winter pollution in north India finds that western disturbances explain a substantial share of the year-to-year variation in winter pollution. Weather systems are only one part of the pollution story, but understanding their role can improve forecasting and help strengthen public-health responses during periods when pollution levels are expected to rise.
Muscle metabolism, healthy ageing
For this month’s Nobel feature we look back at the work of Archibald V. Hill and Otto Meyerhof, whose Nobel-winning research helped establish how muscles generate and use energy. Their independent work helped explain fundamental aspects of muscle metabolism and the relationship between oxygen use, energy production and muscular activity.
And Health Wrap, Episode 50 looks at longevity and the role of racquet sports in healthy ageing, Navin Gnanasekaran, longevity physician and head of radiology, Apollo Hospitals, talk about healthspan, nutrition, sleep, muscle strength, stress, metabolism, inflammation and cognition. The conversation also looks at how racquet sports can bring together physical activity, social interaction and cognitive engagement, making them an interesting part of a broader discussion on maintaining health as we age.
And more:
Shanthi Dass looks at why physiotherapy matters, and the role rehabilitation can play in helping people recover function and manage health conditions.
Dr. Jyoti Bajpai writes about melanoma in India, and why the messaging around this potentially serious skin cancer needs to change to encourage earlier recognition.
Dr. Shivika Gupta looks at what to eat in the weeks before egg retrieval, addressing nutrition in the period leading up to an IVF procedure.
Bindu Shajan Perappadan reports on a WHO-linked study examining smoking and infertility, including the evidence on how quitting smoking can make a meaningful difference.
And in Keralam, health officials have sounded a caution as rising temperatures coincide with a fresh wave of fever cases in Ernakulam, another reminder of how seasonal and environmental changes can intersect with public health.

Iran issues chilling warning to US and its allies as tensions escalate
The State Department published a security alert noting the potential for unpredictable escalation
Iran issued a warning on Sunday against any major new offensive by the U.S. and its partners, saying it had intelligence that such an offensive move was being organized, heightening anxiety across a region already unsettled after recent drone and missile strikes on Saudi Arabia.
Iran’s military central command stated on state media that any fresh assault would provoke sustained retaliation against US military installations and interests, adding that Washington’s regional allies would be regarded as parties to the conflict.
The command did not elaborate on the specific information it claimed to possess regarding an impending US attack.
The State Department published a security alert on Saturday, noting the potential for unpredictable escalation in the Middle East and advising all American citizens to remain vigilant while anticipating potential commercial flight cancellations and possible regional airspace closures.
Nearly seven months after the outbreak of the U.S.-Iran war, neither side appears prepared to offer the significant concessions needed to end the combat.
As global energy markets face severe strain, the conflict continues to spill over into surrounding regional crises.
On Saturday, Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi movement, which made major territorial gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coastline after civil war reignited earlier this month, reported carrying out strikes targeting the Saudi capital Riyadh alongside a major petroleum installation in the kingdom’s Red Sea port of Yanbu.
Footage from Reuters showed a thick plume of black smoke rising near the main international airport in Riyadh following reports of explosions heard overnight in the capital.
Saudi Arabia did not issue a statement on the incident or the Houthi claims, although a Saudi-led coalition fighting the rebels stated it had intercepted separate attacks targeting the kingdom. The US State Department alert highlighted Houthi hostilities against Saudi Arabia, explicitly mentioning civilian airports.
The US Department of Defense did not immediately reply to a request for comment concerning the statement by Iran that it possessed intelligence about a coming American attack.
Recent territorial gains by the Houthis have forced Riyadh into a challenging strategic dilemma: continue airstrikes against the group to block further advances in Yemen, or withdraw to avert drone strikes against critical domestic energy infrastructure.
Houthi positions along the coast place the movement’s forces directly on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, facilitating greater control over commercial shipping traveling between the Red Sea and Asia and enabling a blockade of the crucial maritime waterway.
Because Iran has already blocked most maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, energy exports from the oil-dense Gulf region remain largely cut off from global markets, adding further upward pressure to international oil prices.
A concurrent U.S. blockade of Iranian ports prevents Tehran from selling its own oil, compounding severe economic distress inside the Islamic Republic.
With the conflict inflicting heavy damage on all sides, there is negligible indication of a return to the temporary ceasefire agreement reached in June, which collapsed in July following disputes regarding its precise conditions.
Iran reiterated on Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the terms of the June arrangement, as Tehran interprets them, are met.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf asserted that Iran must maintain both military operations and diplomatic talks to repel its enemies and secure its strategic objectives through diplomacy.

In September 2026, Snopes readers searched this website for information about a video allegedly showing a 104-year-old woman named Mabel Rose Thompson chiding U.S. President Donald Trump.
A search located a Threads post (archived) from Sept. 15 displaying the clip with the onscreen caption, "At 104, I've Seen 18 Presidents. Trump Was the Most Unforgettable." That Threads post featured the TikTok watermark for a user who previously posted (archived) the video and garnered more than 2 million views.
The video begins with the elderly woman saying she's seen 18 presidents during her lifetime — a number that would mean, given her age, that Warren G. Harding would have been her first president:
Mabel Rose Thompson here. I'm 104 years old. I've seen 18 presidents sit in that office. And I'm going to tell you something that will make half of you furious and the other half want to buy me a drink.
Donald Trump was the worst man I have ever watched lead this country. Not because of taxes, not because of tariffs, not because of any policy you want to argue about at Thanksgiving. Because of character, because of what he did to the American heart. Because in 104 years, I have never seen a president who worked harder to make good people hate each other.
Now before you start typing, let me establish my credentials. I was born in 1922. I was 9 years old when Herbert Hoover was still in office. And I remember my father cursing his name at our kitchen table because the man couldn't stop the hunger. I was 20 when Franklin Roosevelt died. My mother wept at the radio. I was 41 when they shot Kennedy in Dallas. I was folding laundry when the news came on. I dropped a towel and didn't pick it up for an hour. I was 53 when Nixon got on that helicopter, waving that ridiculous double peace sign, flying away in shame.
I have voted in every single presidential election since 1944. I have lived under Democrats and Republicans and men so boring you forgot they were there. I have watched them all. And I am telling you plain, none of them, not Nixon, not Johnson, not anyone, none of them damaged the soul of this country the way that man did.
Further searches for the "At 104, I've Seen 18 Presidents" caption, as well as a reverse image search, yielded what appeared to be the original video (archived) posted on the Real Talk With Time YouTube channel (archived). That clip displayed the same title, "At 104, I've Seen 18 Presidents … Trump Was the Worst." It also displayed YouTube's user-enabled label for artificial-intelligence content — a descriptor creators can select when they upload a video.
In sum, the video is fake and was generated using AI. "Mabel Rose Thompson" is a fake name. An AI tool generated the elderly woman, the room in which she supposedly sat and all of the visible objects in it.
Snopes emailed the YouTube channel's owner to ask what tools were used to make the videos, what inspired the clips and whether the channel's content is created simply to make money. The channel's only members-only video (watchable with a free trial that becomes a $9.99 recurring payment in the second month) showed a thumbnail image of a purported 112-year-old woman promising to tell how she avoided the diseases that killed her friends. We'll update this article if we receive further information.
Detecting signs of AI
Beyond the YouTube video's AI label, the elderly woman's waxy-looking skin (another common tell in AI-generated images) confirms its artificiality.
Readers can spot another of the more common signs of AI content by examining the area behind the old woman. The bookshelf is filled with books, none of which appear to have legible letters and numerals on their spines. According to Northwestern University's Kellogg Insight blog, illegible text is often an indicator of AI-generated images and videos.
A scan of one of the video's still frames by the Pangram AI-detection tool displayed a "Fully AI" result: "We believe that this image is fully AI-generated." A separate Pangram scan of the video's spoken text displayed concluded: "100% of this text is AI" and "We believe that this entire text is AI."
Snopes doesn't depend solely on AI detection tools, which vary in reliability, and instead considers the tools' results as one of several data points toward judging an image's authenticity. For Pangram, we bear in mind the platform's strong performance in third-party and internal evaluations, as well as criticisms of the tool.
For further reading, we previously debunked an AI-generated image supposedly showing quadruplet sisters posing with a cake on their 90th birthday.

This past summer, Samsung launched the Galaxy Watch9 alongside the Galaxy Watch Ultra2, its more rugged, shock-resistant smartwatch for outdoor adventures.
The Watch9 is the everyday option, and it’s a solid smartwatch and fitness tracker with a plethora of health features. It’s available in a 40-mm size in cream and graphite, and a 44-mm size in graphite and silver, starting at $80. Compared with last year’s Galaxy Watch8, it’s a modest update, though. There’s a faster processor, a slightly larger battery capacity, and an expanded suite of wellness metrics.
After two weeks of testing the 40-mm model, I wouldn’t necessarily upgrade to the Watch9 from the Watch8. But if you have an older Galaxy Watch or you’re invested in Samsung’s ecosystem and are looking for a smartwatch, the Watch9 is the best choice.
A Familiar (Squircle) Face
The Galaxy Watch’s main hardware update is its new processor. It now utilizes Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite platform, which Samsung claims enhances CPU and GPU performance along with efficiency. In testing, the watch responded smoothly when scrolling menus, launching apps, and dismissing notifications.
Wear OS 7 also adds more customizable widgets and live updates from compatible apps. One of the more exciting new additions is raise-to-talk for Gemini. Lift your wrist toward your mouth, and you can start talking to Google’s AI assistant. The Google Pixel Watch has had this feature for two generations now, so I’m happy to see Samsung finally catch up.
Samsung has also slightly increased the battery capacity. The 40-mm model has a 390-mAh battery (up from 325 mAh), while the 44-mm models get a 445-mAh cell (up from 435 mAh). Unfortunately, that doesn’t translate to an improvement in battery life, which is probably because it’s being used to power the watch’s expanded suite of health features (more on that later). Samsung still estimates up to 30 hours of battery life, but I averaged closer to 25 hours with Always-On Display enabled. That’s enough to get through a full day and night, but not enough to make charging something you can forget about. A full recharge also took me about 100 minutes on average, which is significantly longer than the 45 minutes it takes the Pixel Watch 5 to reach a full charge.
