In Summary
- New Apple CEO, John Ternus, announced a range of products at the Surprise and Shine event.
- While most of the focus was on the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, there was much more to the event than just devices and a CEO debut.
- We bring you eight takeaways that were buried in the buzz around the new devices, which might have escaped your attention.
It might not have surprised too many people – the leaks messed that up – but Apple did a fair bit of shining at its recent Surprise and Shine event. The event, which also marked John Ternus’ debut as Apple CEO at a launch, went on expected lines, with Apple revealing new AirPods, Apple Watches, new iPhone Pros and, of course, the iPhone Duo, which has grabbed the most attention. There was, however, much more to the event than just the launches. Here are our eight biggest takeaways from the day on which the world saw Apple’s new foldable and the CEO on stage:
Table of Contents
New Era? Presentation-wise, Apple is still Cook-ing (Pun intended)
Yes, it was John Ternus who held the reins at Surprise and Shine. But in terms of presentation style, the template that was followed was still from the menu of the preceding chef, Tim Cook. We had multiple speakers, elaborate backdrops, and a similar race through a number of products, leaving the most time for the star of the show (it was the Air last time around, the Duo this time). Yes, in terms of presentation style, Apple remains well ahead of the competition, although we miss the wit and humor of the past; this launch was more from the Cook manual than the Ternus one.
No surprises (Sigh)…
It’s been a while since Apple surprised the Dickens out of us at a launch, but in recent years, the brand’s product announcements have often been leaked out well in advance. And that was pretty much true this time around. From the iPhone Duo to the shades of Burgundy to the fact that there would be no suffix-less iPhone at the event, the leak community got a lot of things right, which, as we have said in the past, takes some of the mystique and surprise out of the event. Mind you, Apple did pull one rabbit out of its hat.
…except for the AirPods 5
There were no suffix-less iPhones at Surprise and Shine, but there sure were suffix-less AirPods. And while most of the noise was about Apple’s first foldable, the AirPods 5 might have emerged as the silent, value-for-money heroes of the show. While most people had been expecting new AirPods Pro with perhaps a camera built into them, Apple brought in a new version of the classic AirPods, complete with better ANC and battery life, even while retaining the “open” fit and, surprise, surprise, the same price tag as its predecessors. Not too many noticed…until the price of the Duo was announced, and suddenly a device with no price increase became the belle of the tech ball.
Hooray, we will now have TWO iPhone launches every year
Surprise and Shine marked the beginning of a new iPhone era, in which Apple will release its iPhones in two tranches over a twelve-month period. While Apple has released iPhones at two different times of the year in the past, the second launch has generally been a relatively low-profile and soft one (of the SE and ‘e’ mainly). That is set to change now. Even if Apple does a soft launch for the iPhone 18, the iPhone Air 2 and the iPhone 18e, rather than a full-fledged event, the fact is that close to half of the iPhone portfolio will be launched in the second half of the year, and the remainder in the first half of the next year. The iPhone schedules just got tweaked.
Apple is getting REALLY serious about AI (no, really, this time)
Two years ago, Apple launched the iPhone 16 series, saying it had been designed from the ground up for Apple’s avatar of AI, Apple Intelligence. However, AI is one area where the Cupertino brand has been found trailing the competition. So it was not surprising that the brand was clearly out to write a new chapter at Surprise and Shine. Every device it announced – iPhones, Apple Watches, AirPods – had a strong element of AI, which different presenters stressed would work wonderfully well, even while preserving the users’ security. Well, we have heard that a few times in the past, but never in such a comprehensive manner. Is Apple finally going to crack the AI puzzle? Based on what we saw, it would be no Surprise if it went on to Shine in that department in the coming months.
Whoop, Whoop, the Apple Watch is now a full-fledged fitness and health device, and is targeting Whoop
It started out trying to be a computer on your wrist, complete with apps, notifications and alerts, but the Apple Watch has of late graduated (or been demoted, depending on your perspective) to being mainly a health and fitness tracking device. And Surprise and Shine saw this trend continuing, with most of the talk about the Apple Watch 4 Ultra and Apple Watch Series 12 revolving around better sensors and measurement. The highlighting of features like Readiness Scores and Health Age seems to indicate that the Cupertino brand now has the screenless Whoop, which popularised these features, in its sights.
The narrative is unmatched, but is now very hardware-driven!
Processors, camera apertures, health sensors, ANC, battery life…these formed the major part of the narrative around Surprise and Shine, showing how Apple’s has shifted from storytelling to specs at its launches in recent times. This might be fine for some, but we do miss the time when an announcer would walk us through nuances of design and amazing (or they called amazing, and often, unbelievable) features on devices.
Yes, Apple remains the lord, master, and commander of product launches, but we prefer tales to tech, and a live presenter on stage to edited videos, no matter how sleekly edited. The fact that the Duo section stood out from the others because of its stress on design and UI only reinforces our belief that Apple might perhaps reconsider going back to its storytelling roots, and leave the specs on the spec sheet, rather than on the speech notes. Everyone else talks specs anyway.
Cosmic orange is out of the Apple cosmos… and Black is back!
This was so typically Apple. After making orange the color of the last twelve months, courtesy of the Cosmic Orange variant of the iPhone 17 Pro series, and making a number of brands come out with orange phones and other devices (JBL even had a pair of headphones in orange), the Cupertino giant pushed the shade out of its color palette. It also brought back the one color that everyone had missed in the Pro series – Black. Henry “Any Color As Long As It Is Black” Ford and AC/DC would approve of the return of the color, and so do we. We are not shedding any tears for orange, although we suspect those orange Pros are going to have great antique value some day.
And one more thing…
Craig Federighi’s hair looks as awesome as ever!

How an Aston Villa fringe player became Europe's most prolific scorer
- Published
Just eight months ago, Donyell Malen was struggling to make a significant impact at Aston Villa.
Today, no player in Europe's top five leagues has scored more goals since his Roma debut on 18 January.
The Netherlands international has enjoyed a remarkable turnaround since joining Roma, transforming from a player who struggled to establish himself in the Premier League into one of the continent's most productive forwards.
Europe's hottest scorer
Since his Roma debut, Malen has scored 20 goals, more than Harry Kane (16), Lamine Yamal (15) and anyone else in the Premier League, La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga and Ligue 1 during the same period.
He also leads the way for combined goals and assists with 22, ahead of Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes (20), Barcelona's teenage sensation Lamine Yamal (19) and Bayern striker Kane (18).
No player across Europe's top five leagues has made a greater contribution in front of goal.
Why Roma's system suits him?
The contrast with his time at Villa could hardly be greater.
In 46 appearances for the Premier League club, the 27-year-old scored 10 goals and registered two assists. Since joining Roma, he has scored 21 goals and provided three assists in just 25 matches.
His scoring rate has improved from one goal every 149.8 minutes at Villa to one every 96.7 minutes in Rome.
On the surface, the figures suggest two very different versions of the same player. But Roma's success with Malen may owe as much to how he is being used as to any change in confidence or form.
The Dutchman arrived in Italy with a proven goalscoring pedigree and the data suggests Roma have found a role that maximises his attacking instincts.
While confidence and form may have played a part, a change in position appears to be a major factor behind the resurgence.
At Villa, Malen was often used across the frontline and spent only 52% of his league minutes as a central striker. At Roma, 99% of his Serie A minutes have come through the middle under manager Gian Piero Gasperini, making him the focal point of the attack and placing him where he can do the most damage.
The stats are backed up by the eye test. After Roma's 1-1 Champions League draw with Fenerbahce last Thursday, when Malen set up his side's goal, French football journalist Julien Laurens told Match of the Day the Dutchman had become central to Gasperini's plans.
"He has been incredible since January," said Laurens.
"He has been really efficient, super clinical. Malen is at the heart of everything they do with the ball."
Following a familiar Serie A trend
Malen is not the only former Premier League player to have flourished in Italy.
Former Manchester United midfielder Scott McTominay has thrived since swapping Old Trafford for Naples. Since joining Napoli in August 2024, only five players have scored more Serie A goals than the Scotland international's 22.
His impact has been such that Napoli supporters have even erected a street shrine in his honour.
Former Manchester United striker Rasmus Hojlund has also enjoyed an upturn in fortunes. His time in north west England divided opinion among supporters and pundits alike.
But since his Napoli debut, only Federico Dimarco, Lautaro Martinez and Malen have recorded more goal involvements than the Denmark international (19).
Their success highlights how a move to Serie A can provide players with the opportunity to thrive in a different environment and role.
For Malen, however, the transformation has been particularly dramatic.
Rather than changing Malen's game, Roma appear to have found a role that gets the best out of him. Used almost exclusively as a striker, the Dutchman has responded by producing the kind of form that first brought him to the attention of Europe's biggest clubs.
For a player whose Premier League spell failed to meet expectations, his resurgence in Italy's capital ranks among the most notable revivals in European football this year.

Protection for women who defy the Mafia is changing in Italy. Does it go far enough?
Practical, emotional toll can be tougher for women who speak out against the Mafia
"Take a map of Italy, tear Sicily from it and throw it away."
That was the advice the late anti-Mafia prosecutor Paolo Borsellino gave a young Piera Aiello in 1991, when she came to him to say she was ready to tell all about the Sicilian Mafia family she had married into.
Aiello's husband had been gunned down in front of her in the pizzeria they ran together. He was the abusive son of the local Mafia boss, and Aiello had been coerced into marrying him as a teen. Still, she wanted his killers caught.
"I have already decided," she recalls telling Borsellino about her decision to testify. "I just need to pack my bags."
Three days later, Aiello left Sicily with two suitcases — one filled with clothes, the other with toys for her three-year-old daughter.
The following year, Borsellino was killed, along with five members of his police escort, in a Mafia car bombing in the Sicilian capital of Palermo.
Aiello would spend most of the next three decades living under another identity, which kept her safe from the Mafia.
But cut off from her Sicily and her old life, building a new one was lonely and arduous.
"I couldn't find work, and I had to support my daughter," she said, explaining how she found work in the countryside harvesting olives, eventually saving enough to open a small business.
Aiello's early years in protection reveal a less visible aspect to Italy's long fight against organized crime: what happens after someone speaks out. For women, the rupture can be both practically and emotionally tougher.
A new Italian law extending protection from organized crime — and providing social, economic, educational and psychological help — to children and the adults caring for them, often their mothers, is designed to address some of those gaps.
Limits of protection
Liberi di scegliere — the "Free to Choose" bill — became law in July and entered into force on Aug. 9.
Sen. Vincenza Rando spent years pushing for the law and working with women who wanted to break away from Mafia families. Many of them, she says, fall outside the categories around which Italy's traditional protection system had been built.
"Women who are neither justice witnesses nor co-operating witnesses, I call them 'cultural collaborators.' They leave that environment and build a culture of legality," Rando said.
They may not be informants or have any useful intel about a murder, a drug shipment or an extortion racket. Their act of rebellion, she says, may simply be deciding that their children will not grow up inside a Mafia family and culture.
Rando says some leave homes flush with cash, only to end up with nothing. Others need a new identity just to sign an employment contract without being traced. Their children are forced to change schools and friends, thrust into a life with entirely different moral codes.
"If you move somewhere where nobody knows you and you cannot even say who you are, who can you talk to?" Rando asked. "Who can you safely tell your story to?"
Under the new legislation, people under the age of 25 and relatives who care for them may be relocated outside their home region, provided with education and psychological support and, where necessary, given new identities.
Critics say the law gives the state too much power over family life, allowing for the separation of children from parents, which could be seen as punishing children for their parents' crime.
But Rando and supporters say the law prioritizes keeping mothers and children together when the mother breaks with the criminal group.
Aiello supports its aims, but worries short-term intervention will not be enough to permanently break the cycle. She says longer-term support through education and job training is essential.
"What does it mean for the State to take responsibility for them for two years?" Aiello asked. "It means nothing."
For Aiello, the lesson from her own experience is that protection has to mean more than physical safety: it also has to provide the tools to build an independent life.
The 'privilege' of never walking alone
Anti-Mafia prosecutor Nino Di Matteo has spent most of his career seeing the cost of protection from the inside.
He has lived under police escort since 1993, at times under Italy's highest level of security. His two children were born while he was already under protection; within days of leaving hospital, he recalls, they too were travelling in an escort car.
Now based in Rome, he says people outside Sicily sometimes perceive police protection as a mark of status, which he says irritates him.
"People can tend to see the protected person as privileged," Di Matteo said. "From that point of view, I would rather not be 'privileged.' People should perhaps think about the sacrifice involved in never being able to take a walk alone."
Di Matteo is equally wary of a lot of the mythology surrounding the Mafia itself. He points to the media's focus on its most cinematic elements of violence and overt criminality — "the so-called military Mafia" — rather than the white-collar Mafiosi who appear to be part of legitimate businesses and cultivate relationships with political and institutional power.
And he says women's roles in that world have also frequently been misunderstood.
"Women have always played a fundamental role, for both good and bad," Di Matteo said.
Some wives and mothers are the family enforcers of the Mafia identity of husbands and sons. Others have rebelled against it — often painfully breaking away — to become justice witnesses and campaigners.
"For a woman I imagine it may be even harder," Di Matteo said of criminal organizations built heavily around kinship. "Especially when speaking out means accusing your own son, your own blood."
When Mafia threats reach your family
Federica Angeli came to protection by a very different route.
An investigative journalist in Ostia, Rome's gritty seaside district, Angeli spent years reporting on local criminal clans and their grip on parts of Ostia's lucrative beachfront economy.
In 2013, during one investigation, Mafia boss Armando Spada discovered the hidden camera she was carrying. Angeli says he detained her upstairs in a room, placed a gun between them and made clear that he knew where she was most vulnerable.
"You have three children. What shall we do?" Angeli remembers him saying to another man. "Shall we start with the youngest one, the one with the pretty eyes?"
A month later she witnessed an attempted double murder near her home. She testified and was placed under police protection.
For 13 years, armed escorts have followed Angeli through ordinary life: work, dinner out with friends, a day at the beach, family outings. She says friends stopped inviting her over because security officers first had to inspect their homes. Restaurants meant being seated according to security requirements. Spontaneity vanished.
Angeli chronicled her ordeal in the memoir A mano disarmata (Unarmed), later adapted into a feature film. In 2016, Italian President Sergio Mattarella made her a Knight of the Order of Merit of the Italian Republic.
But despite the public recognition, the beachfront clean-up in Ostia has sometimes generated resentment: Angeli says she hears residents complain that some establishments worked better under Mafia-linked operators. Other criticism aimed at her is more gendered.
"As a woman, and as a mother, I was heavily criticized for my choice," she said. "Everyone said, 'You put your children in danger,'" who for five years were placed under protection, too, due to threats.
But she rejects the idea that there is one correct maternal response.
"There is no handbook for being the right mother," she said of the decision to denounce organized crime. "But I wanted to free my children from having to bow to the Mafia."
Piera Aiello wanted the same thing for her daughter when she left Sicily.
She built a new life near Rome, and in 2018, she was elected to parliament — Italy's first sitting justice witness — after a long battle to regain her real name. She sat on the Antimafia and Justice committees, where she pushed for stronger witness protections.
And, this summer, more than three decades after Borsellino told her to tear Sicily from the map, she moved back to her beloved island.
"I kept that crumpled piece of Sicily in a drawer," she said, "And I picked it up and glued it back on."

Former England forward Andros Townsend was nearly run over by a motorised pitch roller while warming up with his Prachuap teammates at half-time during a Thai League 1 match on Saturday.
The 35-year-old avoided serious injury and later made a brief appearance in the match at Pattani.

Townsend got back up and continued practicing, and came on as a late substitute while Prachuap cruised to a 3-0 victory.
“Turns out Stoke away wasn’t so bad after all,” Townsend later wrote on Instagram, joking about the English side Stoke City’s reputation as a tough place for visiting teams to play.

Trump’s arch would be a ‘military complex’ hosting drones, snipers
Trump has been calling the new White House ballroom a ‘military complex’ while arguing it is necessary for national security purposes
President Donald Trump said on Sunday that the massive arch he wants to build between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery would become a “top grade military complex” able to host drones and snipers while storing ammunition.
It is one more example of how Trump is insisting that his initiatives to beautify the White House and the city are also serving a defensive purpose. Trump has been calling the new White House ballroom a “military complex” and arguing it is necessary for national security purposes.
Trump’s announcement also comes as the arch, like his other projects, faces legal challenges. Though the arch has received early approval from the US Commission of Fine Arts, whose members were all tapped by Trump, a group of three veterans and an architectural historian sued, saying the project needs to be approved by Congress.
The Republican president said in a social media post that he had agreed, at the “strong request” of the military, to convert the planned 250-foot-tall (76-metre) memorial arch “into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch, to house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage.”

Flooding around the city of Malda in the Indian state of West Bengal since Thursday has had a devastating effect. So far, three deaths have been recorded and many areas are still flooded, with numerous villages affected, along with the region of Bhutni. Erosion from the flooding, reported from Khaskol, led to a disruption in river flow which led to a more severe impact in Bhutni. More than 100 boats have been sent out for evacuation.
At East Basudevpur, a 20ft (6-metre) embankment collapsed, reducing the channel from 550ft to under 150ft, which could lead to further flooding unless repaired. This flooding resulted after the Ganges River rose about 75cm above its “extreme danger” level owing to heavy rainfall.
A swell caused by Hurricane Marie led to significant beach erosion across Orange county in California on 7 September. The erosion formed a cliff edge on some of the beaches, along with exposing old asphalt, pipes and even pieces of an old pier. The flooding caused by the swell damaged homes and vehicles, as well as flooding streets, leaving behind a layer of sand. The swell has been estimated to be between 8 and 10ft tall. Local people say it is not uncommon to see beach erosion, but this has been one of the most severe cases.

U.S. childcare costs are astronomical. More families are turning to grandparents
A few years ago, when Stacia Bourne and her husband would talk about having a second child, the conversation often turned to money.
"We were thinking we couldn't afford it," said Bourne, a University of Delaware psychology professor who lives in Maryland.
Their first child, George, was born in 2020 and started daycare when he was 2. "The cost for childcare for him is about the same as our mortgage," Bourne said. The prospect of taking on the expense of another child gave the couple pause when deciding whether to grow their family.
That was until Bourne's mother, Mary Jo Galusha, 67, made an offer: If Bourne wanted to have another baby, Galusha said, she'd retire and relocate from Idaho to the East Coast to help provide childcare.
Several months later, her phone rang. "I got a call that Stacia was expecting and that I better start planning on retiring," Galusha recalled with a laugh.
She retired from her job as a schoolteacher, packed up her belongings and drove cross-country in her red Volkswagen Beetle. The grandmother of five now lives in Newark, Del., and has since traded in the VW Bug for an SUV in order to fit two car seats in the back row more easily. Robin, who was born in late 2024, spends around 30 hours a week in Galusha's care while Bourne and her husband work.
"It's a joy," Galusha said. "It's like magic to watch them grow up."
Grandparents helping to take care of their grandchildren is nothing new. But the surging cost of childcare in the U.S. has made familial support even more critical for some parents who need childcare and may not otherwise be able to afford it.
According to the group Child Care Aware of America, the average annual cost of childcare for children under 5 in the U.S. in 2025 was $13,184. In some cases, even higher childcare costs can rival the price of rent or college tuition.
Families that are unable to shoulder those expenses or find open seats at daycare facilities are increasingly leaning on older generations for help, said Nicole Jorwic, chief program officer at the national caregiving group Caring Across Generations.
"The reality is that because this country hasn't invested in a childcare infrastructure that is flexible and affordable and reliable, grandparents are filling in the gaps that the service system leaves behind," she said.
A growing need for childcare
A heap of factors is making finding suitable childcare a necessity for a growing number of families across the U.S., said Madonna Harrington Meyer, a Syracuse University sociology professor who studies aging and grandparenting.
For one, the number of households where both parents work full time has steadily risen in recent decades. According to Pew Research Center, 52% of different-sex couples with kids had two parents working full-time jobs in 2025, compared with just 31% in 1975.
There has also been a steady increase in the number of single moms in the U.S. over the course of decades. And families of children with disabilities — of which there are a growing number nationwide — often struggle to find childcare providers that can offer the specialized care necessary.
"All of these things are reasons people turn to grandparents," Harrington Meyer said.
One of those grandparents is Jerry Larkin, 66, a former machinist who moved in with his daughter's family in Tulsa, Okla., during the COVID-19 pandemic to help take care of his twin grandsons, one of whom requires additional medical care.
Larkin said he used to think he was alone in devoting so much time to caregiving, until he learned through social media and elsewhere that many families struggle with similar issues and have come to rely on grandparents for an extra hand.
"Being raised in the '60s, there were a lot of stay-at-home moms and everything, so this wasn't really a thing," he said. "But now that everybody's got to work two jobs, it's become a thing."
Why grandparents help
Nowadays, millions of grandparents are pitching in to care for their grandchildren. One poll found that nearly half of respondents with grandchildren under age 18 took care of them at least once every few months.
According to an AARP report on grandparents from June, the top reasons grandparents provide care are the children's parents are working or busy, and it allows the grandparents to spend quality time with their grandkids.
The median amount of time grandparents spent caring for their grandchildren (excluding grandparents who are their primary caregivers as well as those who provide no care) is 200 hours per year, or roughly 3.8 hours per week, AARP data shows.
Harrington Meyer said parents often find it easier to have grandparents look after their children than other childcare arrangements, since they may already have shared parenting philosophies and since the care comes at no or minimal cost. (AARP estimated that grandparents provide around $731 billion worth of unpaid caregiving annually.)
"But perhaps the biggest benefit is that they are so flexible," Harrington Meyer added. "Unlike a formal daycare situation, often grandparents will come to your house, or they'll alternate between watching the children at their own house and at the grandparent's house."
And it's not just kids and parents who benefit, but also grandparents themselves. Older people may experience a mental boost by tending to their grandchildren, with one study showing higher scores on memory and verbal fluency tests in grandparents who provided care.
A sacrifice for grandparents
Yet caregiving is still work, particularly for older people who've raised their own children already and may be contending with health issues or other problems brought on by age. Watching grandchildren can take a physical toll on grandparents and may impinge on their social lives, especially if they've relocated to be closer to their grandchildren and moved away from friends.
When JD Vance suggested during the 2024 presidential campaign that one solution to high childcare costs was for more grandparents to provide care for free, critics pointed out that not all grandparents can or want to provide care, many older people need care themselves, and it would do nothing to address the lack of government investment in the childcare system.
Yalanda Lattimore, 59, thinks about the career trade-off she has made by volunteering to care for her 1-year-old granddaughter, Mavee. Lattimore provides "granny daycare" one and a half days each week.
She has worked as a blogger and podcaster in Atlanta and now also sells handmade soaps online. But when Mavee came along, Lattimore told her daughter she'd help provide care for the infant — even if it meant she had less time for her soap business and media career.
"I felt like I could make the sacrifice more than they could, and it truly has been a sacrifice," she said. "You just put things on hold, because your priorities are different."
U.S. workers are staying on the job longer than they used to, with more than 11.7 million Americans age 65 and older in the labor force last month, according to government data.
Lattimore said she hopes to work more but doesn't want to drive for Lyft again, which she did when she was taking care of her ailing mother. She has otherwise struggled to find a job that would let her take off one weekday for childcare and avoid lifting heavy loads.
"Where does flexibility exist at this point?" she said. "Is it anywhere besides the gig economy?"
Harrington Meyer, the Syracuse professor, said she has heard another complaint in her conversations with grandparents: that they are spending too much time with their "parenting" hats on and have fewer opportunities for carefree fun with the kids, a generally agreed-upon right of grandparenthood.
"They would say, 'I would love to take the grandkids to the zoo, but I'm too busy helping them with their calculus or too busy helping them get to flute lessons on time.'" she reported. "They were doing a lot of things that they regarded as parenting and didn't have as much time left over for a trip to the park or something fun and frivolous that they would like to do as grandparents."
Making it work
For Mary Jo Galusha, who moved to Delaware to help care for her grandchildren, the lack of pay for being with 23-month-old Robin is possible thanks to her pension from her years as a schoolteacher in Idaho. Her Newark home has a bedroom for her grandchildren, a playroom filled with Legos and even a crafting area for 5-year-old George.
Galusha and her daughter share a Google Calendar where they coordinate care for the kids, and the plan is for Galusha to look after Robin until she starts kindergarten. But Galusha and Bourne, her daughter, review the arrangement every six months or so, and Bourne acknowledges that there is little in the way of a backup plan.
"I'd much prefer to have my mom take care of Robin, but then you always worry, like if in six months she decides that she wants to move and be near another grandbaby, then we'll have to scramble and figure out something else," she said. (Galusha replied from across the table: "No plans for that.")
Lattimore, for whom being a grandmother has been an "amazing journey," relishes her days with Mavee. "What you really want is somebody to say you were there, that you were there for them," she said. "Those are the memories that I want."
But Lattimore points out that something has to give in the caretaking formula in general, where parents are often choosing between paying for care or staying home from work. Lattimore remembers trying to "climb the corporate ladder" while she was raising her four and said she wanted to try to spare her daughter the same dilemma.
"When my daughter got ready to start her family, I just didn't want her to go through that," she said. "I wanted her to have the balance. … If work-life balance exists for somebody, I wanted it for my daughter."

Did you know that an Indian woman scientist had a notable role to play in the development of anti-epileptic drugs and anti-malarial drugs? That the same woman also told us most of what we needed to know about the medicinal plants in the subcontinent?
By the standards of her time, unlike other women scientists, Asima Chatterjee did get recognition for her research while she was alive, but it cannot be said that she received the adulation and celebration that her male peers did. That doesn’t make Asima Chatterjee any less tall a figure in the history of Indian science, and the nation must be grateful for her pioneering work in organic chemistry and the sub category of phytomedicine – using plant extracts to treat various conditions, even prevent them.
109 years ago, Asima Chatterjee was born, on September 23. Her love affair with chemistry began at a young age and she went on to pursue this, with a Bacherlor’s degree and a masters in the subject. At a time when few women were able to take up higher education, she went on to complete her Doctor of Science degree in pre-independent India, specialising in phytochemistry. History records her as the first Indian woman to be awarded a Doctor of Science by any Indian university. She went on to gain expertise in research methodology at the University of Wisconsin, Madison and the California Institute of Technology, working with international experts in the field before returning to India.
She took a great interest in a sector that sought to harness the natural plant biodiversty of India and phytochemistry skills to develop newer compounds and drugs that could be used to treat people. Today plant-based extracts form key elements of critical drugs. Plant-derived drugs range from pure compounds extracted from herbs to complex botanical extracts approved as prescription medications. Chatterjee sank herself into the development of clinically useful drugs from indigenous plants – striking success with isolating the chemical constituents of Marsdenia tinctoria – which led to the formulation of the anti-epileptic drug later marketed as Ayush- 56.
Chatterjee also made huge breakthroughs in developing anti-malarial drugs derived from plant extracts. But the greatest achievement that she is credited with is her extensive research on the chemistry of alkaloids found in Caranthus roseus, or the Madagascar periwinkle, which contributed leaps to the understanding of compounds with anti-cancer properties. No less important is the foundation she laid for modern pharmaceutical chemistry, utilising physical and chemical methods to to determine the complex molecular structures of numerous organic compounds, and recording her methodology meticulously.
Beyond her pioneering work in the lab, Chatterjee was also an ace institution builder and educationist. During her academic career, she served as a professor of chemistry at the University of Calcutta at a time of intense gender barriers in academia, and was later appointed as the Khaira Professor of Chemistry, a prestigious chair in the varsity.
Her work in science was recognised with a Padma Bhushan in 1975, Chatterjee creating a record here too, being the first woman scientist to achieve this honour. She was the first female scientist to be elected as the General President of the Indian Science Congress Association and was also a Fellow of the Indian National Science Academy. No wonder then that she was the first female recipient of the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize in Chemical Sciences (1961), India’s top science award, introduced in 1958. She was also awarded the prestigious CV Raman Award and PC Ray Award.
Today, as the debate rages about bringing scientific vigour and scientifically validating traditional systems of medicine in the country, Chatterjee was a beacon even in this area, her work bridged the gap between traditional Ayurvedic knowledge and modern rigorous chemical analysis, to benefit humanity. Legacy
But Asima Chatterjee’s achievements cannot be confined to just the scientific arena, her immense achievement must also be counted at a time when formidable gender barriers stood in the way of female achievements, breaking the glass ceiling and making it possible, even inspiring, generations of women scientists to make their bold foray into the sciences. Being that rare Indian women scientist who got substantial recognition during their lifetime, in the scientific world, and yet she was largely missing from mainstream narratives, and global histories of science.
But today, we say her name, properly celebrate her legacy. Asima Chatterjee, exceptional chemist, phytochemist and extraordinary pioneering scientist who opened the portals the world of science for generations of women. Say her name, say Asima Chatterjee.

WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump’s administration has prepared sanctions against the entire International Criminal Court (ICC) and plans to announce them soon, two sources familiar with the matter said, a move that would step up its attack on the global tribunal that prosecutes war crimes and genocide worldwide.
The Trump administration has made no secret of its disdain for the court and has worked to undermine it. U.S. officials want the court to drop its arrest warrants against Israeli leaders as well as a past probe into American troops in Afghanistan.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio in July announced a campaign to isolate the court, calling on other countries to withdraw from the tribunal. Washington has imposed sanctions on a number of ICC judges and prosecutors but has so far held off from imposing sanctions on the court itself, although the move has long been considered as one of the options.
The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Sanctions against the court have been prepared, the sources said, even though the exact timing of an announcement remained unclear. The Wall Street Journal cited officials who said the decision could be finalized as soon as this week during the United Nations General Assembly meeting.
Targeting the entire organization directly, as well as entities that cooperate with it, could severely undermine the court’s work.
Any entity-wide sanctions imposed by the U.S. Treasury would prohibit U.S. citizens and companies from providing funds, goods, or services to the court without a license from the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). Banks often over-comply with such U.S. sanctions because they depend on access to the American financial system.
Among the court’s operations that could be affected by sanctions against the entire organization are the purchasing of IT services and insurance, the hiring of investigators and conducting everyday financial transactions, such as paying dozens of American employees, the ICC’s registrar and president have warned.
Trump’s opposition to the court goes back to his first term. It surfaced again with a plan to penalize ICC officials, an idea developed in November 2024 when Trump was reelected and the ICC issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza conflict.
The ICC was established in 2002 by the international community to prosecute war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. It asserts jurisdiction only if a member state is unable or unwilling to prosecute atrocities itself.
The United States has never been a member.

Premium flexible workspace operator Innov8 Workspaces sharply improved its profitability in the fiscal year FY26 while rapidly expanding the network of centres it operates across the country. Innov8's net profit surged nearly 11.8X to ₹13.8 Cr in FY26 from ₹1.2 Cr in FY25, as per its annual report. Important to highlight that the startup's profitability took a 97% hit in FY25 from ₹37.7 Cr in FY24. Meanwhile, operating revenue rose 76% to ₹201.3 Cr from ₹114.5 Cr, while EBITDA net of lease increased 64.6% to ₹49.4 Cr from ₹30 Cr. The company had projected its FY26 I-GAAP EBITDA to double to ₹60 Cr back in September 2025. The sharp improvement in the bottom line was also aided by a notable uptick in non-operating revenue. Innov8 reported ₹38.9 Cr in other income during FY26, more than 12X the ₹3.1 Cr recorded in the previous year. A substantial portion of this came from a ₹36.7 Cr gain on termination of lease contracts. Including other income of ₹38.9 Cr, the total income stood at ₹240.2 Cr in FY26, a 104.4% increase from ₹117.5 Cr in the previous year. Revenue Nearly Doubles In Two Years Innov8's growth has accelerated considerably over the past two years. Operating revenue increased from ₹52.7 Cr in FY24 to ₹114.5 Cr in FY25 and further to ₹201.3 Cr in FY26. In this, rental income remained the company's primary source of revenue, contributing ₹173.6 Cr, or around 86% of operating revenue, in FY26. This was up 59.3% from ₹108.9 Cr in FY25. The company also generated ₹27.6 Cr from other operational income, while revenue from the sale of food and beverages stood at ₹15.5 Lakh. Other operational income rose sharply from ₹5.4 Cr in FY25, indicating that ancillary services are becoming a larger part of the company's revenue mix. The annual report says the growth was driven by expansion of the portfolio, higher occupancy, improved pricing and the scaling of its managed workspace business. Innov8 follows a landlord-led capex model in which landlords fund the fit-outs while Innov8 provides the brand, demand generation, design and operations. This model allows the company to expand without taking on the entire fit-out burden for new centres. Innov8 said this asset-light structure has allowed it to open a new centre roughly every three weeks over the past 15 months. Innov8 ended FY26 with 58 operational centres, adding 16 centres during the year. The expansion continued after the end of the fiscal year. The company added another 14 centres in the three months following March 31, 2026, taking its network to 72 centres as of July 2026. It has set a target of reaching 101 centres during FY27. Importantly, the company plans to expand to 22 cities during FY27, with Kochi, Coimbatore, Kolkata and Jaipur among the cities identified for expansion. It continues to focus on business districts and commercial clusters in cities including Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Chennai. Its stated strategy is to prioritise high-density commercial locations rather than pursue suburban volume. Vatika Acquisition Adds Enterprise Business One of the biggest developments after the close of FY26 was Innov8's acquisition of Vatika Business Centres Private Limited. The company entered into a share purchase agreement on June 8, 2026, to acquire the entire share capital of Vatika Business Centres for ₹27 Cr. The transaction closed on June 18, with 80% of the consideration payable at closing and the remaining 20% due three months later. Innov8 paid ₹10.2 Cr at closing, according to the annual report. The acquisition gives Innov8 an established managed-office platform and is expected to strengthen its enterprise workspace business. The company said Vatika brings marquee enterprise clients on long-term commitments and provides further room for expansion in the managed-office segment. "Our ambition has always been to build premium workspaces that combine thoughtful design, vibrant community, enterprise-grade infrastructure and fully managed services, while giving businesses the flexibility to adapt as their needs evolve... A customer can begin with five seats and grow to five hundred without ever leaving the Innov8 network. Our expansion into managed workspaces, including through the acquisition of Vatika Business Centres Private Limited, completes that ladder," said Rakesh Kumar, director and CFO, Innov8. Breaking Down Innov8’s Expenses The company’s total expenses increased to ₹226.2 Cr in FY26, an uptick of 86% from ₹121.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Here is a closer look at the areas where Innov8 spent the most: Depreciation And Amortisation Expense: Constituting 42.7% of the overall expenditure, spending under this head rose 2.3X to ₹96.7 Cr in the year under review, from ₹42.4 Cr in FY25. Finance Costs: Expenses towards interest on lease liabilities, interest on borrowing and bank charges came up to ₹70 Cr in FY26, marking 127.8% increase from ₹30.7 Cr in the previous fiscal. Finance costs contributed to 30.9% of the total expenses. Employee Benefit Expenses: Employee costs, including salaries, wages, bonus, gratuity expense and contribution to PF and other funds rose 75.3% to ₹6.8 Cr in the reported year, from ₹3.9 Cr in FY25.

Michelle Bachelet, a former president of Chile, has withdrawn her candidacy to become the next secretary general of the UN, ending a bid that had struggled to gain traction among security council members.
Bachelet, 74, announced her decision in a video posted on Instagram on Saturday, saying: “I will now continue, with the same determination as always, my international work.”
The two-time Chilean president and former UN human rights chief had positioned her campaign around defending multilateralism and international law at a time when she said both were under sustained pressure.
Bachelet’s exit leaves seven candidates in the race to succeed the secretary general, António Guterres, who will conclude his second five-year term on 31 December. It is still possible for more candidates to enter the contest.
Her withdrawal comes after a third informal straw poll, held on Friday, showed her support had all but collapsed. That same poll put Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan in the lead.
The UN security council will formally recommend a single candidate to the 193-member general assembly for election. The assembly’s approval has long been seen as a formality once the council reaches consensus.

Ed Sheeran admits 'mistakes' as he addresses Macklemore controversy
- Published
Singer Ed Sheeran opened his latest concert alone onstage and apologised to his fans for making "mistakes" as he handled the fallout from the controversy over American rapper Macklemore being dropped from his tour over pro-Palestinian remarks.
"I never wanted to be an activist musician but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about free speech and the most complex political issue on the planet," he said.
Saturday's show at a Philadelphia sports stadium was the first time he has addressed the matter in person.
It was a stripped down event and Sheeran went on without opening acts after several musicians dropped out over the debacle.
The price for tickets dropped and sales declined for the remaining US leg of his Loop Tour due to the controversy.
The singer has said the decision to drop Macklemore was made by his promoters, not him.
"My concerts have always been a safe space for everyone," he said at the start of the show, adding that he is committed to fans and that is why he returned to the stage.
"Now, I want to address the question of where I stand in the situation in Israel and Palestine, and whether my doing this concert here tonight implies where I stand," he said.
"I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division; about humanity, not politics. But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore."
Sheeran said what happened in Israel during the 7 October 2023 attacks was "horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain".
He added: "What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate. My heart has been broken by the scale of of devastation and loss of civilian lives, of children's lives, and this systemic injustice we're seeing unfold in the West Bank cannot be overlooked."
He said he is trying "to work out how to make a contribution that helps victims of these terrible times and listening and learning, because I do not know enough".
Sheeran then closed out his statement by saying that he hoped his concert could be a place where everyone could gather irrespective of their beliefs.
Sheeran's remaining tour dates are scheduled with shows set throughout North and South America. While the mega-star's previous tour was among the highest-grossing of all time, some ticket prices for this show have dropped to $32 (£24).
Fans also reported being able to get ticket refunds, though Ticketmaster and concert promoter Messina Touring Group did not confirm they were being reimbursed.
An hour or so before the show began, hundreds concert-goers began to stream in for the event.
There was a smattering of press cameras outside the entry gates, though most fans skipped talking to the press.
A few dozen protesters turned up outside the nearest tube stop waving flags as ticket holders streamed towards Lincoln Financial Field - but the concert proceeded largely unfettered.
- Ed Sheeran and Macklemore: How a tour spiraled into controversy 
  - Published47 minutes ago
Of the handful of attendees who stopped to talk to the BBC, there was a sentiment of determination to enjoy an evening of music while at the same time supporting freedom of speech.
One married couple, who paid $450 per ticket, said that they respect Macklemore's right to speak freely.
Another group of two ladies, who told us they got a "deal" for tonight's concert after prices dropped, said that they support a free Palestine and at the same time love Sheeran's music.
Finally, one family let their two young teenage daughters, Victoria, 15 and Sadie,13 be interviewed.
When we asked what they thought of the controversy and Macklemore's removal, they replied "Who is Macklemore?".
One protestor, who gave his name as Cooper, told the BBC that he came out "to support the struggle for" the Palestinian people.
"We need more people like Macklemore and other artists who have a voice, who have a public platform, to be able to speak on behalf of the Palestinian people and their struggle for liberation, especially in the United States," he said.
Cooper said that a best-case scenario at the concert would be an apology from Sheeran, but he was not optimistic.
"It's not going to happen. I'd like to hear him say that genocide is real and that we need to do everything we can to stop it. But I'm not really expecting that," he said.
Israel has rejected all allegations of genocide. It says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law.

Rory McIlroy switches focus to battle with Patrick Reed for Race to Dubai title after near-miss at BMW PGA Championship
Rory McIlroy moved within 307.76 points of Patrick Reed in the Race to Dubai rankings with a tied-second finish at the BMW PGA Championship; McIlroy is looking to win the Order of Merit for an eighth time; JJ Spaun claimed a two-shot win at Wentworth
Sunday 20 September 2026 22:49, UK
Rory McIlroy has turned his attention to chasing down Patrick Reed for another Race to Dubai title after a cold putter cost him BMW PGA Championship victory.
McIlroy went into the final round two strokes back at Wentworth, where he recovered from failing to convert numerous birdie chances to briefly grab a share of the lead during a thrilling final round.
The world No 2 stumbled to a closing par to post a final-round 68 and finish in tied-second on 15 under, two strokes behind winner JJ Spaun, leaving McIlroy with a fourth runner-up finish at the DP World Tour's flagship event since his 2014 win.
"I had my chances out there!" McIlroy told Sky Sports. "I felt like I hit the ball really well - probably the best I've hit it all week.
"Had good chances on two, three, five, eight, nine, 10, 13, the last. I felt like I hit good putts but, a bit like last week [Amgen Irish Open], I was just not seeing the lines that well.
"I struggled with some of the reads today and I hit some good putts that didn't go in. I holed a couple coming down the stretch but I think the story of the week was that I didn't hole as much as I should have.
"If I did, it would have been a different story."
Will Reed stop McIlroy's Race to Dubai title bid?
McIlroy ending in a four-way share of second earned him 532 Race to Dubai points and moved him within 308 of Reed, who withdrew mid-round on Friday due to injury, in the season-long standings.
Reed had said he was looking forward to a battle with McIlroy, who will next feature at the DP World India Championship from October 15-18 before the two season-ending DP World Tour Play-Offs in the Middle East.
The Northern Irishman has topped the Order of Merit in four consecutive seasons and is looking to finish No 1 again, which would pull McIlroy level with Colin Montgomerie's all-time tally of eight Race to Dubai titles.
"As soon as The Open was over, really that was the goal for the rest of the year," McIlroy added. "I would obviously love to do it [win the Race to Dubai].
"For Patrick, it was unfortunate this week. Hopefully he's okay and he can play what he needs to going in to really make it a good battle, but I'm excited.
"I'll keep working on my game over the next three weeks, then hopefully have a strong end to the season and give myself a great chance at that eighth one."
'McIlroy missed putt after putt!'
McIlroy's runner-up finish at Wentworth follows previous seconds there in 2018, 2022 and 2024, leaving him still searching for his first worldwide win since successfully defending his Masters title in April.
"I think McIlroy left a little bit behind him on the greens - he had loads of chances," former Ryder Cup captain Paul McGinley told Sky Sports.
"It was surprising for a guy who has really improved his putting over the past couple of years and looks so good over them, but he seemed to miss putt after putt after putt.
"I don't think he has played his best golf from tee to green, I'd rate him 3.5 out of five for what he's capable of. It's almost like he couldn't get out of the starting blocks but still finishes tied-second - it's incredible and shows just how much talent he has."
What's next?
McIlroy is next scheduled to feature at the DP World India Championship from October 15-18, before further appearances at the Abu Dhabi Championship (November 5-8) and the DP World Tour Championship (November 12-15).

From near oblivion to Europe - Brighton celebrate 125th anniversary
- Published
It is Thursday, 9 November, 2023. Brighton manager Roberto de Zerbi is addressing his players in the Amsterdam Arena before their Europa League tie with Ajax.
"There's 3,000 Brighton fans in this stadium tonight," said the Italian. "But there's more than twice that number in the city who have travelled over. Remember that when you go on to that pitch."
A long-standing senior Brighton official was in the dressing room that day. A fan first and foremost, but someone who has spent almost three decades working for the club.
"It made the hairs on the back of my neck stand up," he said.
For some clubs, an encounter with Ajax is commonplace. Not Brighton.
"The royalty of European football," says the official. "From where we've come from, to be in that environment. It was a pinch-me moment."
Brighton won 2-0. It was the high point of the first European campaign in the club's history.
Ask Paul Samrah for his single most memorable moment as a Brighton fan and a very different answer comes back, which goes to the heart of why, as they celebrate their 125th birthday around the visit of Arsenal, the Seagulls are almost unique among English clubs.
August 2007. "After the years of campaigning, the days and nights I spent fighting for regime change and then for the stadium, the moment I heard we'd actually got planning permission, that our objectors had decided not to continue their fruitless efforts to stop the stadium," he explained.
"We'd won our battle."
The two stories highlight the before and after reality of Brighton & Hove Albion.
Formed in 1901, Brighton were a Southern League club for almost two decades before they were voted into the Football League. They had experienced only seven seasons in Division Two when they were promoted to the top flight for the first time in 1979.
For years, they were known outside Sussex chiefly for "And Smith must score..." - the BBC radio commentary, delivered by the late Peter Jones, at a critical point during the 1983 FA Cup final, late in extra time. It was the moment when Gordon Smith, clear on goal with a chance to earn Brighton their first major trophy, saw his shot saved by Manchester United goalkeeper Gary Bailey. United won the replay.
But in 1995, chairman Bill Archer sold Brighton's Goldstone Ground, their home since 1902, because of escalating debts that there was no obvious way of paying. Fans were not consulted and no alternative stadium was put in place.
Brighton did not leave until 1997, although their final season at the Goldstone was only confirmed by the property company who owned the stadium, after the final game of the 1995-96 campaign, which had to be abandoned as thousands of furious fans spilled on to the pitch to demonstrate against the ownership. Both crossbars were snapped amid the tumult.
After two seasons playing 70 miles away at Gillingham, and with the idea of a new stadium in the Toad's Hole Valley area of Brighton a non-starter, the club returned to the city in 1999 and started playing at Withdean Stadium, most famous for being the home athletics track of Olympic middle distance gold medallist Steve Ovett.
That brings us back to De Zerbi's pre-match team-talk at Ajax.
Brighton had more than 7,000 fans in Amsterdam that night. When they moved into the Withdean, its capacity was only 6,000. The modern Brighton really is a totally different club to the one that existed before.
"After the 1983 FA Cup final, players were sold, there was no investment, the Goldstone was decaying and the crowds were dipping," said Samrah. "There was no communication between board and fans, directors came and went. There was no continuity, no leadership, no direction. We were just rudderless."
There are some notable figures in the Brighton story.
Former Football Association executive director David Davies got involved, Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott overturned a rejected planning application for Brighton's current stadium in Falmer. Former chairman Dick Knight stabilised a club that in 1997 came within 27 minutes of being relegated out of the Football League.
Without that trio, and many more, it is quite possible Brighton would not exist.
The contemporary Brighton are different.
They began their second European campaign in the Norwegian city of Tromso last month, knowing the Conference League offers the chance of that elusive first trophy.
They play in a magnificent stadium, a short train journey from the city centre, with its new corporate areas, and, generally, inclusive family atmosphere. Their recruitment model, buying players in and selling them on for vast profits, is envied. The new Brighton just beat Manchester United at Old Trafford for the fifth time in six visits. Four games into their 10th consecutive Premier League campaign, they sit fifth.
The contemporary Brighton exist the way they do largely because of the vision and investment of Tony Bloom.
Born in Brighton, Bloom is a lifelong fan. His connection to the club is through his grandfather Harry, a former vice-chairman, and uncle Ray, a director.
Bloom, 56, is an entrepreneur. He made his money in finance and gambling, largely through the use of data. He became chairman in 2009, and masterminded the rise from League One and move into the American Express Stadium. Last season, Brighton's average attendance was more than 31,000.
In their 125-year history, Brighton have never had it so good.
"Anyone walking into Brighton today compared to even 15 years ago would not think it was the same football club," sporting director Mike Cave told BBC Sport.
"The club has been on an unbelievable journey. We've got staff members and many fans who have done that journey. For those of us who weren't here 15 years ago, our responsibility is to ensure what's to come - and I think there's lots - is better than what's happened in the recent or long-distance past."
As for Bloom himself, he has reflected on Brighton's 125th birthday in the programme for the Arsenal game.
"Since 1901, this football club has been part of the fabric of our city and the broader county of Sussex," he said.
"It has connected generations of families and communities. Grandparents have brought their children and grandchildren to matches. Lifelong friendships have been forged on terraces, in stands and on away trips.
"Through good times and bad, Brighton & Hove Albion has provided so many of us with some of the most memorable moments of our lives.
"This club is in my blood. Some of my earliest and most cherished memories are wrapped up in the sights and sounds of the Goldstone.
"When I had the privilege of becoming owner and chairman, it was like being entrusted with something precious to safeguard and help develop for the future.
"Many of you reading these words will remember those difficult years. The loss of the Goldstone. The long journeys to Gillingham. The challenges of the Withdean era.
"What got this football club through was the determination of its fans. The bucket collections. The protests. The refusal to accept the Albion should disappear. This anniversary belongs as much to those supporters as anyone. Quite simply, without them, we would not be here today."
Whether they beat Arsenal or not, Brighton stands tall, for those who fought to preserve something they felt was special, and a man who had a vision - and finance - to build something better.

Trump’s Monumental Obsession
The president fantasizes about a capital city full of memorials—to himself.
Donald Trump is facing multiple challenges. The United States is losing to one of its worst enemies in a war that has left the American economy mired in the sludge of growing inflation and rising energy prices. His popularity is now hovering around second-term George W. Bush levels, and may even be headed for end-stage Richard Nixon numbers. His party faces the prospect of a crushing defeat in midterm elections that are only six weeks away. (In some places, early voting has already begun.) The country, and the 47th president’s administration, are in trouble on every front.
Despite all this military, economic, and political chaos, Trump has stayed true to a handful of projects: Renaming the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, demolishing the East Wing of the White House and replacing it with a ballroom that even the French kings might have thought over the top, and building a triumphal arch in front of the bridge to Arlington Cemetery whose design looks like it was found in the bottom of Albert Speer’s desk drawer.
 The president is very concerned about these undertakings. He is, as they say in Washington, laser-focused on them. Ordinary folks might say “obsessed,” because at times he seems unable to talk about anything else, even when asked about matters of national importance, including America’s slow-motion defeat in the Middle East.
Perhaps this world of troubles is why Trump is taking refuge in plans of marble and gilt. Even an emotionally healthier man might want an occasional break from the travails of a presidency in crisis: Harry Truman would retire to the White House balcony with a bourbon, Dwight Eisenhower played a lot of golf, Kennedy and George H.W. Bush loved sailing, Ronald Reagan watched hundreds of movies in the mansion theater and at Camp David.
But Donald Trump is not an emotionally healthy man, and his obsession with monuments is not a mere diversion from the pressures of the job. His most recent tirade—posted at 7:34 this morning on his Truth Social site, some six hours after his last post the night before—suggests a president who is now lost in a fantasy city in his mind, a capital where the buildings are festooned with his name, drenched in glitz, and bristling with weapons.
As is often the case with Trump’s more unhinged posts, it is necessary to read his actual words to get a sense of how alarmingly strange they are:
At the strong request of the United States Military, and for National Security purposes, I have agreed to convert the magnificent Triumphal Arch, planned since the Civil War Era many years ago, at the Receptive Circle adjoining the Arlington Memorial Bridge, into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch, to house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage.
Trump goes on to complain that Washington is the only capital city that does not have a “triumphal arch,” and vows that it will now have “the greatest of them all!”
Trump’s pivot from a memorial to a gilded turret is at least in part a legal strategy. When Trump’s ballroom plans faced legal challenges, the president went to the Supreme Court and argued that he had the right to continue with its construction because the bunker beneath it was a matter of national security. (Other presidents have on occasion tried to circumvent checks on their power by invoking national security, but Trump has made it a routine ploy.) The Court agreed, and Trump may now be trying to squash opposition to the arch on the same grounds.
This militarization of Washington ballrooms and memorials, however, is more than politics. Trump’s imaginings of castle-like defenses on the Potomac move beyond mere bad taste to a place of genuine weirdness. He does not merely imagine the new ballroom, for example, as the cap over a new, more secure presidential bunker; he imagines a space meant for parties and celebrations as a fort where he and his guests can celebrate beneath a drone port crewed by military and security personnel, including snipers.
The ballroom, however, almost seems like a rational investment compared to the arch Trump wants to build in front of America’s most hallowed ground. The entrance to the resting place of thousands of the nation’s war dead would be a “top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch”—whatever that means. (Perhaps it should include a portcullis and a drawbridge.) It would also be a permanent storage facility for a lot of ammunition.
What could go wrong? A space open to the public would also be a continuously operating military installation. Just imagine the sense of peace visitors, tourists, and schoolchildren would feel standing atop an ammo dump full of ordnance. But at least it might stop Chinese paratroopers or Al-Qaeda frogmen from seizing Washington with a daring raid after they’d subdued suburban Virginia.
None of this makes sense as a matter of national security. Yes, the White House is one of the most important centers of command and control in the United States, but it already has an array of defenses—including snipers on the roof when the Secret Service determines they might be needed. Other memorials and tourist attractions in D.C. are likewise guarded by layers of security and law enforcement. Trump, however, is imagining permanent military installations, including one on the roof of a White House annex, all because the current president apparently wants his successors to wake up every morning, see a ginormous eyesore, and remember that Donald Trump once lived there.
Militarizing an arch in front of the Memorial Bridge is an even more dangerous and stupid idea than turning a ballroom into a bastion. Motorists crossing the river would have to drive around the structure, potentially creating the kind of traffic jams terrorists could more easily exploit in a city already full of choke-points. (I lived in Arlington and commuted to the District; it’s a messy trip even now.) The arch would also stand close to the approaches to Reagan National Airport, as if that overburdened facility needed more safety and security challenges. And stuffing the arch with weapons would not only contradict the notion of honoring those who have died in battle, it would increase the possibility of a mistake or a malfunction.
The most important reason not to build the arch, of course, is that it is ugly and un-American. It is fascistic bombast, a militaristic yawp in front of a cemetery that is meant to be a place of respect and rest for the dead and quiet reflection for the living. It will loom over the cemetery, insisting that instead of thinking of the honored dead Americans think only of Donald Trump.
The president has never understood why Washington does not look like other capitals. America does not have a “triumphal arch” because Americans are not the kind of people who generally build such things. They do not ask their fellow citizens to swan about in uniform to celebrate foreign conquests. Napoleon broke ground for the Arc de Triomphe in Paris in 1806 to welcome his troops home after their victory at the battle of Austerlitz. It would take another 30 years to complete it, by which time Napoleon had long since returned in defeat from Moscow and then died in exile.
Speaking of Moscow, most of the institutions of the Russian government are surrounded by walls and parapets. The word “Kremlin” comes from the Russian word for “fortress,” and while it is imposing and even beautiful in its way, it is a symbol of centuries of autocracy and paranoia. And yet Trump wants to turn the White House and an outpost on the Potomac into similar citadels, with little regard for why America’s capital city was named for one of its greatest examples of unadorned republican virtue.
Trump clearly cares nothing for such symbolism. His ego wants what it wants. He lives in a city that he evidently hates and which, for the most part, hates him back. But Trump’s obsession with these vulgar memorials to his own vanity is a reminder of the darkness around him, of his hostility to democracy, his loathing of honor, and his disordered mind.
Perhaps the president is looking ahead to the day he is no longer the most powerful man in the world, and it pains him to think that he would be reviled—or worse, forgotten. If so, he seems determined to leave his mark on America’s capital even if it requires scarring it with militarized obscenities.

Trump says his D.C. arch will serve as 'military complex' with snipers and drones
President Trump has revealed plans to make his proposed 250-foot arch in Washington, D.C. serve as a "military complex", including areas for military snipers and large amounts of weaponry. Trump said military operations at the triumphal arch are needed to protect national security, in a post on Truth Social.
"At the strong request of the United States Military, and for National Security purposes, I have agreed to convert the magnificent Triumphal Arch... into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch," Trump wrote on the social media platform.
Trump added that the arch near the National Mall will "house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage."
The administration's plans to build the arch between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial have been met with opposition. It would be twice the height of the Lincoln Memorial. More than 100,000 people submitted comments to the National Park Service as part of its review of the arch proposal.
The arch has also faced legal opposition. Earlier this month, U.S. District Court Judge Tanya Chutkin ordered the government to provide the court with 48 hours' notice before moving forward with any activity on Memorial Circle.
The order warned any construction or demolition before the NPS issues final authorization would be a violation of the court. A group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian filed the lawsuit alleging the arch would desecrate the hallowed grounds of Arlington National Cemetery. The plaintiffs also claim the president doesn't have the authority to build the arch without approval from Congress.
Chutkin's order came the day after Interior Secretary Doug Burgum wrote on X the administration planned to break ground on an arch within two weeks, despite still awaiting final approval from the National Capital Planning Commission and other federal reviews.
Trump's Truth Social post added: "There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World. Out of the 59 top cities and Capitals, Washington, D.C., IS THE ONLY ONE IN THE WORLD THAT DOES NOT HAVE A TRIUMPHAL ARCH, but it will now and, by far, the greatest of them all!"

Mother of three college athletes and a runner herself, a woman from Milford, New Hampshire, has successfully turned her side hustle into her own brand, which hit 2 million in revenue last year. What started as a side project is now available in 13,000 retail stores, including Starbucks and Walmart. Theresa Burnley, 65, was the owner of Wiley Road Foods. The brand is known for creating and manufacturing clean-label baked items for brands like Trader Joe’s and Milk Bar. In 2023, she started her protein-bite brand, Circ, while working full-time. By the end of 2024, Burnley left Wiley Road Foods and shifted her full-time focus to Circ. Two years later, the brand now offers six different flavours of protein snacks. Circ witnessed growth over a short time period, raking in $2 million in revenue last year. Recalling her inspiration behind the brand, Burnley shared in an interview with entrepreneur.com that she always dreamed of building her own independent natural food brand with her family. She said that she was inspired to curate her brand after realising how outdated the protein bar space was. She believed that the protein in the form of bars was no longer adequate to meet the functional needs of people today. This is how she came up with bite-sized, round protein snacks that are easy to eat on the go. Burnley revealed she invested over $1 million initially for the process and product development. The team adapted packaging equipment to form the packs. Each pack could hold five round protein bites, which became the highlight of their product. "We had taught ourselves to make ball-shaped food working for Milk Bar. Our R&D team were pastry chefs, not food scientists, so they knew how to make food that people love. But our innovative packaging, which took a couple of years to develop, was really transformative," she told Entrepreneur.com. The company was fortunate to secure some early retail placements. Eventually, it began generating steady revenue after its launch at Expo West. However, the founder added that Circ took longer before becoming profitable. She said that the company initially faced higher fixed costs than brands that use co-packers because it manufactures its products in-house, but at scale, in-house manufacturing is expected to provide a significant cost advantage. With time, the company went on to generate about $2 million in top-line revenue in 2025. "We will 4X our run-rate this year," Burnley hoped. While Burnley invested very minimal time when her brand was just a side hustle, it changed once the brand started gaining attention. Soon after, she sold her bakery business and joined her brand full time. "The company can’t run itself yet. I’m responsible for everything; the days are long, but it’s very rewarding," she added.
