What holds the Epic Open Sport back is audio quality—the sound isn't very detailed, and it's generally boring to listen to.
Other Open Earbuds I’ve Tested
EarFun Clip for $70: For around $70, these are a solid pick for anyone on a budget. Waniata found the overall package punching above its price point, with a snappy, compact case, comfortable fit, push-button controls, and reliable multiple Bluetooth connections. The problem is our budget pick, the Soundpeats PearlClip Pro, is often on sale for less and offers a similar overall experience. Don't dismiss these earbuds if you find them heavily discounted.
Shokz OpenFit Pro for $250: The Shokz OpenFit Pro has a great premise: open earbuds with noise canceling. Hear the world around you as you would without headphones, and turn on noise-canceling when you don't, just like regular earbuds. And while they do cancel some noise, it's not much. The bigger issue is price: for $250, you could get open earbuds and great noise-canceling earbuds that do a better job for each task.
Suunto Wing 2 for $179: These open-ear headphones are designed for endurance athletes—they have a long 12-hour battery life but also come with a wireless power bank you can take on the go. Dock the headphones in the power bank for up to 36 hours of battery life total. There's nothing inherently wrong with these headphones, but I don't see a world where I would recommend them over the Shokz Openrun Pro 2, which retail for the same amount and offer more comfort, a sleeker design, better sound, and a more robust app.
Suunto Spark for $179: The Suunto Spark has a similar story to the Suunto Wing 2: with athletes in mind, it has features that sync with Suunto fitness watches, but it is outclassed in the areas that matter (comfort, sound quality, battery) by the similarly priced Shokz Openfit 2.
What Are Open Earbuds and How Do They Sound?
At a glance, open earbuds seem a lot like typical wireless earbuds. The big difference is that, instead of going inside your ear canal, they rest somewhere on the outside of your ear, leaving it open so you can easily hear the world around you. I use them all the time for outdoor exercise like running or biking, where I want my music but also need to hear other runners, bikers, and cars to stay safe.
Because they leave your ears open and the sound comes from farther away (outside your ear rather than inside), audio performance isn't as clear, intimate, or bassy as regular earbuds. They also typically don't have noise-canceling features, so they are not a great fit for the office or air travel.
When or Where Would I Use Open Earbuds?
Open earbuds are perfect for outdoor activities, or when you want to talk to other people without taking off your headphones. When I run or go for a bike ride, I only use open earbuds so I can hear my surroundings and stay safe. I also like using them around the house when I am cooking or doing laundry.
What About Semi-Open Earbuds?
Semi-open earbuds, like Apple's AirPods, sit inside the ear but don't have eartips that create a sound seal. They can offer better audio quality than other open earbuds because the speakers and microphones are closer to your ear and mouth. Semi-open earbuds are comfortable, but they're usually pretty loose—they can fall out easily and may be a poor option for fitness activities.
How Do I Test Open Earbuds?
I test open earbuds like I test any pair of headphones: in the real world, in my daily life. I wear each pair for at least a few weeks to test comfort, battery life, ease of use, and onboard controls. I listen to podcasts, watch TV shows, jam out to my favorite playlists, and call friends.
With open earbuds in particular, I also wear them on jogs, bike rides, and errand runs to get a better feel for how stable they are on my ears. I do not expect them to cancel any noise, so I don't make a point of testing them on airplanes or loud commutes—they aren't really made for that. My main audio source is Spotify Lossless, but, when possible, I test other formats and codecs as well.

How to customize the side button on your Samsung Galaxy phone
You might be surprised at all the things it can do.
Did you know that Samsung stopped making phones with traditional power buttons in 2019? That button beneath your Samsung phone's volume button is actually a multifunctional and customizable side button. If you used any Samsung flagship phone between the S8 and S10, you probably noticed a fourth physical button on the side of the device: the infamous Bixby Button. That fourth button didn't disappear; it actually got merged with the power button on Galaxy phones from the Note 10 series and beyond.
By default, a short press on the side button turns the screen on and off, a long press activates Samsung's Bixby assistant, a double press opens the camera; long-pressing the side button plus volume-down button opens the power menu, and a short press of the same buttons takes a screenshot. The good news is that Samsung lets you remap nearly every action tied to the side button, so a phone that keeps accidentally summoning Bixby can instead open a favorite app with the same press. Even devices that still rock the dedicated Bixby button from the S8 to S10 era can be customized. And everything can be done right in your phone's settings, no super-secret menu or code needed. Do note that for Galaxy Z Flip owners, the functionality of the side button can change depending on whether the device is open or closed.
How to customize the side button on a Samsung phone
Customizing your Samsung phone's side button is pretty straightforward; go to Settings > Advanced features > Side button. From here, you can remap the button; a double press can be set to open Camera, Flashlight, Magnifier, Voice Recorder, Samsung Notes, Modes and Routines, Samsung Capture or a chosen app. Unfortunately, the long-press option is limited to just assistant apps like Bixby, Google Gemini, and other AI assistants including ChatGPT and Claude. Otherwise, you can set the long press to pull up the power-off menu.
On Samsung devices with a separate physical Bixby button, namely the Galaxy S10 series, S9 series, S8 series, Note 8 and Note 9, a long press will always open Bixby Voice. You can customize the button's double-press and single-press functions, but not at the same time; one has to open Bixby Home.
To remap the button, open Settings > Advanced features > Bixby Key. Here, you can customize the button to either open any app of your choice or run a command.
Cool ways to customize the side button
Using Modes and Routines is one of the best ways to take advantage of your side button. For example, if you spend a lot of time driving, you can set the side button to turn on Driving Mode. You can make this mode trigger actions including hands-free calling, opening maps, reading messages aloud and auto-replying to texts. There are myriad things you can do when you pair Modes and Routines with your Samsung phone's side button.
If you like to take down quick thoughts or capture the beginning of a meeting before you can grab a notepad, you can use the side button to start recording. In your settings, you can assign Voice Recorder to begin recording with a simple side-button double press. No need to unlock the phone or hunt for the app; you can begin recording the moment inspiration strikes.

Wembley welcomes 'rabid' college football fans
- Published
It wasn't even gameday in London but the rivalry had already begun.
Fans of the Kansas Jayhawks and Arizona State Sun Devils gathered at a pre-game party in Waterloo on Friday.
Kansas fans shouted their rallying cry "Rock Chalk, Jayhawk", while their rivals replied with "ASU, ASU".
After hosting 42 NFL games since 2007, this was London's introduction to a different kind of American football and a different kind of fandom.
Wembley hosted its first American college football game on Saturday, with 46,523 fans attending the inaugural Union Jack Classic (UJC).
Battle of the marching bands
UJC organisers vowed to create an authentic college gameday in London, and they began with tailgate parties.
Fans enjoy food, drink and music for hours before the game, and they are far bigger for college games than in the NFL. One American fan told BBC Sport she prefers the tailgate to the game itself.
The main tailgate at Wembley opened at 10am - seven hours before kick-off - with Kansas City rapper Tech N9ne helping to entertain the crowd.
Arizona State alumni held their own party, with nearly 2,000 fans packed in, while ASU's marching band and cheerleaders performed on stage.
But the wildest party was on Wembley Way, where Fox Sports had an outdoor studio for its live pre-game show.
It was surrounded by fans and the Fox crew kept trying to stoke the rivalry, while the Kansas and ASU bands battled it out on Wembley Way and on the pitch before kick-off.
Why are college fans so passionate?
The pageantry and passion of college football is what makes it different. NFL fans often choose their team, whereas college teams tend to be passed down through families.
"You feel a loyalty to your lineage," said Kansas fan Hannah, who added that college football fans are not just fanatical but "rabid".
BBC Sport spoke to families at Wembley who have had multiple generations attend the same school and alumni who now live all over the US but travel thousands of miles to watch their alma mater.
Current ASU student Sophie said her family "bleeds maroon and gold". Her friend Amelia has ASU merchandise all over the house. She just got a car that's maroon too.
About 15,000 fans travelled from the US for Saturday's game - 9,000 rooting for ASU and 6,000 Kansas.
College games in the US rarely have away fans but, with both teams having a sizable contingent at Wembley, as well as playing at a neutral venue, some visitors said the atmosphere was like a play-off game.
Why UK fans are learning about college football
Fans from 35 countries bought tickets and, as with NFL games in London, they represented several teams, not just those playing.
Neutrals wore NFL jerseys and college jerseys, of bigger schools such as Oklahoma, Miami and Texas. There were even some British university jerseys.
More than 100 universities in the UK have American football teams, and UJC organisers targeted those players, partly because, as students, they often find college football more relatable than the NFL.
They formed partnerships with the British American Football Association, British Universities and Colleges Sport and the Jacksonville Jaguars to establish links with the grassroots game in the UK.
The UJC has helped to train more than 1,050 British coaches and referees this year, some of whom were at Saturday's game.
Cambridge University player Alex said it has been "cool" to learn the stories of Kansas and ASU and he would probably go to more college games in future "if they're teams we can rally behind".
Will there be another London game?
After planning for an attendance of 60,000, Wembley was about half full at 46,523, with some ticketholders moved to the bottom tier to keep the top tier empty.
Although there were some big plays, the game was not as entertaining as anticipated as ASU claimed a 24-17 win that flattered Kansas.
Music acts played throughout the game and there was a light show in the third quarter. It gave UK fans a flavour of college football, but it lacked the pomp and circumstance of regular games in the US.
There were fewer band members and cheerleaders than normal, and the crowd was not as loud as during ASU home games – they averaged 54,000 last season.
Both teams took 105 players (or student-athletes), 90% of which did not have a passport before this trip.
Many fans and members of the coaches' families also visited London for the first time, and ASU head coach Kenny Dillingham said they had "an experience they will remember for the rest of their lives".
Kansas head coach Lance Leipold added that the hospitality was outstanding, while the hotel and practice facility "was a win".
Both teams are part of the Big 12 Conference, whose commissioner Brett Yormark said: "It exceeded my expectations, from the crowd to the logistics to how the local community has embraced us. It's been fantastic, so we want more."
UJC organisers have signed an exclusive multi-year deal with Wembley, and Yormark says other Big 12 colleges are interested in playing in London.
Big 12 teams also played two games in Dublin over the past 13 months, and the conference could expand to another international market.
Yormark said: "There's not a two-week period where I don't get a call to say 'take some of your product to this country or that country', so we're exploring that right now."
He said there will be an announcement about next year's London game "within the next month or two".
That will give UK fans plenty of time to swot up on the next two teams who will make their presence known across the pond.

Google’s AI models may not be in the lead by most measures right now, but the company does have one key advantage: your data. If you’re deep in the Google ecosystem, Gemini models have a lot of context on you already. Google’s latest Google Labs experiment, known as CC, aims to expand that kind of customization to the whole family.
CC is an evolution of something that Google announced in 2025. The original CC eventually became Gemini’s Daily Brief, which churns through the data in your Google account to offer daily action items and suggestions. The new CC has a similar goal, but it’s designed to be a shared resource for up to six users in a family.
Google says that CC has its own Google account, allowing each family member to interact with it (or not) as they choose. For example, CC only sees emails from its connected users if they are explicitly shared. You can do that by designating certain addresses as always available to the agent—something like school scheduling emails. You can also send content to CC via email or Google Chat. The agent can even monitor a shared Google Drive folder, into which you can dump invitations, documents, and other content.
One of CC’s main functions is, unsurprisingly, a lot like Daily Brief. Each morning, all the registered users will get a shared “Your Day Ahead” email that pulls together the day’s events and updates on previous tasks. It can also add items to shared calendars, remind you about important tasks, and create documents based on your instructions that are accessible to all CC users.

Kylian Mbappe, Vinicius Junior and Ibrahima Konate rolled up their pre-game T-shirts ahead of Real Madrid's match at Elche on Tuesday to obscure the message of support for the people of Ceuta.
Ceuta is a Spanish autonomous city on the North African coast, bordering Morocco and separated from mainland Spain by the Strait of Gibraltar.
Players from both sides walked on to the pitch at Elche's ground, Martinez Valero, wearing white T-shirts carrying the message "Todos somos caballas" – translated as "We are all Ceutans" – along with references to the Spanish autonomous city.

This is not the first time Real Madrid have shown support for Ceuta. At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.

Locals have expressed safety concerns and some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.

How to use Xbox mode on your Windows PC
Xbox mode doesn't reinvent the PC gaming experience, but it has a few nice touches.
2026 is the year when Microsoft finally seemed to notice how nightmarish of an experience Windows 11 has become. Windows 11 has received updates to make it suck less and even new features to help it feel fresh.
One of the biggest new additions to Windows 11 is Xbox mode. It's hard not to see this as a response to Valve's SteamOS, which is increasingly spoken about in messianic tones by gamers hoping to jump ship from Microsoft's slop-laden ecosystem. When you activate Xbox mode on a PC, Windows ditches the taskbar and adopts a controller-friendly layout, dropping you into a redesigned Xbox app with all your game libraries loaded up.
Xbox mode started landing on Windows 11 PCs in May, so everyone who regularly installs updates should have it by now. But how to actually get it running isn't obvious, and neither is how to use it once you do. Before we dive in, make sure you have a gamepad connected — Xbox, PC and PlayStation controllers all work based on our testing. It will also speed up the process later on if you open your digital storefront of choice now.
How to enable and open Xbox mode in Windows 11
The first step to using Windows 11's Xbox mode is to ensure that it's turned on, which it may not be by default. To do so, open Settings by using the Win + I shortcut, then select Gaming > Xbox mode.
Here, if you see an Enable Xbox mode slider, enable it. You may also see a Choose home app section, where you should select Xbox. If you want quicker access to Xbox mode from the desktop, also enable Show Xbox mode in Task View. And if you end up loving the feature and only use your PC for gaming, Enter Xbox mode on startup will save you some time.
Xbox mode is accessible through several paths. The keyboard shortcut Win + F11 toggles between the desktop and Xbox mode. You can also use Win + G to open the Game Bar, click the gear icon in the bar centered at the top of the screen, then choose Enter Xbox mode. If you're in the Xbox app, you'll see a shortcut at the top-right of the home page. Lastly, if you enabled the Task View option above, press Win + Tab and you'll see an Xbox mode shortcut to the right of your open desktops at the bottom of the screen.
While playing, pressing the Windows key on your keyboard enters a task view where you can access the Windows desktop, as well as shortcuts at the top of the screen. To exit Xbox mode, return to the Xbox app home screen and click the Exit Xbox mode button in the top-right. You can also use Win + F11 again.
A common misconception is that Xbox mode brings under-the-hood improvements to performance while gaming, but Microsoft has made no such claim. This is handled by a separate toggle: Settings > Gaming > Game Mode, which "turns things off in the background" to improve your gaming experience. While vague, it's worth turning this on if you don't have it enabled already.
What Xbox mode does is get the most computer-y parts of Windows out of the way, replacing them with a full-screen experience dedicated to gaming that's friendly to use with either a controller or keyboard and mouse. In other words, it's Microsoft's answer to the Big Picture Mode in Steam.
What does Xbox mode actually do in Windows 11?
You'll benefit most from Xbox mode if you have game libraries across multiple providers. If you've got World of Warcraft, Fortnite and Counter-Strike on your PC, you need at least three launchers to run them (Battle.net, Epic Games and Steam, respectively). Xbox mode shows you games from all those libraries, as well as Ubisoft Connect and Humble Launcher, in a centralized place. We didn't test other launchers like the EA App. If you don't see a particular title, you can pull it into the Xbox app by selecting the plus icon from the top-right of the Library tab.
Launching a game from the Xbox app sidesteps the need to open its launcher, as Xbox will simply target the game executable, which boots the necessary software in the background. This process wasn't the quickest or smoothest in our testing. Although games launch every time, we recommend opening third-party launchers before starting Xbox mode to speed up the process.
If you're subscribed to Xbox Game Pass, you'll be able to access its library through Xbox mode. Surprisingly, the Cloud Gaming tab doesn't lock you to Microsoft's services. You can set Nvidia GeForce Now as your default streaming service in the Xbox app's settings.
Ultimately, Xbox mode in its current form is little more than a souped-up Xbox app with controller mapping and a few extra settings to prevent you from needing to interact with Windows. It's more useful on handhelds and living room PCs than on a standalone gaming PC. Regardless, with more gamers switching to Linux than ever before, it's good to see Microsoft exploring improvements to the Windows 11 gaming experience.

Health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced Thursday a new effort to improve autism diagnoses, arguing that the current model is outdated, too time-intensive, and overreliant on professionals with limited availability.
“We are not satisfied simply for describing autism and managing its consequences. We are asking what drives the different forms of autism, and why developmental trajectories differ, why some children regress, and which interventions work for them,” Kennedy said during his keynote address at a conference for Children’s Health Defense, an anti-vaccine organization he previously led.
The initiative calls for organizations to submit “solutions” — tools and technologies that will not only speed up assessments but also improve autistic people’s quality of life. The program will be administered by the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, which funds novel health research. The announcement does not provide financial details for these grants.
“It’s exciting that ARPA-H is focusing on autism, and I think the idea of exploring ways that technology can transform aspects of diagnosis, interventions, and support is timely,” said Helen Tager-Flusberg, director of the Center for Autism Research Excellence at Boston University, in a text. “We can only hope that the review process will lead to an unbiased selection of projects!”
Autism care is facing some headwinds right now. Wait times to receive an assessment can stretch months or even years as prevalence has increased in recent decades. Health insurers have started pulling back from covering the main therapy used to treat kids after the field was rocked by allegations of fraud.
The autism community has also had to contend with Kennedy’s repeated use of dehumanizing language to describe the condition — he called autistic kids “damaged” during Thursday’s keynote — and his insistence that autism is correlated with vaccines, though there is no scientific evidence for the link. Kennedy and President Trump have also asserted, without evidence, that autism is connected with Tylenol use during pregnancy.
Many autism researchers have been wary of the federal investigations of autism launched by Kennedy, though they remain cautiously optimistic about the Autism Data Science Initiative, which awarded $50 million to 13 projects through the National Institutes of Health in June.
SPECTRA — or Systems for Phenotypic Evaluation, Clinical Trajectories, Response, and Agency — is a bet that greater understanding of interactions among genetic, environmental, microbiome, and other factors will provide advances in the field.
It will be overseen by ARPA-H Program Manager Russell Shilling, who has two kids with autism and used to sit on the Medical and Science Advisory Committee at the influential nonprofit Autism Speaks.

Hundreds of drones targeting Moscow and its surrounding region killed at least two people and damaged a major refinery on the final day of the country’s parliamentary elections, authorities said on Sunday.
The capital’s mayor said that more than 1,600 drones had been intercepted and shot down, 450 of which were aimed at Moscow.
Sergei Sobyanin accused Ukraine of attempting to interfere with a tightly controlled three-day election that is set to tighten president Vladimir Putin’s 26-year grip on power.
“The unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed,” he said on Telegram.
Moscow’s regional governor said at least two people were killed – a 44-year-old woman and an elderly man – in two separate locations.
A fire triggered by a drone crashing into a 21-storey building also led to 400 people being evacuated, said Moscow regional governor, Andrey Vorobyov, without specifying the drones’ origin.
The attacks come at a time when Kyiv stepped up its long-range drone strike campaign against Russia in recent months, particularly against energy infrastructure to target a vital source of the Kremlin’s revenue to fund its war effort – now in its fifth year.
Ukrainian strikes have knocked out a significant part of Russia’s oil refining capacity, triggering oil product shortages, fuel price increases and long queues at filling stations in many regions across the country’s 11 time zones.
A facility on the territory of the Moscow oil refinery had been damaged, Sobyanin said. No casualties had been reported so far and emergency services were on the scene.
That major refinery has already been hit by Ukrainian strikes in recent months.
Ukraine has not commented on the attacks. Both sides say they do not target civilians.
The latest strike comes after the US president, Donald Trump, said on Monday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities.
It also comes after Russians began voting on Friday in the country’s first parliamentary election since Moscow invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
Only parties that support Putin and the Kremlin’s military campaign have been registered to run. Moscow has also organised voting in occupied Ukraine.
Few Russians doubt Putin’s United Russia party will coast to victory again, but the vote offers a gauge of public support for the war.

Flock Safety announced a voluntary employee separation program on Friday, offering a “generous” severance package to those who want to leave amid growing backlash against the surveillance technology company, according to an internal email shared with WIRED.
Applications for Flock’s voluntary severance program opened Friday, and employees have until October 2 to decide whether to leave the company. Flock expects to grant buyouts to the majority of workers who apply, according to the email. People familiar with the program but not authorized to discuss it publicly say they believe that a significant number of the startup’s roughly 1,500 employees may try to depart.
Flock is making the severance offers as it continues to lose customers amid growing frustration across the US about its sprawling network of license plate readers, which have raised concerns about privacy and misuse. In the last month, WIRED has documented officers allegedly abusing Flock to track former romantic partners and colleagues, exposed how widely some agencies share access to the system, shown how little is known about the manufacturing of the devices, and revealed in new detail how much information Flock’s cameras collect based on data from a dismantled Flock device.

Founded in 2017, Flock raised money at a valuation of more than $8 billion in a funding round that closed in April. The company has had many of its contracts either not extended or dropped this year, which could leave it short of revenue goals, according to two of the people. A wave of vandalism targeting its cameras has unexpectedly increased expenses. Without buyouts, Flock almost certainly would have to lay off some staff, one of the people believes.
In an internal announcement, Flock said the separation program provides “greater agency” for its workers and “treats employees with transparency, respect, and choice.” It also described the package as the “most generous” ever offered by the company, roughly double its previous severance offers.
Flock did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Some Flock employees have said they have received buyout offers in the range of tens of thousands of dollars, one of the people said. The package also gives employees several months of health care coverage and the ability to exercise stock options within two years after separation, a longer period than the company typically offers resigning employees, according to the email and people familiar with the offer.
Flock employees are expected to learn whether their applications were accepted on October 9, according to the email. Most accepted employees would leave the company by October 29, though in some cases Flock may ask employees to remain for another one to three months.
People familiar with Flock’s severance plan tell WIRED that some employees may take the offer amid speculation that the company, which has raised about $1.2 billion in venture capital, might resort to selling off parts or all of its business to stay afloat. “When you see enough of the vandalism” targeting Flock cameras this year, one of the people says, “you know the writing is the wall” that something has to change.
Flock CEO Garrett Langley said on the All-In podcast last month that “the biggest damage” caused by the backlash against the company had been “internal morale.”
“Because you go on to X or you go on to Reddit and you go, why are people so mad at us when we've been doing the same thing for nine years?” Langley said. “And why are they so mad at us for things we don't do? And we just want people to be safe.”
One advocacy group identified 93 city and county governments that cut ties with Flock in August alone. Overall in 2026, roughly three times as many local governments have dropped Flock compared to the previous five years.
Flock has recently been building products that extend the company beyond its core license plate reader offering. WIRED reported last month that the company has developed AI-powered investigative software to identify drivers, find potential associates based on patterns of movement, and search across police records and other data.
A separate WIRED analysis of Flock’s software found tools designed to continuously search camera feeds for people matching written descriptions. WIRED’s analysis of Flock’s code also found potential integrations with drones and other surveillance systems.

Over 30 people across four states have been poisoned by bacterial toxins after getting intravenous (IV) drips at wellness clinics, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Food and Drug Administration.
The people had received IV drips containing glutathione, which is sold—without evidence—for purposes like detoxification, immune support, increased energy, and skin brightening. Glutathione is an antioxidant that’s found naturally in the body. It has been studied as a potential treatment for various ailments, but so far there is little to no evidence-backed use for the tripeptide; there are no FDA-approved glutathione products in the US.
Nevertheless, it’s commonly used as a supplement and promoted as having various benefits. It’s most often used in supplement pills, taken by mouth. But popular wellness clinics offering IV drips of vitamins and other supplements have also been offering glutathione. According to the CDC and FDA, the problem is that specialty drug makers, called compounding pharmacies, are making these IV drips using glutathione powders that are graded for dietary supplements taken orally. This grading is critically different from that of purified products graded for use in sterile injectable drugs.
In an announcement late last month, the FDA said it had learned that at least two compounding pharmacies had been doing this and that people were getting sick. At the time, the FDA had gotten reports of at least 30 sickened people.
Illnesses
The IV glutathione products involved appeared to be made from glutathione provided by Medisca Inc., headquartered in Plattsburgh, New York. “The glutathione was labeled as dietary supplement grade, which is not an appropriate ingredient to make injectable drugs,” the FDA said. Medisca told the FDA that it had informed its pharmacy customers not to use the product for injectable drugs.

The southwest monsoon has begun withdrawing from parts of northwest India, with the withdrawal line moving across western Rajasthan and adjoining areas, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said on Sunday. As of 20 September, the line of withdrawal passes through Ramgarh, Mohangarh, Phalodi and Khajuwala. The development marks the onset of the annual retreat of the southwest monsoon, which typically begins from western Rajasthan in September. The withdrawal process is expected to progress gradually towards other parts of northwest and central India, depending on rainfall and atmospheric conditions, the weather office said. The southwest monsoon typically starts withdrawing from the North-West in September, with its retreat progressing gradually towards the South and the East. The development will be closely watched as the monsoon accounts for about 70% of India's annual rainfall, and its withdrawal marks the transition towards the post-monsoon season. Meanwhile, the IMD in its latest forecast also stated that rainfall is likely to remain active across several parts of the country over the coming week, with widespread showers forecast over parts of eastern, central and southern India. In eastern India, widespread rainfall is likely over the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Gangetic West Bengal during 21-26 September, while Odisha, Jharkhand and Sub-Himalayan West Bengal and Sikkim are expected to receive widespread rain from 22-26 September. Bihar may see widespread rainfall during 24-26 September. Central India is also likely to witness significant rainfall, with Chhattisgarh forecast to receive widespread showers throughout 21-26 September. Vidarbha is likely to see widespread rainfall during 21-26 September, while east Madhya Pradesh is expected to receive rain during 23-26 September. In southern India, widespread rainfall is forecast over Kerala, coastal Karnataka, and parts of Karnataka during the week, while Telangana and coastal Andhra Pradesh are likely to receive rain at different times. The North-East is also expected to see widespread rainfall and thunderstorms over Assam, Meghalaya and parts of the region during 21-25 September. In northwest India, east Uttar Pradesh may receive widespread rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms and lightning on 25-26 September, while isolated rain is likely over other parts of the region. The southwest monsoon season has so far brought cumulative rainfall of 695.6 mm during 1 June-19 September, 15% below the normal of 817.2 mm. A silver medal can be a bittersweet achievement. It can mean you came second. Or, depending on how the competition unfolded, it can leave you wondering how close you came to winning gold.
There was perhaps a hint of that feeling in the first call Elavenil Valarivan immediately made after finishing second in the women’s 10m air rifle competition at the Nagoya Asian Games.
“I missed a gold! I was so close!” she told her coach, Neha Chavan, back in Chennai.
You could understand why she felt that way. The 27-year-old opened with a perfect 10.9 and led for much of the 24-shot final. She kept the Chinese shooters off the podium and pushed Olympic champion Ban Hyo-jin into third place. Gold had seemed within Elavenil’s grasp before a late stumble in the final three shots opened the door for Japan’s Hinata Taichi to move in front and win the title by 0.6 points, 253.0 to 252.4.
But Elavenil’s post-match call conveyed only part of how she felt. The rest is written in a scrapbook in which she makes a little note every time she shoots. But more on that in a while.
Elavenil’s medal is no ordinary silver.
You could see that in the beaming smile on her face as she held it up on the podium.
Follow | Asian Games Highlights, September 20
“I have a lot of gratitude. I’m trying to practise saying these words a lot more frequently and I’m just grateful I could win these medals,” she told Sportstar outside the Aichi Prefecture Shooting Range.
This was India’s first individual medal of the Nagoya Asian Games. It followed the team silver alongside Vidarsa Vinod and Sonam Maskar that Elavenil had helped secure in the qualification round earlier that morning.
More personally, both were the first medals Elavenil had won at a multi-sport Games.
“I’ve been competing at these multi-event Games for the last eight years. I’ve finally got my first medals,” she said.
When you look at her career, that statistic seems a strange sort of anomaly.
Ever since Olympic medallist Gagan Narang spotted her as a 14-year-old in Ahmedabad, there was a sense that Elavenil had something special. She has been competing internationally since 2018, when she was 18, and has since won medals at the Asian Championships, World Cups, World Cup Finals and World Championships.
She has also represented India at three major multi-sport Games — the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta, the Tokyo Olympics in 2021 and the Paris Games in 2024.
Yet she had never had a medal from one of them to show for it. At all three, she failed to make it beyond the qualification round.
There was more than enough time, then, for memories of those past disappointments to flood her mind during the one-and-a-half-hour drive from her team hotel in the port city of Nagoya, through winding hairpin bends and up into the hills towards the Shooting Range.
Instead, she looked out at the verdant mountainside and plugged in her earphones. Her playlist was a smorgasbord of Western rock, Punjabi belters, Bollywood hits and Tamil film classics.
“I’ve had a long journey from the time I first started competing. So when I got selected for these Asian Games, the first conversation I had with my coach Neha was that I had got my second opportunity to compete at an Asian Games eight years after my first. I was just grateful that I was getting the chance to be part of an Indian contingent and represent the country,” she said.
Before the competition, Elavenil had spoken to Neha, who has been part of her journey since she first picked up an air rifle 13 years ago.
“Neha just told me that I’d put in all the hard work already. She said, ‘You’ve trained your absolute best. Just trust your technique and be courageous,’” Elavenil recalled.
The first step was simply qualifying for the final. There was no guarantee that would happen.
After the first series of shooters had completed their qualification round, Elavenil knew she would need to be at her best not only to make the individual final but also to keep India in contention for a team medal.
At the start of her series, India trailed Japan by 0.7 points and Korea by 2.9 points in the team event. Those were the gaps Elavenil had to close.

She did so without missing a beat, shooting an unruffled 633.5 to qualify for the final and help ensure India finished ahead of both Japan and Korea.
That is why Elavenil’s emotions cannot simply be summed up by how she felt after the final.
Alongside the various odds and ends of equipment, snacks and kit in her shooting kitbag, Elavenil carries a small scrapbook to every competition. Once she has finished competing, she writes down how she thinks she has done. It is an immediate and honest assessment of her emotions, one she says she uses to get better in the future.
On Sunday morning, at the end of the qualification round in the women’s 10m air rifle competition, Elavenil fished it out and wrote down a single sentence.
“I did my best today.”

In New Orleans, an empty building becomes a free store — and roller skating rink
New Orleans — Scars from Hurricane Katrina are still visible in the Lower Ninth Ward more than 20 years later: empty lots where people never rebuilt their homes and boarded up storefronts where businesses never came back.
On one corner, an old Family Dollar store stands covered in graffiti. It looks abandoned. But twice a week people line up outside, and when the doors open, they rush in to find racks full of clothing and shelves piled high with household goods, toys, food, books — even packs of birth control. Mattresses and furniture line the walls and there are bins full of purses and shoes.
And it's all free for the taking at the New Orleans Free Store, where Ernestine Lane is shopping with a friend from church. They're trying on boots and winter wear even though it's mid-August and pushing 100 degrees. "The problem is, we're not used to cold weather," says Lane, "so when it gets cold, you're naked."
In this heat, several industrial fans cool the space: there's no air conditioning in the 9,000 square foot building. Lane says people might be skeptical at first, because of how the free store looks from the street. "They see the graffiti on the outside of the building and it's a misconception. I say 'Go in, there's blessings in there, go in.'"
Inside, it's a treasure trove.
"People who are struggling don't just want the bare necessities," says Dan Bingler, founder of the Greater New Orleans Caring Collective, a local mutual-aid organization that runs the free store. "They want nice things, too, because they deserve nice things, too," he adds. "People want comfort. People want care. People want fun objects in their house just for the sake of those existing."
Bingler, who is 42-years-old, has a history degree and used to work as a server and bartender in fine dining restaurants. When he was sent home at the beginning of the Covid-19 pandemic, Bingler says he started organizing grocery deliveries to older folks in the community, meal delivery to families, and help with laundry for people who couldn't safely get to a laundromat. "It blew up locally," he says.
Then, when Hurricane Ida hit Louisiana in 2021, "that put us in a position to have kind of like a community resource center," Bingler says. "We had so many objects and things people had donated."
The parking lot outside the abandoned Family Dollar was already being used in a similar way, but Bingler made a deal with the owner of the property to use the building rent-free. He just has to pay the utilities. That way the property is kept up until the owner is ready to redevelop it in the future.
"It's just a crazy opportunity," Bingler says. "I don't think it's really been tapped." He thinks the idea could be replicated at empty storefronts around the country.
That was more than three years ago. On this day, Hilsa Rodriguez, a 37-year-old mom who lives nearby is shopping with her stepdaughters, Angela and Gloria Calix.
Angela, 8, says she likes the free store "a lot." She's picked out some animal-print hair clips for school, which she shows to her sister. Gloria, 9, is shopping for baggy jeans. "I like to look for shirts in the summer," she says. She shows off a small, furry vest and explains, "My stepmom is a babysitter. I thought I could be nice and give this to the baby." She's also picked up some towels in case she goes to the beach and flip flops that she's not sure will fit: "I have big feet," she adds.
As the two older girls dig through bins and happily run around with their shopping bags, their stepmom peruses the shelves with her 4-year-old, Galya. The free store "helps us a lot," says Rodriguez, who has six kids at home. "To have all the donations that they have here," she adds, "we're very grateful."
In addition to clothing and housewares, the New Orleans Free Store opens its doors for other services twice a week. "We do free STI testing," says Bingler, as well as "some food handouts and some basic medical care." Plus art classes, free punk shows and even roller skating. "Somehow the ground is just the perfect, polished concrete for it," Bingler says.
On a Wednesday night, the overhead lights are dimmed, the industrial fans are whirring and Chrishana Simon is gliding around the makeshift roller rink. "It just feels good when you're on the wheels and you skate and the floor feels nice," she says.
Simon is relatively new to roller skating. She learned by coming to the free store, where they have skates available to rent, but she already looks like a pro, wearing a furry trapper-style hat with headphones over it and gracefully crossing one foot over the other as she skates laps around the floor.
"It's a beautiful resource for the community," Simon says during a break. "I come to skate mostly… then they have the pole, right?" She's talking about a dance pole attached to a table, surrounded by some couches — another fun feature of the free store. "I definitely skate better than I pole dance," she laughs. Simon and Diana Ledet, who volunteers during free skate, practice some moves on the pole before grabbing hands and skating off together, talking and laughing.
The store operates with the help of several neighborhood ladies who volunteer their time. Phyllis Matthews, who goes by the name 
"Queen" is sorting newly donated clothing. The retired social worker says she does a little bit of everything. "I'm all over," she says. 
"I'm like an octopus." She's on a mission now to find a truck that the store can use to pick up large donated items. Matthews says there's much need in the Lower Ninth Ward.
Erin Sims agrees. She's setting up a hot dog stand behind a counter near the back door. "I raised three kids in the Lower Ninth Ward," she says, "and my momma raised me and four of my other siblings down in the Lower Ninth Ward. I've been here all my life."
The only time Sims left was during Hurricane Katrina. When the levees broke, her house was submerged. It took her a year and a half to rebuild, but she doesn't think the neighborhood ever fully recovered. "We still have a lot of abandoned places," Sims says. "You can't get groceries... Even to get medicines you have to go to the Walgreens or Walmart. There's nothing down in the Lower Ninth Ward for that."
"It's the number one food desert in Louisiana," adds Dan Bingler. It's a void he's trying to help fill in the community with the Greater New Orleans Caring Collective. Because, as he puts it, the next storm is coming. "When something happens again, number one is we're closer. We're more prepared," he says. "We'll be doing hurricane relief... and we'll be a shelter, if need be... Even if it's just skating with a generator," Bingler says, the New Orleans Free Store will be there.

‘I'm so, so sorry’: Ed Sheeran addresses Gaza on stage after losing every opening act
About a week after the widespread international backlash for dropping his pro-Palestinian support act, Ed Sheeran made his first public comments on stage, apologising to fans and saying that what Israel is doing in Gaza is "unjustifiable".
Last week, American rapper Macklemore announced online that he had been removed from Sheeran's Loop Tour, which is due to stop at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, where Sheeran has shows on 25 and 26 September.
Macklemore was to open for Sheeran, but the stadium's owner, Robert Kraft, wanted him removed over his pro-Palestine speeches on stage, threatening to cancel Sheeran's stadium concerts if he stayed, and lobbying other stadium owners to join him in applying pressure.
"I've had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I'm so, so sorry," Sheeran told his audience in Philadelphia, where he performed for the first time since Macklemore was taken off the tour.
Pro-Palestinian protesters gathered outside the venue hours before Sheeran's concert was due to start.
At the start of the concert at Lincoln Financial Field, Sheeran called Israel's war on Gaza "catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate".
According to US media reports, the start time of Sheeran's concert was pushed back by two and a half hours because of the withdrawal of all the opening acts, and Sheeran performed solo.

German Chancellor Merz vows to stay on despite 'disaster' in state election
- Published
Embattled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay on despite exit polls in two local elections suggesting damaging defeats for his centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party.
In the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the party was projected to only just scrape into parliament, while the AfD was on track to win the most votes. Merz called the result "a disaster" for his party.
In Berlin, the ruling CDU was also expected to be beaten by Die Linke (The Left).
Merz is under mounting pressure, with poor approval ratings and rumours he could even be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap.
Votes took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt.
Echoing comments he made after that defeat, Merz told reporters on Sunday that he would forge ahead with his coalition government's plans to push through a package of economic, tax and welfare reforms.
"The reforms have to come," he insisted. "I am taking on this responsibility, because I want to move our country forward".
"I would even go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the authoritarian poison that, with the fascination of authoritarianism, is penetrating ever deeper into our society," Merz added.
Polls for both states closed at 18:00 local time (17:00 BST), with a final result expected in the coming hours.
According to public broadcaster ZDF, the AfD was projected to take 38% of the vote share in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. It was followed in second place by the centre-left SPD, on 36%.
However, the AfD is unlikely to govern in the state as other parties refuse to work with it.
For Berlin, the broadcaster put the CDU on 20% of the vote share when polls closed, behind Die Linke on nearly 26%.
Prior to Sunday's elections, there had been intense speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced unless his party's political fortunes improved.
Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz, who has only held the post for 16 months.

- A rumor circulated online in September 2026 alleging several images show the moment immediately before an Israeli "double tap" airstrike reportedly killed a Gazan child attempting to help a wounded person.
- Research on this subject concluded the images were enhanced, likely with artificial intelligence. However, further examination found an authentic video served as the reference point for the enhanced images.
- According to news reports, the video shows a boy named Muhammad al-Zinati dying in an airstrike that took place moments after an earlier strike injured or killed a man in the Sheikh Radwan neighborhood in Gaza City on Sept. 15. Getty Images hosts authentic photos that appear to match the same neighborhood, date and story.
- We contacted Palestinian news agencies reporting on the matter, as well as the Israeli government, Israeli military, Pentagon and White House, to ask about the incident. The Pentagon referred us to the Israeli military. We will update this article if we receive further information.
In September 2026, people shared various images online allegedly showing the moment immediately before an Israeli "double tap" airstrike reportedly killed a Gazan child who was attempting to help a wounded person. The images show one adult lying on the ground and the child, a boy, reacting to an incoming missile or other type of aerial weapon about to strike the ground.
A Snopes reader emailed an X post attachment, asking, "Very curious to understand if this picture posted to X is real. Stating it's a missile about to hit a child in Gaza."
(@mhdksafa via X)
A reverse image search found users sharing the same image (archived), as well as a slightly different image on Facebook (archived) and X (archived) — featuring differences in the appearance of the purported missile, debris from a destroyed building and a person lying on the ground.
(@PalPress24 via X)
The same reverse image search located posts of a third image showing the same scene, including on Instagram (archived) and X (archived) — also with differences in the appearance of the aerial object, the building debris and the person lying on the ground.
(@hasoonmasre via X)
In sum, the images provided a cropped and enhanced look at a real moment sourced from an authentic video, likely achieved with the help of artificial intelligence. One low-quality, blurry frame of that same genuine video, highlighted in other posts, truly appears to show a missile or other aerial weaponry right before a fiery explosion. For example, this post (archived) shows the authentic, unaltered moment:
(@Hakeam via X)
Two comparisons of the enhanced and original (blurry) frames confirm they were shot from the same perspective, ruling out the idea a photographer also separately captured a still picture at the exact same moment.
A Threads post hosts the authentic (and graphic) video. That post also displays one of the altered and enhanced images to the left of the genuine clip. The video itself doesn't display any signs of AI. The clip's one-minute length serves as a credible indicator of its authenticity (most AI-generated videos on social media are extremely short, lasting only seconds).
Snopes emailed the Israeli government (including the Israeli military) to pose questions about its purported participation in the airstrike. We also emailed the Pentagon, whose spokesperson referred us to the Israeli military, and emailed the White House, as well as news media outlets reporting out of Gaza, for comment. We will update this story if we receive further details.
More about the airstrike deaths
The Arabic-language Al Jazeera and Turkish state-run Anadolu Agency, as well as Palestinian outlets Al-Resalah and Shehab News Agency, all reported the news of the airstrikes.
Some of these outlets shared the enhanced images without making note of the alterations, reporting the location of the incident as the Sheikh Radwan neighborhood of Gaza City, the date as Sept. 15 and the identity of the young victim as Muhammad al-Zinati (الل محمد الزيناتي), a boy described as "no more than 15 years old" who was reportedly walking from a Quran memorization circle. According to the outlets, the video shows him approaching the man lying on the ground, identified as Sharif Shadi Labd (شريف شادي لبد), who was injured by an Israeli airstrike moments earlier.
The Shehab article and that publication's Telegram feed host other videos of al-Zinati's death, including clips reportedly showing his body covered in blood at the scene of the airstrike, as well as several moments with his father crying over him (longer video).
Getty Images hosts photos of the purported father, identified as a relative in several of the pictures, crying over a body, possibly al-Zinati. Its caption and other images match the neighborhood and date. The media-licensing company credited the pictures to photographers Ahmed Younis and Saeed M. M. T. Jaras.
Some of Shehab's still-image content appear to feature AI editing, for example the overly smooth look of an image showing the two victims posing together, possibly created from two authentic photos. The Al Jazeera (Palestine) Facebook page also featured (archived) one of the enhanced images, as well as other video clips allegedly from the same scene.
Via Messenger, we contacted Al-Resalah (archived) and Al Jazeera (Palestine) (archived) to inquire about the altered images in their Facebook posts, as well as Shehab News Agency via X to ask about another enhanced image in one of its posts (archived) — mainly whether the images were edited with AI or reposted from elsewhere. Al-Resalah and Shehab are both affiliated with the militant and political group Hamas, according to The New York Times and BBC News. We will update this article if we receive further information.
We found some of the aforementioned reporting by using Google Translate to search for the victims' Arabic-language names, a research strategy that can display results that may not show up in an English-only search.

Long-standing Winnipeg hotel reconnects with 'piece of history' after nearly 120 years
Antique mechanical cash register built in 1907 returns to Northern Hotel
A long-standing Winnipeg hotel has reconnected with a piece of its history, after an Alberta-based antiques dealer stumbled upon a cash register made for the business more than a century ago.
The register, built by National Cash Register Company in 1907, is engraved with the name of the Northern Hotel and was once a critical part of the Main Street establishment's daily operations.
"It's kind of neat. It's all mechanical — and the fact that it still works, a lot of it is just a testament to the craftsmanship that they did 120 years ago," said hotel owner Keith Horn.
"It's a piece of history."
Horn purchased the register in late July from Franz Giesen, co-owner of Frantic4tiques — an online business based in Mannville, Alta., east of Edmonton.
Giesen said he spotted the cash register for sale on Facebook Marketplace and made the nearly 1,200-kilometre drive from Mannville to Winnipeg to collect it.
"I thought on the way in, I'm like, how cool would it be if I was able to reconnect this cash register with the owner of the Northern Hotel? So then, when I got to the city, I made the phone call," Giesen said.
Horn said he was initially skeptical about buying the antique, but came around to the idea after learning more about it.
Giesen used a serial number stamped on the register to determine when it was built. He believes the machine, which is covered in embellishments, was cast in metal.
It weighs more than nine kilograms and still makes a satisfying ring when punching in the numbers, which range in value from five cents to $10.
"Just wondering what, back in 1907, was $10, when rooms back then [only cost] up to $2," Horn said, smiling.
"I guess they were very hopeful."
This particular model included specialty buttons that allowed the hotel to track how many meals or cigars it sold, and was capable of keeping a running total of the day's earnings.
While the exact history of the cash register is murky, but it's nearly as old as the hotel itself, which was built in 1906. Giesen learned the register wound up in the care of a former radio repair shop a short distance from the Northern Hotel sometime in the 1950s.
It was then inherited by the daughter of the radio shop owner, who kept it in her basement until he bought it from her, said Giesen.
"Everything from back then is just out of this world, right? Things were made to last, nothing was made to be tossed away. There is a reason why these things still exist," he said.
Horn said he plans to clean the register, and then put it on display inside the Northern Hotel.

The world is bracing for a “super” El Niño, and its effects are already being felt in India, where the monsoon has brought less rain than average but more intense downpours.
Meteorologists predict that the current El Niño, which is developing over the Pacific, could be one of the strongest in living memory. India is likely to be heavily affected, particularly later in the monsoon, when El Niño’s influence tends to strengthen.
But, as Ligin Joseph of the University of Southampton explains in The Conversation, its effects on India’s monsoon are not straightforward. A previous study in Science found that El Niño tends to bring more extreme summer monsoon rainfall to India.
This year, the southern state of Kerala has felt the brunt of the building super El Niño, with about a fifth less rain than normal. Yet intense downpours in the first week of August triggered flash flooding and landslides, killing 26 people.
The super El Niño is expected to peak after India’s monsoon season, but Indians are already keeping an anxious eye on the skies, wondering where and when the next deluge may come.

Rangers look like they know where they want to go - Celtic just look lost
- Published
At the end, every fibre of Derek McInnes' being must have wanted to have one of those Steven Gerrard moments, a scream of delight and relief into a Celtic Park camera lens, a human reaction to a significant victory on hostile terrain.
McInnes, though, showed little emotion. He shook hands with a now beleaguered Martin O'Neill and pretty much got out of there.
Later, the first words he uttered on radio were about not going "overboard" after back-to-back wins against their city rivals. "Just three points." he said. "Three points closer to Celtic."
That's true, of course, but it was also the first time a Rangers manager has won his first two games against Celtic since Graeme Souness in 1986. McInnes was 15 years old at the time.
So there was historical context but also deep relevance in the here and now. Rangers were good, and clearly deserving of the win, but they didn't quite hit the levels of ruthlessness of a week ago at Ibrox.
They can be better and yet they won as comfortably as it's possible to win when the margin at the end is just a single goal. Their superiority would have been better reflected had they won by two.
O'Neill has problems mounting game-by-game
O'Neill said there was "not much between the sides" but nobody was really buying that, Celtic folk chief among them.
The Celtic manager has problems and they're mounting game-by-game. His team is physically weak and mentally substandard. They have lost the elan they had in a few games in early season. They were out-played, out-muscled and out-coached. Again.
O'Neill has time to pause now, time to reassess. Time, perhaps, to question whether he's got the answers to the myriad ills of his team.
He doesn't have robust players in midfield because his board has not delivered them. He doesn't have the kind of wingers the club had when Daizen Maeda, Liel Abada, the still unfit Jota and Nicolas Kuhn were knocking around.
In Yang Hyun-jun's absence - and week on week he appears to be spoken about as an absent world beater - James Forrest is the best winger they have. So says former captain Scott Brown, who knows Celtic players. Forrest is 35-years-old.
Neither does O'Neill, at present, have good instincts.
Starting Sebastian Tounekti at Ibrox last week was an odd call and he changed it at half-time. Going with Sam Johnstone in goal at Rangers back-fired.
Giving Luke McCowan his first start of the season on Sunday was another curious decision that didn't work. The midfielder was off the pace and never came out for the second half.
O'Neill's famed ability to problem-solve and inspire has deserted him, for now. When set against the newfound organisation and vigour of this Rangers set-up then Celtic look jaded.
Their supporters are being cast into a scenario that none of them want to be a part of - wondering aloud, or just quietly, if the icon still has it in him. He sounds like he does. If that is the case then he needs more from his assistants - or just better ones.
From board level to coaching and playing, the whole operation looks humdrum and in need of a mighty shake. It's as if the 5-1 Champions League disintegration against LASK has removed not just confidence but heart and soul.
There was little gumption at Ibrox in the 3-0 League Cup loss, there was only a brief early reaction against Ferencvaros in the Europa League before another beating, and now there's a third poor loss in a row and a fourth inside a month.
McInnes has really hit upon something
How quickly things turn. A few short weeks ago, as Rangers exited Europe to the sound of booing, McInnes didn't hold back when assessing the problems in his team.
Not a possession team, not a pressing team, not a counter-attacking team, he said. They were also too young and too inexperienced, a collection of individuals but not a unit - no identity, no discernible style of play.
What were weaknesses then are, in the blink of an eye, strengths now. Callowness has become youthful excellence.
For the second straight week, Olwethu Makhanya was the most dominant and classy defender on the pitch. He's 22.
For the second straight week the hardest-working and most effective attacking player was Ryan Naderi. He's 23.
Dan Neil and Nico Raskin, aged 24 and 25, were once again hugely influential in the middle of the park. Neil looked fairly ordinary not that long ago. Now he's growing fast as Rangers captain.
The oldest Rangers player from the start was James Penrice, who is 27. Celtic had six guys who were older than him in their team. The average age of the line-ups was 26.7 versus 24.4.
McInnes has moulded them all into a group of players who have, against Celtic, shown maturity and togetherness. He has really hit on something.
Certain things stood out. At half-time, Rangers were not just ahead thanks to Naderi's goal, they were winning battles all over the pitch, just as they had done last Sunday.
They were winning aerial duels by 67.6% to 32.4%, they had eight shots to Celtic's one, six on target to Celtic's zero.
Camilo Duran had eight touches of the ball, Kevin Kelsy had 13 and Naderi 23. All the individual match-ups were more or less Rangers victories.
Even when Celtic's club record-signing Kasper Hogh came on, not a lot changed. Rangers had more chances in the second half.
Hogh got no service again, but he's beginning to look like a player so devoid of belief that even if service did come his way there's no guarantee that he'd execute the way he did so often for Bodo-Glimt.
When your star striker can't get a start and when your leader, Callum McGregor, is getting over-run, then you have problems, too many for O'Neill to solve.
McInnes was right about the three points thing, but the momentum in Glasgow is his now. The energy, the clarity, the optimism is blue and not green. The power has switched with breakneck speed and, of course, it could switch back again if Celtic get their act together.
There are massive questions now, though. More than O'Neill would have ever faced in the city before.
Rangers look, at the moment, like a club that knows where it wants to go. Celtic, by contrast, look lost in a haze of confusion and uncertainty.

Veteran goalkeeper Savita Punia became the Indian women’s hockey player with the most international appearances on Monday.
She made her 321st senior international appearance during India’s 17-1 thrashing of Indonesia at the Asian Games 2026, surpassing former India forward Vandana Katariya’s record.

Hailing from Sirsa district in Haryana, the 36-year-old became only the sixth woman hockey player to be conferred the prestigious Padma Shri earlier this year. She was also awarded the Arjuna Award in 2018.
Speaking after the match, Savita said, “I want to start by saying thank you — to my family, my coaches, my teammates and every single person who has stood behind me since I was a young girl learning to save my first penalty corner. Honestly, I never thought I would reach this milestone.”

* Arjuna Award: Recipient in 2018
* Padma Shri: Recipient in 2025
* Hockey India Baljit Singh Award: Goalkeeper of the Year in 2015 and 2024
* Hockey India Balbir Singh Senior Award: Player of the Year in 2021, 2022 and 2024
