Here's why an Arizona medical examiner is working to track heat-related deaths
Greg Hess deals with death day in, day out.
Hess is the medical examiner for Pima County, Ariz., a region along the United States-Mexico border. His office handles some 3,000 deaths each year — quiet deaths, overdoses, gruesome deaths, tragic ones.
From April through October every year, Hess is confronted with an increasingly obvious and dramatic problem: His morgue drawers fill with people who died sooner than they should have because of Arizona's suffocating heat.
Pima is hot, but it's not the hottest county in the country. Nor the biggest; the most humid; or the most populated. But Hess and his team are at the country's forefront in one key way: They have developed some of the most innovative strategies to accurately count the number of people dying from heat-related problems. Those efforts could redefine how the United States understands the growing cost of climate change, because right now, the human toll of climate-worsened disasters is dramatically undercounted.
A small group of health experts across the country has concluded over time that thousands of Americans die every year because of climate-fueled disasters, like stronger, more dangerous hurricanes or heat waves so intense they obliterate historical records. And no one is keeping official track of the scope of the problem — not government agencies, researchers or state officials.
Those omissions aren't just painful for the loved ones of the dead, says Kristie Ebi, a public health and climate epidemiologist at the University of Washington. They have concrete consequences: Without an accurate count of the human toll of weather disasters, it is hard — or sometimes impossible — to understand their full impact on families and communities. By extension, Ebi says, an incomplete count impairs the ability to plan for and prevent such losses in the future, like knowing when and where to locate cooling centers during a heat wave.
"If you don't know how many people suffer and die in disasters, then you can't set priorities appropriately," she says.
But now a small contingent is trying to count better — a critical goal as climate change pushes heat to nearly unlivable temperatures, makes hurricanes deadlier and chokes communities with wildfire smoke. The ranks are diverse, from those on the front lines of death, like Hess, to epidemiologists and public health experts. And their goal is to provide insights based on their data so that policymakers, city leaders and advocates have the information needed to save lives.
A heat-curious medical examiner
Hale, ruddy-cheeked Hess grew up in Wisconsin, but he has thrived in the desert. He rides his bike to and from work, even through the blazing Arizona summer heat, and he is the undisputed champion of the office's ongoing pickleball competition (evidence: a small silvery cup on his office shelf, a pickleball jammed inside and a stamped label reading "CHAMPION").
When he was in medical school, he rotated through a forensic pathology stint, which other students avoided. After all, wasn't being a doctor about saving people, they asked? What was the point of working on someone who was already dead? But that was part of the appeal for Hess. There was a mystery in these people on the autopsy table, entire lives encapsulated in the bodies that remained.
Plus, upon first meeting, his new department head asked Hess about his beer preferences. This was the place for him, he thought: on a team of people who were, despite their deeply serious work, playful, thoughtful and creative.
Hess did a residency in Wisconsin and a stint as an Air Force doctor in California. But when he took the lead medical examiner position in Pima County, Ariz., in 2011, he ran headlong into a crisis — one that would inform his work for years to come.
Pima County is tucked up against the U.S.-Mexico border in southern Arizona. It's a small county — about a million people, most of whom live in Tucson. The rest is rural, swaths of desert crisscrossed by roads stripped pale by the incessant sun. When Hess arrived, the county was a hot spot for people attempting to cross the border on foot from Mexico into the U.S. But the desert was punishing. Every few weeks during summer after summer, Hess got a call asking his death investigators to go to a scene where two, or six, or eight people had been killed by heat and exposure. The annual counts ran into the hundreds.
The nonstop stream of complicated deaths pushed Hess' team to develop innovative protocols. They learned how to thoroughly investigate each death, identify those lost, and track down family members left behind, to give them some sense of closure. Hess developed a deep appreciation for the data his team produced and what it could do.
A few years later, the opioid epidemic slammed into Pima and filled the office's autopsy tables. Once again, Hess and his team leaned into their experience collecting thorough, complete data describing and humanizing the deaths. And as always, Hess collated all the data into neat annual reports. But he suspected they sat on someone's desktop, unread. The reports were packed with valuable insight, but their utility was limited because they were "not very timely," he said.
But around this time, during the height of the opioid epidemic, other officials — from county public health, the mayor's office, the police force, the federal government — realized that death data could help prevent more deaths by identifying patterns quickly and figuring out how to intervene. But that would require a faster exchange of data. So in 2022 Hess got the go-ahead to hire an epidemiologist, Tasha Tully, to mine the rich seam of information the team collected. She developed a near-real-time dashboard that tracked opioid deaths and funneled useful insights to the city and state offices.
Before long, Tully and Hess realized such efforts could help them understand another, quieter epidemic: the avalanche of deaths from each hotter and hotter summer.
Why heat?
The biggest, most obvious, directly climate-influenced risk to people's lives comes from heat.
Climate change has dramatically increased the risk of heat in every state and territory of the United States in recent years. Nationally, summer high temperatures have increased by just under 2 degrees Fahrenheit since the 1970s. But that small number belies the dramatic impact: A small shift in the average temperatures means extremes become much more likely — and much more deadly. Events like the 2021 heat wave that shattered temperature records in the Pacific Northwest would have been virtually impossible absent human-driven climate change, scientists found. So would 2023's 31-day-long run of 110-plus F temperatures in Phoenix, Ariz.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that each year about 1,200 people in the U.S. die of problems directly caused by heat, such as heatstroke; that number has risen from about 700 just a few years ago. But that's a vast undercount, says Greg Wellenius, an environmental epidemiologist at Boston University. The true toll, according to a 2020 statistical estimate from Wellenius' lab, is likely at least 10,000 people every single year.
The discrepancy arises, in part, because the CDC's estimate is based on whether heat is recorded on someone's death certificate. But for a host of reasons, heat is rarely listed as a cause of death — even when it plays a major role.
"If somebody doesn't report it, we don't know about it," says Kathryn Pinneri, a former president of the National Association of Medical Examiners.
Heat is not commonly mentioned on death certificates because heat alone is rarely the main thing that kills people. Typically, hyperthermia deaths are easy to spot, Hess says: What's trickier to identify, yet much more common, are deaths from other health problems that were exacerbated by heat.
There is no doubt that heat worsens health problems. In hot weather, the number of cardiac arrests rises. The number of strokes goes up. Complications from diabetes increase. Deaths associated with neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's increase.
But linking a heart attack to heat is trickier. For that, you need data, collected at the very place where someone died: Was it 120 degrees Fahrenheit inside the home? Was someone working on a roof hours before they collapsed? That specific evidence is what Hess' office now excels at uncovering.
Hess describes a scenario he's encountered more times than he can count. His office gets a call about an unhoused person found dead in a park, drug paraphernalia next to them on the ground. At autopsy, the forensic pathologists find drugs in the deceased's bloodstream. In the past, when they filled out their software and death certificate, they almost certainly would have noted it as an overdose death alone, Hess says. But heat makes drug use more dangerous: Methamphetamine inhibits sweating. Opioids like fentanyl inhibit users' awareness of heat. Cocaine makes people more active.
"We sure do get a lot more of those unhoused people dead in the park with overdoses in July than we do in December," Hess says. "And so, why? 'Why' is because heat may contribute to those deaths."
So now, when death investigators go out to the body, they'll note that it was 115 degrees outside. Then, when they fill out their paperwork, they will note the heat — and likely enter it as a contributing factor to the death. That attribution then shows up on the death certificate.
Sometimes the connection between heat and someone's death is even harder to figure out. What if an older person with a heart problem dies in their home, a trailer that has never had air conditioning, Hess asks? How hot does the room have to be to have been too hot for that person to survive? People who certify deaths are careful: They want real, solid evidence to support their decisions.
If a medical examiner or coroner sees an edge case with no context about heat, "they are going to use their best judgment and say, I don't have enough evidence to make that claim, and therefore I won't make that claim. How would you?" Hess says.
But the evidence does often exist, Hess and other medical examiners say. Creating systems to collect and analyze that evidence is what their offices do differently than many others. The evidence is not as stark as a ligature mark, or chemical traces in someone's blood, but contextual clues instead. It's up to the medical examiner, coroners and the death investigators who go to the scene to collect them.
Clue hunters
Hess knew that another medical examiner had already spent several years thinking deeply about the accuracy of death tolls: Jeff Johnston, the energetic forensic pathologist who had stepped into the lead role in Arizona's Maricopa County in 2013.
Maricopa enfolds Phoenix, the poster child for heat risk. Phoenix's summer temperatures regularly hover well above 100 degrees Fahrenheit for weeks. Nearly 40% of the city is paved, trapping daytime heat in concrete and asphalt and keeping overnight temperatures stifling. Doctors, houseless advocates, government officials and residents have recognized for some time that the conditions in Phoenix have made it a deadly place to live.
The problem was, no one really knew exactly how deadly. Like Pima, Maricopa based its estimates on the number of death certificates that mentioned "heat" as the primary cause of death or as a major contributing cause.
But in 2018, Johnston told the 16 forensic pathologists on his team to try something new: Think about heat deaths more expansively. They would track not just heat-caused deaths — the obvious cases, like heatstroke — but heat-related deaths as well.
They came up with a protocol. Every time the office gets a call about a body, they send a "death investigator" to suss out the context in which someone died. Between April and October, those investigators ask about heat. They check the temperature of the rooms people were found in. They ask whether they were having trouble paying their electric bill because of air conditioning. They see whether a phalanx of fans was set up in front of the chair in which someone died.
All that context feeds into the decisions pathologists make when examining the body and filling out death records and goes into the official records themselves. They coined the term "environmental heat exposure" to encapsulate heat-related factors that contributed to someone's death without necessarily being the primary driver.
"There is some art in deciding what's significant or not," Johnston says. Hard science, yes, but also nuance, and curiosity and creativity in trying to piece together the last fragments of someone's life. "It's hot every summer: 103, 105. The question is, what's too hot?"
In the mid-2010s, Maricopa reported 61 to 182 heat deaths per year. But after they changed their count technique, the numbers swelled: In 2020, there were 323; 339 in 2021; and 645 in 2023. The numbers were alarmingly large. But they were certainly more representative of what had been happening for years — just not recognized.
None of the changes were complicated. But the shift in mindset is revolutionary, says Rebecca Sunenshine, head of Maricopa County's Public Health Department.
Data from Johnston's office was used to make the case that utilities shouldn't shut off people's power in the summer, even if their bills were overdue. That 2019 policy shift has likely saved lives, says Sunenshine. In Pima, the Public Health Department is exploring ways to use Hess' data to figure out where to put cooling centers and to identify those at excessive risk from heat, such as people who live in mobile homes.
Tully, the forensic epidemiologist in Pima, sees the data she produces as the foundation for better decisions. "It's the beauty of my job, I think. It's being able to be like, OK, we're going to put information out that people haven't had before," she says. "If public health officials don't have those numbers, they can't identify a problem. They can't try to address a problem, and they certainly can't find solutions to a problem they don't know exists."
The way forward
Johnston and Hess were among the first medical examiners in the country to adopt the new protocol, with a few tweaks that made more sense for his smaller office in Pima County.
Adoption elsewhere has been slow. "We have a fragmented death investigation system right now in this country," says Kelly Keyes, president-elect at the International Association of Coroners & Medical Examiners. There is no nationally consistent method by which the people involved in death investigations decide whether a death is related to a disaster in the first place, she says. On top of that, Keyes says, "There is no central repository of death information other than the death certificates." So if crucial information doesn't make it onto those certificates, there's little or no hope of retroactively finding that lost context.
This burst into public awareness after 2017's Hurricane Maria, the storm that devastated Puerto Rico. Initial government counts suggested 64 people died in and after the storm. But Puerto Ricans knew that number was an extreme undercount. Statisticians looked at the number of deaths recorded in the weeks following the storm and compared that to previous years with no storms, a technique to calculate "excess mortality" from an event like a hurricane or a disease wave (the technique was used to estimate COVID-19 deaths, as well). Those estimates put the true numberin the thousands. The official record now stands at 2,975, nearly 50 times the original.
Afterward, a congressional bill required the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine to assess the disaster-death counting capabilities in the U.S. The ensuing report explains that "there are no standard practices" for deciding whether deaths are disaster-related, and it identified "persistent, systemic" flaws in the current system, from inadequate guidance on how to count disaster-related deaths to poor use of the invaluable data that does exist. It recommended systemwide reform of death-assessment efforts nationwide.
But that change has not happened. The CDC last published best-practice guides for how to more expansively account for disaster-related deaths in 2017 and has conducted just a few training sessions for death certifiers since then.
In the meantime, the National Association of Medical Examiners has been pushing its members to adopt standards it recommended in 2022. Johnston presented on Maricopa's strategies at a late 2023 meeting of medical examiners, and other jurisdictions are considering adopting similar measures. But overall, it is slow going, says Pinneri.
"It really is going to vary amongst the jurisdictions and how the deaths are actually reported to the medical examiners and coroners," she says. "And that is something we cannot control at all. We can beg and plead and say, 'You need to report these,'" but the standards are voluntary, and offices are often overstretched, Pinneri says.
The challenges are not unique to heat. Climate change is also raising the risks from hurricanes and wildfires — and death tolls of those events are similarly hard to track.
Wildfire smoke inhalation is rarely, if ever, documented as a primary or even contributing cause of death, though many medical professionals and public health experts think it is driving hundreds, or even thousands, to premature death each year. Similarly, medical examiners, coroners and doctors struggle to attribute many people's deaths to hurricanes, especially if those deaths aren't immediate. When a falling tree branch kills someone during the storm, that would be tallied. But what about the case where the storm knocks out the power to someone's ventilator, asks Keyes? Or someone who couldn't get dialysis because the clinic flooded? "Where is that on the scale?" she asks.
The omissions are not purely academic. The Federal Emergency Management Agency, or FEMA, provides funds for funeral costs if someone's death is associated with a federally declared disaster — but it has to be listed on the death certificate. Many who lost family members to Hurricane Maria were denied those funds, absent direct attribution on the certificate. And heat isn't even considered a "natural disaster" eligible for federal aid.
Other challenges abound. Of the 3,000 different medical examiners, coroners and justice of the peace offices nationwide, only about 50% of them are even using computerized case management systems, Keyes says. And in recent years, the field of death has been "extremely taxed," she says. The opioid crisis, COVID-19 and ongoing disasters — the relentless crises have stretched thin the few thousand people in this line of work nationwide.
Five years into Johnston's experiment in Maricopa, there's just starting to be enough years of data to show that the office's new protocols are effectively revealing the scope of the heat problem.
So far, though, the deaths are only increasing. The 2023 summer broke nearly every heat record in Arizona. The 35-day stretch of 110-plus temperatures pushed the office near a breaking point.
"It's really an emergency response, a crisis response, these last two summers," Johnston says. In a normal summer, the office handles about 25% more bodies than during the rest of the year. "We're prepared for that. That's our norm," Johnston says, but "the last two summers, they've been 63% above that."
Some weeks saw twice as many bodies as usual. His team of 30 was doing 80 scene investigations a week. They rotated shifts so the exam tables in the mortuary were constantly in use, just to keep up with the flood of bodies coming in. Maricopa released the final count of 2023's heat-related deaths in April of this year: 645.
"It's all a balancing act of trying to respond to what is essentially a mass fatality event," Johnston says. "It's really hard. The last two summers have been really, really hard."
In April of this year, just a few days after the 2023 Maricopa death toll was issued, the heat in Arizona was back. The temperatures at Hess and Tully's midday pickleball competitions cracked 100 in April. The death investigators are packing thermometers in the bags they take to scenes. Hess sent around an email reminding the forensic pathologists to go through a heat-focused checklist in their autopsies. By April, Pima recorded its first heat-related deaths of the season; the teams are bracing for another challenging year.
Hess knows there's only so much his office can do. But "if you can't articulate what the problem is, then how can you talk about solutions?" Hess asks. "We're not the solution people. We're just the medical examiner's offices, the objective data people. And we just give other people the data and say, here, figure it out."

Dutch riot police break up far-right protest in The Hague after violence erupts
Dutch riot police have dispersed several hundred far-right protesters in The Hague after violence has erupted
THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- Dutch riot police dispersed several hundred far-right protesters in The Hague on Saturday after violence erupted and local authorities banned a planned march in the city against immigration and asylum policies.
Police officers made several arrests after some protesters started throwing fireworks and other projectiles at them.
Justice Minister David van Weel called on X for an “extremely firm” response to what he described as “disgusting scenes” at the protest. He said that demonstrators made Nazi salutes, chanted antisemitic slogans, attacked police and threw fireworks at riot officers.
“Thanks to all the police officers who are once again standing up for our democratic rule of law,” he wrote.
The Hague municipality banned the march after violence broke out among demonstrators gathered at the Malieveld, a park in the city center, and later ordered the crowd to disperse.
Saturday’s unrest came a year after rioting erupted around a right-wing demonstration. A police car was set on fire during clashes between black-clad protesters and police, and the headquarters of the centrist D66 party — whose leader, Rob Jetten, is now prime minister — was attacked.

A surprising statistic about health equity
Before writing this newsletter for you all, I sat on a panel at the National Academies of Science. The session was part of an all-day roundtable about studying population health and communicating that information to the public. A common thread was how the way we talk about research impacts trust in science, something we have been thinking a lot about at STAT. We discussed some of my reporting over the past year on health equity researchers, who have felt political pressure not to speak publicly about their work.
But my co-panelist, Phillip Alberti from the Association of American Medical Colleges’ Center for Health Justice, raised polling he conducted showing that most American adults favor efforts to achieve health equity, though the amount of support varied a bit based on how you framed the question.
“When we asked a representative sample of U.S. adults … ‘Do you support the goal of health equity’ without any definition, 65% of self-identified conservatives said ‘I do.’ So I think even though there was a difference, it’s not as big as maybe we are being told it is,” he said.
Alberti also noted that the AAMC will have more data in coming weeks about how trust in health care institutions has changed. You can watch a recording of the panel here. Relatedly, I had a story late on Wednesday about some researchers pushing back on the National Institutes of Health’s screening of grants for specific keywords by suing the agency.
Kennedy goes on offense against vaccines
Speaking of trust in science, Isa Cueto brings us a dispatch from the Children’s Health Defense conference in Washington, D.C., where CHD founder and current health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. gave the keynote. At points during his tenure, Kennedy has downplayed his skepticism about vaccines, but that attitude was not present on Thursday. For more than 20 minutes, he cast doubt on shots, saying he feels the public has “no idea” about the risk profile of vaccines that have been administered tens of millions of times.
You can read more about Kennedy’s “victory lap” here. And it’s worth revisiting Daniel Payne’s reporting on CHD from last year here as well.
The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force has all new members
On Thursday, Kennedy also named new members to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. The committee has largely stayed mum throughout the second Trump administration — last year Kennedy announced he would fire task force members because they were too “woke,” and the panel has not met in over a year. The group is tasked with determining which preventive measures insurance companies cover.
Kennedy’s USPSTF is now made up of specialists instead of generalists, which the American Medical Association called a “significant departure from the Task Force’s traditional membership.” One expert added that specialists often don’t sit on the panel because they may introduce conflicts of interest. (The page intended to host conflict of interest disclosures says it is being updated). Read more about the eight new members of the task force here. You can also revisit this write-up of the 2025 Supreme Court decision that handed Kennedy the power to remake the committee.

ARPA-H announces new grants to speed up diagnoses
Yesterday, the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health announced a new effort to improve autism diagnosis. “We are not satisfied simply for describing autism and managing its consequences,” Kennedy said of the initiative in his speech at CHD. “We are asking what drives the different forms of autism, and why developmental trajectories differ, why some children regress, and which interventions work for them.”
The effort calls for “solutions” that speed up the time to diagnose autism. Wait times for an assessment can take months, if not years, as the number of people with autism increases. The issue has also received more attention under the Trump administration. You can read Rose’s story about the announcement here.

That lingo comes from the looksmaxxing community, a male-dominated group that seeks to improve their attractiveness at all costs. Fair skin, curly hair, tall height no basis to determine caste, religion: Madras HC
The court made the observation while setting aside an order, which held that a community certificate held by a man was not genuine citing physical attibutes.
The Madras High Court recently said that physical attributes including fair skin, tall height and curly hair, without any evaluation conducted by an anthropologist, could not be used to determine someone's religion or community.
The court made the observation while setting aside an order of the District Level Vigilance Committee – which had held that a community certificate held by a man was not genuine. The committee had decided that the man did not belong to the Adi Dravidar community, which is a Scheduled Caste community, Live Law reported.
The HC was hearing a petition filed by M Ravikumar, who had challenged the order deeming his certificate invalid. Ravikumar had, in his petition, stated that his father belonged to the Adi Dravidar community but had converted to Christianity. However, Ravikumar said both his father and him had reconverted to Hinduism later.
Also Read | SC rejects presumption of child sale, orders custody to adoptive parents in Telangana
“While, whether the petitioner follows the Hindu gods or Christianity, will be relevant, the reasoning that the petitioner and his family members are very fair in colour, they are tall and having good physique and speak Tamil and English and have curly hair, may not have any relevance,” Live Law cited the HC as saying.
What was the case?
Ravikumar had, in his plea, argued that his father originally belonged to the Hindu Adi Dravidar community, but had converted to Christianity. Ravikumar was born when his father was a practicing Christian, according to Live Law.
However, Ravikumar and his father later reconverted to Hinduism, with the petitioner submitting that both had gone to the Arya Samaj centre, where the re-conversion ceremonies took place.
Ravikumar stated that he had obtained a community certificate after reconversion and was working as Assistant Commissioner in Chennai General Commissionerate. However, right before his superannuation in May earlier this year, the authorities had initiated a verification of the genuineness of his community certificate, with the commissioner later conveying the finding that the certificate was not genuine.
What were the arguments made?
Ravikumar argued that his family was practicing Hinduism, while submitting that both his and his daughters' marriages had been solemnised according to Hindu rites and customs.
Regarding the mention of appearance, he said that the certificate was held as not genuine while only considering their looks, fair colour, height etc, adding that this did not stand the scrutiny of law, Live Law reported.
Meanwhile, the authorities submitted that the petitioner and his family were only claiming to practice Hinduism to get employment and reservation status, but were actually professing Christianity. The defendants further argued that the petitioner's father was buried in a Christian cemetery, and said that while the petitioner had claimed reconversion back to Hinduism, the community people had not accepted it.
What were the court's observations?
Justice Bharatha Chakravarthy set aside the District Level Vigilance Committee order, saying the complexion of a person, their height and proficiency in Tamil alone are not enough to prove that they practice Christianity.
“The manner, in which the said reasons are mentioned in the impugned order, is also not in the context of any evaluation by any anthropologist in this regard,” the court added. The HC noted that the Commission had stated that in the 1994 ration card, the petitioner's daughter's name was in Christian, however, as per the petitioner, he got married in 1994 and the daughter was born in 1998.
The high court directed the petitioner to be given an opportunity of personal hearing, according to Live Law, and asked Ravikumar to appear before the authorities within four weeks and submit all documents, including the photographs and other materials, to prove that he was following Hinduism. The Madras HC also directed the vigilance committee to pass orders within eight weeks of the enquiry.

How the race they said women couldn't run took centre stage
- Published
For 32 years, the women's 800m was absent from the Olympics, with its competitors deemed too frail. Now, it is one of the most hotly anticipated events on the track.
This extraordinary story starts at the 1928 Olympic Games, which represented a huge - if temporary - step forward for women's sports.
The Amsterdam Games were the first to allow women to compete in track and field events. Five women's events were added to the programme - the 100m, high jump, discus, 400m hurdles and, controversially at the time, 800m.
The progress, however, was temporary.
German athlete Karoline Lina Radke, external became the first woman to win Olympic gold in the 800m - but she would also be the last for another 32 years.
The event was removed from the Games after reports - later proven to be false - claimed competitors suffered extreme exhaustion after the race, and the International Olympic Committee decided women were too frail to compete, external over the two-lap distance.
Fast forward almost 100 years and the event now gets headline status at major events.
In recent times, it's been the battle between Britain's Olympic 800m champion Keely Hodgkinson and the Swiss European champion Audrey Werro that has captivated fans.
So how did the 800m become the 'one to watch'? BBC Sport spoke to the women who helped shape the race to find out.
'You don't realise what you've done'
It was the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, and Ann Brightwell (nee Packer) had just crossed the finish line of the women's 800m to take gold - and set a new world record.
In doing so, Brightwell became the first British woman to win an Olympic gold on the track, in a time of two minutes 01.1 seconds.
She told BBC Sport: "My husband, who was my fiance then, said to me, 'you don't realise what you've done'.
"I didn't give it a thought at the time… but now I realise I played a very small part in women running longer distances."
But the controversy hadn't completely gone away. Brightwell knew all about the claims that had seen women unable to compete for 32 years after the 800m was removed from the Olympics.
Brightwell adds: "Men weren't happy about women competing in these very high profile events…we were considered too frail and too delicate.
"And they took it upon themselves to make it look really bad. They were saying women were collapsing on the way round. But it was all a lie."
After 1928, women's middle-distance shrunk into the shadows for the next few decades.
The 800m was finally reintroduced to the Olympic programme in 1960 and, four years later, the then-22-year-old Brightwell went to her first Olympics, fitting training around her job as a teacher.
"Many people in my era either had to take unpaid leave or resign, or they got sacked because they were trying to juggle their sports with their career," she said.
"My school was very tolerant towards what I was doing, so I was fortunate."
Going out for a run around the local streets or countryside - which seems so commonplace today - was unusual in the era Brightwell was competing.
"If I just felt like an easy run, I would run around my village, around the streets… people commented on it or tooted their horns. And it was funny looking back, but it never troubled me," the now 84-year-old told BBC Sport.
Brightwell's 800m time of 2:01.1 stood for almost three years, before Australian Judy Pollock broke that with a new time of 2:01 flat in 1967.
The next target was to go under two minutes.
Breaking 'sub-two' - and a stubborn world record
"Records are great and medals are the best, but when you break a barrier it's a fantastic feeling," said Christina Boxer-Cahill (nee Boxer).
It was at the 1979 European Cup final in Turin that Boxer-Cahill looked up at the clock and realised she'd gone under two minutes.
She added: "I knew this would probably be my last chance, because there were other girls in Britain trying to do it."
In 1971, Germany's Hildegard Falck, external had become the first woman to break the two-minute barrier.
Eight years later, it was the 22-year-old Boxer-Cahill who became the first British woman to do so, in a time of one minute 59.05 seconds.
"It's a bit like when Roger Bannister broke four minutes for the mile. Once he'd done it everybody did it because you see what's possible," Boxer-Cahill, who is now 69 years old, told BBC Sport.
"I just think I'm so fortunate that I was in a sport where everybody accepted that you have men and women's races in the Olympics."
From 1971 to 1983, the women's 800m world record would be broken six times.
But the 1983 record stands to this day.
It belongs to Czech athlete Jarmila Kratochvilova, who ran a time of one minute 53.28 seconds at a meeting in Munich.
Kratochvilova's record has been questioned, with claims it was assisted by her country's doping regime that existed at the time, something she has strenuously denied.
In 2017, European Athletics proposed wiping out records set before 2005 - sending a strong signal that records set before then were disputable.
Several Soviet satellite states - including East Germany - are known to have been operating state-sponsored doping programmes throughout the 1980s.
At the 1988 Seoul Olympics, Boxer-Cahill finished fourth in the 1500m, behind a Russian athlete who was later banned for doping.
Boxer-Cahill said: "I was running during that Eastern Bloc era when, you know, they've looked back and some of the performances, there's sort of a cloud over it.
"I'd just have loved to have been on that rostrum. I wish the Eastern Bloc system hadn't been there, but that's what it was.
"Politics in sport, when you're the performer, it frustrates you. But if you get too frustrated, all it's going to do is upset your own performance."
Women's 800m 'stronger than ever'
"We've got not just two but several girls who are running under two minutes every time they turn out," Brightwell told BBC Sport.
"It's stronger than it's ever been."
Kratochvilova's 43-year-old record is looking increasingly precarious.
The 800m European champion Werro has come closest, running a time just 0.42 seconds shy of the record at the Zurich Diamond League.
Keely Hodgkinson, the current 800m indoor world record holder, told BBC Sport earlier this year that she's never felt closer to breaking the outdoor record.
She said: "I really do believe we can break it, but a lot of things have got to come together."
Hodgkinson is one of six athletes competing in the 800m at Athlos, the all-female athletics event taking place in London, on Friday.
"I do think the [800m] world record will go in the next year or two, and hopefully this season, because we're on a real high, aren't we?" Boxer-Cahill told BBC Sport.
"If it happens towards the end of the season, 2026 [would be] the year of women's 800m running."

Pragati, an Indian influencer who runs the Instagram account Lucknowi in Japan, has left viewers amused after sharing a video about losing her iPhone 16 Pro in Japan - again. The influencer said this was the fifth time she had misplaced her phone there, only to eventually find it at the exact spot where she had left it. In the video, Pragati joked about her habit of forgetting where she puts her phone. “Sab kehte hai ki phone ki lat hona bohot kharab cheez hai, lekin mere liye phone ki lat na hona bohot kharab cheez hai kyunki main apne phone kahi bhi bhool jati hu aur phir 2-3 ghante baad mujhe yaad aata hai,” she said. She then used another phone to locate the missing iPhone through Apple’s Find My feature. As she walked towards the location shown on the map, she recalled several previous incidents in which she had misplaced her phone. Pragati said she had previously found her phone at a police station and another time in a vegetable market. She also recalled leaving it behind in a trial room on two occasions. What surprised her was not simply that the phone was recovered each time, but that it was still where she had left it. Japan does have a formal system for dealing with lost property. The National Police Agency says people who find belongings can hand them to a police station or police box, while items found at a particular facility should generally be reported to the manager. Police can then cross-reference recovered property with lost-property reports and return items to their owners. The system handles millions of lost-and-found items every year. In 2024, around 31.28 million found items were reported, including those retained by designated facilities, with about 11.41 million articles returned to their owners. Pragati ended her video by reflecting on how unusual her repeated experiences seemed. “I don't know agar ye koi country mein possible hai but kasam se Japan mein mere saath ye 4-5 baar ho chuka hai,” she said. She then joked, “Toh aap log dekh sakte hai main apne phone se kitna detached hu.” Her husband, who was laughing during the recording, then asked her to return his own phone - the device she had been using to film the video. Sharing the clip on Instagram, Pragati wrote that losing the iPhone 16 Pro had happened “AGAIN” and called it the fifth time. She asked followers how often they had lost their phones and whether they had managed to get them back. The comments quickly turned into a discussion about Japan’s reputation for returning lost property. One user mentioned experiencing similar safety in Dubai, while another joked that Pragati’s repeated phone losses were simply an excuse to make her husband walk after eating. Others contrasted her experience with their own experiences in India. For Pragati, however, the recurring pattern has become almost a running joke - she loses her phone, forgets about it for hours, and somehow finds it waiting exactly where she left it. Germany’s embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has vowed to stay in office and fight for future-proofing economic changes despite heavy losses for his conservatives in two state elections, one to the far right and the other to a leftwing party.
Preliminary results indicated Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) tallied just over the 5% threshold to enter the state parliament in the coastal region of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, its worst-ever state score, which he called a “disaster”.
The anti-immigration, Kremlin-friendly Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party extended a streak of strong showings by coming in first in the former communist region with nearly 38%, more than doubling its previous score.
In the capital, Berlin, one of Germany’s 16 federal states, the far-left Die Linke looked on course to win with about 25% of the vote, ahead of the incumbent CDU by a five-point margin. The AfD made headway there too, with a clear double-digit result.
The deeply unpopular Merz has been fighting for his political survival after a humiliating series of setbacks with voters this year.
Speculation about his ability to hold on as chancellor reached fever pitch after Saxony-Anhalt state’s AfD chapter routed the CDU with a record 44% for the party in an election two weeks ago.
The Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania result marked the third time the AfD has emerged as the strongest party in a region, although the party seemed likely to remain shut out of power in the state because of a “firewall” of non-cooperation agreed by the other main parties.
In a rare speech on a state election night, Merz admitted the CDU had been bitterly deprived of “tailwinds from Berlin” in both of Sunday’s races. But he said he would remain chancellor and party chair and continue a reform drive on fronts including taxes, healthcare, pensions and reducing bureaucracy.
Merz said the German economy was facing “profound upheaval”, while public discourse had become “harsher and more irreconcilable”.
“Trust in our country’s institutions is waning and is being actively undermined by radical parties on both the left and the right,” he said.
But he added: “Germany is capable of reform. I would even go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the poison of authoritarianism, which is penetrating ever deeper into our society as the fascination with authoritarianism grows.”
A jubilant AfD co-leader, Tino Chrupalla, mocked Merz before his speech, saying voters had given his own party a “very clear result” and called on the chancellor to resign.
About 2.5 million people were eligible to vote in Berlin and nearly 1.3 million in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
The stinging blows from the latest elections had been expected to put pressure on Merz at a minimum to cede the CDU leadership, which would have in effect ruled out a run for re-election at the next national poll, due in 2029.
Merz’s eroding support has created a sense of instability in Europe’s top economy, which is struggling with deindustrialisation, sluggish growth and soaring energy costs.
If the AfD’s surge led Merz to abandon the chancellery prematurely, it would give the far right further momentum as France, Italy, Spain and Poland head into elections next year with nativist parties on the march.
Germany has high constitutional hurdles to replacing a chancellor against their will and any appointed successor would need to demonstrate a ruling majority. A failure to do so could trigger a new election.
The AfD is the biggest opposition force in parliament and is leading national opinion polls with about 30%. It has called for Germany to quit the euro, end support for Ukraine and carry out mass deportations of “irregular” migrants, while citing the “destruction” of the CDU as one of its central goals.
The CDU’s debacle in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania – a small, relatively poor state – is particularly bitter for Merz as it was home to the constituency of his arch-rival, Angela Merkel. While she governed Germany for 16 years, Merz appears to be on the ropes after no more than 16 months.
Merz took office in May 2025 at the helm of a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) promising to restore the German economy to strength and slash the AfD’s support.
A failure to make decisive headway on either front has produced profound disappointment in his leadership, with only one in 10 Germans saying they are satisfied with his performance. An inability to connect with voters appears particularly marked in the former communist east, where the AfD is strongest.
In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the Social Democratic party state premier, Manuela Schwesig, distanced herself during the campaign from a key pension change backed by her party in Merz’s coalition government.
She was expected to hold on to power in a left-leaning coalition even if the AfD came out on top when all the votes were counted. Despite leading the polls for months, the far right failed to garner enough support to govern alone and the remaining parties have ruled out working with it.
A confirmed win by Die Linke in Berlin, where the far-left party has called for expropriation of corporate landlords to fight rising housing costs, could see its candidate, Elif Eralp, become the capital’s first leader of Turkish origin.

We are unable to determine why the forklift was running into the pillars, and cannot confirm whether it was a malfunction or intentional.
In mid-September 2026, the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C., announced it would be closing its doors to the public due to financial concerns and renovations. Soon after, U.S. Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, a Kennedy Center trustee, filed a motion requesting an emergency hearing for officials to explain the closure.
A claim then spread online that a court document said a legal observer witnessed a forklift ramming into columns at the Kennedy Center columns. Snopes readers sent us the following post (archived), asking whether the forklift was intentionally damaging the building:
We had thought the "safety issues" at the Kennedy Center were caused by the Trump administration. It appears that might be the case. In a sworn declaration filed today, a legal observer said she witnessed a forklift carrying fencing drive to the north side of the building and repeatedly run into and hit the Kennedy Center's pillars. They had to damage the building to make it unsafe so they could close it for renovations.
A legal observer did indeed write in a court document about witnessing a forklift repeatedly strike the columns of the Kennedy Center on Sept. 16, 2026. Therefore, the claim is true.
We cannot, however, determine why the forklift was ramming into the pillars.
We reached out to the Kennedy Center to learn more about the forklifts at the venue and ask why one was striking the pillars. We will update this post accordingly.
On Sept. 16, the legal team representing Beatty in her case against President Donald Trump, submitted a declaration (archived) to the court describing what a member of their team witnessed. Bridget Kennedy-Bailey of the Washington Litigation Group described her visit to the Kennedy Center on Sept. 16:
I saw a forklift carrying what appeared to be a more permanent form of fencing drive over to the north side of the building. I saw the forklift run into and hit the pillars on the building several times.
Kennedy-Bailey described arriving that morning and being told by an employee that the Kennedy Center was closed for the day and that the order came from "higher-ups." A public relations representative told her the building was closed for repairs, she said. Kennedy-Bailey also described other forklifts moving white-and-orange gates to the front of the building.
At the bottom of the declaration, Kennedy-Bailey wrote, "I declare under penalty of perjury that the foregoing is true and correct."
We cannot determine the intention behind the forklift ramming into the pillars until we hear from the Kennedy Center or an employee willing to speak on the record.
The forklift rumor came after a judge said changing the building's name to include Trump's name would require congressional approval, while the Trump-appointed board argued that the Kennedy Center's survival depended on the name change.
Beatty described Trump having a "tantrum" during a closed-door meeting with the trustees on Sept. 15, after the judge blocked his bid to have his name on the Center. "He went into name-calling, from everything from trying to say that I was an obstructionist, I was dumb," Beatty said on MS NOW.
For further reading, Snopes has covered numerous claims about the Trump administration's work on the Kennedy Center.

While more than 80.62 lakh names were deleted from the draft roll after being marked as shifted or absent, and these voters were asked to fill Form-6 to be included in the final rolls, only 6.66 lakh Form-6 applications have been received so far — less than one in 10 of those marked as shifted or absent have applied for inclusion. The figure also includes applications from new voters.
While 24,328 Form-6 applications were received on September 19, during the second campaign when BLOs were instructed to help the public with the inclusion and correction process, 6,42,670 applications were received between June 16 and September 17.
While people can fill Form-6 even after the final rolls are published, the current figures suggest that the number of net additions could be low in the final roll.
When The Hindu spoke to several voters who had been marked as absent or shifted, many said they did not know about the deadline (September 23) or how to fill the form. Several said their applications encountered multiple glitches when they tried to apply online, while others said they did not know whether their names were marked as shifted or absent in the ASDDO list.
Voters marked as permanently shifted or absent account for the largest share of ASDDO deletions, with more than 80.62 lakh names marked under the two categories out of 1.07 crore deletions. More than 15 lakh were marked absent because they were not present during the enumeration phase, while the remaining had a different address in the current and previous rolls, something many said was common as rising rents and changing jobs have made it difficult to stay in one place in the city. Many also said they were wrongly put under the ASDDO category and did not know about it, as they returned the enumeration form as directed.
Even in States where the SIR has been completed, the pattern suggests that the net additions have not been enough to offset the large-scale deletions. The claims and objections process, along with fresh registrations, brought some voters back into the rolls, but the total electorate still remained substantially lower overall.
For instance, Bihar, where the SIR was first conducted, had 7.89 crore electors before the exercise. Although 21.53 lakh eligible electors were added through Form-6 during the revision, the final roll had about 7.42 crore electors — nearly 47 lakh less than before the SIR. Moreover, the figures do not establish how many of those added through Form-6 were electors who had been excluded from the draft roll and subsequently restored.

Apple’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, could give the stagnant foldable market a much-needed push. It may not reinvent the category, but Apple’s reach, software focus, and mainstream appeal could make foldables far more popular.
September is here and so are the new iPhones. This year at Apple’s Surprise and Shine event, the Cupertino tech giant came with a number of changes, not just in terms of devices but in terms of management too. There was a new CEO – it was John Ternus’ first event as CEO – as well as new Apple Watches, AirPods and, of course, new iPhones too.
The Duo dominates the new iPhones
Even though Apple showcases a number of products during its September event, it is mainly the iPhones that the world waits for. And even in iPhones, it is usually the Pro and Pro Max iPhones that make the headlines (barring the odd occasion when the Air popped up). The plain iPhones are usually pushed to the sidelines and launched as the more “economical”, “affordable” iPhones whose price tags and generally minor upgrades in specs and design are the only things that get them any attention.
For the longest time, we have been feeling for the plain iPhones because they are quite capable and bring in big sales numbers (especially in markets like India, where they are bestsellers) and yet do not get the hype they deserve. Well, this time around, the iPhone Pro and the Pro Max got the taste of this bitter medicine. The two smartphones had to fold (pun intended) and give up all their headline space for the more expensive, exclusive, and most different iPhone since the inception of the original iPhone: the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable iPhone.
With the iPhone Duo, Apple has finally marked its official entry in the world of foldables. It comes with a starting price of Rs. 299,900 in India ($1,999 in the US), which has naturally inspired a tsunami of reinvented kidney jokes and all sorts of comparisons about all that you can buy for that price. It has also got many competing brands scoffing at Apple’s very late attempt at foldables, calling the Duo a “copy”. While some of the criticism and cynicism around the Duo is valid, we think a foldable phone from Apple is just what the foldable market needed to make foldables mainstream. Not because the Duo is an out-of-the-tech-world, never-seen-before, and extraordinary folding smartphone (hey, we haven’t reviewed it yet), but for much simpler reasons.
Ghost of foldables past: A story mainly of Samsung
Samsung is considered by many to be the modern foldable phone pioneer. It was the trailblazer that was responsible for actually bringing in foldable phones that not only landed on the tech moon but also managed to stick around for seven2 years – Samsung’s first Galaxy Fold arrived in 2019, followed by the Galaxy Z Flip in 2020. The brand did not really have a working blueprint that they could have used back then to have perfected their foldables and technology around it, but it enjoyed an early mover’s advantage in the segment and managed to create a very strong reputation for itself. They built a strong rapport with the consumers that none of the other brands could develop, even after launching just as good, just as powerful foldable smartphones.
Following Samsung’s start, many leading tech brands have been surfing the foldable wave for a while now. The OG flip phone master, Motorola; the Android originator Google; the flagship killer OnePlus; the Chinese Apple, Xiaomi; Vivo, Oppo, and others have created foldables with their own touches and twists. Huawei has gone one step further and has launched a tri-fold – a smartphone that folds twice. But even after all this effort, none of them could really be a standout foldable smartphone brand. Only Samsung did.
But in spite of Samsung’s consistency and the efforts of other brands, foldable smartphones have not become mainstream. They have never really made impressive numbers or become popular/common devices. Yes, most of them come with premium price tags, but even those that are relatively affordable – mostly flips or budget foldables (yes, there are some) – have not gained the kind of traction that had been expected. The foldable revolution that many had predicted seemed to have stalled, and apart from a few devices (mainly from Samsung), growth was largely limited.
Apple and the tech snowball effect… could it come to foldables?
Now Apple has stepped into the foldable ring, and while there are many contenders in it already, we think the Cupertino tech giant might get the buzz around foldables going. It has been quite a trend setter in the tech world, and is identified with premium innovation. Features, functions, and devices that existed long before Apple “reinvented” them suddenly became popular once they started shipping with an Apple logo and Apple’s own unique take on them. They not only became mainstream but also often became a common sight on products from other brands as well. Touchscreen phones, apps and app stores, music stores, portrait mode, notches (Dynamic Island), are just some of the products that Apple did not invent, but made a part of
everyday technology.
Of course, every time this happens, the Internet is flooded with techies pointing out how the particular feature or product has been around for years and how Apple is not really innovating or, rather, thinking differently (Apple’s very tagline). Despite all the chatter and gossip around this topic, somehow the feature picks up momentum, and soon enough the world gets interested in knowing how it works and then owning a device that lets them use it. This initiates a snowball effect of sorts, which leads to that feature or device becoming extremely popular.
We will keep it simple: quite often, it basically takes an Apple device or feature to grab mainstream attention. It happened with GUI, MP3 players, ultra-portable notebooks, touchscreen phones, tablets, TWS, smartwatches, and we think it could happen with foldables too. The Duo has the potential to put the seemingly jammed foldable wheels in motion.
It is important to remember that it is not like whatever Apple does just becomes a hit automatically. The brand has a loyal following, but it has released many features, devices, and functions that did not strike a chord with consumers and have faded away. The Apple Vision Pro, HomePod, iPhone Mini and iPhone Plus, the Touch Bar on the Mac…Apple’s failure list is quite long. It may be one of the most successful tech brands in history, but Apple is no tech Midas – there is no real guarantee that the iPhone Duo would be an absolute hit. The stakes are quite high for the Duo, especially given its price tag (which is even higher in India).
It has got the hype, but what would make the Duo click?
Unlike Samsung, Apple has not had to reinvent the foldable wheel. It has had time to read, research, develop, try, and make mistakes, and fix them all, even while observing the efforts of other tech brands. And while the Duo’s design and specs, and indeed, many of its features, are nothing we have not seen before, these are not areas where Apple differentiates itself from the regular crowd. The iPhone Duo needs to bring Apple’s attention to detail when it comes to user experience, and software tuned exactly to suit the needs and capabilities of the device it supports.
We have not yet had the pleasure (or pain) to experience the device but so far, from the looks and the videos on the Internet, we can tell you there are a few things we love about the iPhone Duo – the TouchID on the side (yes, we actually love it), the vertical tool bar for easy access, the matte display layer which makes the crease largely invisible, and yes, of course, the animation that blurs out the side/front screen when the phone is being opened or folded. But it’s not all pink skies and red roses. We are not very convinced by the asymmetrical shape of the device, the insanely high price tag, and, well, even the name. Duo? Really, Apple? We are also really curious about how Apple has worked on apps for the cover display as well as the inner ones.
But these are early days. The iPhone Duo is more than a month away, and we are sure Apple will fine-tune it even further before releasing it. In the meantime, we expect the kidney jokes to continue and even gather momentum, but on the flip side, curiosity will also grow, as we are sure more will be revealed about the device and its features and functions.
The iPhone Duo has generated more buzz about the foldables in a few months than other players in the field got in years, but it is all going to boil down to how well and how differently it works from other foldables. Given the interest levels around it, it might just prove to be the elixir that foldables need.

Dr. Reddy's Laboratories on Friday (September 18, 2026) entered into an exclusive distribution agreement with Takeda Pharmaceutical Company to promote and distribute its dengue vaccine, QDENGA, in India's private market for pediatric and adult vaccination.
Subject to local regulatory processes, the vaccine is expected to be available in the first half of 2027. The vaccine received marketing authorisation by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) in July 2026 for individuals aged 4-60 years, Dr. Reddy's said in a press release.
QDENGA, a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine, aims to strengthen dengue prevention and management by providing broad immune coverage across all four circulating dengue virus serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4). Administered as a two-dose regimen given three months apart, it is India's first approved dengue vaccine, according to the release.
While Dr. Reddy's will exclusively manage private-market distribution, disease awareness, and healthcare professional engagement, Takeda will retain rights for the public market, legal ownership, and overall medical and brand oversight, it said.
"As the second-largest vaccine player in India, we believe the introduction of India's first approved dengue vaccine is an important development for the country's healthcare landscape," said M. V. Ramana, CEO, Global Generics, Dr. Reddy's Laboratories.
"Through our collaboration with Takeda, we look forward to making QDENGA available to eligible individuals and contributing to efforts aimed at addressing the country's dengue burden," Mr. Ramana said.
Dr. Mahender Nayak, Head of Intercontinental Markets, International Business Unit, Takeda, noted, "In parallel, our private-market collaboration with Dr. Reddy's will help enable timely private-market access for eligible individuals once QDENGA becomes available in India." Approved in 43 countries, QDENGA has seen over 32 million doses distributed globally.

A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia’s cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living cat species has been formally named and described in more than a century.
The cat, called Tilcayo by local communities, is part of a group called tiger cats found across much of South America. It was found in Bolivia’s lush Yungas forest, a mountainous region where forests are often covered by clouds and surrounded by high humidity, according to researchers. It measures about 18in (46cm) long and weighs about 3lbs (1.4kg), making it smaller than the average domestic cat.
Researchers used genetic data to confirm that the cat is a new species, and gave it the scientific name Leopardus tilcayo, retaining its local name.
“Its fur is light brown ... with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body,” said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer and one of the authors of the study describing the newly identified species published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology.
Little is yet known about the cat’s biology and lifestyle. Remains of small rodents in scat samples suggest they may form part of its diet, while camera-trap evidence indicates it could be more active at night, Nogales-Ascarrunz said.
Tiger cats are so-called cryptic species, meaning they cannot easily be distinguished merely by appearance, said evolutionary biologist and study co-lead author Jonas Lescroart of the University of Antwerp in Belgium.
Tiger cats previously had been considered a single species, but genetic studies decades ago suggested the existence of multiple species.
Referring to the new species, Lescroart said: “Our information at this moment is limited to the two live individuals that we examined, and a small number of camera-trap records.”
One of the live cats is a 10-year-old male that now lives in the Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary after being kept by a local family in their home.
Observing the Bolivian cat drew interest because “its characteristics did not match the descriptions, most of them based on Brazilian cats,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “This made us wonder: what tiger cat do we actually have in Bolivia?”
The team analysed DNA from 38 cats sampled across several South American countries, including eight museum specimens. The study found that tiger cats are in fact five genetically distinct species.
“We never expected this Bolivian tiger cat to be a separate species, and no one had ever proposed it as a different animal, subspecies or otherwise,” Lescroart said.
Genetic analysis suggested that the Tilcayo lineage separated from other tiger cats about 1.4m years ago.
“The more differences in their DNA, the longer the time that we estimate those lineages to have been physically separated,” Lescroart said, adding that such a gap is generally considered a species-level divide in cats.
The research team also described a new tiger cat subspecies in Peru’s Yungas, naming it Leopardus tigrinus antisuyo after Antisuyu, the region of the old Inca empire that included the area it inhabits.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) red list tracking the status of species currently treats tiger cats as two “vulnerable” species with declining populations.
The researchers have shared their findings with the IUCN, whose upcoming review will assess the five lineages separately. That could give a more accurate picture of risk, Lescroart said, and species such as the Tilcayo could be considered endangered when assessed on their own.
The need for a clearer assessment is particularly acute in the Yungas, one of the region’s most threatened ecosystems.
The mountain forests face growing pressure from deforestation, agricultural expansion, human-caused fires and mining, Nogales-Ascarrunz said. Restoring forest patches damaged by fires, protecting remaining native forest and maintaining connections between habitats are urgent priorities, Nogales-Ascarrunz added.
“Showing the general public that even in a flagship group such as cats ... there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message,” said Eduardo Eizirik, an evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil and senior author of the study. “There are many undiscovered species out there in the world, and they are at risk of disappearing before we even discover them.”

Next month’s budget will be made more difficult by Donald Trump’s war with Iran, one of Andy Burnham’s cabinet ministers has said, while adding she did not expect the prime minister’s previous disparaging comments about the US president to be an issue.
Burnham is expected to meet Trump early next week at the UN general assembly summit in New York, the pair having previously spoken twice by phone since Burnham entered No 10.
As Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham said Trump would not be welcome in the city, saying also that UK politicians who indulged him “should be ashamed”.
Asked about the comments, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair and minister for women and equalities, told Sky News: “Look, I think what you’ve just described there is politics. The president knows that. This is far from unique.
“People will express views at different points on different topics. And that’s no bar to having a strong relationship.”
She nonetheless repeated UK condemnation of Trump’s on-and-off military campaign against Iran, which has disrupted global oil supplies, causing significant inflationary pressures, saying this would make life more difficult for John Healey, the chancellor, as he plans the budget.
The economy was, Phillipson said, “in a strong position”, especially with growth figures.
She said: “But that’s not to take away from the very real challenges that you identify, particularly where it’s come to the conflict we’ve seen in the Middle East and the impact that that’s been having on businesses and on families close to home.
“We took the decision not to involve ourselves in that conflict. That was the right call. The US will take their own foreign policy decisions, but I believe, and still believe now, it was the right decision for us as a country not to get involved in that conflict. Of course, something that, had Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage been running the country, we would have jumped headlong into a conflict with it without end.
“And yet, and we do see the consequences here at home and as we go into the budget, making sure that we are doing everything we can to give people that breathing space to tackle those challenges around the cost of living has been at the forefront of everything that Andy Burnham has done since becoming prime minister.
“I know it’s at the forefront of the chancellor’s mind as he’s planning for that budget later on next month.”
In a later interview with the BBC, Phillipson was dismissive of comments by Jim Ratcliffe, the petrochemicals billionaire, who said this week he had lost confidence in the UK due to levels of immigration and taxation.
She said: “You’ll forgive me if I do take with a pinch of salt what someone who is a tax exile has to say about our country.” Ratcliffe is resident for tax in Monaco.
Burnham has previously defended his comments about Trump in a similar way, saying of the US president: “Well, he’s said things as well, and everyone says things as politicians. In the moment, you meet people where they’re at, and you find a connection with people, and that’s always been my style.”
With the wider UK-US relationship, there were “differences of opinion”, Phillipson said, while arguing that Burnham could see beyond those differences with Trump in maintaining invaluable ties.
She said: “We don’t have the same political outlook, but the relationship between the UK and the US goes beyond any one president, any one prime minister.
“It’s something that has stood the test of time over many centuries, despite political differences. They come and go. What matters most is the British national interest. And that’s what Andy Burnham will deliver for our country.”

When a woman has difficulty conceiving or experiences repeated pregnancy loss, the focus often turns to the uterus, the quality of the embryos or ovarian reserve. However, hormones, too, can play an important role, and one hormone that deserves attention is prolactin.
Prolactin is produced by the pituitary gland and is best known for its role in breast milk production. Its levels naturally rise during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Outside these periods, however, persistently elevated prolactin, a condition known as hyperprolactinaemia, can interfere with normal reproductive function.
The symptoms are not always obvious. Some women may have irregular or absent periods, difficulty conceiving or an unexpected milky discharge from the breasts. Others may have no noticeable symptoms at all.
Prolactin and fertility
Reproductive hormones work as a closely connected system. Prolactin is part of this system, and when its levels remain elevated, it can interfere with the hormonal signals required for ovulation.
High prolactin can suppress the release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone from the brain. This can subsequently affect Luteinising Hormone (LH) and Follicle Stimulating Hormone (FSH), which are involved in follicle development and ovulation. As a result, some women may ovulate irregularly or stop ovulating altogether. Their periods may become longer, unpredictable or absent, making conception more difficult.
Prolactin also interacts with reproductive hormones after ovulation. This is one reason why its possible role in the early stages of pregnancy has attracted clinical attention, although the relationship is more complex than simply linking one abnormal hormone level to pregnancy loss.
The link to repeated pregnancy loss
The relationship between elevated prolactin and recurrent pregnancy loss is documented in clinical literature but described with appropriate caution. A 2025 guideline published in the Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada found that elevated prolactin is associated with pregnancy loss and may contribute to luteal phase deficiency. The guideline recommends prolactin testing in women with recurrent pregnancy loss who also present with irregular periods or unexplained breast discharge.
The clinical nuance here is important. Hyperprolactinaemia is one contributing factor among several more established causes of recurrent pregnancy loss, such as chromosomal abnormalities in the embryo, uterine structural issues, antiphospholipid syndrome, and thyroid dysfunction. This does not reduce the clinical relevance of elevated prolactin, but it does mean that a single elevated test result should not be treated as the explanation before other causes have been assessed. The 2025 guideline is explicit on this: elevated prolactin should be confirmed through repeat testing before any treatment is initiated, and thyroid function should be checked first, as hypothyroidism can independently raise prolactin levels.
The connection with PMOS
Among women with PMOS, earlier known as PCOS, mildly elevated prolactin levels are occasionally found alongside the more typical hormonal pattern of the condition. Some research has found a mean hyperprolactinaemia prevalence of 11.9% in women with PMOS, though the range across studies is wide, reflecting how variable the relationship is across different populations and diagnostic thresholds. Hyperprolactinaemia is not considered a clinical manifestation of PMOS, and the two conditions are assessed and managed independently.
Why the elevation
The causes of elevated prolactin are varied. A benign, prolactin-secreting pituitary tumour called a prolactinoma is among the more significant causes and is identified through an MRI when prolactin levels are substantially elevated. Hypothyroidism, certain medications including antipsychotics and some antihypertensives, and occasionally stress or intensive exercise can also raise prolactin levels transiently. This is why repeat testing under standardised conditions such as fasting and avoiding physical stress before the blood draw, is important before a diagnosis of hyperprolactinaemia is established.
When true hyperprolactinaemia is confirmed, dopamine agonist medications such as cabergoline or bromocriptine are effective at normalising prolactin levels in most cases. Research has demonstrated successful restoration of ovulation and term pregnancy outcomes in women with hyperprolactinaemia following dopamine agonist therapy, including in cases involving pituitary tumours. The condition, when properly identified and treated, is one of the more manageable contributors to fertility challenges.
What women should know
For women experiencing recurrent pregnancy loss or difficulty conceiving, prolactin testing is a reasonable part of a comprehensive hormonal evaluation. The results need to be interpreted alongside thyroid function, ovarian reserve, and a full assessment of both partners, because the factors that influence reproductive outcomes are rarely operating in isolation.
(Dr. Prachi Benara is a fertility specialist at Birla Fertility and IVF, Gurgaon. prachi.benara@birlafertility.com)
